News.title: Man, 44, fired multiple shots & hurled petrol bombs at home in ‘deliberate and terrifying’ attack which sparked blaze
News.content:
HOUSE ASSAULT Man, 44, fired multiple shots & hurled petrol bombs at home in ‘deliberate and terrifying’ attack which sparked blaze

A VIOLENT man who fired shots and hurled petrol bombs at a house in a “deliberate and terrifying” attack has been jailed for 15 years.

Iain Boddy, from Bishop Auckland, was found guilty of arson with intent to harm and possession of a firearm at Durham Crown Court on Thursday.

It comes after emergency services were called to an address in Burnhope, Durham, on December 5 last year at around 5.15pm.

Glass bottles containing petrol had been launched at the house, sparking a fire in the property’s garden which was quickly extinguished.





Fortunately, no injuries were reported.

Boddy, 44, was identifed as the prime suspect and arrested and charged with a number of offences, all of which he denied.

However, the wick of the petrol bomb was found to contain his DNA.

Similar bottles launched at the property in Burnhope were found at his workplace.



Temporary Detective Chief Inspector Hannah Wilson, of Durham Constabulary, said: “The attack in Burnhope was deliberate and terrifying for those who live there.

“It could easily have ended in tragedy.

“This level of violence will not be tolerated in County Durham, and we will remain relentless, with the support of our partners and our communities, in our pursuit to disrupt and dismantle criminal fraternities that operate across our county.

“I would like to thank the community for their support, and the assistance of partner agencies throughout our investigation.”



She added that anyone with concerns about criminal activity in their area should contact police on 101.

It follows a devastating case of mistaken identity in January, which saw an innocent family’s home petrol bombed by two balaclava-clad men.

Jody Lynam and an unknown offender crept up to the property in Manchester during the early hours, thinking it was empty, and hurled a bomb through the window.

News.title: Tourist, 27, BANNED from Brit holiday hotspot for 10 years after being ‘filmed having sex with woman on public driveway’
News.content:
A RANDY tourist accused of having sex on a public driveway has been deported and banned from a beloved Brit holiday hotspot for a decade.

Cops claim to have caught Billy Aspinall, 27, with his pants down after CCTV allegedly showed him engaging in a sex act with a woman in Bali, Indonesia.



The Australian national was arrested at Bali’s International Airport as he tried to board a flight home on August 25.

His arrest came two days after the local’s security camera caught him and the woman in North Kuta.



Footage shows Aspinall and the woman in an uncompromising position in front of iron gates and – ironically – a welcome sign.

A stunned local woman stumbled across the pair in the middle of the alleged sexual act as she was on her way to prayer.



She reportedly shouted at them to stop what they were doing, but they appeared to ignore her.

The alleged romp lasted 15 minutes before the pair walked away.



Balinese locals held a cleansing ceremony at the property to purge it of bad energy.

Following his arrest Aspinall spent the next two weeks in immigration detention.

On Wednesday, it emerged that the Sunshine Coast man had been deported from the island and received a ban on entering the country for the next 10 years.

The head of the Ngurah Rai Immigration Office, Muhamad Novyandri said: “We will continue to strengthen immigration supervision and maintain close co-ordination with law enforcement authorities, while taking firm action if violations of immigration regulations are found in the future.”

The strict 10 year entry ban means that Aspinall will not be permitted to return to Indonesia in any capacity during the period of the sanction.



North Kuta chief police commander Ketut Sukadana said at the time that the alleged “indecent acts have the potential to cause public concern”.

He continued: “Particularly among the residents of Tibubeneng, and may negatively affect the image of security and tourism in the North Kuta area if the matter is not addressed and handled seriously by taking firm action against the perpetrators, whether under local customary law or national law.”

The woman in the video has not yet been identified by authorities, although she is believed to be a foreign citizen who was drinking with Aspinall prior to the act.

Public acts of indecency and sex outside marriage are illegal in Indonesia, and foreigners caught can face jail time.

Although Bali is predominantly Hindu, Indonesia is a Muslim nation with strict laws regarding pornography and conservative social norms around intimacy.



Last year OnlyFans star Bonnie Blue made international headlines after she was detained in Bali over alleged “pornographic activities”.

Like Aspinal, Blue was banned from the state for 10 years after she was accused of filming X-rated content which is strictly forbidden under Indonesia’s harsh morality laws.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

While she was not convived over her aleged sexual activity, Blue was fined £9 and received the ban for breaking road rules related to her blue pickup truck the “Bangbus”.

The adult film actress was ordered “not to violate Bali’s traffic laws again” to which she replied: “I understand.”

News.title: Labourer was buried alive after trench collapsed and covered him in soil as two firms blasted over ‘preventable’ death
News.content:
FATAL CONSEQUENCES Labourer was buried alive after trench collapsed and covered him in soil as two firms blasted over ‘preventable’ death

A LABOURER was buried alive after a trench collapsed and covered him in soil as two businesses are blasted over his “preventable” death.

Gheorghita Arsene, 33, was fatally crushed while working on a construction site in Banstead, Surrey.



The firms were fined £1million over Mr Arsene’s “horrifying” death in June 2020 and one employee has admitted to failing to discharge his duties.

Mr Arsene had told his mother he thought the 10ft ditch was too deep on the day of his death, the court heard.



The Romanian national was clearing soil when one or more of the trench walls suddenly collapsed.

A colleague ran for help and tried to clear the soil from Mr Arsene’s face and body.

When fire and ambulance crews arrived at the scene they struggled to dig out his body due to the weight of the earth.

Inspectors later found the trench was lacking supports and the excavated soil had been dumped too close to the ditch.

Appledorn Developments and T Vaughan Limited (TVL) were fined £500,000 and £650,000 plus £40,000 costs, respectively, following a three-month trial at the Old Bailey.

Judge Judy Khan KC said the now-defunct Appledorn were “motivated by the desire to get things done quickly and cheaply” and had failed to ensure a safe system of work.



Meanwhile, TVL had not “sufficiently adhered to or implemented” systems in place.

Contracts manager Anthony O’Connor was sentenced to 10 months in custody suspended for 18 months, alongside 150 hours’ unpaid work.

The jurors failed to reach a verdict on whether he was guilty of manslaughter.

A Health and Safety Executive spokesperson said: “Gheorghita Arsene’s death was as horrifying as it was preventable.”

They continued: “Basic precautions were not in place to protect workers from the well-known risks that come with excavation work.



“This case is a stark reminder that when basic safety standards are ignored, the consequences can be fatal.

“Companies and individuals alike have legal duties to protect workers.”

Mr Arsene’s mother Ienuta said her son was a “good man” who was trying to support his family.

He had told her of his concerns about the ditch over the phone on the day of the accident, her statement read.

She added: “I have a depression that is eating me away and a constant feeling of loneliness.



“Everyone in the family was devastated by Gheorghita’s death.”

Mitigating for O’Connor, Mark Balysz KC said he was sorry for his role in Mr Arsene’s death and “clearly regrets the catastrophic mistake he made”.

Prashant Popat KC, who was representing TVL, said the company did everything “as safely as possible”.

The business had spent £3m on health and safety he added.

Site manager Peter Wraith, 54, was acquitted of manslaughter.



Assistant site manager Gregory Peake, 51, was found not guilty of failing to discharge his health and safety duty.

Senior Investigating Officer, Detective Inspector Debbie Birch, said: “Gheorgita Arsene’s death could have been avoided if the appropriate health and safety measures had been followed.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“It can be easy to cut corners to save time and money but this tragic death highlights just how important health and safety legislation is on all building sites.

“Sadly, this resulted in the death of a 33-year-old man who was simply trying to do his job, and our thoughts remain with his family and friends at this difficult time.”

News.title: Waitrose issues urgent ‘do not consume’ warning on olives over fears they could contain rare invasive bacteria
News.content:
A MAJOR UK supermarket has announced an urgent recall on its olives over fears they contain a rare, invasive bacteria.

Waitrose issued the alert after finding listeria monocytogenes in 120g packs of its Essential Pitted Black Olives with a use-by date of September 13, 18 and 27.

Customers who bought these packs are being advised not to eat them.



They have been told they will receive a full refund when they return them to a Waitrose store.



The Food Standards Agency has said symptoms of listeriosis resemble the flu, including soaring temperatures, muscle ache, chills, nausea and diarrhoea.

Healthy adults will often recover from the infection in a few days, without the need for antibiotics.

In rarer cases, the infection can cause major complications, like meningitis, an inflammation of the membrane in the brain.

Severe literiosis has a high mortality rate, at about 20 to 30 per cent, especially among newborns and the elderly.

Unlike many other foodborne bacteria, it can grow and thrive even at fridge temperature.

Waitrose apologised for the recall and inconvenience caused.

It comes as Sainsbury also issued a recall on its pitted black olives three days ago, after the same bacteria was discovered in its product.

News.title: Five Mexicans charged with running meth lab in quiet UK countryside after cops uncovered secret ‘kitchen’ on farmland
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BREAKING BAD Five Mexicans charged with running meth lab in quiet UK countryside after cops uncovered secret ‘kitchen’ on farmland

FIVE Mexicans have been charged with operating a meth lab in a remote rural hideout after cops discovered a “kitchen” on some farmland.

The men are allegedly part of a criminal gang making methamphetamines near the hamlet of Furnace End, in North Warwickshire.

All five defendants denied their involvement at the hearing at Warwick Crown Court on Thursday, with one insisting they were a chef, another that they were a construction worker.

The case was adjourned and a trial set for the same court on February 15.





The men are currently being held in custody.

The defendants include Alejandro Ambriz Dimas, 45; Victora Ramirez, 47; Fausto Beltran, 33; Lioncio Moso Borja, 37; and Jose Nunez Angolo, 44.

They are all from northwest Mexico, except for Dimas, who is from the south, the National Crime Agency said.

They were arrested on August 13 and initially appeared at Coventry Magistrates’ Court, where they were held in custody.

The men are understood to have conspired “together and with others” to produce the Class A drugs between February 6 and August 14.

Ambriz, who is fluent in English, denied the allegations.

The remaining men entered their pleas with the assistance of two Spanish interpreters.

Informally known as crystal meth, or ice, methamphetamines are highly addictive stimulants.



While they have yet to fully take hold in the UK, several other countries already battle severe meth addiction problems, including Australia and the US.

It comes after builders used a drone to chase a hapless cannabis farmer across a £1million hidden drugs factory in Essex back in August.

The workers were able to track him down until he reached a main road, where he was nabbed by cops.

News.title: Oil prices rocket as Houthi militants capture key port city and try to paralyse another supply route vital for West
News.content:
OIL prices rocketed yesterday after a raid by Iran-backed Houthi rebels tried to paralyse another oil route that is vital for the West.

The price of benchmark Brent Crude soared four per cent to $105.26 a barrel after ­militants captured the key port city of Mocha in Yemen.



Houthi forces also advanced on islands in the key Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea and the Suez Canal to the Arabian Sea and the Indian Ocean.

Closing that would mean a fresh blow to oil supplies of western economies including Britain — adding to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively shut by Iran since February.



US president Donald Trump’s forces are still struggling to secure safe passage for tankers through the waterway that usually carries 20 per cent of the world’s oil.

Trump has struggled to contain the economic ­fallout from his war with Iran and is imposing a naval blockade to halt its oil exports.



The Houthis yesterday said they would “respond to the blockade with a blockade” and launched strikes on the US’s ally Saudi Arabia.

Salvos of the rebel force’s drones and missiles wounded at least 73 people – including children – in Saudi cities and oil plants on Tuesday.

It comes as tit-for-tat strikes escalated in recent days as Washington and Tehran blitzed several targets in the region.

The regime reportedly used electro-optical missiles for the first time in the war.



Iran said it used them to strike two US warships and eight oil tankers on Wednesday, as well as a military base in Jordan, according to The Telegraph.

The air assaults came in response to Washington blitzing five Iranian oil tankers, according to Tehran.

News.title: Charlie Kirk statue unveiling sparks Times Square chaos with far-right activist Jake Lang punched by leftist
News.content:
CHAOS erupted in Times Square following the unveiling of a $100,000 statue honoring slain conservative figure Charlie Kirk, as far-right activist Jake Lang was punched by a protester.

The dramatic scenes unfolded on Thursday as supporters and opponents gathered on the first anniversary of the Turning Point USA founder’s assassination.



A 6ft 5in bronze-painted sculpture depicting Kirk seated with a microphone and wearing a “FREEDOM” T-shirt was unveiled in the tourist hotspot in his memory.

But tensions boiled over shortly afterward when Lang, a pardoned January 6 defendant and controversial far-right activist, arrived at the scene.



Lang was immediately heckled by protesters, including some who accused him of being a Nazi.

He hit back at the taunts, insisting he was not a Nazi and declaring that “Nazis are losers.”

An eyewitness told The U.S. Sun that Lang showed up shortly after the statue unveiling at around 2:35pm before becoming engulfed by the crowd.

They said they saw Lang running through Times Square as he was chased by a huge group of people.

Video obtained by The U.S. Sun shows Lang attempting to get into a taxi as the crowd surrounded him, shouting, “Back the f*** up.”

Moments later, a tall man appears to strike Lang on the side of the head.



Lang was then seen lunging toward the man as others attempted to keep them apart and police intervened.

He eventually escaped the crowds by disappearing into the subway, the eyewitness said.

One conservative Kirk supporter who attended the unveiling told The U.S. Sun he had come to Times Square to help keep the activist’s legacy alive.



He said: “First of all, I’m definitely a conservative person. I’m also a proud American.

“I’m also a fan of Kirk. I’m here to support the cause and also to spread his legacy and his name.”

The supporter said Kirk’s assassination should transcend political divides, adding: “Whether you’re liberal or conservative, it’s definitely wrong to shoot one of us in cold blood.

“Especially a person who’s a Christian man and also has kids and a wife.”

Another man at the scene, Dan Roth, told The U.S. Sun he had come to confront those whose views he considered intolerant.



“My political agenda is I don’t like intolerant people,” he said.

“I saw a bunch of people preaching intolerance, and I felt the need to tell them that they’re not American.”

Lang has become a controversial fixture at political protests since being released from federal custody following President Donald Trump’s sweeping clemency for January 6 defendants.

He had faced charges over his role in the January 6, 2021, Capitol attack, including allegations that he assaulted police officers.

Lang appeared in New York after recently descending on Plymouth, Massachusetts, during the high-profile Lindsay Clancy murder trial.



He has also staged anti-Muslim demonstrations and faced accusations of antisemitism in the past.

Thursday’s confrontation came amid continuing political divisions over Kirk’s legacy a year after his murder.

Fox News host Will Cain, who was Kirk’s friend and interviewed him the day before his death, told The U.S. Sun this week he had been troubled by the reaction to the assassination.



Cain criticized mocking responses from parts of the left while also hitting out at figures on the right who he said had turned Kirk’s death into a “soap opera” for content.

He warned the fallout had fractured parts of the conservative movement in ways that “may not be easily healable.”

Meanwhile, tributes poured in across the country on Thursday to mark the anniversary.

Trump honored Kirk at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday night, telling the crowd, “We love you, Charlie,” as his widow Erika received a standing ovation.

Vice President JD Vance also paid tribute to his late friend, while Utah Governor Spencer Cox declared September 10 “Charlie Kirk Day” and called on Americans to reject political violence.



Italian-born artist Sergio Furnari spent around $100,000 of his own money creating the Times Square sculpture, which depicts Kirk clutching the microphone synonymous with his campus debates.

Furnari has said he was disturbed by the reaction to Kirk’s death and intended the monument to promote freedom of speech and conversation rather than deepen political divisions.

Kirk, 31, was fatally shot in the neck while taking questions during an outdoor event at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025.

He had been discussing gun violence moments before a single shot rang out.

Tyler Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to charges including aggravated murder over Kirk’s killing.



A judge recently ordered Robinson to trial, with prosecutors seeking the death penalty if he is convicted.

Kirk co-founded Turning Point USA and became one of the most influential figures on the American right before his death.

His widow Erika has since taken over as CEO and recently opened up about grief.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Kirk’s killing sparked condemnation of political violence from across the political spectrum.

A year later, the heated scenes surrounding his Times Square memorial showed how deeply divided reactions to his death and legacy remain.

News.title: Fury as Labour accused of making disability benefits EASIER to claim as welfare bill balloons
News.content:
LABOUR was tonight accused of making disability benefits easier to claim while failing to tackle Britain’s ballooning welfare bill.

PIP claimants could face a new “light-touch” initial assessment and be offered more digital services under reforms being considered.



Those with lifelong or degenerative conditions could also be spared repeated reviews, while some awards could include services or other non-cash support alongside payments.

The plans come with no overall cut to PIP spending, which is still forecast to hit an eye-watering £41.5billion by 2030/31.



Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary Helen Whately branded the review a “wasted opportunity” and accused Labour of watering down checks.

She said: “The benefits bill is out of control. Yesterday the Prime Minister admitted Labour have no plan to cut it. Labour puts social security before national security.



“Welfare should be a safety net for disabled people. Instead, the system is being abused.

“But their ‘Timms review’ will do nothing to tackle that abuse or make savings.

“Labour’s answer is to make PIP easier to claim, offer more online assessments, hire more people to wave claims through, and water down checks further.

“It’s extraordinarily out of touch.”



It comes as more than four million people now claim PIP in England and Wales – twice as many as in 2019.

Annual spending has risen from an inflation-adjusted £16.3billion in 2019/20 to £27.3billion in 2024/25.

The Timms Review must work within that forecast but has not proposed an overall cut to the cost of PIP.

Its draft recommendations say cash should remain the “foundation” of the benefit while some awards could include services or other non-cash support.

They also propose reducing “unnecessary” reviews and ending the suspension of PIP for people who spend more than 28 consecutive days in hospital.



The review is also considering more face-to-face capacity alongside greater use of digital services.

Sir Stephen Timms said PIP was “widely valued” but “no longer fit for purpose”.

He was appointed after Labour was forced into a retreat over welfare reforms after a major backbench rebellion under Sir Keir Starmer.

Sir Stephen is expected to publish his final recommendations later this autumn.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It comes after Andy Burnham sparked uproar at PMQs this week by refusing to back Tory plans to cut welfare to boost defence spending.



The Prime Minister said “national security can’t come at the expense of social security” as he rejected proposals to find billions from the benefits bill.

News.title: Andy Burnham warns terror 'still knocks at door of democracy' on 9/11 anniversary
News.content:
Andy Burnham warns terror 'still knocks at door of democracy' on 9/11 anniversary

As the world pauses to remember the 9/11 atrocities 25 years on, Prime Minister Andy Burnham says the UK and the US 'stand together' in the war against terror

View 5 Images The September 11 terror attacks were the deadliest in human history and changed the world forever (Image: Getty Images)

Andy Burnham has warned that the threat of terror still looms large and forever "knocks at the door of democracy” as he reflected on the trauma of the 9/11 attacks that shook the world 25 years ago.

‌



As millions of people across the globe pause to mark the sombre milestone today, the Prime Minister said the UK and America “stand together in memory of those we lost, and in defence of the values we cherish”. Mr Burnham recalled how, in the wake of terrorist outrages in Manchester during his time as mayor of the city region, messages of support had been received from across the US, including the children of those killed on September 11, 2001.

‌



Meanwhile, Tony Blair, PM at the time of the murderous atrocity and had to deal with its aftermath, said the anniversary was also a time to “commemorate the unshakeable and essential bond” between the two countries.

‌



View 5 Images Andy Burnham has sent a warning as he expressed the nation’s unity (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

US ambassador to the UK Warren Stephens said Britain had rallied in support “in one of America’s darkest hours” and that “despite our disagreements and debates”, the transatlantic relationship “has kept us safe for centuries”. His comments follow strained relations with President Donald Trump’s White House, most notably over the Iran war, which have tested long-standing ties with traditional allies.

It was on a bright, cloudless day 25 years ago that 2,977 people – 67 of them British – were killed when passenger jets hijacked by al Qaida terrorists struck the twin towers of the World Trade Centre in New York, causing both to collapse, and the Pentagon outside Washington DC. A fourth plane seized by extremists – United Airlines Flight 93 – crashed into a field in rural Pennsylvania after the crew and passengers fought back with the famous line “let’s roll”, and so prevented it from hitting another target, thought to be the congressional building, which houses the US legislature.

‌



5 View 5 Images It is 25 years since the harrowing events on September 11 (Image: NY Daily News via Getty Images) 5 View 5 Images The PM says the free world 'refuses to be defined' by any terror attacks (Image: AFP/Getty Images)

It remains the worst terrorist outrage of all time, claiming the lives of victims from more than 90 nations. In response, the US became the first and only ever country to invoke Nato’s “all for one, and one for all” collective security clause, where members rally to the defence of an ally under attack – a commitment now called into doubt by the current president.

‌



It led to the large-scale deployment of UK forces to conflicts in both Afghanistan and Iraq, which left hundreds of British troops dead, thousands more injured and continue to have global repercussions. Mr Burnham said: “On the 25th anniversary of 9/11, we remember the nearly 3,000 people who were killed, including 67 Britons.

“My thoughts are with all those who lost friends and family members that terrible day. Time may pass, but I know the grief is still felt just as deeply today. On this anniversary, we must remember that hatred and fear did not have the last word on 9/11.

View 5 Images Almost 3,000 people perished in 2001 after hijackers flew planes into buildings (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



“The terrorists sought to weaken and divide America, and everyone who believes in the values our countries share. But our response was clear: those who seek to destroy our way of life will never win.”

He added: “I saw that same defiance in Greater Manchester. When I was mayor, Manchester was the victim of two horrific terrorist attacks. I will never forget the messages of support and friendship from people across America who knew better than anyone the suffering of our city.

“Some of the children of those killed in the 9/11 attacks wrote to the families of the people killed in Manchester, and they said this: 'We are you and you are us. We are one.' We will never forget these terrible events, but we refuse to be defined by them.

‌



"Terror still knocks on the door of democracy, but the United Kingdom and the United States stand together in memory of those we lost, and in defence of the values we cherish. We are you and you are us. And we will prevail.”

9/11 The Day The World Changed

Reflecting on the anniversary, Sir Tony said: “I will forever remember 11th of September 2001, as a leader but also as a citizen. 9/11 was the worst terrorist attack ever perpetrated, the greatest loss of life through an attack on American soil in the history of America and the largest death toll of any act of terrorism in respect of the British people. That day changed the world and 25 years on, changes the world even now.”

‌



He added: “We remember those who lost their lives, 3,000 of them on that day. We remember their families. We recall the courage of the responders, many of whom also sacrificed themselves in that moment. And we remember the incredible fortitude of the people of New York and the other cities affected. And we recognise that, though thankfully such an attack has never been repeated in America, the struggle against terrorism in all its forms continues.

“We should all recommit ourselves to confront and defeat those who engage in such terrorism, and to pursue the cause of peaceful co-existence between people of all faiths, cultures and nations. Here in Britain, as we remember this day, we also commemorate the unshakeable and essential bond between our country and the United States of America.”

Speaking at a ceremony at the American embassy in London to dedicate a memorial stone to the victims of 9/11, the US ambassador said following the 2001 attack “a new chapter was added to the world’s most historic partnership”. Mr Stephens recalled: “As America grieved, the people of the UK rallied to stand beside us in sympathy and solidarity.”

Article continues below

As well as the public displays of unity, the ambassador said: “Away from the public eye, our military and intelligence communities began to work together on a level unseen in international relations: sharing information, conducting joint operations and disrupting threats in the weeks and months after 9/11.

“That co-operation saved countless lives – and it continues to save lives today. We must always remember the painful lessons 9/11 taught us. Because despite our disagreements and debates, the US-UK partnership has kept us safe for centuries: helping us overcome threats from Nazi tyranny to communist ideology to terrorist insurgency.”

He added: “In one of America’s darkest hours, the UK – a nation attuned to grief and terror – rose as one to stand alongside their American brothers and sisters.”

News.title: Delay in action on cosmetic procedures 'prolonging risk to public safety', warn MPs
News.content:
Delay in action on cosmetic procedures 'prolonging risk to public safety', warn MPs

MPs criticised the Government for for a 'lack of a timely response' to their report on cosmetic surgery reforms, warning they are 'deeply disappointed by this significant delay'

View Image Ministers are 'not moving quickly enough' in introducing a licensing system for non-surgical cosmetic procedures, MPs warned (Image: Getty Images)

A delay in action on high-risk cosmetic procedures “is prolonging a significant risk to patient safety”, MPs have warned.

‌



The Women and Equalities Committee (WEC), a cross-party group of MPs, said it is "deeply disappointed" by a lack of Government action to address cowboy practitioners. It said ministers are “not moving quickly enough” in introducing a licensing system for non-surgical cosmetic procedures and “should accelerate regulatory action”.

‌



The powerful Commons committee in February called for procedures including the liquid Brazilian butt lift (BBL) and liquid breast augmentations to be banned from the high street immediately. It also demanded ministers “require all practitioners performing invasive surgical cosmetic procedures to have specialist training and hold appropriate board certification in the procedures they undertake”.

‌



The Mirror's three cosmetic demands 1. Cosmetic operations such as liposuction, surgical face lifts and surgical eye lifts, should only be carried out by properly trained surgeons on the GMC specialist register. These surgeons should have UK Board Certification in Cosmetic Surgery for their area of practice. 2. All operations and high risk procedures must be surgically safe and carried out in clinics and hospitals inspected by the Care Quality Commission (CQC). 3. Make it a legal requirement for beauty clinics who offer non-surgical interventions to have malpractice insurance.

But today, the committee said it is still yet to receive a response from the Government despite a reply being due in April. The WEC said: “The lack of a timely response to our report risks reinforcing concerns that women who have experienced adverse health impacts after having breast implants are not being taken seriously by healthcare authorities.”

‌



Among its findings, the WEC's inquiry heard horrifying stories of women contracting sepsis and needing to undergo extensive corrective surgery after receiving botched cosmetic procedures. It also heard about a failure to protect the public from rogue operators. This included people facing dodgy requests to pay for their surgery in advance or women suffering "aggressive" responses if they tried to raise concerns about their treatment.

Interim committee chair Christine Jardine, who is a Lib Dem MP, said: “MPs are deeply disappointed by this significant delay. It leaves important recommendations unaddressed and patients’ safety at significant risk. It is clear that high-risk procedures are still being carried out and that they are being delivered by unqualified practitioners and in unsafe settings. This delay in government action in this area is prolonging a significant risk to patient safety."

She continued: “While it is positive to hear a licensing system for non-surgical cosmetic procedures will be introduced within this Parliament, this issue requires much faster regulatory progress, particularly in high harm areas, and the Government is not moving quickly enough."

Article continues below

The Mirror is campaigning for tougher rules on cosmetic surgery to stop cowboy practitioners putting lives at risk. Among demands, this newspaper wants cosmetic operations such as liposuction, surgical face lifts and surgical eye lifts, to only be carried out by properly trained surgeons on the GMC specialist register. We also want it to be made a legal requirement for beauty clinics who offer non-surgical interventions to have malpractice insurance.

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “This government is committed to protecting the public and keeping them safe from rogue practitioners. We have worked with experts to develop tough new measures to ensure only qualified healthcare professionals can perform these high-risk cosmetic procedures.

“We will soon be consulting on this new legislation including restricting all cosmetic surgery to doctors who are regulated to strict standards set by the General Medical Council and who work from Care Quality Commission regulated settings. For anyone considering a cosmetic procedure, please check the provider’s qualifications and insurance - and avoid treatments that appear suspiciously cheap.”

News.title: Waitrose recalls popular food item over health risk as ‘do not eat’ warning issued
News.content:
Waitrose recalls popular food item over health risk as ‘do not eat’ warning issued

The Food Standards Agency has issued a recall notice for Waitrose Essential Pitted Black Olives because of contamination with Listeria monocytogenes

View 2 Images A food item is being recalled by Waitrose (Image: In Pictures via Getty Images)

Waitrose has recalled a popular food item after bacteria which can cause serious illness was found in the product.

‌



Shoppers have been warned by the Food Standards Agency not to eat Waitrose Essential Pitted Black Olives after Listeria monocytogenes was detected.

‌



The recall affects 120g packs with use-by dates of September 13, September 18 and September 27, 2026.

‌



Customers are being advised to return the olives to their nearest Waitrose store for a full refund.

View 2 Images Some packs of Essential Pitted Black Olives are being recalled (Image: Waitrose)

"Waitrose is recalling Waitrose Essential Pitted Black Olives because Listeria monocytogenes has been found in the product," the agency stated.

‌



"If you have bought the above product do not eat it. Instead, return it to your nearest Waitrose store where you will be given a full refund. For further information, please contact Waitrose Customer Care on 0800 188 884, Option 4."

And it says of the bacteria: "Symptoms caused by Listeria monocytogenes can be similar to flu and include high temperature, muscle ache or pain, chills, feeling or being sick and diarrhoea. However, in rare cases, the infection can be more severe, causing serious complications, such as meningitis.

"Some people are more vulnerable to Listeria infections, including those over 65 years of age, pregnant women and their unborn babies, babies less than one month old and people with weakened immune systems."

‌



A statement from Waitrose confirms that a refund will be made for people returning the olives as it also issued an apology.

"We are recalling Waitrose Essential Pitted Black Olives 120g as a precautionary measure due to the potential presence of listeria which may cause illness if consumed," it said.

"We apologise that it has been necessary to recall this product and for the inconvenience caused."

Article continues below

Meanwhile, last week Sainsbury's recalled its Inspired to Cook Pitted Black Olives after Listeria monocytogenes was found in the product. The recall affected 120g packs with use-by dates of September 6, September 7 and September 10, 2026.

Customers who bought an affected pack were similarly told not to eat the olives and instead return them to their nearest Sainsbury’s store for a full refund.

News.title: Child makes miraculous escape from jaws of giant Florida alligator after entering ‘no swim zone’
News.content:
Child makes miraculous escape from jaws of giant Florida alligator after entering ‘no swim zone’

A terrified child survived with minor injuries after coming face-to-face with an alligator in Florida, weeks after a woman was ripped to pieces by one of the giant beasts

View 2 Images Officers respond to the alligator attack at Weeki Wachee Preserve in Florida (Image: Hernando County Fire Rescue)

A child has managed to survive an alligator attack after being grabbed while swimming in a restricted nature reserve.

‌



The incident, at the Weeki Wachee Preserve in Spring Hill, Florida, saw the youngster released from hospital hours later after sustaining minor injuries. The victim, who has not yet been identified, sustained puncture wounds to the leg and the arm from the 12-foot long creature.

‌



The terrified child, along with several others, became stranded on a sandbar after the attack. The group were returned to the mainland after being rescued, before being taken to Bayonet Point Hospital for further treatment. An alligator trapper then laid traps in the area to try and catch the beast.

‌



View 2 Images The alligator, similar in size to this one, attacked the child (stock photo) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission is investigating after they ventured into a 'no swim' area on Monday afternoon. The state is home to around 1.3 million alligators and Christopher Gillette, the owner of Bellowing Acres Animal Sanctuary in Interlachen, told Fox News Digital that people must only swim in designated areas - or they could meet the reptile's jaws.

"That's really kind of the root of the issue here: You're swimming in the no-swimming zone," Gillette told the channel. "We're very fortunate that the kid did survive. If you're going to go swimming, only go swimming in designated swimming zones where we know there are not alligators."

‌



He added: "The three biggest problems that we run into are people swimming in alligator habitats, people feeding the alligators, or having kids and pets near the water's edge. My advice is don't end up there in the first place. It's incredibly dangerous even for someone who knows what they're doing."

Despite the huge numbers of the beasts, Florida averages about eight unprovoked alligator bites per year that require professional medical treatment Out of those 500 total bites in almost 50 years, 32 resulted in deaths - averaging less than one fatal attack per year.

Experts suggest that the chance of a resident being seriously injured in an unprovoked alligator incident is about one in 3.1 million. One deadly attack happened in July when an alligator ripped a woman to pieces in a horrifying attack in front of her boyfriend.

Article continues below

Brittany Clark, 31, had both of her arms ripped off by the 13-foot beast on June 29 while taking a dip in a river during a hike through the Little Big Econ State Forest in Florida. Investigators said she was killed in a "death roll" while swimming in shoulder-deep water with her boyfriend, Chance Allison, and roommate.

She was dragged under the water by the alligator during the attack, with Mr Allison trying urgently to rescue her from the jaws of the beast as it started trying to rip her arm off. A report from the Orange County Medical Examiner's Office stated that both were pulled under water, with the crocodile releasing its grip, only to clamp around the desperate woman's other arm.

The report stated:“While they were swimming an alligator grabbed [Brittany] by her arm and began the ‘death roll’."

News.title: Mum and dad to face trial over death of one-year-old son who died of 'severe malnutrition'
News.content:
Mum and dad to face trial over death of one-year-old son who died of 'severe malnutrition'

Parents Adam Johnson and Kylie Smith are alleged to have caused or allowed the death of their one-year-old son Maero Johnson in 2023 and both will stand trial next year

View 4 Images (Image: Liverpool Echo)

A mother and father will stand trial after pleading not guilty to causing the death of their one-year-old son.

Adam Johnson, 26, and Kylie Smith, 25, of St Helens, Merseyside, were charged last month in connection with the death of Maero Johnson three years ago. Police previously said a postmortem examination confirmed Maero died in August 2023 of ketotic hypoglycaemia and severe malnutrition.

The couple appeared at Liverpool Crown Court today where their trial, expected to last four to six weeks, was listed for April 19 next year. Smith, wearing a white polo shirt and with her hair in a long plait, and Johnson both pleaded not guilty to causing or allowing the death of a child between June 5 2023 and August 24 2023.

4 View 4 Images Johnson outside Liverpool Magistrates' Court today (Image: Liverpool Echo) 4 View 4 Images Kylie Smith covered her face as she leaves court (Image: Liverpool Echo)

Charge sheets state that the pair were "aware that there was a significant risk of serious physical harm being caused to" Maero "by the unlawful act of a member of his household". The count also accuses them of "failing to take reasonable steps to protect him from that risk".

They also denied two counts of cruelty to a person under 16. Johnson, wearing a shirt and with facial hair, pleaded guilty to a charge of possessing cannabis. The pair were granted unconditional bail ahead of a pre-trial hearing on April 5 2027, the LiverpoolEcho reports.

Judge Brian Cummings KC, presiding, said: "Adam Johnson, you have pleaded guilty to one of the charges, the drugs charge, but otherwise you have both pleaded not guilty to the indictment. There will be a joint trial on April 19.

View 4 Images Little Maero Johnson was found to be severely malnourished three years ago (Image: Facebook)

"It may seem a long way away, but you may find it comes around sooner than you think. There is a lot of preparation before the trial so please cooperate fully with your legal team."

According to court sentencing guidelines, the charge of causing or allowing the death of a child can carry a maximum penalty of life imprisonment. A post-mortem examination showed Maero died in August 2023 of ketotic hypoglycaemia and severe malnutrition, Merseyside Police has said previously.

Merseyside Police previously said: "Two parents have been charged following the death of their child three years ago in St Helens. Just after midnight on August 23, 2023, we received a report that a one-year-old boy, Maero Johnson, had been taken to hospital, but, despite medical staff's best efforts, he sadly passed away.

"A Home Office postmortem confirmed Maero died of ketonic hypoglycaemia and severe malnutrition."

News.title: Mum put on child abuse register and given suspended sentence after letting son walk to pond
News.content:
Mum put on child abuse register and given suspended sentence after letting son walk to pond

Karyann Parkinson has left parents divided after being placed on the child abuse and neglect register for allowing her son, 5, to walk to a nature spot on his own from their home in Virginia

View 3 Images Parents are debating at what age a child should be allowed to walk on their own (stock photo) (Image: Getty Images)

A mother has sparked a parenting debate after she was arrested for allowing her five-year-old son to walk on his own to collect feathers near a pond.

‌



Mum-of-five Karyann Parkinson from Virginia has been handed a six-month suspended prison sentence and will remain on the child abuse and neglect registry for seven years after her lad Samuel was spotted on his own 800 meters from his home. She was charged with contributing to the delinquency of a minor, despite nothing happening to him, and was convicted by a judge after a trial in the Williamsburg Juvenile & Domestic Relations District Court.

‌



She was told if it happens again, she will go straight to jail. The treatment of Karyann has split many mums and dads after she allowed the boy to walk to the nature spot on his own, stressing that she could trust him - and that he was ready to show he could make the short trip without supervision.

‌



3 View 3 Images The mum was given a suspended jail sentence and placed on the child abuse and neglect registry (Image: Karyann Doty Parkinson/Facebook) 3 View 3 Images She let Samuel out on his own to collect goose feathers (Image: Karyann Doty Parkinson/Facebook)

She said that after the family went for a bike ride near their community pond, they made the short trip home. When they returned, Samuel asked if he could walk back and gather some more feathers - so the mum decided the time was right to see if he was ready to make a trip on his own.

But minutes later, the boy was stopped by a security guard, who alerted the police before Child Protective Services were called. Karyann told the authorities she hadn’t been breached any laws by allowing her son to walk on his own, but two weeks later she was charged - and is now is not allowed to volunteer at any of the schools her children attend.

‌



There is no official minimum legal age in the UK for a child to walk outside or walk to school on their own. The NSPCC state that kids usually start walking to school or outside independently between ages 9 to 11.

Karyann has spoken out to defend her parenting, and told Reason.com that her life was turned upside down just two weeks before the birth of her fifth child. She said: "Everyone in our neighborhood was close-knit and knew each other. There was 24-hour security, a 25-mph speed limit, sidewalks, and wide grass verges.

‌



"Sam was a responsible and independent kid. He'd made that journey hundreds of times with me, my husband, Dallin, 37, and our other children. Neglect occurs only when you put your child in serious or obvious danger, with no lower restriction on their age. Independence should be age-appropriate, taking into account the child's individual maturity and abilities."

As parents remain divided, she told Fox News: “I didn’t send him to play at the pond, I sent him down the path that happens to go past the pond to collect goose feathers. I know that a lot of people have seen the headlines and seen ‘five-year-old alone at a pond' - I think if I saw that in isolation, I’d probably be alarmed, too.

“We need to stop parenting from a place of fear and a place, you know, of obsessing over the unknown or some boogeyman who’s going to jump out from behind a bush.”

Article continues below

The mum says the family have filed an appeal because they want her case decided by a jury and are hopeful of hearing the outcome before Christmas.

News.title: Dad of teen killed in A66 crash charged with attacking mourner 'over comments made' at son's funeral
News.content:
Dad of teen killed in A66 crash charged with attacking mourner 'over comments made' at son's funeral

It has been claimed Gye Worthy, the father of 17-year-old crash victim Cole, allegedly took exception to comments made during his son's funeral service at Teesside Crematorium

View 4 Images Gye Worthy was arrested at his son Cole's funeral (Image: Facebook)

The father of one of the teenagers killed in the A66 crash has been charged with attacking a mourner at his son's funeral.

The remembrance ceremony for Cole Worthy, 17, was reduced to chaos when his father, Gye, 39, allegedly took exception to comments made during the service. He is accused of assaulting the mourner and of obstructing police who were called to deal with the disturbance.

A source close to the family said that Cole Worthy's mother Natalie McConnell had been "devastated and shocked" by the disruption to her son's memorial. Ms McConnell has long been separated from Gye Worthy and both now have new partners. A spokesman for Cleveland Police said Gye Worthy will face court next month.

4 View 4 Images Cole Worthy, right, was killed in the catastrophic crash last month 4 View 4 Images Police officers embrace before the funeral of PC Matthew Blades (Image: Owen Humphreys/PA Wire)

In a statement the force said: "The 39-year-old man arrested yesterday (Wednesday 9 September) at Teesside Crematorium, following a disturbance during a service, has now been charged with common assault, public order and obstructing police. He is due to appear before Teesside Magistrates’ Court on 2nd October."

Sarah Moloney, a friend of Ms McConnell, thanked mourners for their attendance on her behalf. In a social media post she said: "To everyone who came today for our Coley, thank you from the very bottom of our hearts.

View 4 Images A house in Ruskin Avenue, Middlesbrough, after being rammed by a car (Image: Owen Humphreys/PA Wire)

"Seeing so many faces who loved him cared for him and held him close means more than we can ever put into words, your presence your hugs your kind words and every beautiful memory you shared. Cole was so loved and today showed us just how far that love reached.

"Thank you for walking this hard day with us, thank you for loving him, for remembering him and for being here for us He will live on in all our hearts forever. Rest peacefully our beautiful Coley, we love you more than anything."

Gye Worthy, from Acklam, Middlesbrough, works as an offshore deck foreman and is the boss of his own specialist lifting company which operates on offshore platforms. His semi detached £200,000 home recently suffered serious damage in a criminal act currently under investigation by Cleveland Police.

Cole Worthy was killed within minutes of his father's home being attacked, alongside four of his associates and two police officers, PC Matthew Blades, 37 and PC Tom Clough, 38. They were all killed at 3.39am on Saturday August 22 when the police armed response vehicle was struck at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, by a speeding VW Passat containing the five youths and young men aged between 17 and 23.

Worthy, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Michael Cahill, 23, and Theo Rae, 17, were also killed in the smash. Police said the five all had links to organised crime and had been trying to flee police when they drove the wrong way up the A66 into the police vehicle.

The incident was blamed on a tit for tat gangland turf war over the supply of drugs on Teesside. PCs Clough and Blades died from severe head and neck injuries at the scene.

The final funeral of the five youths in the Passat was also taking place today in County Durham as family gathered to mark the death of Michael Cahill. At an earlier vigil held in his honour, a number of cars - including a £80,000 Porsche - were driven at speed around a field at Haswell, near Peterlee, and set ablaze.

News.title: Toy firms prepare to tap into booming 'kidult' craze as Christmas 2026 trend predictions released

News.title: Labour mayors in England vow to cap tourist tax at 5%
News.content:
Labour's regional mayors in England have pledged to cap a new fee on visitors' overnight stays at 5%, after hospitality bosses warned it could put jobs at risk.

Local leaders are set to gain new powers to charge an uncapped levy, dubbed a "tourist tax", as a percentage of the cost of hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation.

But the Labour mayors in 10 city regions said they would voluntarily limit the charge if they do apply it, adding that they had listened to concerns over costs.

Reform UK's two regional mayors and the two Conservative ones are likely to oppose any levy given criticism from their national parties of the policy.

In a letter to Chancellor John Healey and Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner, the Labour metro mayors said 5% represented a "reasonable ceiling" on the tax.

"It provides a balance of ensuring that local levies are not excessive, or vary significantly between regions, while also leaving room for local variation as appropriate," they added.

They added this would still allow for "meaningful investment" in local areas, whilst stressing any future levies in their areas would be "subject to local consultation".

The letter was signed by Labour mayors in London, Greater Manchester, Liverpool City Region, West Midlands, North East, West of England, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, East Midlands and York and North Yorkshire.

The government had earlier pledged to protect budget holidays "by making sure low-cost accommodation always pays lowest levy" and said the extra cash could be invested in high streets and local transport.

While Labour mayors have backed the new levy, others have expressed caution or signalled they will not bring it in.

Local leaders, including heads of Foundation Strategic Authorities where there is no mayor, will need to clarify by early 2028 how the revenue raised should be reinvested.

They will also be allowed to offer exemptions, such as for campsites.

However, mayors will not be allowed to exempt whole localities within their regions from the tax, to avoid creating confusion for visitors and businesses.

The government said it would introduce a bill to Parliament "in due course" to bring in the levy, which would apply to both Britons and people visiting from abroad.

News.title: Oil, gas and borrowing costs surge as fears over Middle East escalate
News.content:
The price of oil has jumped to $105 a barrel amid signs the conflict in the Middle East will not be resolved quickly, fuelling fears that inflation could accelerate.

With the conflict between the US and Iran in the Gulf intensifying in recent days, the cost of both crude oil and gas has been rising sharply. Brent crude went back above $100 a barrel on Wednesday and has continued to climb.

The war has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, preventing supplies of oil and gas from the Gulf from reaching global markets.

US and UK long-term borrowing costs also surged to their highest level in decades.

Speaking at a Republican Party convention in Texas on Wednesday, President Trump said he did not think the fighting would end until after the US mid-term elections in November.

Analysts said the combination of rising energy costs and higher borrowing costs was adding pressure on financial markets.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at trading platform IG, said investors were becoming increasingly concerned about the economic impact of higher oil prices.

"It feels like investors worldwide are now waking up to the crisis in oil markets," Beauchamp said. He warned that the surge in energy prices could weigh heavily on the global economy if it continues.

Concerns have also grown after Iran-aligned Houthi forces were reported to have seized Yemen's port of Mokha, a key Red Sea port.

The move could elevate fears of further shipping disruptions.

The price of natural gas has also been soaring on wholesale markets. In the UK, it rose above 200p a therm for the first time since the end of 2022.

Storage levels in Europe are much lower than normal for the time of year, and the need to fill reserves ahead of the winter has helped to push up prices.

News.title: Use all powers necessary on anti-migrant protests, home secretary tells police
News.content:
"These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," the Home Secretary said.

"This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."

The BBC understands that police chiefs are now actively considering using recently-granted powers to completely ban face coverings in specific areas, in light of that demonstration.

Saturday's protest was followed 24 hours later with another in which men blocked the only road out of Langstone Harbour, near Portsmouth, after the RNLI had brought ashore 120 migrants.

It's unclear at this stage whether further such protests will go ahead - but in some areas of England local groups that have associated themselves with the Patriot Platform umbrella group have called for more demonstrations.

The meeting discussed the emergence of Patriot Platform with ministers believing the group aims to intimidate communities.

Mahmood is said to have told police chiefs to make better use of intelligence to make sure they had better plans in place ahead of this weekend.

That call came after Kent Police had earlier admitted it had been made aware of a potential demonstration in Dover but had not "fully assessed" the warning before the town's nationally critical port road was brought to a standstill.

During the meeting, Mahmood is said to have made clear the government expected police to make full use of powers and to deal robustly with any criminal offences.

Speaking after the meeting, Deputy Chief Constable Andy Mariner, the National Police Chiefs Council lead for public order, said forces were "continually assessing and preparing for protests and any potential impact on public safety".

This includes working closely with "local forces, specialist teams, communities and partners" to ensure support is available when needed.

He added: "Our priority is to keep people safe, maintain public order and support the right to peaceful and lawful protest. While people are entitled to express their views, anyone committing criminal offences can and should expect police action."

Major changes to protest law in the last three years mean officers can now intervene more quickly to end demonstrations that block critical national infrastructure, such as roads to ports.

They can also designate an entire area a face mask-free zone for the duration of a protest.

It's that second power that police chiefs are now considering using.

Police chiefs also say they have initiated an "enhanced and co-ordinated" approach to gathering as much intelligence as possible in the days ahead.

News.content:
Visitors flocked to the British Museum in London on Thursday as the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition opened its doors to the general public.

The Bayeux Tapestry is an embroidery almost 70m (230ft) in length and nearly 1,000 years old. It tells the story of the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

Adult tickets to see the tapestry are priced at Â£33 during peak times and Â£27 at off-peak times, with an additional Â£3.50 donation.

The BBC's Katie Razzall asked the first visitors if it was worth the price.

News.title: Four hurt and seven arrested in London stabbing
News.content:
Seven people have been arrested after four men were stabbed in south-east London, the Metropolitan Police has said.

One of the men remains in a critical condition in hospital, while the other three are being treated for injuries that are not believed to be life-threatening.

Paramedics and the London Air Ambulance were called at about 14:20 BST to Bromley High Street, where one eyewitness reported seeing a man wielding a machete.

A KFC spokesperson confirmed a "serious incident" had taken place at its Bromley High Street restaurant and an altercation had begun there. The company said it was assisting police and "supporting our team members and customers at this difficult time".

News.title: Drone display recreates the Twin Towers over New York City
News.content: According to organisers, 2,977 drones recreated the Twin Towers at full scale with each light representing a victim of the 9/11 attacks. The artwork, titled "2,977 Lights Over New York Harbor", is a commemorative public art installation in collaboration with artists, producers, and members of the 9/11 community, including victims' families, survivors, and first responders.

News.title: Esther Rantzen says she is too fragile to travel to Switzerland to end life
News.content:
Dame Esther Rantzen has said she is now "too physically fragile" to travel to Switzerland to end her life at an assisted suicide clinic.

The veteran broadcaster, 86, said she would have to fly to the country, where the practice is legal, alone, which she could only have done before her life became "unbearable" and before she was ready to end her life.

The Childline founder, who is terminally ill with cancer, first revealed in December 2023 that she had joined the Dignitas clinic.

Dame Esther used her statement on Thursday to reiterate a plea for MPs to vote in favour of legalising assisted dying in England and Wales when proposed legislation is revisited by Parliament on Friday.

She announced she had joined Dignitas about a year after being diagnosed with stage four lung cancer.

"Unfortunately, when I was strong enough to make the flight and go to Dignitas, my life was not unbearably painful, indeed I was able to relax in my beloved cottage in the New Forest," she said.

"And by the time life did become unbearable, I was too physically fragile to make the journey and go through the Dignitas process.

"So even though I had spent the money and made the plans, I was not ready to end my life back then, and did not realise that would be my last chance."

Dame Esther added that "everything I didn't want to happen I'm having to go through now", with loved ones either unable to visit her or "see me suffering pain or indignity" when they do.

The prominent assisted dying campaigner said the law - which she described as "messy and cruel" - must "change and change quickly".

Helping someone end their life is currently considered a criminal offence across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Jersey legalised assisted dying for terminally ill adults earlier this year.

MPs are considering a draft law that, if passed, would make it legal in England and Wales under specific circumstances for people who are terminally ill with less than six months to live.

While Dame Esther, who is best known for presenting the BBC programme That's Life! for 21 years, is among several leading figures in favour of the bill, there are also campaigners against it, including Paralympian Baroness Grey-Thompson

They fear that a change in the law could mean that disabled and other vulnerable people could be pressured to end their lives, while also criticising the wording of the proposed legislation as not providing strong enough safeguards.

The bill has been through several drafts and has been scrutinised by several Parliamentary committees and the House of Lords, which submitted 1,200 amendments.

The bill was previously introduced in 2024, but the last session of Parliament ran out of time before it was passed.

It was reintroduced in this Parliament and a second vote will be held on Friday afternoon. If it passes the House of Commons, rarely invoked powers could be used, meaning it would not need the assent of the Lords to become law this time.

Proponents of the bill have indicated they would try to bring legislation again as soon as possible were it to be voted down on Friday.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he would not be voting on the issue and has suggested that palliative and social care should be better funded before legalising assisted suicide is considered.

Assisted dying is legal in a number of countries - including Canada, Australia and Belgium - as well as in Switzerland, though the circumstances under which it is legal differ between those nations.

News.title: Police and army attend funeral for officer killed in wrong-way A66 crash
News.content:
Police officers and army veterans gathered for the funeral of the second officer killed in a head-on crash.

PC Tom Clough, 38, died on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 22 August with his colleague PC Matthew Blades when a Volkswagen Passat hit their marked police car. Five young men in the Passat also died.

Members of the public also gathered for the funeral at Kirkleatham Walled Gardens, in Redcar, along with family, friends and former colleagues from British Transport Police and the Civil Nuclear Constabulary in Sellafield, Cumbria.

Cleveland Police Federation chair Lauren Somerville said PC Clough's partner said public support "brought them so much strength".

The ceremonial procession made its way along Plantation Road towards the Walled Gardens, accompanied by the music of a lone piper.

The road was lined on both sides with standard bearers who had lowered their flags before the cortege went past.

At its head was a mounted police unit of four horses.

Immediately behind them came the hearse carrying PC Clough's coffin, draped with the Union Flag and topped with his custodian helmet.

The hearse was flanked by officers in ceremonial dress escorting the coffin to the service.

News.title: Bayeux Tapestry unveiled to UK public for first time at British Museum
News.content:
Cecilia and Fabio Zanini were completely wowed by the scale of the Bayeux Tapestry.

"I was amazed by the vibrancy of the colours. The detail of the characters," Cecilia said. "It gave both of us goosebumps."

Fabio said he was constantly looking left and right to see all the action and he was surprised by the scale of the tapestry, particularly the number of Norman boats and cavalry.

"It feels like you're in the battlefield," he added, praising the "real sense of movement" in the embroidery.

"It really allowed you to go back to 1066."

But others told the BBC the event was "out of reach" because of its cost and London location.

Angie in Leeds said the "historic event" was "out of reach for many, many families in the north" when you factor in the cost of train tickets and food costs on top of the museum tickets themselves.

"London-only cultural events alienate many families north of Watford," she added.

Another man spoke of the "extreme queuing" required to view the exhibit. Hadyn Blakeston said he felt like he was on a "conveyor belt" while moving along the tapestry.

"It's one long queue," he said. "I know we're supposed to love queuing, but it was extreme queuing."

News.title: Teacher sexually abused pupils at multiple schools
News.content:
A teacher has been found guilty of sexually abusing a 16-year-old boy after previously admitting offences against two teenage girls.

Former PE teacher Bronwen James, 30, of Chippenham, Wiltshire, admitted nine sexual offences against two teenage girls - one a pupil at Bitterne Park School in Southampton and the other at Hardenhuish School in Chippenham.

She was convicted earlier at Winchester Crown Court of three counts of sexual activity with a 16-year-old boy who also attended Bitterne Park School.

During the trial the prosecution said James "craved" attention and "abused the trust put in her" as a teacher.

The jury found James guilty of the three counts of sexual activity with a child by a person in a position of trust by a majority of 11 to one and acquitted her of a fourth charge.

Due to legal restrictions covering the trial, media had been unable to report James' guilty pleas against two girls - which she made in January - and the jury were not told about them until after they had passed their verdict.

News.title: Theatregoer who throttled woman at show is jailed
News.content:
A 75-year-old man who strangled a woman after she started to sing along at a West End show has been jailed for two years.

Malcolm Potier was sitting near victim Kirsty O'Donnell in the audience at We Will Rock You at the London Coliseum in June 2023.

He said he had no recollection of being at the show, or of attacking O'Donnell, but was sentenced at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday after being found guilty of non-fatal strangulation by jurors.

Potier, a businessman and surveyor of Sarratt near Watford, was already jailed in Australia two decades ago having twice tried to arrange the murder of a former partner following a dispute over their child.

He is also the former laird - a Scottish term for someone owning a large long-established estate - of the Hebridean island of Gigha.

Judge Dafna Spiro said his behaviour was "extreme and horrific".

"It is an unusual offence," she said. "It's not a situation I have ever come across before."

She said there was a "thread" of "dominance, control and lack of accountability" in Potier's behaviour.

News.title: Father of A66 teen charged with funeral assault
News.content:
The father of one of the five men who were killed in a wrong-way crash with a police car has been charged with assaulting someone at his son's funeral.

Gye Worthy, 39, was arrested at Teesside Crematorium in Middlesbrough following a disturbance during the service on Wednesday.

His son Cole Worthy, 17, died when the Volkswagon Passat he and four others were in collided with a marked armed police car on the A66 in South Bank in the early hours of 22 August.

Cleveland Police said Gye Worthy has been charged with common assault and obstructing police and is due to appear at Teesside Magistrates' Court in October.

Cole Worthy's funeral was held on the same day as that of PC Matthew Blades, 37, who was one of the officers killed in the crash.

PC Blades had been travelling along the A66 with his colleague PC Tom Clough when their car was struck head-on by the Passat travelling in the wrong direction.

The pair were in a vehicle looking for the Passat after its cloned registration plates triggered a camera, although they were not involved in the pursuit which preceded the crash, according to the Independent Office for Police Conduct.

News.title: Ex-Tory campaign chief pleads guilty over election bet
News.content:
The Conservatives' former director of campaigning and his wife have pleaded guilty to cheating at gambling by placing bets on the date of the 2024 general election.

Anthony Lee stood to win approximately Â£15,000 after placing more than 60 successful bets totalling Â£1,549, the Gambling Commission said.

He passed confidential information to his wife about when former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak was planning to call the general election.

Laura Lee, who was a parliamentary candidate at the time, placed eight successful bets on the election date totalling Â£535 and would have profited by around Â£5,000.

On Thursday at Southwark Crown Court, Anthony Lee pleaded guilty to two offences and Laura Lee pleaded guilty to one offence.

They will be sentenced in October.

The trials of 10 other defendants will take place in September 2027 and January 2028.

Former MP Craig Williams, who was Sunak's closest parliamentary aide at the time, pleaded guilty in June and will be sentenced at a later date.

In Williams' case, the prosecution said he bet Â£250, Â£100, and Â£22.50 on the date of the 2024 election, telling the court he "used highly sensitive and confidential information".

When details of the scandal first emerged in June 2024, Williams admitted making a "huge error of judgment".

Sunak's decision to call the poll was a surprise to many, including many Conservative MPs, who were expecting an autumn date.

The Conservative Party has been approached for comment.

News.title: Catherine joins William as he says sport can save lives from suicide
News.content:
It was important that sports stars admitted their own vulnerability, said Olympic cyclist Dame Laura Kenny.

She spoke movingly of how a family member had tried to take their life and how she felt "almost ashamed to admit that this could happen in my family because it's not a subject that is easily spoken about".

The cyclist also described the darkness of her feelings after the loss of two babies, through a miscarriage and an ectopic pregnancy, "which ultimately ended up in an emergency situation".

On Your Side aims to use the reach of sport to raise awareness about suicide and to show people the help available in a crisis, with the Football Association, Premier League and Team GB providing support.

The level of suicide is disproportionately higher among men than women - it is the biggest cause of death for men under the age of 50 in the UK - and sport is seen as an effective way of communicating that help is available.

"My hope is that every sporting organisation in the country will look at what is being launched today and ask a question: 'What more can we do?' Because the opportunity before us is enormous," Prince William said.

The royal couple saw a bench at the ground dedicated in memory of Gary Speed, a footballer who once played at the club, and who died by suicide in 2011.

The bench, unveiled last year, is intended to give people a space to speak openly about their anxieties and the royal couple met Speed's mother there.

Shearer was a friend of Speed and is backing the call for people to try to support people they have worries about.

"You don't have to be an expert. You don't have to have all the answers," said Shearer. "But we can all be better at asking, listening, and helping someone find the right support."

News.title: Two arrested in London on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service
News.content:
Two people have been arrested in London on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service, the Metropolitan Police has said.

A 60-year-old man and 42-year-old woman were arrested at properties in London on Wednesday as part of an investigation into suspected National Security Act (NSA) offences.

The suspects, who were both held on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service, have been released on bail under strict conditions until late October, the Met said.

Police said the arrests were not "connected to any of the incidents or attacks" linked to Jewish and Iranian communities across London earlier this year.

The arrests took place following two searches carried out at properties in north and north-west London in June, the Met added.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said she knows "news of these arrests will come as a concern to some members of the public" but stressed she does "not believe there to be any imminent threat to the wider public".

She added: "We've seen a marked increase in the tempo of our work linked to national security and state threats over the past year and this investigation is a continuation of that.

"As we've shown here, if we suspect any activity could threaten the safety of the UK or the public, then we will not hesitate to take action."

She added the UK's terror threat level was severe and called for people to be vigilant.

News.title: Alstom to build new battery-electric train fleet
News.content:
He added: "I've lost count of the number of times someone has stopped me to tell me about the train that never came.

"And when that happens, it means missed shifts, missed appointments, and missed opportunities. Today, that starts to change."

The DfT said the trains would help deliver the Transpennine Route Upgrade's aim to boost capacity by 30%, with thousands of additional seats a day across the Pennines by the early to mid-2030s.

They will run between key destinations across the north including Liverpool Lime Street and Scarborough, Manchester Airport and Saltburn, and Manchester Piccadilly and Hull.

The DfT added that journey times will be cut by up to 10 minutes between Manchester and Leeds and up to 14 minutes between Manchester and York.

The trains will be bought by Rock Rail and leased to TransPennine Express, the government added.

Alstom, which boasts the largest rolling stock train manufacturing site outside of China, secured a Â£370m contract in 2024 to produce 10 new London Elizabeth line trains.

This came less than three months after a redundancy consultation put 1,300 jobs at risk at its Litchurch Lane factory, which dates back to 1876.

Rob Whyte, managing director UK at Alstom, called the latest agreement a "landmark moment for Britain's railway".

He said: "We couldn't be prouder that the country's first main line battery-electric trains will be designed and built in Britain.

"The fleet will transform journeys across northern England while showcasing the very best of British engineering, innovation and advanced manufacturing."
