World.title: Liberia: SpoonTV CEO Cuts a Deal, Trades Prison for Testimony
World.content:
Monrovia — SpoonTV CEO Stanton Witherspoon has secured his release after prosecutors credited him with providing substantial assistance in the investigation and prosecution of a multimillion-dollar scheme involving the sale of fraudulent nursing diplomas and transcripts.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Witherspoon, who pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud, was originally sentenced in November 2023 to 41 months in prison and three years of supervised release.

But on September 9, 2026, U.S. District Judge Rodney Smith granted a government motion under Rule 35(b) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, reducing Witherspoon’s sentence to time served and eliminating the supervised-release requirement. The remaining counts against him—Counts 2 through 6 and Count 8—were dismissed.

The $5.17 Million Scheme

According to prosecutors, Witherspoon was a 50% owner of Siena Education Center LLC and Siena College of Health II LLC, as well as founder and president of Nursing Education Resource Center LLC (NERC).

Prosecutors said Witherspoon worked with Rene Bernadel, Alfred Sellu and Cimoyne Alves through NERC to recruit and train aspiring nurses.

He later worked with Eunide Sanon and Siena to provide fraudulent nursing-school diplomas and transcripts. The documents were used by students to obtain fraudulent certification as registered nurses or licensed practical nurses.

Witherspoon was held responsible for approximately $5.17 million in losses.

His total offense level was calculated at 26, with a criminal history category of I, resulting in a federal sentencing guideline range of 63 to 78 months. He ultimately received a 41-month sentence in 2023.

Testimony Against Co-Conspirators

The government’s decision to seek a reduction in Witherspoon’s sentence was tied directly to his cooperation with federal investigators and prosecutors.

Before entering his guilty plea, Witherspoon was interviewed by agents from the FBI and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General about individuals involved in nursing-school fraud schemes.

Prosecutors said his cooperation subsequently contributed to cases against several defendants.

Among those was Carleen Noreus, who operated a separate fraudulent nursing program known as Carleen Health Institute. Witherspoon testified against Noreus at trial, and she later pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money-laundering conspiracy charges. She is awaiting sentencing.

Other defendants who pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy charges included Cimoyne Alves, Lemuel Pierre and Cleophat Tanis.

Witherspoon also provided an affidavit identifying nursing students who had received fraudulent degrees and transcripts. That information was forwarded to the National Council of State Boards of Nursing, allowing state licensing boards to take remedial action.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida, together with HHS-OIG and FBI investigators, supported the reduction, citing the scope and usefulness of Witherspoon’s cooperation.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Christopher J. Clark filed the Rule 35(b) motion on behalf of the government.

From Conviction to Freedom

The court’s decision means Witherspoon has now completed his federal prison sentence and will not be required to serve the previously imposed three years of supervised release.

His release has generated considerable reaction in Liberia, where Witherspoon is a prominent media personality and the head of the Spoon Network.

Witherspoon was a vocal supporter of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and the Unity Party Alliance during the 2023 Presidential and Legislative Elections.

He used the Spoon Network to campaign for Boakai, then a former vice president and opposition candidate, and helped to organize political events involving the Boakai campaign in the United States.

The media entrepreneur was subsequently credited by supporters with playing a role in mobilizing Liberians abroad and helping the Unity Party candidate defeat then-President George Weah.

Despite his support for Boakai, however, Witherspoon has since used his media platform to criticize aspects of the administration, regularly highlighting what he describes as policy failures and missteps by officials of the government he once strongly supported.

‘Now That We Are Free, We Will Talk’

Following the court’s decision, Witherspoon appeared on his Spoon Network and thanked his wife, relatives, pastor, staff and Liberians who supported him during his legal ordeal.

He also sought to separate his release from Liberia’s political divisions.

“God didn’t do this for me. God did it because He is God,” Witherspoon said.

“This is not about the Unity Party, not about CDC, not about who is in government. We will continue to talk; we are not going anywhere. Now that we are free, we will talk.”

He thanked Liberians, politicians and private citizens who had contacted him, prayed for him and wished him well.

The news of his release has produced mixed reactions, with supporters celebrating the decision while others have questioned the court’s action in reducing his sentence.

Spoon Network Celebrates

Tetee C. Karneh, CEO of the Spoon Network, also appeared briefly on Spoon Talk following the ruling and thanked the network’s staff and Witherspoon’s wife for standing by him throughout the legal proceedings.

Karneh, who previously served as General Manager of Spoon FM before being elevated to CEO as Witherspoon focused on his legal case, attributed his release to divine intervention.

She also thanked the Liberian people for their support and expressed appreciation to the U.S. court system.

Snowe Welcomes Release

Bomi County Senator Edwin Melvin Snowe also welcomed Witherspoon’s release in a statement posted on Facebook.

“My dear friend, Stanton, through it all, you looked unto the hills from whence cometh your help. You kept the faith, you trusted God, and today, your prayers have been answered,” Snowe wrote.

He described Witherspoon as “a free man” and said he shared in the relief and gratitude surrounding the end of the difficult chapter.

“May this experience strengthen your faith even more and remind you that no matter how difficult the journey becomes, God remains faithful,” Snowe added.

For Witherspoon, the federal court ruling closes one chapter of his legal battle—but his active role in Liberia’s highly charged media and political landscape could open another, particularly after his declaration that “now that we are free, we will talk.”

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Puts Banks, Borrowers and Government on Notice As NPLs Hit 19%, Demands Urgent Fix
World.content:
Monrovia — President Joseph Boakai has called for urgent and coordinated action to resolve Liberia’s persistent non-performing loan (NPL) problem, warning that the crisis is restricting access to credit and threatening the country’s broader economic growth.

Jaheim T. [email protected]

Speaking Wednesday, September 9, at the opening of the National Conference on the Resolution of Non-Performing Loans at the Ministerial Complex in Monrovia, President Boakai said the issue must no longer be treated as merely a technical banking concern, but as a national development challenge.

The three-day conference, convened by the Central Bank of Liberia, is being held under the theme, “Resolving Non-Performing Loans to Unlock Access to Finance for Private Sector Growth and Job Creation.”

The gathering brings together government officials, commercial banks, regulators, the judiciary, the Legislature, private sector representatives and development partners to examine the causes of distressed loans and develop measures to improve credit recovery and expand access to financing.

President Boakai said the consequences of unpaid loans extend far beyond bank balance sheets.

“This issue, in my view, is really about people,” the President said, pointing to farmers seeking financing to expand production, young entrepreneurs looking for capital, businesses hoping to expand and create jobs, and depositors whose funds must be protected.

He warned that when loans remain unpaid, money that should circulate through the economy becomes trapped, forcing banks to become more cautious and making credit harder and more expensive for legitimate borrowers.

“That is why the theme of this conference … is both timely and important,” Boakai said. “This is not simply a banking problem. It is a national development challenge.”

Liberia’s NPL Burden

CBL Executive Governor Henry F. Saamoi provided a stark picture of the problem, revealing that Liberia’s banking sector recorded a non-performing loan ratio of 19.1 percent at the end of 2024, nearly twice the prudential benchmark.

Although the ratio declined to 12.9 percent in 2025, Saamoi cautioned that the improvement was driven largely by loan restructurings and write-offs rather than sustainable recoveries.

The figures, he said, underscore the need for structural reforms aimed at strengthening repayment performance, credit discipline and debt recovery.

“Liberia’s elevated level of non-performing loans demands decisive action,” Saamoi said.

He compared Liberia’s situation with other countries, noting that Ghana recorded an NPL ratio of 21.8 percent in 2024, while Nigeria recorded 8.1 percent, Guinea 6.7 percent and The Gambia 4.6 percent.

According to Saamoi, international experience shows that systemic NPL problems cannot be resolved through isolated action by regulators or banks.

“Governments must play their part. Regulators must play their part. Banks must play their part. The judiciary must play its part. Borrowers must play their part and development partners must play their part,” he said.

Boakai Demands Accountability

President Boakai stressed that resolving the existing stock of bad loans must be accompanied by measures to prevent new ones.

He called for stronger credit reporting systems, improved land administration and collateral registration, better use of technology, expansion of responsible digital financial services and reforms to Liberia’s insolvency framework.

He also placed responsibility on both lenders and borrowers.

“Banks must lend responsibly and conduct proper assessments of those to whom they lend,” Boakai said. “Borrowers must also understand that loans are obligations that must be repaid.”

He further emphasized the importance of enforceable contracts and collateral, as well as an effective judiciary capable of resolving disputes fairly and efficiently.

“Contracts must mean something. Collateral must mean something,” he said.

But the President reserved some of his strongest remarks for what he described as Liberia’s tendency to produce recommendations without sufficient follow-through.

“The success of this conference will not be measured by the speeches we make or the recommendations we write. It will be measured by what we do after we leave this room,” Boakai said.

“Liberia has had many conferences. We have produced many good reports and recommendations. What our people need now is implementation.”

He urged participants to leave the conference with clear commitments, assigned responsibilities, realistic timelines and a mechanism for monitoring implementation.

Finance Minister Links Government Arrears to Bad Loans

Finance and Development Planning Minister Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan broadened the discussion, arguing that government’s own payment practices can contribute to the accumulation of non-performing loans within the banking sector.

Ngafuan explained that when government fails to pay contractors, suppliers and service providers on time, those businesses may struggle to service loans they previously obtained from commercial banks.

“What begins as a government arrear can eventually end up as a non-performing loan on the balance sheet of a commercial bank,” Ngafuan said.

He said the Boakai administration is therefore seeking to restore government’s credibility as an economic actor by honoring legitimate financial obligations.

“When this government contracts with you, government must pay you,” Ngafuan declared.

He acknowledged that the administration inherited significant legacy obligations but said the government is addressing them within available fiscal space while seeking to avoid creating new arrears.

Ngafuan said the current national budget provides nearly US$235 million for debt service, including more than US$90 million for commercial debt.

He also cited approximately US$25 million budgeted for debt service to the World Bank, arguing that government must demonstrate the same repayment culture it expects from citizens and businesses.

“We cannot call upon citizens and businesses to honor their obligations to banks while government fails to honor its obligations to those banks,” he said.

From Bad Loans to Productive Capital

For the CBL governor, the ultimate objective is not merely to reduce the NPL ratio but to free up capital for productive economic activity.

Saamoi said the conference is expected to produce three key outputs: a conference communique, an NPL resolution policy roadmap and a reform action plan.

The roadmap is expected to identify practical reforms in credit risk management, debt recovery, collateral enforcement and credit discipline, while also assessing the regulatory, legal and judicial systems governing loan recovery.

Ngafuan said resolving distressed assets should ultimately redirect capital toward agriculture, manufacturing, construction, trade, technology, housing and other productive sectors.

He argued that government alone cannot employ every Liberian and that sustainable job creation requires a stronger private sector capable of investing, innovating and expanding.

President Boakai similarly linked the NPL crisis to his administration’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development, which seeks to expand employment, empower women and young people, strengthen agriculture and food security, improve infrastructure and grow Liberian businesses.

The President said those ambitions cannot be achieved without a financial system capable of providing affordable and reliable financing.

A Test of Implementation

The conference comes at a time when Liberia’s financial sector continues to face the twin challenge of improving loan recovery while expanding access to credit for businesses and households.

For Boakai, the challenge now is to move beyond diagnosis.

“We know the problem. We have brought the right institutions together. Now we must move from discussion to action,” he said.

Saamoi echoed that position, describing the conference as an opportunity to establish a new chapter in Liberia’s financial sector—one marked by stronger banks, healthier balance sheets, greater financial inclusion, expanded access to credit, increased investment and more jobs.

“The ultimate measure of success of this conference will not simply be a lower NPL ratio,” Saamoi said. “Success will be reflected in greater access to credit, better repayment terms and performance, stronger businesses, expanded investment, increased employment opportunities and improved livelihoods for our people.”

For the Boakai administration, the resolution of bad loans has therefore become part of a broader economic question: how to unlock capital trapped in distressed assets and put it back to work in an economy where farmers, businesses, entrepreneurs and young Liberians are demanding greater access to finance.

World.title: Liberia: McGill Rejects Costa’s Drug Cartel Allegation, Demands Evidence
World.content:
Senator Says Claims Linking Him to Alleged Narcotics Network Are “False, Malicious and Unsupported”

Monrovia — Senator Nathaniel F. McGill has strongly rejected allegations by political commentator Henry Pedro Costa seeking to link him to an alleged drug cartel, describing the claims as false, malicious and unsupported by credible evidence.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The allegation comes amid heightened public scrutiny of Liberia’s ongoing investigation and prosecution of individuals accused of involvement in the country’s recent high-profile narcotics cases, with competing claims and counterclaims increasingly playing out in the media and political space.

In a recent podcast, Costa allegedly claimed that Gerald Smith told investigators that Senator McGill was linked to a drug cartel. The allegation has not been independently substantiated by FrontPage Africa.

Responding through an official statement, the Office of Senator McGill categorically denied any connection between the senator and drug trafficking or an alleged narcotics organization.

“The Office categorically rejects these allegations as false, misleading, malicious, and entirely unsupported by credible evidence,” the statement said.

The senator’s office maintained that McGill has never associated himself with a drug cartel, drug-trafficking operation or illegal drug business.

It cautioned against presenting allegations based on insinuation, speculation or unverified claims as established facts before the Liberian public.

Denies Financial Link to Gerald Smith

A central aspect of the statement was the office’s denial that McGill ever received money from Gerald Smith or anyone associated with him in connection with alleged drug-related activities.

“The Office further states unequivocally that Senator McGill has never received money from Mr. Gerald Smith or from anyone associated with him in connection with any alleged drug-related activity,” the statement said.

According to the senator’s office, McGill’s relationship with Smith was strictly professional and arose from their respective government positions.

At the time referenced, Smith served as Deputy Director of the National Security Agency, while McGill served as Minister of State.

Their interactions, the office said, occurred within the normal course of official government responsibilities.

‘Produce the Evidence’

McGill’s office challenged anyone making allegations against the senator to take the claims beyond public commentary and submit whatever evidence exists to Liberia’s investigative and judicial authorities.

“If any individual possesses evidence establishing otherwise, the appropriate course is to present that evidence to the relevant investigative and judicial authorities,” the statement said.

The office emphasized that allegations and repeated references to unverified claims should not be confused with evidence.

It argued that accusations involving serious crimes such as narcotics trafficking should be handled through credible evidence and established legal processes rather than political rhetoric.

The statement also referenced what McGill’s office described as previous attempts by political actors associated with the Unity Party to connect the senator to the reported US$317 million cocaine seizure.

The office maintained that no credible evidence has been publicly established linking McGill to the narcotics seizure.

Drug Investigation Becomes Political Battleground

The latest dispute adds another layer to an increasingly contentious national debate over Liberia’s drug investigations.

The government’s prosecution of suspects in connection with major cocaine seizures has generated intense political controversy, with opposition figures, political commentators and government officials trading accusations over who may have known about, facilitated or benefited from the alleged narcotics operations.

McGill’s office warned that reducing serious narcotics allegations to political accusations could undermine public confidence in legitimate investigations.

“The Office considers it inappropriate for serious matters involving alleged narcotics trafficking to be reduced to political accusations without substantiating evidence,” the statement said.

It argued that unsupported allegations could distract from the need for transparent and evidence-based accountability.

The office therefore called on those making allegations to produce the evidence underlying their claims and, where appropriate, submit that evidence to competent authorities for independent investigation.

McGill Says He Is Ready to Respond

Despite rejecting the allegations, McGill’s office said the senator remains willing to respond to legitimate questions and credible evidence.

“Allegations of criminal conduct must not be presented as established facts in the absence of verifiable evidence,” the office said.

It maintained that the appropriate test for the allegations is evidence, not political assertion.

The statement concluded with a direct challenge to those advancing the claims: if evidence exists, it should be submitted to the authorities; if no evidence exists, the allegations should not be used as political propaganda or as a basis for publicly characterizing the senator as involved in criminal conduct.

The statement was issued by the Office of Senator Nathaniel F. McGill, Republic of Liberia.

World.title: Liberia: Bishop Brown Cautions Opposition Leaders Amid Ongoing Collaboration Talks
World.content:
Monrovia — Former Liberia Council of Churches President, Bishop Kortu Brown, has urged opposition politicians to approach Liberia’s political challenges with greater responsibility, cautioning them against allowing the pursuit of political power to overshadow the national interest.

By Obediah Johnson, [email protected]

Brown, who is Founder and General Overseer of the New Water in the Desert Apostolic Pentecostal Church, said Liberia’s political class has a responsibility to create an environment where disagreements can be managed through dialogue rather than confrontation.

His appeal comes at a time when political actors from opposition parties and members of the governing establishment have increasingly engaged in discussions aimed at addressing national issues and exploring areas of common interest.

While welcoming recent roundtable engagements involving opposition leaders and lawmakers associated with the ruling Unity Party, Brown said such meetings would only be meaningful if they produced discussions centered on the welfare of ordinary Liberians.

He made the remarks during a thanksgiving service at his church in Brewerville, outside Monrovia.

For Brown, Liberia’s political future should not be reduced to the question of who will control the Executive Mansion after the 2029 elections.

He argued that political leaders should be more concerned about the decisions they make today and how those decisions affect the country’s stability and future generations.

Brown acknowledged that politicians naturally seek state power, but maintained that the outcome of elections ultimately cannot be determined solely by political calculations.

“Liberians have seen everything. We’ve seen war and peace, CDC and UP,” he said, emphasizing that Liberia’s political history should encourage leaders to act with greater responsibility.

He called on opposition politicians to become a constructive force capable of criticizing government while also contributing ideas toward solving the country’s problems.

Brown said opposition leaders should not view political engagement solely through the lens of gaining power, but should also consider their responsibility to maintain peace and national cohesion.

His message was particularly directed at political leaders preparing for the next electoral cycle. He urged them to engage one another, communicate with government officials and seek common ground on issues affecting Liberians.

Brown believes political disagreements are inevitable, but warned that the manner in which those disagreements are handled can either strengthen or weaken the country.

He therefore encouraged opposition leaders to maintain dialogue among themselves and with those currently exercising state authority. “God is in control of this country,” Brown said, stressing his belief that Liberia’s political destiny cannot be determined entirely by human calculations.

He urged opposition leaders to make peace and demonstrate political maturity as they prepare for the 2029 elections.

The religious leader also cautioned Liberians against allowing historical grievances to dictate contemporary relationships.

He warned against attempts to punish or seek revenge against members of the present generation because of wrongdoing committed by their ancestors.

According to Brown, Liberia’s history contains numerous examples of conflicts that began with disputes involving families and communities and later developed into wider divisions.

His appeal was therefore not limited to political parties. He called on Liberians generally to resist the temptation to inherit conflicts and grievances from previous generations.

Brown’s remarks also reflected on Liberia’s turbulent political history.

His reference to “war and peace” and successive political administrations underscored the dramatic changes the country has experienced over the years.

For him, those experiences should provide sufficient lessons for the current generation to avoid repeating the mistakes that contributed to division and instability.

He maintained that Liberia still has people capable of contributing positively to national development if given the opportunity. “But Liberia still got some good people that can be used to produce more good people,” he said.

The statement appeared to be a call for greater confidence in Liberians themselves and for the country’s political and social institutions to encourage citizens who can contribute constructively to national life.

Brown also commented on the legal situation involving former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor, whose temporary release on medical grounds has attracted considerable political attention.

He commended the court for granting Taylor compassionate relief and placing her under house arrest in connection with the ongoing cocaine case.

The former vice president’s detention had become a politically sensitive issue, particularly among supporters of the opposition National Patriotic Party and other political actors who had raised concerns about her health and treatment.

Brown argued that Taylor’s release had helped ease political tensions surrounding the case. He said the development should provide an opportunity for Liberians to redirect their attention toward issues affecting their daily lives rather than allowing political disagreements to escalate.

His comments came against the backdrop of wider concerns over political polarization and the increasingly heated exchanges among supporters of rival political camps.

Brown also challenged Liberians to reconsider what he described as a culture of constant complaint. Rather than spending their energy blaming government, relatives or other people for their difficulties, he encouraged citizens to make productive use of whatever opportunities and resources are available to them.

His appeal extended beyond politics to personal responsibility. Brown suggested that national progress requires citizens to recognize their own capacity to improve their circumstances while simultaneously holding public officials accountable.

The distinction, he implied, is between constructive criticism and a culture in which citizens remain focused entirely on what others have failed to do.

With Liberia’s next presidential and general elections still ahead, Brown’s intervention places renewed emphasis on the conduct of political actors before the campaign period intensifies. His message is that the competition for political power should not come at the expense of national peace.

He wants opposition parties to remain engaged, but responsible; critical, but constructive; and ambitious, but mindful of the consequences of political confrontation.

The 2029 elections will inevitably produce competing interests and competing visions for Liberia. But Brown believes the country should not have to pay the price for those differences. His broader appeal is for political leaders to learn from Liberia’s history rather than reproduce it.

For Brown, the most important political calculation is not simply who wins an election, but whether Liberia remains peaceful, united and capable of giving its citizens a better future.

World.title: PPP happy with Ndola-Mufulira road rehabilitation works
World.content:
Public-Private Partnership (PPP) Technical Committee Vice Chairperson, Richard Banda says the rehabilitation of Ndola-Mufulira road is progressing well.

Dr Banda said the project is among key infrastructure developments being implemented through the PPP framework to improve connectivity, facilitate trade and stimulate economic growth.

Speaking during a monitoring visit to the Ndola-Mufulira road project, Dr Banda said once completed, the highway will significantly reduce travel time between Ndola and Mufulira.

He said the 25-year concession provides for three years of construction, with the remaining section towards Mufulira expected to be completed within the agreed timeframe.

Dr Banda, who is also Ministry of Infrastructure, Housing and Urban Development Director of Planning, Monitoring and Research, said 17 kilometres of the road, stretching from the Ndola roundabout to the Sakania border, have so far been completed.

He said the project has also seen the construction and operationalisation of the Tom Mtine Toll Plaza and a one stop border post.

Dr Banda however, disclosed that the government identified sections of the road that developed defects after it was opened, prompting immediate remedial works.

“Entering into PPP has seen the rehabilitation of the Ndola-Mufulira road, which also includes the construction of a toll plaza and a modern Sakania border post. Once this road is fully completed, trade will be enhanced significantly,” Dr Banda said.

He further said the government is taking measures to ensure that the project meets the required quality standards by engaging an independent engineering firm tasked to ensure quality works are rolled out on the project.

“I can confirm that the government, together with the concessionaire, has engaged an independent engineering consultant to monitor the quality of works being undertaken on the project,” he said.

Dr Banda further said the Road Development Agency (RDA) will continue monitoring the road throughout the 25-year concession period to ensure that required standards are maintained.

Meanwhile, Jaswin Ports Limited, a concessionaire working on the road, explained that the entire Ndola-Sakania stretch has been completed, while the stretch from Sakania to Mufulira is scheduled for completion by June 2028.

Jaswin Ports Limited Project Manager, Deng Jianping said the construction of the new One Stop Border Post at Sakania has reached 70 percent completion.

He said the modern border facility is expected to improve the movement of goods and services between Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) once it is operational.

Mr Deng said the new Sakania border post will include a police post, clinic, fire-fighting section and other essential facilities designed to improve border operations.

Meanwhile, the Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) has lauded the construction of the state of the art Sakania border post.

ZRA Examining Officer, Rex Nketani, observed that once fully completed, the new facility will accelerate economic growth as revenue collection will improve significantly.

World.title: Government commits to upscale suicide prevention
World.content:
Government has reiterated its commitment to up scaling efforts aimed at preventing suicide incidents.

North-Western Province Permanent Secretary, Grandson Katambi, said government aims to provide improved health scale, top among the list is prevention and management of suicide cases.

Colonel Katambi stated that mental health issues should not only be discussed when there is a crisis, adding that systems must be strengthened for identification, support and prevention.

He said this at the commemoration of world Suicide Prevention day in Solwezi today.

He revealed that suicide still remains a concern, with the latest World Health Organisation’s latest estimates indicating that 1,397 people died by suicide in Zambia in 2021.

He noted that the figures call for concerted efforts to prevent the vice.

Meanwhile, North-western Province Health Director, Luckson Chidikita, said suicide is affecting not only communities but the health workers fraternity as well.

He said there is need for delivery decisions among stakeholders in dealing with suicide.

The World Suicide Prevention day also marked the launch of the 30 days of mental health awareness, which will culminate into the official mental health day commemoration on 10th October 2026.

World.title: ‎Chisi Mbewe appointed  U23 coach
World.content:
The Football Association of Zambia (FAZ) has appointed Chisi Mbewe as Zambia Under-23 Men’s National Team Head Coach ahead of the Egypt 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers.

‎

‎Announcing the appointment today, FAZ General Secretary Charles Chakatazya said Mbewe, who is also head coach of Super League side Red Arrows, will lead an all-local technical bench.

‎

‎“The appointments have been made after a rigorous exercise that saw FAZ pick some of the best local coaching talents,” Chakatazya said.

‎

‎Mbewe will be assisted by Numba Mumamba as First Assistant, George Chilufya as Second Assistant, and Kalililo Kakonje as Goalkeeper Coach.

‎

‎The rest of the bench includes 2012 Africa Cup of Nations winning vice-captain Chintu Kampamba as Physical Trainer, Mumba Mwila as Team Manager, Dr. Ndaba Sipuke as Team Doctor, Nimrod Musongwa as Physiotherapist, Luka Kaunda as Video Analyst, Nchimunya Mwila as Security Manager, and 2009 CHAN Golden Boot winner Given Singuluma as Equipment Manager.

‎

‎Chakatazya said Mbewe brings vast youth experience, having previously coached the U15 and U20 national teams.

‎

‎He was head coach of the U20 squad that qualified for the 2023 U20 AFCON in Egypt.

‎

‎“Mbewe has been part of the Zambian youth system for some time… and knows his way around the current generation of players,” Chakatazya said.

‎

‎“He will be assisted by an equally competent ensemble of local coaches that we have tasked to firstly qualify to the U23 AFCON and subsequently the Olympics in 2028.”

‎

‎Zambia has been handed a second-round tie against either Sierra Leone or Burkina Faso in the qualifiers for the 2027 U23 AFCON in Egypt.

‎

‎Mbewe’s charges will enter at the second round, with the first leg scheduled for 9 November 2026 and the return leg eight days later.

‎

‎The last time Zambia qualified for the U23 AFCON was in 2019 in Egypt under Beston Chambeshi, where the team exited in the first round.

‎

‎FAZ says the long-term target for the new bench is to qualify for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.

World.title: Kopala inter-company relay moves to Chingola
World.content:
Zambia Athletics President Maj Bernard Chola Bwalya has called for stronger corporate partnerships to drive health, wellness and athletics development as he officially launched the KCM Kopala Inter Company Relay 2026 at Nchanga Stadium.

The event, sponsored by Konkola Copper Mines (KCM) for the second consecutive year, is scheduled for Saturday, 17th October 2026 at Nchanga Stadium under the theme: “Celebrating Corporate Partnerships, Health & Wellness”.

MajBwalya thanked KCM for backing the relay, noting the company has gone further this year by combining it with KCM Sports Day and other activities.

“This demonstrates that KCM believes in the value of sport, health and wellness, corporate engagement and, importantly, the development of athletics in Zambia,” he said.

The Zambia Athletics boss said the federation is building on the foundation laid by Elias Mpondela and others, and is taking the relay to more towns.

After Kitwe last year, Chingola is hosting in 2026, with ambitions to take it to Choma, Kaputa and every province.

Bwalya said the relay is about more than running. It’s a platform for talent identification, employee wellness, networking and community engagement.

“Our vision goes beyond organising events. We want to identify talent wherever it exists and create a strong pool of athletes across our country… Talent is everywhere in Zambia. Our responsibility is to create platforms where that talent can be seen, identified and nurtured,” he said.

He added that events like this help Zambia Athletics discover young athletes and feed them into provincial, national and international structures.

The 2026 edition is expected to attract more than 50 companies, over 1,000 participants and thousands of spectators with a budget of approximately K850,000.

Bwalya called on more companies to come on board, saying the funds go toward *youth development, grassroots structures, athlete preparation and international competition*.

“To the corporate world, I say: come and partner with us. Come and run. Come and walk. Come and exhibit. Come and network. But most importantly, come and invest in the future of our young people and the future of athletics in Zambia,” he said.

World.title: EU Election Observation Mission donates equipment, materials
World.content:
The European Union Election Observation Mission (EOM) in Zambia, has donated equipment and material worth 4.9 million Kwacha to selected organisations which are involved in community work across the country.

Speaking during the handover ceremony, EU Ambassador to Zambia and COMESA, Karolina Stasiak said the donation of the equipment, which was used by the EOM, marks the mission’s closure, pending the release of a report.

Ms Stasiak noted that the Observation Mission represents the EU’s engagement aimed at strengthening the quality of the electoral process in Zambia.

She added that the exercise reflects a strong partnership between Zambia and the EU, built over many years and a shared interest in supporting credible, transparent and inclusive electoral processes.

She stated that as the Mission comes to a close, the expert team is preparing its final report, which will provide a full assessment of the entire electoral process and include recommendations to help improve future elections.

“These recommendations are part of the European Union’s continued commitment to strengthening democratic processes as well as government and oversight institutions,” Ms Stasiak explained.

Ms Stasiak has also acknowledged the recipients of the donation noting the important role they play in responding to communities and helping them stay informed.

Among the recipients of the donation are Healing Balm Foundation of Livingstone, Namusola Community School of Chongwe, Prisoners’ Future Foundation of Kabwe and Kitwe District Land Alliance of Kitwe.

Others include community radio stations supported through BBC Media Action, the Media Self-Regulation Council and Free Press Initiative in Lusaka, In & Out of the Ghetto, Zambia Open Community Schools, Undikumbukire Zambia, and St. Lawrence Home of Hope Foundation.

And speaking on behalf of the recipients, Healing Balm Foundation Executive Director, Sepiso Mushoke expressed gratitude to the EU for the equipment.

Ms Mushoke noted that the equipment will greatly help in reducing her organisation’s operational costs as funds meant for purchase of such equipment will be saved and channeled to other needs.

“These are not donations that usually come to our organisations especially us who are based in rural communities”, she explained.

World.title: Benin, World Bank Group congratulate President Hichilema
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has continued to receive messages of congratulations from international leaders and institutions following his re-election as President of the Republic of Zambia.

President of Benin, Romuald Wadagni, has congratulated Mr Hichilema on his re-election, underscoring the need to strengthen relations between Zambia and Benin.

Mr Wadagni said the two countries should give fresh impetus to bilateral relations and align their efforts towards economic transformation and continental integration.

He noted that enhanced cooperation between Zambia and Benin will contribute to the mutual benefit and prosperity of citizens in both countries.

“There is need to give fresh impetus to relations between Zambia and Benin and align our efforts towards economic transformation and continental integration,” Mr Wadagni said.

Meanwhile, the World Bank Group has also congratulated President Hichilema on his re-election.

The World Bank has reaffirmed its commitment to supporting the Zambian government’s development priorities through financing, knowledge sharing, technical assistance, private investment and capital mobilisation.

The Bank further said the support is aimed at helping Zambia accelerate sustainable and inclusive economic growth.

“We reaffirm our commitment to support the government’s priorities and help accelerate sustainable and inclusive growth for Zambia,” the World Bank said in a congratulatory message.

The messages of goodwill underscore continued international confidence in Zambia’s development agenda and the importance of strengthening partnerships to advance economic transformation and national development.

World.title: PIDG, IFDK invest US$11.5 million in Africa GreenCo
World.content:
Africa GreenCo has announced an additional US$11.5 million investment from its existing shareholders, the Private Infrastructure Development Group (PIDG) and the Impact Fund Denmark (IFDK), to support the growth of its renewable energy trading platform in Southern Africa.

The latest investment, delivered through PIDG’s project development solution, InfraCo, brings Africa GreenCo’s total third-close fundraising to US$21.5 million following a recent investment by Sanlam Alternative Investments.

Africa GreenCo is a regional energy trader and intermediary off-taker that supports renewable energy Independent Power Producers by providing bankable power purchase arrangements and payment security.

The company has been actively trading for less than five years after joining the Southern Africa Power Pool (SAPP) in 2021.

It is licensed to operate in Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia and South Africa, and has traded more than 1.4 Terawatt-hours of electricity so far this year.

Africa GreenCo said its model is aimed at strengthening energy security, reducing emissions and supporting regional power integration by facilitating the movement of clean energy across multiple markets.

Founder and Group Chief Financial Officer, Pug Bennet, said the additional investment demonstrates strong confidence from both new and existing shareholders in the company’s business model.

Mr Bennet explained that the increased financial strength, together with guarantee facilities provided by GuarantCo and the European Commission under its EFSD+ programme, will enable Africa GreenCo to further support the region’s energy transition.

Meanwhile, IFDK Managing Director and Co-Head of Green Energy and Infrastructure, Thomas Hougaard, said the institution is proud to have supported Africa GreenCo since its first capital raise.

Mr Hougaard said IFDK’s support in 2025 helped mobilise a 50-million-Euro guarantee facility, enabling the company to attract additional private capital and accelerate the energy transition in Southern Africa.

And PIDG Head of Business Development for Africa at InfraCo, Omar Jabri, observed that the latest investment will enhance Africa GreenCo’s capacity to scale its renewable energy model across the region.

Mr Jabri said the company’s work aligns with PIDG’s mandate of mobilising infrastructure finance to address climate change while promoting sustainable economic development.

Sanlam Alternative Investments Executive Head of Infrastructure Finance, Mark Moorhouse, said Africa GreenCo plays an important role in creating the market infrastructure required to deliver new power generation.

Mr Moorhouse revealed that Sanlam’s investment is consistent with its long-term commitment to infrastructure development and supporting Africa’s transition towards reliable and increasingly low-carbon energy.

Africa GreenCo further noted that the additional investment and guarantee support will strengthen its liquidity and risk-bearing capacity.

It added that this will enable it to support up to 900 megawatts of renewable energy power purchase agreements and provide the payment security which is needed to make renewable energy projects bankable.

The development comes at a time when demand for electricity across Africa continues to grow, increasing the need for energy projects capable of attracting private-sector investment while addressing climate change.

World.title: Suspected anthrax recorded in Muchinga Province
World.content:
The National Disaster Risk Management Division (DRMD) has alerted the public on suspected anthrax cases and environmental pollution reported in three districts of Muchinga Province.

The affected districts are Mpika, Lavushimanda and Shiwang’andu, where approximately 40 animals have reportedly died, while 11 people are suspected to have been affected.

DRMD Senior Communications Officer Mathews Musukwa told the media in a statement today that the government has since launched assessments to establish the extent of the suspected outbreak and contain the situation.

Mr Musukwa added that the assessments are being undertaken through Provincial and District Disaster Risk Management structures to protect communities and safeguard livelihoods.

He noted that the National Disaster Technical Committee of Permanent Secretaries also met on September 8, 2026, to review the reports and make recommendations.

Mr Musukwa has since strongly urged members of the public in the affected areas not to consume, sell, distribute or handle meat from animals that have died suddenly or are suspected to have died from anthrax.

“Members of the public are further strongly advised to stop handling wild animals until further notice, particularly in areas where animal deaths have been reported,” he said.

He has further cautioned the public against handling infected animals and carcasses as these can expose people to anthrax.

Mr Musukwa also advised the public to avoid getting in contact with blood, tissues and other materials from suspected infected animals and urged them to promptly report unusual or unexplained animal deaths to veterinary, health or disaster management authorities.

“Government, through the Disaster Risk Management Division and other appropriate Ministries, will continue to assess the situation and coordinate interventions with relevant stakeholders,” he added.

The DRMD Senior Communications Officer has further urged the public to remain calm, follow official health and veterinary guidance and avoid spreading unverified information as the government continues monitoring the situation.

World.title: Mozambique: Opposition Leader Venâncio Mondlane to be Tried for Treason
World.content:
Venâncio Mondlane has been charged with treason for his role in the demonstrations November 2024-March 2025 protesting the fraudulent elections of 9 October 2024. More than 350 demonstrators were killed by police, who have not been charged. More than 1000 demonstrators are improperly still being held in jail without trial.

Mondlane says he is accused of committing the crimes of publicly condoning a crime; publicly instigating a crime; inciting collective disobedience; instigating terrorism; and inciting terrorism. He is accused of committing these crimes during the post-election protests. (Carta de Moçambique 24 July)

Because Mondlane officially came second in the presidential elections, he is automatically a member of the Council of State, with immunity. The Council lifted his immunity on 10 June at a meeting Mondlane did not attend, but this was kept secret until 25 August. But because of his membership of the Council of State, he will be tried by five members of the Supreme Court.

By law, Mozambican justice is politicised. The president and vice-president of the Supreme Court (Tribunal Supremo, TS) are named by President of Mozambique and the 11 judges are nominated by parties in parliament in proportion to their seats (subject to qualifications criteria), which gives Frelimo overwhelming control of he Supreme Court and the judicial system.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Savana (4 September) gave detailed profiles of the five judges in the Venâncio Mondlane case. (Two judges are also named Mondlane, a common name in southern Mozambique.) Luís Mondlane and António Paulo Namburete are the two leading judges for the trial. Luís Mondlane earlier was named president of the Constitutional Council (CC) by President Armando Guebuza, but resigned in 2011 when he was accused of misusing $400,000 for personal expenses, and returned his previous post on the TS.

Namburete was named Attorney General by President Joaquim Chissano in 1998. Chissano dismissed Namburete and six of his deputies in 2000 after they were accused of not investigating the $14mn thefts from Banco Commercial de Moçambique (BCM). (Moçambique recolonizado através da corrupção, pp 162-3). Investigative Journalist Carlos Cardoso was assassinated in November 2000 while he was investigating the BCM case and the seeming protection of the culprits. In 2012 Namburete was made a member of TS.

Isabel Rupia was named a Deputy Attorney General by Chissano in 2000 as part of replacing the dismissed group, and concentrated on corruption. But she was dismissed in 2005 by Attorney General Joaquim Madeira; Savana says she has been investigating high figures in the nomenklatura and in Frelimo. In 2009 she was proposed by Renamo for the CC, but this was blocked by Frelimo. She was named to the TS in 2024.

João Beirão was a member of the National Elections Commission 2013-5. He was named vice president of the TS in 2015 by President Filipe Nyusi and after 10 years stepped down to be an ordinary TS judge.

Carlos Mondlane was a member of the Standing Committee of the Superior Council of the Judiciary 2019–2024, and was named to the TS in 2025. Savana says that Isable Rupia and Carlos Mondlane are considered ‘the most level-headed judges in this group’.

But the real issue of this trial will be Frelimo using the law for overtly political processes, against people of whom it is frightened. In the case of Venâncio Mondlane, he was first prevented from standing for parliament when the his party Democratic Alliance Coalition (CAD) had its registration revoked after it was too late to stand for another party. He could stand for President because under the constitution all presidential candidates stand as individuals. That election was so corrupt that no one knows who really won, but Mondlane was officially second. He is clearly the most important opposition figure, but he was then banned from participating in the ongoing ‘National Dialogue’ because it was restricted to parties having seats in national or provincial parliaments. The move to try him for treason is seen as an attempt to prevent him standing in the next elections, by jailing him or forcing him to flee from Mozambique. But many civil society leaders argue that organising legal protests against manifestly corrupt elections cannot be seen as treason.

Close 

The prosecution will use videos of his speeches and social media broadcasts to try to show that in promoting demonstrations he was ‘inciting collective disobedience’ and violence. The defence will be that his political statements and the civic protests were legitimate and within constitutional rights, and that he repeatedly opposed violence in his broadcasts. (Evidências 8 Sep)

It has already been decided that the trial will be in a small room without space for many press and public, according to Raul Sende and Cleto Duarte of Savana. Civil Society is pressing for the trial to be broadcast on TV, and the decision is up to the two trial leaders, Luís Mondlane and Namburete.

World.title: South Africa: Six South Africans Remain Unaccounted for After Nepal Flash Floods
World.content:
Six South African nationals remain unaccounted for, following the devastating flash floods in Nepal, the Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO) confirmed on Thursday.

DIRCO said it had, following a formal request from the Nepalese government, arranged with the South African Police Service (SAPS) for the collection and coordination of DNA profiles from biological relatives of the missing South Africans.

The profiles were collected through the Victim Identification Centre under the SAPS Division: Detectives and Forensic Services and have been sent to police in Nepal and Interpol in Kathmandu.

South African diplomatic missions in New Delhi, India, as well in Beijing, China, are also liaising with their respective host countries to coordinate the response to the disaster.

"Regrettably, there is still no confirmation from the authorities in Nepal or China/Tibet regarding any of the six South African nationals. We will continue to monitor the situation closely and provide updates to the families as more information becomes available," DIRCO said.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Will Monitoring of Eastern DR Congo's 'Ceasefire' Improve Compliance?
World.content:
analysis

The first deployment of the monitoring mechanism is positive, but current conflict conditions should temper expectations.

The first mission to verify the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) ceasefire agreed in November 2025 began its work in South Kivu on 24 August. But can facts be established in a fragmented and polarised context? And can the mission's findings change how warring parties assess the costs, risks and benefits of continued fighting?

The Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+) was activated following August talks in Switzerland between the DRC government and Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC)/M23. Qatar, the United States (US) and African Union (AU) helped mediate.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Established through the Doha negotiations between the DRC and AFC/M23, the EJVM+ reports to the Ceasefire Oversight and Verification Mechanism, which supervises implementation and aims to create conditions for de-escalation and dialogue.

Kickstarting the EJVM+ is one of the most tangible signs of progress under the Doha framework, providing a way to verify alleged ceasefire violations by the DRC government and AFC/M23.

However current conflict conditions should temper expectations. Both the government and AFC/M23 continue to contest territory through drone strikes, recruitment and alliances with other armed groups. Belligerents often use ceasefires to reposition or rearm forces, establish new 'facts' on the ground and consolidate territorial control.

The ceasefire also fails to separate forces and reduce the risk of renewed fighting, which could have been done by providing clear ceasefire lines, force withdrawals, cantonments and buffer zones.

Choosing South Kivu's Minembwe for EJVM+'s first verification mission is significant as the area embodies many of the complexities that make ceasefire monitoring in eastern DRC difficult.

First is worsening violence. Following M23's withdrawal from Uvira, the DRC government launched an offensive towards Minembwe in early 2026, trapping citizens, restricting humanitarian access and the movement of goods. In early July, rebels consolidated control in the highlands, where fighting continues.

Second, the conflict does not involve only the government and AFC/M23. In Minembwe, the armed movement of the Banyamulenge - a Congolese Tutsi community whose citizenship and security have been contested - has aligned with AFC/M23, while the Congolese army collaborates with fragmented Wazalendo groups.

Heightened tensions between Burundi and Rwanda also make ceasefire monitoring difficult. With Burundian troops deployed to back Kinshasa, and Rwanda supporting AFC/M23, the war risks escalating longstanding rivalries and fuelling proxy conflicts, including through increased Rwandan support for Burundian armed groups.

A central EJVM+ weakness is that its scope is limited to a two-party ceasefire in a conflict involving regional actors and multiple armed groups that rarely consider themselves bound by such a ceasefire.

Fragmentation of diplomatic efforts is another complicating factor. Alongside the Doha process, the US is mediating between the DRC government and Rwanda. As the implementation of that peace agreement stalls, Rwanda's military involvement in eastern DRC, along with the Forces Démocratiques de Libération du Rwanda (FDLR), has continued.

Developments arising from these parallel tracks are beyond the EJVM+'s remit. Rebel withdrawals from Uvira and the Ruzizi Plain in January and May resulted from US diplomatic pressure rather than the Doha negotiations and lacked neutral verification.

Although it has been suggested that the EJVM+ mandate be extended to the Washington Accords, the ceasefire excludes the withdrawal of Rwandan forces and the disarmament of the FDLR. That means the EJVM+ cannot verify those commitments and lacks direct links to the mechanisms overseeing the DRC-Rwanda agreement.

This reflects a broader problem: fragmented peace initiatives have produced overlapping monitoring and verification mandates tied to partial ceasefire arrangements lacking clear political objectives.

The EJVM+ also faces operational constraints. Investigating violations across an extensive and difficult conflict zone strains its limited funding, personnel and logistics. The downsizing of the United Nations Organisation Stabilisation Mission in the DRC (MONUSCO) compounds the problem. Since its 2024 withdrawal from South Kivu, MONUSCO has no civilian protection mandate or capacity to respond to human rights abuses there.

Another challenge for EJVM+ is the specialised expertise needed to investigate drone strikes that can reach beyond front lines. Recent attacks have been attributed to both AFC/M23 and the DRC army. Sophisticated equipment capable of causing GPS interference further complicates monitoring and verification.

Access is another constraint. AFC/M23's parallel administration and the many armed groups in North and South Kivu could limit EJVM+'s movement. An overreliance on armed groups' consent could undermine its neutrality and deter people from engaging with the mechanism freely. This is particularly concerning because the ceasefire arrangement does not explicitly cover violence against civilians.

Still, the EJVM+ remains unique. It is the only recognised ceasefire mechanism and is supported by the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) and MONUSCO. It can help establish facts, reduce competing narratives and build confidence in the Doha process.

But the EJVM+ needs financial support and specialised training to investigate and document violations. In the longer term, sustainable funding from ICGLR member states can reduce the mechanisms' dependence on external support and maintain regional ownership. To protect EJVM+'s neutrality, external actors supporting the peace process, including Qatar, the US, AU, ICGLR and UN, must counterbalance the mechanism's reliance on warring parties' consent.

Close 

Strong guarantees of freedom of movement and security are needed for MONUSCO and EJVM+ personnel. Clear procedures are also required when third-party actors supporting the ceasefire want to initiate a verification mission. Steps to address non-compliance are also vital. Verified violations must generate political follow-up, sustained external engagement and accountability that can influence the actions of the DRC government and AFC/M23.

The EJVM+ would also benefit from a more robust ceasefire arrangement that accounts for actors outside the Doha process, and has provisions for humanitarian access and peacekeeping.

Ultimately, eastern DRC needs a peace process that incentivises honouring a ceasefire, not just a record of who broke it.

Bram Verelst, Senior Researcher, Conflict Prevention, Management and Peacebuilding in the Great Lakes Region, ISS

Nicodemus Minde, Researcher and adjunct faculty member at United States International University - Africa, Nairobi

World.title: Texas A&M's Mike Elko describes fight between LSU, SEC over former NFL players as 'parenting'
World.content:
The SEC, no stranger to attention, is once again the center of the college football world. Though not necessarily due to a dominant dynasty racking up championship after championship.

Lane Kiffin, also no stranger to attention, immediately invited controversy after taking over as head coach of the LSU Tigers by working to bring in former college players who have signed contracts to play in the NFL. The SEC and Big Ten immediately moved to ban pro players from playing, leading to a series of court battles to settle the issue.

While LSU ultimately prevailed, with a judge granting an injunction to let two players, Dae’quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, play this season, the SEC and other teams signaled their intention to fight back. Hard.

LSU LEAVES FORMER PRO-ATHLETES OFF FINAL ROSTER, ONE NIGHT BEFORE SEC TAKES LANE KIFFIN AND TIGERS TO COURT

The conference cited Kiffin’s flippant, sarcastic comment before halftime during the game against Clemson in a new amended complaint: "Imagine if we had pro players."

It was then widely reported that the conference’s other 15 schools would vote to kick the Tigers out at a meeting scheduled for Sept. 10.

A brief war of words ensued, resulting in the Tigers seemingly backing down by adding two non-pro players to the roster and filling out their final two spots.

Some commentators, like Stephen A. Smith, have defended LSU’s actions, while many opposing coaches have expressed a mixture of skepticism, bewilderment or anger over how Kiffin and the Tigers’ administration handled the situation.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

One of Kiffin’s rival SEC coaches, Texas A&M’s Mike Elko, just added to it Thursday with a colorful explanation of the dynamic between the two opposing sides.

"This is a little bit like the son figuring out where the limits are until dad comes home and raises his voice, and then the son goes, ‘I was just kidding, I didn’t mean any of that,'" Elko said. "I think that’s what you’re seeing. LSU will be in the SEC…This is just a little bit of parenting going on right now."

Mike Elko, never one to shy away from a great quote.

There’s some truth to that, and it’s evidenced not just by how the administration and Kiffin have handled this situation, but how the governor of Louisiana handled it too. After seemingly backing the Tigers, Gov. Jeff Landry issued a statement to Yahoo Sports! regarding the potential vote which said simply, "Ridiculous. Can we just play football?"

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Well, that’s part of the problem, isn’t it? Kiffin’s search for any advantage, no matter how minute, led the Tigers to push the boundaries of what other teams and, ultimately, fans find acceptable. For weeks, LSU backers proudly insisted they were right about bringing NFL players back to college football. As soon as the stakes were raised — for example, with the possibility of expulsion from the conference — the message became, "Can we just play football?"

The turn of phrase Elko used might be colorful, but it’s right. LSU was the upstart teenager, who got his bluff called by dad. Dad won out, and now the tone of the conversation has changed.

LSU and Texas A&M play on Sept. 26 in Baton Rouge, without any NFL players on the field. There will be, however, a must-see postgame handshake between these two coaches.

World.title: Dolly Parton’s sister reveals ‘last thing’ country legend asked of her before death
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Dolly Parton's sister is sharing the final request she received from the musician.

During a recent interview with "CBS Mornings," Stella Parton shared the last thing her sister asked of her before her death.

"That’s the last thing Dolly asked me for, was prayer," she recalled.

The legendary musician died Aug. 25 at the age of 80 after a "brief battle with cancer," which she hid from her fans and even some family members.

DOLLY PARTON OFFERED TO TRY EXPERIMENTAL DRUGS IF ‘NO HOPE’ FOR CANCER BATTLE TO HELP OTHERS, SISTER SAYS

Stella noted that the family would not be sharing what type of cancer Dolly had "out of respect for her" since Dolly "didn't tell us that we could say it." She added that she is able to speak about her love for her sister, but when it comes to her health, "it's not my business to tell her business."

Concerns over the "Jolene" singer's health first arose in September 2025, when she made the difficult decision to postpone a number of shows in Las Vegas, telling fans she needed to undergo a "few procedures."

"I want the fans and public to hear directly from me that, unfortunately, I will need to postpone my upcoming Las Vegas concerts," Parton shared online at the time. "As many of you know, I have been dealing with some health challenges, and my doctors tell me that I must have a few procedures."

Shortly after Dolly made her announcement, concern among fans increased when her sister Freida asked fans to pray for Dolly, saying, "Many of you know she hasn’t been feeling her best lately."

When speaking with "CBS Mornings," Stella noted, "I think Dolly got on to Freida about that.

DOLLY PARTON’S ONGOING HEALTH BATTLE FORCES COUNTRY LEGEND TO MISS MAJOR DOLLYWOOD EVENT

"I'm pretty sure Dolly said, 'You're going to, you know, pipe it down,' because that was the first time people thought 'Oh,'" she said. "And she knew that Freida was just upset and hurt, but she thought, 'Don't be telling my situation, Freida. Don't be spilling my business.'"

According to Stella, Dolly decided to keep her diagnosis a secret because she "could not bear negative things" and didn't want her fans to worry about her.

Her death came a little over a year after the death of her husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Dean, who died in March 2025 at the age of 82. While some have speculated Dolly died of a broken heart, Stella doesn't agree.

"I think she was very sad, but I don't think that's why she got sick," Stella said. "I think she worked too hard and didn't maybe take as good a care of herself as she should have. She, at one point, she said, 'You know, I spent a lot of time caring for Carl that maybe I neglected myself.'"

DOLLY PARTON LAID TO REST AS NIECE SHARES EMOTIONAL TRIBUTE TO ‘GRANNY’

She went on to say that while it "broke her heart to see him in the shape he" was in before he died, she ultimately believes Dolly's determination to continue working "so hard for so long" contributed to her death.

When speaking about Dolly's relationship with Dean, she referred to it as "very unique and very deep and loyal" and gave Dean credit for being supportive of Dolly and loving "her enough to let her be what she was."

Stella explained that while Dolly was a huge star across the globe, Dean "didn't care about that at all," and if it was up to him, she would have been "at the house with her hair up in a ponytail and barefooted cooking in the kitchen." Stella said even family members rarely saw Dolly without her signature glamorous look after she became a star.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Not after she got to be Dolly Parton. No. She would sleep in her makeup when she'd come spend the night with me," Stella said. "Oh, I knew what she looked like. She looked like me without her makeup. So, I knew what she looked like without it."

Her sister also credited Dolly for being a good businesswoman, saying that while she had opinions on politics and other controversial topics, she never shared them because "she would never have offended anyone."

Although Dolly was battling cancer, Stella says she knows her sister was at peace in her final moments.

"She knew where she was going," she said. "She wasn't going anywhere bad. She was going to be with mom and daddy. She was prepared. Yeah, she was definitely prepared."

When it comes to how she hopes her sister is remembered, Stella said she wants people to think of her as "very sweet, kind, loving, brilliant and so talented."

"Her creativity had no bounds, and she could dream bigger than anybody," Stella said. "And I want young people, young girls and boys that may think they have no opportunity to dream. Coming from our situation, she gave us permission to dream that way."
