World.title: Nike shareholders reject transparency proposal as faith-based firm questions DEI commitments
World.content:
Tim Schwarzenberger’s last pair of Nike sneakers is about 10 years old and the shoes have holes in them.

But the Christian investor who helped lead a shareholder campaign demanding more transparency from Nike says he wants a reason to buy another pair.

"For me, what resonates is forgiveness," Schwarzenberger told OutKick. "If companies make changes, we need to applaud them."

NIKE FORGOT THAT REPUBLICANS BUY SNEAKERS, TOO, AND NOW IT'S GETTING BOOTED FROM THE S&P 100

"I would like to get back to buying the shoes, but I can’t rationalize doing that when Nike has become so activist," he said. "If the company can change, I would be the first to applaud them and get in line."

Schwarzenberger is a portfolio manager and director of corporate engagement at Inspire Investing, a faith-based firm that represents investors who own Nike stock. Those investors make money if Nike succeeds, not if it collapses.

"We’re long-term investors," he said. "Our primary goal is to earn competitive performance for the investors we serve, and we want companies to do well."

Nike shareholders rejected Proposal 5 during the company’s annual meeting Sept. 8. Inspire backed the proposal on behalf of client William C. Cunningham.

The resolution asked Nike to evaluate and issue a report analyzing the "benefits, costs, and legal, reputational, competitive, and other relevant risks" associated with its charitable support.

The proposal’s supporting statement specifically cited Nike’s verified score of 100 on the Human Rights Campaign’s Corporate Equality Index. Inspire argued that the score raises questions about whether Nike’s employee health plan covers gender-transition procedures for minors, including surgery, cross-sex hormone therapy, menstruation suppression and puberty blockers.

Schwarzenberger said Nike has not publicly answered whether it provides those benefits to minor dependents.

HRC's 2026 criteria require transgender-inclusive health benefits for full credit, but Nike's public HRC profile does not disclose the company's age limits or dependent-specific plan terms.

The proposal also pointed to Nike’s broader DEI initiatives and argued that its charitable relationships with advocacy organizations could create legal, reputational and financial risks.

Nike’s board recommended that shareholders reject the proposal, arguing in its 2026 proxy statement that the company already evaluates those risks.

"The company’s current approach to charitable giving, together with our existing disclosures and guidelines, appropriately serves the best interests of our shareholders," Nike stated.

The company also said creating another report would consume time and resources without providing additional value to investors.

Detailed vote totals were not yet available when OutKick interviewed Schwarzenberger. Nike disclosed the results in a September 10 SEC filing, showing the proposal received less than 1% of votes cast for or against it.

"Most shareholder proposals do not receive majority support, so that was not a surprise," Schwarzenberger said. "But we were able to make the case to shareholders and raise issues that I think are on the minds of many shareholders."

Inspire questions Nike’s ‘robust’ review

Nike said charitable partnerships are approved only after what it described as a "robust due diligence review."

"Any time I hear the word robust, it kind of scares me," Schwarzenberger said. "Are they actually concerned about the end investor?"

Proposal 5 focused heavily on Nike’s relationship with the Human Rights Campaign and its Corporate Equality Index, which evaluates companies on their LGBTQ workplace policies and practices.

Nike received a verified score of 100 on the 2026 Corporate Equality Index. The Human Rights Campaign recognizes companies receiving that score as leaders in LGBTQ workplace inclusion.

Schwarzenberger said the score means Nike is complying with what Inspire considers an increasingly left-wing set of corporate requirements.

"They’re doing all the things that the Human Rights Campaign has asked for," he said. "It’s really been like a moving treadmill where they’ve upped the ante every single version. The goalposts are always switching."

Participation in the survey declined sharply this year. According to HRC’s own report, the number of Fortune 500 companies submitting information fell 65%, from 377 companies in 2025 to 131 in 2026.

HRC said the decrease in public reporting does not necessarily mean the companies changed their underlying workplace policies.

Nike remained a participant.

Schwarzenberger argued that Nike’s continued participation in HRC’s Corporate Equality Index raises questions about whether the company has adequately considered the legal, reputational and financial risks of its partnerships.

"Our ask is simply to provide transparency into what Nike is doing," he said. "If the company has analyzed the risk of these organizations, then let us see it."

Nike’s problems go beyond politics

"Nike is set to be removed from the S&P 100 before trading begins Sept. 21, after nearly 18 years in the blue-chip index.

S&P Dow Jones Indices said the rebalance is intended to make its indexes more representative of their market-cap ranges.

The company’s market cap has fallen by more than $200 billion since its November 2021 peak. Nike has also lost ground to newer competitors and faced product challenges, while Greater China revenue fell 13% on a currency-neutral basis in fiscal 2026.

TED CRUZ TAKES VICTORY LAP AS ICONIC AMERICAN BRAND'S STOCK PLUNGES TO 12-YEAR LOW

Schwarzenberger acknowledged that Nike’s political decisions cannot be blamed for all of that.

"It is hard to dissect exactly what is causing the share-price decline," he said. "There are many factors, including China and perhaps some missteps with the company’s approach there and with various campaigns."

Still, he believes Nike has made its recovery more difficult by taking positions that anger some potential customers.

"At the very least, don’t do things that are going to upset your customers further," Schwarzenberger said. "If you are alienating half of your customer base, it is difficult to quantify exactly what percentage of the share-price decline is caused by those activities. But it is certainly a distraction."

OutKick has previously detailed Nike’s history with Colin Kaepernick, the canceled Betsy Ross sneaker, Dylan Mulvaney and a proposed study involving transgender youth athletes.

Schwarzenberger said Nike does not need to move toward conservative politics to correct course.

It just needs to stop making politics part of the product at all.

"The company does not need to take sides," he said. "It does not need to go right or left. It needs to stay in the middle, focus on its business and acknowledge its mistakes."

Schwarzenberger said Nike CEO Elliott Hill’s comments about refocusing on athletes were encouraging, but not strong enough to convince him that the company was committed to changing course.

"The CEO’s statement at the annual shareholders meeting about focusing on the athlete was good, but it was kind of a lukewarm response," he said. "They really need to take a very strong approach and say, ‘Look, we’re going to focus on manufacturing athletic apparel, and that’s going to be our focus. We’re not going to wade into hot-button political issues.’"

He also wants Nike to produce better products.

"If Nike does that and begins showing innovation in its products, that would be progress," he said. "Nike should get back to focusing on its core business and show that it is not an advocacy organization. It is an apparel company."

Schwarzenberger compared Nike’s lack of product innovation to Disney’s reliance on brands from the 1990s.

"It’s kind of like Disney. When’s the last time you’ve seen a good Disney movie?" he said. "We’d like to see some innovation."

How conservative investors can pressure companies

Schwarzenberger said Inspire filed dozens of shareholder resolutions last year, and roughly two-thirds of the targeted companies made the changes the firm requested.

"The point I would make to conservative investors is that you have a voice," Schwarzenberger said. "For far too long, we have delegated that voice to others who are doing things completely contrary to our values."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

That leverage is not limited to professional investors. Millions of Americans own shares in major companies indirectly through mutual funds held in their 401(k) accounts. Fund managers generally determine how those shares are voted in corporate elections.

Schwarzenberger said workers can review how their fund managers vote and ask their employers or plan administrators to offer additional investment options.

"You have a tremendous voice and a responsibility," he said. "If we show up and start pressuring these companies to get back to business, I think we can see even more success than we have seen so far."

World.title: Fatwas, holy wars and socialism: Inside the Islamic conference where El-Sayed drew a hero’s welcome
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

DETROIT, Mich. — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed headlined an Islamic conference over Labor Day weekend where the United States was described as an empire in decline, early Islamic conquests were praised and the aftermath of 9/11 was framed around Islamophobia and discrimination.

The event, held annually by the Islamic Society of North America, featured a range of speakers discussing topics from Muslim civic participation to the ongoing conflict between Israel and Hamas.

Over the course of the conference’s speeches and panel discussions, participants took positions that were generally critical of the United States and the broader Western world and expressed opinions that some may regard as extreme.

EXILED MUSLIM SCHOLAR WARNS FAR-LEFT–ISLAMIST ALLIANCE BEHIND ANTI-ISRAEL PROTESTS ECHOES IRAN’S RISE

Fox News Digital attended the event over the weekend, sitting in on many of the panels held on Saturday and Sunday before and after El-Sayed's speech. The Michigan Democrat is running in one of the most hotly contested Senate races of the 2026 cycle, the outcome of which may decide control of the Senate.

At one panel, "Rising Islamophobia in the U.S.," a speaker described recently passed legislation that could bar colleges participating in certain commercial boycotts of Israel from receiving some federal higher education funds as "an anti-Muslim bill."

Shortly after that, a man in the audience wearing a Pakistani flag pin stood up and called for a fatwa to be issued against the bipartisan group of lawmakers who voted for the bill. A fatwa is a religious ruling or opinion that can range from a formal condemnation to, in some cases, a call for or justification of violence.

The legislation was introduced by Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., and co-sponsored by Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J.

After the man called for a fatwa against members of Congress, members of the audience — and one panelist — applauded.

Earlier, during the same discussion, a panelist criticized Congress for moving to censure Reps. Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib for making "​​the most lighthearted comments"

Tlaib was censured in part for endorsing the phrase "from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free," which calls for the destruction of Israel as bounded by the Jordan River in the east and the Mediterranean Sea in the west. Critics characterized the phrase as a call for ethnic cleansing, while the congresswoman defended it as "an aspirational call for freedom, human rights and peaceful coexistence."

ISNA is a nonprofit Muslim religious organization established in 1981 to provide America's growing Muslim population with a platform for civic coordination and education. Detroit, where the event took place, is situated in a metropolitan area that has a significant Arab American population concentrated in areas such as Dearborn and Hamtramck.

EL-SAYED CAMPAIGN BACKED BY OVER $100,000 FROM DOZENS OF MEMBERS OF GROUP WITH ALLEGED TERROR TIES

Panelists also accused billionaire Elon Musk of funding a White supremacist global anti-Muslim movement, suggested that some of the narrative regarding 9/11 taught in American schools has been "debunked" and asserted that Muslims were treated unfairly in the wake of the 2001 attacks.

Criticism of America’s response to 9/11 surfaced repeatedly across the conference’s events and breakout sessions. One speaker asserted that one of the most important things to reflect on as the 25th anniversary of 9/11 approaches is that "Islamophobia is at an all-time high." Another called the War on Terror, a series of post-9/11 military operations that claimed the lives of over 7,000 U.S. military personnel, the "War of Terror."

El-Sayed has sought to moderate his public image since launching his Senate campaign, even as he has maintained ties to prominent socialists and socialist-aligned activists. His attendance at the recent ISNA conference is the latest in a series of associations that have drawn criticism, including ties to Nation of Islam figures, Muslim clerics accused of expressing support for terrorist organizations and activists on the socialist left.

In response to these charges, the Democrat has pointed out that GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers has links to individuals who echo conspiracy theories about the 2020 election or who have called for bans on gay marriage.

EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS

Before the event, El-Sayed’s campaign moved to distance the candidate from other conference speakers.

"Abdul is not affiliated with and does not endorse any other participant of the conference," a spokeswoman for his campaign told media outlets in the lead-up to the event.

The statement followed reports that he would appear alongside Islamic clerics who defended child marriage and praised U.S.-designated terrorist organizations, including al Qaeda. Of the controversial speakers, only the cleric who had defended child marriage was ultimately disinvited, The Washington Free Beacon previously reported.

ISNA appeared to anticipate scrutiny over some of the speakers it invited to the conference. In the conference venue’s main hallway, the organization posted a prominent sign which says, "ISNA does not endorse the actions of convention participants and explicitly disclaims any responsibility for the views expressed, information provided, or materials displayed, sold or distributed by convention speakers, performers, exhibitors, vendors, or attendees."

COUNTERTERRORISM EXPERT WARNS ABDUL EL-SAYED SENATE BID RAISES HOMELAND SECURITY CONCERNS

While ISNA sought to distance itself from the controversial views expressed by some conference speakers, the organization itself took actions that also drew scrutiny.

Fox News Digital spoke to three Christian evangelists outside the conference who claimed they were removed from it without warning. Each of them said they were simply having conversations with individuals who wanted to speak with them before they were escorted outside by security.

Attendance at the conference was open to people of all faiths, and registration did not require attendees to be Muslim. The conference also held an interfaith banquet on Sunday.

The disclaimer took on added significance in light of books available for purchase at the conference’s on-site bazaar. Fox News Digital found books that defended Islamic warfare while portraying Christianity as uniquely violent.

"Christians are the last people on earth who should bring the charge of bloodshed and cruelty against followers of any other system, for it is a well-established fact that no religion known to history has such a horrible sanguinary record as church Christianity," one book sold at the conference reads.

Another book argued that all Islamic warfare is defensive, defended non-Muslims being forced to pay a discriminatory tax and claimed that Christian civilization has killed nearly 200 million people by attributing wars that did not have religious motivations or were not initiated by Christians.

The French Revolution, which was instigated by individuals hostile to Christianity, for instance, is counted toward Christianity’s death count. The Korean War, which was launched by communist North Korea, is also counted toward the body count of Christianity.

UNEARTHED INTERVIEW REVEALS EL-SAYED’S SHARIA ‘OBLIGATION’: ‘NOT BECAUSE OF FEAR’

The conference also featured s for "Sharia-compliant" mortgages and other financial products.

El-Sayed held a quasi-celebrity status among the conference’s attendees. Campaign buttons were nearly ubiquitous at the conference, and his campaign’s booth was easily the busiest of those located in the main hall, Fox News Digital found.

When the Senate hopeful walked on stage to address the conference, he was greeted with a thunderous standing ovation. Calls of "we love you" rang out from the crowd.

El-Sayed’s speech was ultimately measured and largely focused on unity, representation and the idea that Muslim and American identities are compatible.

"As we leave here tonight, I’ve got a challenge for each and every one of you," El-Sayed said with a measured cadence reminiscent of former President Barack Obama.

"It’s the question of how you show up in the spaces in which you show up everyday, as wholly and 100% yourself. Because we are a community as Muslim Americans who believe in the rhyming of our Muslim ideals and our American ideals. That those two things are not mutually exclusive, in fact, that at their best being Muslim makes us better Americans and being Muslim enables us to be better Americans."

‘DESTROYING THE AMERICAN WAY OF LIFE’: EL-SAYED’S POLITICAL ORBIT COMPLICATES EFFORT TO MODERATE HIS IMAGE

But elsewhere at the conference, speakers offered a markedly different assessment of America and its place in the world.

"The world has become multipolar, and we see almost like the fear and insecurity that the empire has at this moment if we think through the lens of the U.S. So, I like to think that we are on the very end of an ending empire," an academic speaking at a session about the conflict between Israel and Hamas said. "I'm very positive about it."

The same panelist later argued that referring to the river next to Detroit as the "Detroit River" was an immoral act of colonialism because Native Americans had a different name for the waterway.

In a similar vein, a speaker at one of the conference’s main sessions criticized American foreign policy after the 9/11 terrorist attacks, then credited the "TikTok generation" with mobilizing in favor of Palestinians following the Oct. 7 terrorist attacks.

Some speakers, however, made a clear effort to connect El-Sayed’s socialist project with his Islamic faith.

"Islam historically was not just spread by the instance of Dawah. It was spread by socialism," said a cleric who would go on to speak positively about early Islamic conquests.

ISNA declined comment. The El-Sayed campaign did not respond to requests for comment after being reached by Fox News Digital Wednesday.

World.title: Suzy Kolber opens up about ESPN firing, emotional reaction: 'I lost it'
World.content:
Suzy Kolber was part of a 20-talent layoff at ESPN in June 2023, along with Steve Young, Max Kellerman and Jalen Rose. At the time, Kolber hosted the network’s "Monday Night Countdown" pregame show.

Kolber spoke about her firing for the first time during a conversation on the "Sports Media with Richard Deitsch" podcast this week.

"He [ESPN president Jimmy Pitaro] said, ‘Suzy there’s a whiteboard and your name’s on it. I don’t really know for sure right now but your name is on it,'" she said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

It’s unclear how the head of the company didn’t know whether Kolber was safe. Nonetheless, she recalled coming home that night and having a conversation with her daughter.

"I remember that day sitting next to my daughter in the kitchen. For years I’ve said ‘You never know.’ And I sat down next to her and I cried. And I said, ‘I think this is really happening.’"

The following week, Kolber received a call from then-ESPN executive Norby Williamson, best known as a supporter of Mark Jones.

Kolber said she "lost it" when Williamson told her she couldn’t say "anything disparaging about the company or we can take the last year of your contract."

Before her layoff, Kolber had agreed to take a pay cut.

"I did think the 39% cut was going to get me to the end [of my career]," she said.

Perhaps Kolber should have remained silent about her firing. She didn’t help herself with these comments.

For one, she comes off as entitled. We understand that a layoff can be emotional, regardless of the circumstances. However, a non-disparagement provision is standard. Kolber is no different from any other talent laid off with time remaining on their contract.

There was hardly a reason to "lose it," as she put it, over the clause.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Kolber also worked at ESPN for 27 years. She is now 62. She hosted the network’s top pregame show. ESPN didn’t owe her anything else. And yet, she suggested that she was unhappy with the lack of appreciation she received during her departure.

"I just thought after 27 years of, I was the first person hired for the launch of ESPN 2. I was the first person assigned to the X Games," she continued. "I went and shot the marketing tape for it. ‘Monday Night Football’s’ move to ESPN, I was part of some pretty big franchises. You’re not going to say a word? Not thanks for 27 years, just acknowledge it? I didn’t understand that."

At least her bosses didn’t fire her on-air, mid-show, as they did Ryan Clark in an apparent attempt to spite OutKick.

Our understanding is that Kolber’s firing was about the numbers. The network needed to shed a certain amount of talent salary, and she became expendable because ESPN employed other anchors who could fill her role. ESPN eventually tapped Scott Van Pelt to replace Kolber on "Countdown."

ESPN likely would have made a change at the position regardless, with its first-ever Super Bowl broadcast coming this fall. The anchor of "Monday Night Countdown" will also host the Super Bowl and its halftime show.

As one of the faces of the network, Van Pelt was a favorite for the position before 2023.

The network arguably has more NFL hosts than it has major sports. Van Pelt hosts Mondays. Mike Greenberg hosts the Sunday morning pregame show. Laura Rutledge, the host of "NFL Live," would be the lead football anchor at most networks and arguably should be at ESPN.

Therefore, Kolber became the odd person out.

Still, Kolber was a good host. Her talent and production were not the issues. In fact, since executive Burke Magnus is in the business of rehiring previous anchors, he should have brought her back.

Instead — in what appears to be a make-good for firing Ryan Clark — Magnus rehired Stan Verrett, who has a weird obsession with OutKick and race talk, to anchor a show on NFL Network.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Kolber has since shifted her focus, creating a new interview series called "The Originals" on the Scripps Sports Network. Her first episode airs Sept. 15 at 8 p.m.

Several performers have pulled out of an international festival in Portugal headlined by comedian Jerry Seinfeld, with some citing concerns related to the Israel-Gaza conflict and others giving no public explanation.

The withdrawals come ahead of the inaugural MEO Commedia a La Carte Fest in Lisbon, scheduled for Oct. 29 to Nov. 1. While some acts left the lineup without a public explanation, others cited political differences with performers involved in the festival.

On Saturday, actress Inês Aires Pereira announced on Instagram that she was withdrawing her show Namastê from the festival lineup.

In one image, Pereira wrote in Portuguese that "one of the names persistently defends ideas and acts that I consider indefensible. We cannot minimize or normalize a genocide," according to a translation by The Hollywood Reporter.

COMEDIAN DECLARES HUGH LAURIE 'CAN'T BE CANCELED' AS ACTOR COMES TO SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM'S DEFENSE

Musical comedy duo Cebola Mol also addressed their exit on Instagram, writing in a translated caption, "We will celebrate justice, freedom and joy with you on another occasion." The post included a cartoon watermelon, which is widely used as a symbol of Palestinian solidarity.

Several departing acts did not disclose their motives. High-profile performers, including pop musical project Tributo Pop, comedian Pedro Tochas, the group Conjunto Cuca Monga and visual artist Vhils all withdrew from the festival lineup without publicly stating a reason.

MICHAEL RAPAPORT SLAMS 'CLOWN' MACKLEMORE FOR ANTI-ISRAEL PERFORMANCE

Seinfeld is the festival’s main headliner and has publicly supported Israel. The festival’s website still lists him as a performer.

His support for Israel during the conflict has drawn accolades but also fierce criticism. In June, while leaving a New York Knicks game at Madison Square Garden, Seinfeld told a streamer asking for a "Free Palestine" shoutout that "it doesn’t exist."

During an event at Duke University, Seinfeld also discussed pro-Palestinian protests, saying, "Free Palestine is, to me, just — you’re free to say you don’t like Jews. Just say you don’t like Jews.

RABID ANTI-ISRAEL ACTIVISTS SET TO HIT THE STREETS TONIGHT IN MAMDANI'S MANHATTAN

"By saying ‘Free Palestine,’ you’re not admitting what you really think," he continued. "So, it’s actually — compared to the Ku Klux Klan, I’m actually thinking the Klan is actually a little better here because they can come right out and say, ‘We don’t like Blacks, we don’t like Jews.’ OK, that’s honest."

Fox News Digital reached out to Seinfeld’s team but did not hear back.

Comedian and media analyst Tim Young argued that the withdrawals hurt the departing performers far more than Seinfeld, whom he called "uncancellable."

"It was a total eye-roll for me," said Young, who also serves as a Media Fellow at the Heritage Foundation and media editor at The Dallas Express.

"I think anybody who is a comedian, anybody who is a performer, would want to work with basically the most successful, if not one of the most successful comedians in world history at this point. The guy's a billionaire from his comedy and his writing, and I don't know why you would want to walk away from it," he added.

Young suggested the withdrawals were simply catering to their existing fan base, calling the move "a group of woke people performing for woke people."

"They know who their audience is. They're behaving the way that their audience would behave and just playing into it," he said, adding the performers are likely getting more publicity from pulling out than they would have from performing.

Young doesn't believe the withdrawals will have any lasting impact on Seinfeld's standing in the comedy world.

BILL MAHER SAYS IT’S 'SO STUPID' FOR ANTI-TRUMP ARTISTS TO BAIL ON KENNEDY CENTER PERFORMANCES

"You can’t cancel somebody like him," Young said. "Comedy is uncancellable. You get to a certain level, you're not going to be affected by it, and it’s important that people like Seinfeld … come out and say, ‘Hey, you know, this is bad, the things that are happening.'

World.title: Hillary Clinton warns the U.S. has let its guard down on terrorism 25 years after 9/11
World.content:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton warned Thursday that the Trump administration isn’t doing enough to monitor and thwart terrorists who still pose a threat to the U.S., 25 years after the 9/11 attacks.

“I worry a lot that we’ve let down our guard on counterterrorism, and I don’t say this to scare anybody or to exaggerate, but I think we are not paying enough attention to resurgent terrorist actions,” Clinton said in an interview with NBC News’ Andrea Mitchell at the VOICES 25th Anniversary Symposium, an event reflecting on the attacks.

Clinton, who was a U.S. senator from New York on 9/11, said that there have been many “close calls” with terrorist plots in the ensuing quarter century and some that succeeded.

“The threat did not go away — it receded — but it is still there, and there are still many thousands of extremists in the world who wish us a great deal of ill,” she said. Clinton argued that the U.S. needs to overcome its internal divisions and confront threats from both nation-state adversaries, like Russia, China and Iran, and nonstate adversaries, like terrorist groups.

She lashed out at President Donald Trump for spending so much attention on his planned White House ballroom. “When you’re more interested in building your ballroom than figuring out what the intelligence is coming out of Afghanistan — that is absolutely contrary to any kind of sensible decision-making,” she said.

Clinton accused the Trump administration of dismantling parts of the federal government, including within the State Department, that traditionally collected intelligence and evaluated these terrorist threats. As a result, she said, the U.S. doesn’t have “eyes and ears in a lot of these countries,” including in western Africa, where she said extremism is taking hold.

The administration cut thousands of jobs across the federal government last year as part of the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency effort, including at the CIA and the State Department.

“I am increasingly concerned because I don’t think we are focused. I know there are very dedicated people still in the government, you know, in the FBI, in the intelligence agencies. I understand that,” she said. “But they don’t have ... the resources, and they’re not given the kind of mission focus that they need right now to adequately do their jobs.”

Reached for comment, the White House referred NBC News to the Department of Homeland Security, which didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

During the interview, Clinton also reflected on the revelations about the toxic air quality in Manhattan after 9/11, recalling her experience at ground zero. “It looked like a black curtain,” she said. “There was particulates. ... There was, you know, acrid smells. My throat hurt.”

Asked if misleading information about the air from the Bush administration at the time was deliberate, bad science or an effort to reassure the public, Clinton said it was “all three.”

“I think that there was a certain element of some leaders being unwilling to face the truth because they wanted to get the economy going,” she said. “They wanted to get Wall Street open. They wanted people to feel like normalcy was possible, and so they either deliberately ignored or they didn’t ask the right questions.”

She also responded to Jon Stewart, comedian and 9/11 health advocate, who said that the U.S. has lost nearly 10,000 people to 9/11-related illnesses, which is three times as many people as the nearly 3,000 killed in the twin towers.

Addressing the fact that there are people experiencing these health effects that aren’t registered for programs intended to help these victims, Clinton said, “There needs to be a concerted effort to fund this expanded outreach and screening and treatment. And I would hope that the city, the state and the federal government would join together to do that.”

World.title: Prosecutor who led ‘grand conspiracy’ probe of Trump targets resigns without charging anyone
World.content:
Joe diGenova, the 81-year-old Trump loyalist who had headed a sprawling investigation in the Southern District of Florida that targeted President Donald Trump’s perceived political enemies, has resigned from the Justice Department.

“It was an honor and a privilege to serve the president and the department,” diGenova said Thursday.

Asked why he is leaving, diGenova declined to comment.

“I’m moving on,” he said.

ABC News first reported diGenova’s departure.

While diGenova resigned from the Justice Department and was not fired, a source familiar with the determination told NBC News that Justice Department officials had already lost confidence in his leadership skills and his ability to run the investigation.

Justice Department leadership felt the investigation was not moving quickly enough, even though diGenova was provided with a team of Justice Department lawyers from Washington, according to the source familiar with the determination, who said the hope is the probe can get back on track with those attorneys at the helm.

For now, a specific person will not be named to take diGenova’s place, and the investigation is expected to move forward without delays.

The Justice Department declined to comment on diGenova’s resignation.

DiGenova, a top federal prosecutor under President Ronald Reagan, was part of Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election in his favor. He made headlines this year when it was revealed that he would head the Florida-based investigation into Trump’s foes.

DiGenova’s probe has not produced any prosecutions, though shortly before he resigned there was a recent burst of activity in the wide investigation. The Justice Department is seeking testimony from multiple former officials before a federal grand jury, people familiar with the probe told NBC News. The Associated Press first reported the subpoena activity.

The probe reached back a decade, revisiting a Justice Department inquiry into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election. That posed a major hurdle for the investigation, given that the activity took place nearly a decade ago, far outside the typical five-year statute of limitations for most federal crimes.

DiGenova stepped in to replace career prosecutor Maria Medetis Long, who had objected to advancing an investigation into former CIA Director John Brennan, whom Trump allies were pushing to be charged for allegedly false testimony.

The grand conspiracy investigation was taking place in a legal district that has historically been advantageous for Trump, overseen by the Trump-appointed U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, Jason A. Reding Quiñones, and using a grand jury in a Fort Pierce court run by U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, a Trump-friendly judge.

Then-acting Attorney General Todd Blanche appointed diGenova in April, shortly after Pam Bondi was fired. DiGenova, joined by his wife, Victoria Toensing, whom he brought into his team along with Rudy Giuliani and Sidney Powell, was part of a group that repeatedly tried and failed to overturn Trump’s 2020 election loss.

World.title: ‘We felt defeated’: Lindsay Clancy juror provides new details about the lone holdout
World.content:
A juror in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial provided new details Thursday about the lone holdout on the panel, including that he acted out the killings on a water bottle during deliberations.

Nick Dargie, 25, was one of the three men on the 12-person jury tasked with determining whether Clancy should be held criminally responsible for the 2023 strangulation deaths of her three young children: Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months old. He told “Good Morning America” on Thursday about his frustrations with the holdout juror, who has yet to be publicly identified.

“I think we felt defeated,” Dargie said about the case’s conclusion. “We spent seven weeks on this trial, almost two months of, you know, all of our lives dedicated to it.”

He is among at least five jurors — and the first male — who have spoken out about the case and what happened inside the deliberation room at Plymouth Superior Court last week. After more than 38 hours, the jurors could not reach a unanimous decision, forcing Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial after they deadlocked three times.

On Thursday, defense attorney Kevin Reddington filed a renewed motion to find Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility on each of the three charges, arguing that the prosecution did not prove, beyond a reasonable doubt, that Clancy was not in psychosis at the time of the killings.

Dargie told “Good Morning America” that toward the end of deliberations, the holdout juror would not engage in discussions with others or provide evidence that supported his reasoning, instead choosing to scroll on his phone.

Ultimately, Dargie said, he confronted the holdout juror after the man mimicked the killings, tying an exercise band entered into evidence around an empty water bottle and pulling it tight. Dargie said he is not sure why the man did that.

“I was shocked. It didn’t make any sense to me,” Dargie said. “We’re not in here to play detective or it’s not a game of Clue. This is serious.”

Nick Dargie on "Good Morning America." ABC News

Throughout the trial, Clancy’s defense attorney argued that she was in a state of psychosis when she strangled the children with exercise bands and therefore was not aware of what she was doing. The prosecution, however, argued she was not actually experiencing postpartum psychosis and planned the killings ahead of time.

Three women on the jury told NBC Boston that the 11 jurors agreed to find Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility. The holdout wanted to convict, they revealed, but admitted he expressed doubt in the prosecution’s case.

“It was definitely frustrating, mainly frustrating when [the holdout juror] explicitly said, ‘You know, I don’t know if the prosecution or the defense proved their case,’” Dargie told “GMA.”

Reddington in the motion also pointed to the fact that in this case, every juror except one — who did not apply the reasonable-doubt standard — came to that same conclusion.

“No rational jury could find beyond a reasonable doubt that she had no mental disease or defect when the Commonwealth’s own proof established that she did,” the motion said, noting the 11-1 jury split.

And at first, Dargie said, a number of jurors thought Clancy was guilty of the crimes, and at times the jury’s votes differed day to day.

A female juror who spoke with WBZ-TV of Boston anonymously said many people on the jury were initially “firm in their beliefs,” and that she was one of the people who, at first, agreed with the holdout and thought Clancy was guilty.

She explained how there was so much “gray area” and doubt in the case, and that ultimately, she switched her tune because she thinks Clancy is mentally unwell and that she’d get better help in a state mental health facility than in prison.

Dargie told “GMA” that “once we laid out all of the evidence and how we saw it, that really brought everyone kind of on the same page, except for this one juror.” The female juror chalked it up to one person being unable to let go of their convictions.

When that one juror didn’t agree with the group, Dargie said, he asked him to show evidence that “helped to prove what he was saying, but he couldn’t.” That’s what led the jury foreperson to send a note to the judge about the holdout during deliberations, explaining that he wasn’t meeting the burden of reasonable doubt the prosecution must overcome.

Dargie acknowledged that it’s fair for someone to have a differing opinion but said this particular juror would not engage and could not “find something to support his view.”

Now, prosecutors must decide whether they want to retry Clancy. The next hearing for the case is scheduled for Sept. 29.

Dargie, who was serving in the military overseas, said he’s “haunted” by the case. Specifically, he said, the recording of the 911 call made by Clancy’s then-husband, Patrick Clancy, when he found the dead children that night is seared into his memory. The recording was played in court and was not released to the public.

Patrick Clancy on the stand. David L. Ryan / The Boston Globe via Getty Images file

“I’ve never heard something like that, like a scream like that, come out of someone’s mouth,” Dargie said of the recording. “It’s horrifying.”

The anonymous female juror told CBS Boston that she will “never be the same after that 911 call.”

Dargie also rejected online conspiracy theories that Patrick Clancy was actually the one who carried out the killings, noting that if anyone had heard the 911 calls, they would change their mind.

“I think if they tried the trial again the way they did, I think nine times out of 10, I think the jury would come back with not guilty by reason of insanity, no doubt,” Dargie said.

World.title: Heart damage may occur from getting too much light at night while we sleep, study finds
World.content:
Exposure to light during nighttime sleep may lead to potentially harmful changes in the structure and function of the heart, according to a study published Wednesday in the European Heart Journal.

Previous research had shown a link between nighttime sleep while exposed to light and an elevated risk of coronary artery disease, heart attack, heart failure and stroke. The new study is the first to examine how it also affects the structure and function of the heart.

Changes to the heart — known as remodeling — can help explain the elevated risk for heart problems associated with too much nighttime light, said lead researcher Dr. Lu Qi, of Tulane University’s Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public Health & Tropical Medicine.

“The takeaway is clear: darkness deserves recognition as a vital sign, as essential to cardiovascular health as blood pressure control and clean air,” Dr. Thomas Münzel, an environmental cardiologist at the University Medical Center of Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, and colleagues wrote in an accompanying editorial.

The researchers analyzed data from 11,071 participants enrolled in the UK Biobank, a massive database that began recruiting participants in 2005 and collects data about demographics, health and lifestyle. The people in the study wore light and motion sensors on their wrists for seven days, and a few years later, they were given MRIs of the heart. They did not have cardiovascular disease starting out.

The researchers compared people who were exposed to almost no nighttime light during sleep to people who were exposed to at least 3 lux — lux is a measurement of illumination — which would still be a very dim room, said Kristen Knutson, an associate professor of sleep medicine at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine who has no connection to the study.

Your closed eyes, however, would be able to detect the light, she said.

Street light leaking through window shades, clock radio illumination and LED lights on equipment like room air purifiers or humidifiers were possible sources for nighttime light in the study, said Qi.

After adjusting for demographic, lifestyle, health and environmental factors, the researchers found that any increase in light exposure above 3 lux during nighttime sleep was associated with measurable, subtle cardiac damage.

For example, participants in the highest light exposure group had, on average, a 2.4% larger left ventricle (a chamber of the heart), a 1.5% thicker heart wall and a 1.9% reduction in the heart’s ability to contract, compared with participants sleeping in the darkest rooms.

Each of those changes in the heart looks small, but they have been linked with cardiovascular disease and stroke.

“If we look at the various different functional and structural outcomes together, they are pretty considerable,” Qi said.

In fact, the researchers looked for those kinds of health events. They found that after up to 10 years of follow-up, the highest light exposure group showed a 29% increased risk of heart failure, a 24% higher risk for heart attack, a 33% elevated risk for stroke and a 26% increased risk for cardiovascular death compared with the lowest light group.

Nighttime light can affect how long someone sleeps, and the paper found that nearly half of the changes in the heart’s structure and function could be attributed to lack of sleep. Another potential pathway could be nighttime light’s effect on the body’s circadian rhythm system.

That system, or clock, controls 24-hour patterns in a wide range of areas, from sleep, to hormones, to blood pressure, to inflammation, among others. Nighttime light can confuse the body’s circadian system, which can lead to cardiovascular consequences down the road, said Knutson.

The paper has limitations. The participants wore the wrist sensor for only a week. It also measured only illumination, not light spectrum, and so the study couldn’t say anything about the impact of different kinds of light, for instance LED light versus fluorescent light, on heart remodeling. In addition, the participants were mostly white, and so the results may not apply to other racial groups.

Most important, the study was observational, and so it can’t be firmly established that nighttime light caused the heart changes.

A future study about nighttime light could include people who start out with cardiovascular disease or are at high risk for it, said Knutson. “Are they more vulnerable, less vulnerable?” she asked. Future studies could also include measurements of the light spectrum and the body’s circadian rhythm.

The study’s implications are clear, wrote Münzel and colleagues. People can make simple and inexpensive fixes, such as installing blackout curtains, using warm-colored bedside lighting and covering the small standby LEDs on household electronics.

Cities can also take action, from using dimming and motion-activated streetlights to shielding streetlights so they don’t shine into buildings.

The study, the editorial said, provides a crucial link between “a planet growing ever brighter at night, and the clinical reality unfolding inside our chests: hearts that are becoming stiffer, weaker, and less efficient.”

World.title: Surrogate appeals to Supreme Court in custody dispute over baby with heart defect
World.content:
A California couple's surrogate who refused their wishes to have an abortion has asked the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene in a custody dispute over the 4-week-old child, who was born with a serious heart defect.

McKenna West filed the emergency appeal Wednesday amid a legal battle over surrogacy and abortion that has won the support of Republican officeholders and anti-abortion groups. West, a nurse who lives in Alaska, traveled to Dallas to give birth in August. Most abortions are banned in Texas.

West is asking the nation's highest court to halt a California court order that recognizes Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar as the parents of the child whom she calls Gabriel, and they call Rumi.

West wants final custody or conservatorship because she believes the couple will not provide lifesaving care, citing their request for an abortion at 23 weeks.

The boy was born Aug. 12 with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a life-threatening condition that prevents normal blood flow to the organ.

Just before his birth, the office of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton intervened in the case and obtained an emergency court order requiring that the boy receive lifesaving medical care.

"It was scary to think that something might be wrong, and that I may be the one that's not able to make a decision about the treatment," West said in an interview last month with Live Action, an anti-abortion rights organization.

He underwent surgery soon after he was born. The couple's attorney, Lee Budner, said in August that the newborn was in critical condition and appeared to be "suffering from potential complications."

Surrogacy is not regulated at the federal level. Each state has its own laws, which can leave room for gaps in interpretation. The Supreme Court is not obliged to hear the case.

Ahmed and Gilkar have not yet responded to the Supreme Court filing. CBS News has reached out to the couple's attorney for comment on the emergency petition.

The couple previously said West violated the surrogacy contract, and they obtained a restraining order from a Texas court preventing her from seeing or holding the child. That court also ruled that Ahmed and Gilkar, not West, are responsible for medical decisions.

Gilkar called West "mentally unstable" during a hearing Aug. 25 in Dallas, telling the court West was trying to take their baby away.

"He's our child," Gilkar said, wiping away tears.

During that hearing, Gilkar testified that West never told her or Ahmed that she was traveling to Texas, and alleged that West withdrew access to the child's medical records, a claim which West admitted to in the hearing.

Gilkar told the court that she and her husband did request to terminate the surrogate pregnancy back in May because of the heart defect.

In the hearing, West said that she wanted custody of the child, but was open to the idea of dropping any custody claims if the couple agreed to the baby's lifesaving care.

"Denying lifesaving care is not true," Gilkar said in court. "We are devastated ... We've never wanted anything more than those babies."

McKenna West, center, leaves a courtroom after a court hearing regarding the surrogacy baby case, on Aug. 25, 2026, in Dallas, Texas. Chitose Suzuki/The Dallas Morning News via Getty Images

West and her attorneys argue that Gilkar and Ahmed are not committed to guaranteeing the baby will undergo surgeries or "life-saving care."

Both sides were publicly silent after the Aug. 25 hearing, and the case file was sealed, but West's Supreme Court filing says she lost her plea in Texas to win conservatorship of the child.

The Texas court granted full credit to the California judgment on Sept. 2, according to the filing.

The odds of the Supreme Court granting the appeal are low, said Marla Neufeld, an attorney who represents parents, surrogates and donors but who isn't involved in this case. Emergency relief is usually extraordinarily difficult to obtain and the Supreme Court doesn't usually get involved in family disputes, she said.

"The stakes of the decisions below are enormous," West's lawyers wrote in her plea to the Supreme Court, asking that she be recognized as the mother under Texas law. "But because of the unlawful California judgment, she has been dismissed with prejudice from the Texas proceedings and denied any information about or control over the medically fragile child."

West believes Ahmed and Gilkar plan to put the baby into hospice care in California rather than let him undergo surgery that could save his life, according to the filing.

Without treatment, hypoplastic left heart syndrome can lead to death within days or weeks. Surgical repairs are not necessarily cures and additional surgeries or heart transplants may be needed, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

According to the Cleveland Clinic, the baby will need a second surgery between 4 and 6 months of age, and then a third surgery between 18 months and 4 years old.

The couple has said they will not provide any updates to West about the child's condition, the filing states.

World.title: Trump's $5,000 payments would reignite inflation, economists say
World.content:
President Trump's vow to send $5,000 to every U.S. adult if the Republican Party keeps control of Congress in the midterm elections would drive up the federal deficit, reignite inflation and alarm investors, according to economists.

After Mr. Trump raised the idea of such a dividend on Wednesday night at the Republican National Committee's midterm convention, Vice President JD Vance told Fox News that the U.S. would fund the payment using tariff revenue collected by the Trump administration, and that it would be aimed at the middle class.

Those tariffs are generating about $125 billion in annual revenue — one-tenth of the $1.25 trillion that would be required to pay $5,000 to each of the nation's roughly 245 million U.S. adults, Erica York, senior economist with the Tax Foundation's Center for Federal Tax Policy, told CBS News.

Because tariff revenue would fall short, the U.S. would likely need to issue government debt to pay for the dividends, raising the federal deficit to $3 trillion, up from its current level of about $1.8 trillion, York estimated.

Why the dividend would drive inflation

The one-time payments would also likely stoke inflation by fueling a surge in consumer spending, as did the multiple federal stimulus checks during the pandemic.

Economists say those payments contributed to consumer prices reaching a 40-year high in June 2022.

A $5,000 giveaway would also rattle financial markets, York said. With the nation's debt recently surpassing $40 trillion for the first time, Treasury bond buyers would likely demand higher yields to offset increased fiscal risks, she added.

"If financial markets are already concerned about U.S. budget deficits, which are historically large and are projected to grow, and the message that you're giving is, 'We don't really care. We're almost going to double our deficits' — that's madness," York said of Mr. Trump's proposal.

Offering such a payment to Americans would be "fiscally dangerous," Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a nonpartisan think tank that favors reducing the U.S. deficit, said in a statement on Thursday.

"It's hard to understand how anyone could look at our current fiscal and economic situation and think we need to borrow another $1.2 trillion to send everyone cash," she said.

The White House said that Mr. Trump has "consistently proven his doubters wrong."

"The doomers and naysayers have consistently doubted President Trump: when he pledged to create the historic Trump Accounts, lowered prescription prices with Most Favored Nations, secured the border with no crossings, cleaned up our streets, ended taxes on tips, grew real wages, renegotiated broken trade deals and reshored key manufacturing back to the United States," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement to CBS News.

Piling on debt

Many fiscal hawks have urged lawmakers to start addressing the mounting federal debt, which has doubled in less than a decade due to multiple tax cuts and COVID-related spending, among other factors.

Adding $1.25 trillion in debt to the nation's ledger is "completely detached from fiscal reality," York said.

Rising U.S. debt has pushed up the nation's interest costs, with the U.S. government now spending more on servicing its debt than on national defense or Medicare. Investors are demanding higher Treasury yields due to the worsening federal fiscal outlook. That, in turn, is pushing up borrowing costs for consumers, including mortgages, auto loans and personal loans.

"The bond market is already nervous about inflation and America's $40 trillion debt," Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union, said in an email. "This would likely cause borrowing costs to jump even further."

Long added that because of those issues, Wall Street is "largely ignoring" the Trump administration's dividend plan, writing it off as unlikely to gain traction with Congress, which would need to approve it.

In an exclusive interview with CBS News Texas, President Trump said on Thursday that he doesn't think lawmakers would need to approve the $5,000 payments.

During his speech on Wednesday, Mr. Trump also proposed other ways to lower the cost of living for Americans, which polls show is a key campaign issue ahead of the November elections. That includes possibly eliminating credit card swipe fees, which he said could save the typical family about $1,200 a year.

But the $5,000 payment has garnered the most attention, likely because many consumers say they're struggling with the cost of living, with gas prices remaining above $4 a gallon and inflation still elevated.

Consumer Price Index data for August, set to be released on Friday, is expected to show inflation rose at an annual pace of 3.3%, well above the Federal Reserve's annual target of 2%.

While a $5,000 payment might initially help struggling consumers, such a program would soon backfire by driving inflation even higher, York told CBS News. The COVID stimulus checks caused inflation to rise by 2.6% during the pandemic, according to 2023 research from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

"We would be stimulating the economy in a really massive way with $5,000 payments, when the economy is not really calling for that," she said. "You're really kind of worsening the problem that you're supposedly trying to address with this proposal."
