World.title: Orange Shirt Day founder says her truth is being 'pushed aside' by controversial shirts
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The founder of Orange Shirt Day says she was sick to her stomach when she learned orange shirts with slogans like "Dig deeper" and "Still no proof" were being sold online.

Holding back tears and speaking from Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc in B.C., which announced a discovery of potential unmarked graves near a former residential school site in 2021, Phyllis Webstad said her campaign was being used in a "hateful way."

"I've been trying to understand why they believe that it's OK to hurt people," she said.

In 1976, Webstad wore a present from her grandmother, an orange shirt, on her first day at a residential school at St. Joseph's Mission, in Williams Lake, B.C. The shirt was taken from her by school officials and never returned.

Webstad founded Orange Shirt Day on Sept. 30, 13 years ago, to honour Indigenous children who were forced to attend residential schools.

In late August, Rebel News announced it was selling orange T-shirts on its website for the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation and that the shirts are about "challenging the identity politics that Canadians are increasingly pressured to accept and standing up for the whole truth in our complex Canadian history."

Statements printed on the shirts include "Still no proof," "You can't handle the truth," "Buried Truth" and "Dig Deeper," as well as "Canada was built not stolen."

Webstad called the sales a direct attack on her work with the Orange Shirt Society.

"It's my truth and what I know is the truth," Webstad said.

"It seems like this truth is not being respected. It's not being understood. It's being pushed aside."

Orange T-shirts with various slogans were posted to the Rebel News store at the end of August. (Rebel News Store)

In an emailed statement, Ezra Levant, founder and owner of Rebel News, pointed CBC News to a video on its website launching the sale of the shirts, saying their reporter "approaches these issues with compassion."

"The stated purpose of the National Truth and Reconciliation Day is noble – to honour residential school survivors and their communities by recognizing the lasting impacts of Canada's residential school system, so Canadians can better understand its legacy as part of our ongoing journey toward truth, healing, and reconciliation," Levant quoted what was said in the video.

In the video, the Rebel News reporter goes on to say "But five years later, Canadians are still being told that there are some truths they're not allowed to question."

Levant added in the statement that Rebel News staff are "dedicated to freedom of expression including the right to seek the truth" and "these orange shirts are a response for people who are forced to wear orange shirts at school or at work, as part of an 'official' political narrative."

"No Canadians should be compelled to support any political view, including Orange Shirt Day’s politics."

In the video promoting the shirts, the Rebel News reporter says "what's more than likely underneath the apple orchard soil at the Kamloops site is probably an old septic plot."

Webstad pointed to the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, which has so far documented more than 4,000 deaths of Indigenous children in Canada's residential school system.

WATCH | B.C. regional chief speaks on residential school denialism: ‘Denialism is not an academic debate. It’s hate speech,' says regional chief | Duration 1:32 Regional Chief of the British Columbia Assembly of First Nations Terry Teegee said violence, anti-Indigenous rhetoric and hate speech are linked to residential school denialism and that, if left unaddressed, denialism ‘undermines truth and reconciliation.'

She said her own auntie, Agness Jack, shared a personal story about what it was like living in the Kamloops Indian Residential School in a book published in 2001, Behind Closed Doors: Stories from the Kamloops Indian Residential School.

Webstad also said her grandmother and her grandmother's 10 children including Webstad's mom were all forced to attend residential school.

"My mother was so traumatized that she could not take care of me; thank God my Granny was there, thank God my auntie was there," said Webstad.

"I want to say that we aren't liars. Indian Residential School survivors are not liars. Have some respect and give us the space and time to do what we need to do as individuals, as family, as a community, as a nation."

The orange shirts available on the Rebel News website are listed in youth sizes as well as adult.

"That is a whole new level of every word in the book: disgusting, unbelievable, sickening. Where are their minds?" said Webstad about the youth sizes.

MPs and ministers condemn shirts

Last week, the Liberal Indigenous Caucus published a statement that said merchandise "that mocks survivors' experiences and dismisses their truths is reprehensible and beneath any organization."

A request for comment from Conservative MP Billy Morin, the party's shadow minister of Indigenous Services, was not returned by time of publishing.

Morin told APTN News last week, “I find it racist and I find it absolutely disgusting that they’re attempting to make a profit off the pain and suffering of residential schools."

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty, who is a member of the Waswanipi Cree Nation in northern Quebec, said people across the country have raised concerns about the shirts to her.

"Not just people living in my riding but also from Canadians who are appalled about this really disgraceful and grotesque attempt to exploit human suffering for financial gain," said Gull-Masty.

Gull-Masty's mother and grandmother were both forced to attend the La Tuque Indian Residential School in Quebec.

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty, a member of Waswanipi Cree Nation in northern Quebec, says she heard concerns from people all over Canada about the shirts being sold online. (Marie-Laure Josselin/Radio-Canada)

Gull-Masty said she expressed her concerns to Justice Minister Sean Fraser, but didn't say what avenues the government would explore. She said she felt Fraser understood how serious the matter is.

"I think this is one of the areas where we are seeing behaviour that is not only being perpetuated more commonly but it is reaching a level that is unacceptable," said Gull-Masty.

In a statement to CBC Indigenous, a spokesperson for Fraser said, "Seeking to profit from Indian residential school denialism is deeply disgraceful and represents a cruel and grotesque attempt to exploit human suffering."

"Residential school denialism is a serious and distinct issue, and our government has said this issue warrants dedicated further parliamentary study," the statement said.

"Any legal response should be developed carefully in consultation and co-operation with Indigenous Peoples and the communities most affected."

Earlier this year, Canada's Senate voted down an amendment to Bill C-9 that would have criminalized residential school denialism, by making it illegal to wilfully promote "hatred against Indigenous Peoples by condoning, denying or downplaying the Indian Residential Schools System."

Webstad said she supports the idea that residential school denialism should be added as hate speech to Canada's Criminal Code.

"I believe what Rebel News is doing right now is what is needed to convince our Canadian government that yes, a law needs to be passed," said Webstad.

Shirts designed to provoke conflicts in schools, says academic

Sean Carleton, an associate professor in history and Indigenous studies at the University of Manitoba, said he feels the shirts monetize anti-Indigenous racism and deliberately profit off of pain and suffering.

"Thousands of Indigenous children died, we know that," said Carleton.

"So what [Rebel News] is trying to do is cast doubt, shake public confidence and are trying to convince Canadians that maybe we shouldn't care about Indigenous people and reconciliation anymore."

Carleton said the easiest way to understand denialism is to look at the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's simple formula.

Sean Carleton, an associate professor in history and Indigenous studies at the University of Manitoba, says the shirts monetize anti-Indigenous racism, and deliberately profit off of pain and suffering. (Submitted by Sean Carleton)

"We've got to have truth first," he said.

"Truth will lead to healing and justice. Healing and justice will lead to reconciliation. Denialists know that and what they're trying to do is keep us stuck in the truth part."

Carleton said he believes the inclusion of youth sizing is a tactic designed to provoke conflicts within schools where parents may be influenced by denialist rhetoric and use their children to challenge school policies.

He said the slogans on the shirts not only defend the colonial status quo but promote colonization as a compassion project, and said they question survivors' lived experiences.

NDP MP Leah Gazan tabled a private member's bill in Parliament last fall to criminalize residential school denialism.

In a letter to the Indigenous Liberal Caucus on Tuesday, Gazan said anti-Indigenous racism and denialism are growing and have now resulted in "the production of merchandise denying genocide and mocking the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. We must respond to this as what it is – the incitement, monetization and promotion of hate."

Gazan called on the Indigenous Liberal Caucus to table her bill as a government bill.

A national 24-hour Indian Residential School Crisis Line is available at 1-866-925-4419 for emotional and crisis referral services for survivors and those affected.

World.title: Carney says he's regularly speaking with Trump and still believes there's a deal to be had
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says he's still in regular contact with U.S. President Donald Trump despite the ongoing trade rift and some unsavoury remarks from administration officials.

The prime minister suggested that his recent conversations with Trump have been focused on global events, including how the wars in Ukraine and Iran are impacting international energy and grain markets.

"In terms of playing that [international] role, we continue to work with the United States. We can compartmentalize," he said during a news conference alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Calgary on Thursday.

"I spoke to [Trump] recently in the last few days, a couple of times, related to issues [in Ukraine], related to issues in Iran, other global developments. Because that's part of our responsibility."

WATCH | Carney gives examples of topics of discussion with Trump: Canada ready to support Russia-Ukraine ceasefire where U.S. can play 'decisive role': Carney | Duration 2:17 Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said a cessation of hostilities between Russia and Ukraine offers a possible 'shorter-term solution' to global issues around access to energy and agricultural goods.

Tariff negotiations between Canada and the U.S. fell apart last month, with both sides hurling blame at the other.

The U.S. immediately slapped 50 per cent levies on hundreds of Canadian goods, and Canada countered with new tariffs on roughly an equivalent value of U.S. imports on Monday. The Trump administration responded on Wednesday by announcing it would place further tariffs on some Canadian imports and outright ban others later this month.

Carney didn't say whether his government would respond with more counter-tariffs on U.S. goods.

"We're looking closely at the measures the Americans just recently announced," he told reporters later on Thursday.

Carney said that even though talks have stalled, he believes there's still a deal to be had with the U.S.

"Canada's always ready to strike a fair deal. We believe there's still a mutually beneficial deal for Canada and the United States," he said at the news conference with Zelenskyy.

WATCH | Carney says government is reviewing Trump's latest trade actions: 'We're looking closely' at Trump's import bans and tariffs, Carney says | Duration 1:03 Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday that the government is looking at U.S. President Donald Trump's recent measures which include bans on Canadian imports including most alcohol products and new 50 per cent tariffs on a series of other products. 'We fully recognize that for individual companies and in individual sectors these are significant, and there's a response there,' Carney said.

Trump and some of his key cabinet members have disparaged Canada in the media and online in recent weeks.

The president notably decided his government would refer to Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have both derided the Canadian Armed Forces. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told the Financial Times that it's "unhinged" for Canadian leaders to characterize the administration's tariffs as a trade war.

Carney has pushed back when asked about some of the Trump administration's more unsavoury remarks, saying they're "beneath their office."

WATCH | More about the trade war: Is toilet paper an unlikely pressure point in the Canada–U.S. trade war? | Duration 2:28 U.S. President Donald Trump dropped tariffs on certain Canadian products, including toilet paper, cement and salt. In 2024, Canada exported approximately $328 million worth of the product, making it the largest international provider of toilet paper to the U.S.

When asked about why he thinks Trump has continued to disparage Canada since talks fell apart, Carney wouldn't speculate.

"I can't look deeply into the souls of other people and see their emotions. This isn't a question of emotion, it's a question of sovereignty for Canada," he said.

World.title: Man accused in Mexican condo scheme claims he was a victim, too
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A U.K. man facing accusations he took part in a scheme that wiped out a Canadian couple's retirement savings says he's provided proof to Mexican authorities probing the case that he never touched a dime of the vanished funds, and that he's also a victim of his co-accused.

Harry Robinson, 66, is accused of working with a Mexican national named Jacqueline Herrera Herrera to defraud Cindy Thompson and Glenn Brown of Curve Lake, Ont., of $280,000 by offering them a fake deal to buy and flip seven condos.

Robinson provided CBC News with a memo and HSBC bank records, both filed with the state attorney general's office of Quintana Roo, that he says proves Herrera redirected Thompson and Brown's money — sent over three installments — through cashier's cheques and transfers to other, unknown accounts.

The memo, filed Aug. 24, alleges that Herrera had total control over the account which was under the name of Xen Investments, their former joint venture. It claims Herrera put the account under a "lock" to prevent Robinson from accessing or moving funds.

CBC News was not provided with any documented proof outlining the alleged lock on the account.

The memo asks state investigators to seek a judicial order to obtain the names linked to the cashier's cheques and other bank accounts to trace the final destination of the funds.

"If you watch any criminal show on TV, the one statement that is made all the time: Follow the money," Robinson told CBC News in his real-estate office in Puerto Morelos, a small port town between the tourist hotspots Playa del Carmen and Cancun.

Cindy Thompson, right, and Glenn Brown of Curve Lake, Ont., sent $280,000 to a company co-owned by Robinson and his co-accused Jacqueline Herrera Herrera. (Submitted by Cindy Thompson)

"And yet, here we are in a fraud case with missing money and no one has made any attempt to follow the money."

However, state authorities are not focusing their case against Robinson and Herrera on what happened to the money, according to other court records. There have been no applications yet before the courts to trace the movement of Thompson and Brown's funds after they landed in Xen Investments's account.

The investigation is simply focused on proving there was fraud by deceit — that Herrera and Robinson did not have any access or control over the seven condos they offered Thompson and Brown as part of a deal, which promised the couple 100 per cent profit.

"This operation evolved as more resources were collected, without the existence … availability or actual allocation of the promised units being documentally proven," says a state prosecutor's filing seeking arrest warrants against Herrera and Robinson, which was obtained by CBC News.

"For months [Thompson and Brown] were kept in a narrative of extensions, new fund requests … and imminent refunds that never materialized."

Herrera was co-owner of a company called Xen Investments, which is registered in Mexico. She pitched the sale of a condo to Thompson. (Jacqueline Herrera Herrera/Facebook)

A state judge issued those warrants on July 24. Herrera and Robinson both obtained stays in Mexican federal court against the warrants, but their state-level criminal proceedings are waiting on a judge to set a date to commence.

"I don't think I'm being fairly treated … by the prosecutor's office. I think they're not going after the true criminal in this case," said Robinson.

"I've lived my whole life honest, no problems, no criminal record, nothing … and all of a sudden I'm now some sort of master criminal? Nobody makes that transition like that."

Publicly available records show Robinson was born in Liverpool and that he worked in Australia and the U.S. before moving to Mexico. CBC News could find no evidence of any sanctions against Robinson or court cases involving him or his businesses.

Robinson says he moved to Mexico around 2020 and also has Australian citizenship.

A fraud by deceit conviction could lead to a prison sentence ranging between three to 12 years.

Robinson says he's asked the U.K. Embassy for help.

The 'middleman'

Thompson said that Robinson was the "middleman" throughout the months of attempted dealmaking, which started in 2024.

"I had 100 per cent faith in [Robinson]," she said.

"He was very convincing … anytime we had any questions or concerns, he always had an answer … I would get: ‘relax, calm down, everything's going to be fine, it's just taking a long time. It's Mexico, right?'"

Robinson says he was also duped by Herrera and believed the deal was real — though he put none of his own money into the pot, despite telling Thompson he would also go in as an investor.

"The deal was that all my time and effort, everything else, was going to be paid in commission. That commission was set aside and put toward the deal," he said.

This condo building in Playa del Carmen was part of the alleged scheme that is now under investigation by Mexican authorities. (Gustavo Huerta/CBC)

"And I would see it one day. So I didn't even get anything upfront."

Robinson said he met Herrera around three or four years ago and attended several private events with her and that she seemed to be well connected and respected as a Cancun realtor with 30 years of experience.

"Everybody seemed to now have gone out of their way to tell me how good a person Jacqueline was, how trustworthy she was, how I couldn't have found a better business partner," said Robinson. "I was a mark in exactly the same way [Thompson] was."

Seeking settlement

Herrera claims Robinson also took some of Thompson and Brown's money. She is seeking to avoid criminal proceedings by offering to repay part of the missing money through an alternative justice channel that is part of the Mexican system.

Herrera is offering to repay $2.4 million pesos — roughly $196,000 — in two installments to Thompson and Brown under a court-authorized settlement. Herrera has claimed — through her lawyer, according to Thompson — that Robinson is responsible for the rest.

Herrera declined an interview request, but told CBC News it was "never" her intention to defraud Thompson and Brown.

Thompson and Brown say they are facing a tough decision on whether to proceed with Herrera's settlement offer.

"Our biggest worry is, if we accept that, do we get the rest of the money?" said Brown.

World.title: Edmonton Oilers facing online backlash after signing Alex Formenton
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Edmonton Oilers decision to sign a hockey player who was acquitted last year of sexual assault has sparked a wave of disappointment and calls for the team to "do better."

The intensely negative reaction started rolling in Wednesday after the team announced it had signed Alex Formenton to a one-year contract worth $850,000 US.

Formenton was one of five players from Canada's 2018 world junior team accused of sexual assault, charges that stemmed from an encounter with a woman after a Hockey Canada gala in London, Ont.

"The initial reaction from the fan base has been really, from what I’ve seen on social media, pretty overwhelmingly negative," Daily Hive sports journalist Preston Hodgkinson told CBC News on Thursday.

"I remember the pushback for Corey Perry was one; Mike Babcock just happened this summer, even Stan Bowman. There was a lot of pushback for all that. This one seems more intense."

On an Oilers Instagram post about the signing, commenters said they were "embarrassed," "disgusted" and "disappointment." While some defended the Oilers' signing, many said they would not support the team as long as Formenton was on it.

"T o the Oilers organization: you need to do better for your female fans," said a comment posted by @ireland1102 that had received more than 4,200 likes as of Thursday morning.

"This isn’t just about hockey, it’s about the message you are sending to the women and girls who wear your jersey, buy your tickets and have supported this team their entire lives. "

A screen capture of the Edmonton Oiler Instagram post about Alex Formenton's signing, along with some reaction. (Edmonton Oilers/Instagram)

One of the team's most high-profile fans echoed the sentiment in her own social media post.

"Although he was acquitted in court, I cannot ignore my conscience or what this decision represents to me," wrote Mary Loewen, who dresses up during NHL playoffs as a sequined Stanley Cup known as "Mama Stanley."

Loewen wrote on her Instagram page that she was a sexual assault survivor, adding, "For that reason, as long as Formenton remains an Oiler, I CANNOT AND WILL NOT support or cheer for this team."

On Thursday, she launched an online petition calling for the Oilers to end Formenton's affiliation with the team. Loewen did not immediately respond to a request from The Canadian Press for an interview.

Acquitted in July 2025

The five accused hockey players — Formenton, Cal Foote, Carter Hart, Dillon Dube and Michael McLeod — were acquitted in July 2025. The NHL later reinstated all five players after charges were dropped.

Last month, a n independent appeal board ruled that all five breached the Hockey Canada code of conduct, and recommended continued suspensions from any Hockey Canada-sanctioned program for four of the players.

Only Formenton was named eligible for immediate reinstatement.

Formenton has said he is grateful to join the Oilers after what he called a "difficult road."

The 26-year-old native of Barrie, Ont., spent three of the past four seasons playing in Switzerland for HC Ambri-Piotta and the other not in hockey at all. He recorded 33 goals and 19 assists for 52 points over 88 games with HC Ambri-Piotta. He last played in the NHL during the 2021–22 season with the Ottawa Senators.

Hodgkinson said he is baffled why Oilers management would take on the "baggage" of signing Formenton given his on-ice performance in recent years.

"It’s not like you’re bringing in a star player," he said. "You’re bringing in a bottom lineup guy and you have to deal with all this. It doesn’t really feel worth it to me."

While the outcry has been fierce, Hodgkinson noted that there are some people who have expressed support for giving Formenton a chance in light of the acquittal.

He also pointed out that among those vocally criticizing the signing are people, like Loewen, who have identified themselves as being survivors of sexual assault "and this is a blatant 'eff you.'"

Late Wednesday, the Sexual Assault Centre of Edmonton (SACE) issued a statement that noted Oilers announcement " may be difficult for many survivors and members of our community.

"If this news is bringing up hard feelings or emotions, please know that you don’t have to carry them alone. SACE is here. We hear you, we believe you, and we stand with you."

World.title: These tiny endangered raccoons make their own toys out of trash
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Interview with biologist Nessie O'Neil: As It Happens 6:22 Endangered Mexican pygmy raccoons make their own toys out of trash

The first time Nessie O’Neil witnessed a pygmy raccoon making a toy ball out of trash, she didn't realize that she'd just made a major scientific discovery.

"My first thought was, oh my gosh, this is adorable," O’Neil, a biologist at Miami University in Ohio, told As It Happens host Nil Köksal.

Then she showed the footage to her advisor.

"She was like, 'Nessie, this is very important. Do not post this on social media because we need to write a paper about this.'"

That paper, now published in the journal Wild , documents the itty bitty Mexican critters rummaging through bins for paper and other materials, crafting those scraps into balls to play with, and teaching their family members how to do the same.

The authors say this is first documented evidence of “material culture” — socially shared cultural information about objects — in the Procyonidae family, which includes raccoons, ringtails and other similar creatures.

"We know that raccoons are very playful animals. If you give them a cat toy, they will bat it around or chew on it and chase it," O'Neil said. "But up until now, we have not seen anything like this."

Pygmy raccoons are a critically endangered species found only on Cozumel Island off the coast of the Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico.

Weighing about three to four kilograms, they are much smaller than the chunky mainland raccoons who dwell in Canadian and American cities. They have long limbs, which they use to navigate their native mangrove forests and forage for crabs and other shoreline prey.

But as their natural habitat is increasingly razed for development, O'Neil says they've turned to tourist scraps and to garbage bins for sustenance.

In fact, O'Neil was observing a family of raccoons at a beach club when she first witnessed the toy-making behaviour.

"I actually saw one of the juveniles go into a trash can and dig through and pull out a rather long receipt. And she brought the receipt back to a stainless steel water bowl that one of the staff members had put out for her and began to dunk it in the water," she said.

"She started to roll it between her hands and shape it into a ball. And then she would roll it in the sand and maybe dump it back in the water a little bit and then go back to the sand and work on shaping it. And after she got it how she wanted it, she began to play with it like a cat with a little mouse toy."

WATCH | Pygmy raccoon crafts her own toy: Watch this pygmy racoon make a toy ball out of trash | Duration 0:28 Pygmy raccoons in Mexico have been documented fishing scraps of paper out of trash bins, then using water and sand to form them into little balls to play with. Credit: Nessie O'Neil/Miami University.

Then, O'Neil says, she shared her skills.

"Her sister learned how to do this behaviour, too. She would watch and practise alongside her," O'Neil said.

The mother raccoon also tried to make a ball, the study noted, but gave up when was unable to retrieve her paper towel from the water dish.

"The success of the mother during this attempt might have been influenced by her earlier consumption of one ounce of a margarita, which appeared to lower her dexterity," the study reads.

Novel behaviour

Benjamin Beck, a retired scientist from the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute and co-author of the book Animal Tool Behavior, says he's seen many instances of animals playing using random objects as toys.

But he says he's never heard of an animal making its own toy.

"I think it's a distinct category to say that you made your play toy as well as used your play toy," he said. "What that distinction means, I'm not absolutely sure. Maybe it suggests a higher level of foresight and creativity."

What's even more interesting, he says, is that the raccoons were seen batting the ball back and forth between each other.

"That's social object play," he said. "And that I have no record of."

The researchers observed at least six instances of the raccoons playing with the balls they'd made. (Submitted by Nessie O'Neil)

Still, he says, he'd be hesitant to label the behaviour as an example of culture, given the small sample size.

"You're going to have to look at a sequence of generations to make sure that the behaviour persists, it is being learned intergenerationally, before you can make the leap to any sort of culture," he said

The plight of the pygmy

There are only 200 pygmy raccoons alive today in Cozumel, and O'Neil says those numbers are shrinking as tourist developments destroy their habitat and cut them off from their natural food supply.

In fact, the pygmy raccoon O'Neil first filmed making a paper ball has since died.

"She was so malnourished due to eating almost nothing but tortilla chips," she said.

A pigmy racoon grabs some tortilla from a trash bin on a Mexican beach club. Researcher Nessie O'Neil says the creatures have become reliant on human scraps, and it's leading to malnourishment. (Submitted by Nessie O'Neil)

O'Neil says she hopes this research will shed light on the plight of pygmy raccoons, and inspire people to change their behaviour — especially tourists.

"People need to stop feeding them. Stop feeding them tortilla chips. Stop offering them margaritas. Stop supporting resorts and beach clubs that are destroying their homes," O'Neil said.

"Every animal has an intrinsic value. Even if humans can't see it, they have a right to be there. This is their home."

World.title: From pipelines to railways and AI: Ottawa pitches 167 projects ahead of Carney's investment summit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A floating LNG terminal on B.C.'s coast, a high-speed rail line between Edmonton and Calgary and a pipeline from Alberta to the Pacific Ocean are among 167 possible investment opportunities Prime Minister Mark Carney will show off at next week's investment summit in Toronto.

The projects are outlined in a 66-page "prospectus" obtained by CBC News, which gives the most detailed look yet at the investment opportunities Ottawa and Canadian business leaders plan to showcase at the summit.

The Sept. 14 and 15 gathering, hosted by the prime minister in partnership with the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Public Sector Pension Investment Board, will bring together deep-pocketed international investors and Canadian business leaders in hopes of drumming up $1 trillion in investment.

CBC News previously reported that invitations went out to some of the world's biggest investment firms and sovereign wealth funds as part of a broader push to attract capital at a time of trade upheaval and geopolitical uncertainty.

With the U.S.-Canada trade war escalating, the government is also under pressure to deepen economic ties beyond the United States.

The document groups the pitches into eight areas of investment: 11 conventional energy projects, 31 clean energy projects, 63 in mining and metals, 16 in marine and port infrastructure, 11 in power and utilities, 10 in digital technology, 19 in advanced manufacturing and six transportation projects.

Each pitch highlights the project's current stage, the capital expenditure needed and the kind of investment being sought to help it get built.

Some of the priciest projects on the list include a $57-billion US expansion of the Port of Churchill; a $44-billion investment in Nova Scotia's Wind West offshore wind project, led by the province; the proposed $35-billion West Coast oil pipeline, which would carry oil from Alberta to B.C.'s coast; and the $28.5-billion Ksi Lisims LNG terminal project.

WATCH | Canada reaches large-scale deal to export LNG to Germany: Canada reaches large-scale deal to export LNG to Germany: sources | Duration 1:43 Sources have told CBC News that the federal government will be announcing a large-scale deal to export liquified natural gas from B.C’s northwest coast to Germany.

Other projects include a float glass manufacturing facility in Manitoba, expanded manufacturing capacity for night-vision technology used in defence and satellite technology for Earth observation, along with the long list of infrastructure projects.

Absent from the list are the Alto high-speed rail project, which would run between Toronto and Quebec City and has received pushback over the land expropriation it would require, and any plans to privatize airports, which Carney's government has been weighing .

Some projects are also closer to reality than others. The Ksi Lisims project, for example, is described as "fully permitted and shovel ready," while a critical-mineral graphite project in Saskatchewan is listed as being in the preliminary stages of economic and environmental assessment.

The prospectus spells out plans for a $57-billion US expansion to the Port of Churchill. Upgrades to Canada's only deepwater Arctic seaport would include a liquefied natural gas (LNG) export corridor, rail upgrades and other modernization aimed at establishing a "four-season trade gateway."

For Alberta, the prospectus spells out a $10.9-billion plan for a high-speed passenger rail line linking Calgary and Edmonton. The document says trains would reach speeds of more than 300 kilometres per hour, completing the trip in about 90 minutes.

For the oil and gas sector, plans include a $35-billion, 1,250-kilometre-long oil pipeline connecting Alberta crude production to a deepwater export terminal in southern British Columbia.

The document also includes a $2.1-billion US proposal for Calgary-based South Bow's Prairie Connector pipeline expansion. The proposal would add 380 kilometres of new pipeline to transport Canadian crude to U.S. refining markets in the Midwest. Prairie Connector would use parts of the cancelled Keystone XL pipeline previously built on the Canadian side of the border.

A grain vessel at the Port of Churchill on Monday, Aug. 31. An expansion of the port is one of the projects included in the prospectus for the summit. (Josh Crabb/CBC)

For natural gas, the document includes a $28.5-billion pitch for the floating Ksi Lisims LNG export facility on the B.C. coast. Currently, 99 per cent of Canada's natural gas exports are destined for the United States . Amid ongoing trade tension, Carney's government has sought to diversify the pool of buyers for Canada's energy exports.

In clean energy, the federal government is attempting to sell investors on access to "the world's cleanest and most reliable energy systems." Proposals span nuclear power generation in New Brunswick, carbon capture in Saskatchewan and wind power and green hydrogen in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Aside from natural resources and hard infrastructure, the document frames Canada as a pioneer in artificial intelligence, with a national strategy dating back to 2017.

World.title: Generic acetaminophen pills recalled due to possible 'foreign material' contamination
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An over-the-counter pain reliever is being recalled due to the possible presence of "foreign material" that could harm the digestive system.

Teva Canada is recalling a lot of 500-milligram Nov-Gesic Forte acetaminophen "due to the potential presence of phenolic resin or epoxy," according to a Thursday news release from Health Canada.

Health Canada says the pills from Lot No. 100083040, with the expiration date of Jan. 31, 2029, were supplied to pharmacies in 1,000-count bottles and dispensed to patients in smaller quantities.

"Immediately stop using the affected product and return it to your local pharmacy for replacement and proper disposal," the release states. "If you are unsure whether your product is recalled, check with your pharmacy."

The agency says anyone who has used the affected product and has concerns about their health should contact their health-care practitioner, and should report any product-related side effects or complaints to Health Canada.

Customers can also contact Teva Canada Customer Care by calling 1-800-268-4129 or emailing customer.service@tevacanada.com.

World.title: Colombia announces new aerial fumigation pilot program
World.content:
Colombia’s National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine.

In a resolution, the CNE ordered “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

In a public statement, the National Police’s counternarcotics unit said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo and would not affect indigenous and afro-descendant communities, who would need to be asked permission.

The exclusion of environmental protection zones and protected areas, zones associated with bodies of water, rivers, and other environmentally sensitive areas is contemplated, as well as those territories that, in accordance with current regulations and the corresponding technical studies, must be excluded. National Police Counternarcotics

The purpose of the pilot program is to “evaluate the effectiveness of aerial spraying, as well as its application under the established technical and operational conditions, said the police.

The police stressed that “this experimental phase does not constitute the resumption, adoption, or definitive authorization of a widespread or nationwide aerial spraying program,” which was banned by the Constitutional Court in 2015.

In order to resume aerial fumigation, health and environmental authorities must sign off on the program and the police would only be allowed to use airplanes with the approval of the court and local communities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella vowed to resume aerial spraying more than 330,000 hectares while on campaign and after taking office last month as part of his hardline approach to organized crime.

Former President Ivan Duque also vowed to resume aerial spraying, but failed to comply with the norms established by the court.

World.title: Court orders Colombia’s government to remove images of slain “narcoterrorists”
World.content:
A Bogota judge ordered Colombia’s government to remove images and videos of President Abelardo de la Espriella walking through the remains of slain suspected guerrillas from its social media accounts.

The judge also ordered the government to remove images and videos of the body bags containing the lifeless remains of four members of organized crime group ACSN who were killed in La Guajira.

According to the judge, the images could be harmful to minors.

The decision was celebrated by congressman Santiago Osorio (Green Alliance), who sued the government over the controversial social media posts.

The State and the National Government cannot engage in a contest with crime to see which of the two is the most cruel; in this regard, the Office of the President of the Republic, Mr. Abelardo de la Espriella, were ordered to promptly remove images that may have reached the cell phones of children across the country, showing a state displaying corpses as trophies. Congressman Santiago Osorio

Th publications were previously rejected by the Ombudsman’s Office, whose director, Iris Marin, urged the government not to “compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power.”

In the first video, De la Espriella and Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora walked through rows of body bags, displaying the remains of 23 alleged members of FARC dissident organizations EMC who were killed in the southern Guaviare province.

Among those killed in Operation Azarias were two minor victims of forced recruitment by the guerrillas.

The videos sought to promote the government’s hardline security policy, which vows to kill “narcoterrorists” who refuse to surrender.

World.title: US, Colombia sign memorandums of understanding amid “rebirth” of relations
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the “rebirth” of bilateral relations as they signed memorandums of understanding on nuclear energy and rare earths.

The two leaders met in Barranquilla, where De la Espriella lives, as part of Rubio’s tour through allied countries in the Andean region.

The president and the secretary of state hailed the improvement of ties that were severely disrupted when former President Gustavo Petro was in office.

During a joint press conference, Rubio stressed the need for security in the region, claiming that “the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people.”

De la Espriella said that as part of the “Barranquilla Agreements,” he asked the US for support for his hardline security policy.

We have proposed to the government—and today I reiterated this proposal to the secretary—the 21st-Century Patriot Plan to modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president promised to “start spraying, we are going to target the laboratories, the precursors, the trafficking routes, the drug trafficking kingpins, the armed narco-terrorist organizations—we are going after the money launderers, their criminal assets, and those international networks that pose a grave danger not only to the hemisphere but also to humanity.”

Rubio did not openly commit any US support other than the memorandums of understanding.

The unbinding agreements were part of Rubio’s wish list as the US seeks new sources for rare earths and miners that can be processed outside of China, which the US Government sees as its rival.

With the nuclear energy agenda, Colombia seeks to “strengthen its capacities” with US support. Both governments “reaffirm their commitment to international development and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.”

In order to create policy regarding the memorandums, De la Espriella would need congressional support, which he has yet to seek openly.

World.title: De la Espriella lifts Colombia’s 10-year gun ban
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella lifted a gun ban that had been in place since 2015.

According to De la Espriella, the decision seeks to give “good citizens” a way to defend themselves against “criminals.”

“For years, law-abiding citizens were restricted, while criminals continued to arm themselves to the teeth illegally. That has to change,” said the president on social media platform X.

99.9% of crimes committed with weapons are committed with unlicensed, illegal weapons. Anything said beyond the mathematics is just opinion. Mathematics is an exact science. So I am pleased to sign this decree. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president said that those who want to carry guns legally must comply with strict regulations and can’t have criminal records.

The ban reactivates previously approved gun licenses and allows citizens older than 25 to purchase approved hand guns from Colombia’s State military industry.

In order to be given a license, a potential gun owner must undergo fitness tests and convince the military authority that his position in society merits a firearm.

The decision has long been awaited by conservative and far-right elements in society, who have claimed that the gun ban made them sitting ducks for extortionists, particularly in the countryside.

Experts consulted by newspaper El Colombiano warned that lifting the gun ban could increase deadly violence, particularly considering Colombia’s violent history and evidence obtained in countries where guns are legal.

“There is no evidence showing that these countries have seen a decrease in theft, extortion, and threats following these measures,” said the director of the Central University’s Security Observatory, Andres Nieto. “On the contrary, the evidence does show an increase in violence among citizens,” the scholar added.

The ban was initially imposed by former President Juan Manuel Santos in 2015 and has since been upheld by his successors.

World.title: Liberal Party joins Colombia’s far-right to form majority coalition
World.content:
The Liberal Party announced that it had joined the congressional coalition of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The party, which also supported De la Espriella’s presidential bid, said that it would join the coalition after “extensive deliberation and arduous debate among representatives, senators, and leadership” of Colombia’s oldest political party.

It is worth noting that the discussions between representatives and senators over the past several weeks have revealed disagreements among some members of our caucuses with the current administration, but they also acknowledge President Espriella’s ability to work toward stimulating economic growth, building a talent pool to provide real opportunities for Colombians, and restoring security and respect for institutions. Liberal Party

The liberals’ decision gives the government broad support in Congress and marginalizes the opposition led by the leftist Historic Pact Party.

In the senate, De la Espriella’s right-wing coalition can count on the support of 63 of 103 lawmakers. In the House of Representatives, the coalition consists of 123 of 183 lawmakers.

The Historic Pact, which won the elections and became the biggest party in Congress, was abandoned by the left-liberal Green Alliance party and can count of the support of 28 senators and 44 representatives.

The opposition party has been able to make temporary anti-government alliances with, for example, the far-right Democratic Center party of former President Alvaro Uribe.

World.title: Colombia’s president appoints controversial new spy chief
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella appointed retired army General Jorge Andres Zuluaga as director of the National Intelligence Directorate (DNI) despite pending criminal investigations.

Zuluaga, who spent 30 years with military intelligence, is best known for his participation in Operation Jaque, which liberated former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, three American military contractors and 11 soldiers.

Throughout his career, the 61-year-old former general was deputy commander of the now-defunct Charry Solano intelligence school, commander of the Regional Intelligence #5 and the director of the National Army’s Technical Intelligence Center (CITEC).

Zuluaga received training in the United States and was a diplomatic aide at the Organization of American States.

He was removed as CITEC director in 2014 after prosecution investigators found out that he received intelligence illegally obtained from “Andromeda,” a clandestine intelligence unit that operated from a Bogota internet café.

In October 2024, war crimes tribunal JEP ordered the Prosecutor General’s Office to investigate Zuluaga for his alleged participation in the extermination of the leftist Patriotic Union party when he was the CITEC’s director between 2004 and 2005.

The prosecution has yet to decide whether or not to formally charge the retired general with the crimes he allegedly committed.

Zuluaga, who became a member of the far-right Democratic Center party after he was ejected from the army, has always sustained that he acted within the boundaries of the law.

World.title: Colombia’s government clashes with ombudsman over De la Espriella walking among corpses
World.content:
Colombia’s chief ombudsman, Iris Marin, clashed with the national government after she criticized President Abelardo de la Espriella for walking among the corpses of people killed by the military.

In a public statement, Marin reiterated that “in recent days, we saw the president of the Republic walking among the bodies—in white body bags—of people who were killed during Operation “Azarías” in Guaviare.”

“I don’t recall ever seeing a president walking among the dead and taking pride in those deaths,” said the ombudsman, whose office is independent from the government.

The state and the government cannot allow themselves to be drawn into a competition to see who can be the cruelest. They cannot compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power. Ombudsman Iris Marin

According to Marin, the military has the right to kill citizens, but must do so with respect for the Constitution and International Humanitarian Law, and is responsible for “the way that the State exercizes power and communicates its results.”

In a response, Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara said that the Ombudman falsely equated the State with “narcoterrorist groups as if it wer competing with them in cruelty.”

“Such an equivalence is inappropriate,” said Lara and called on the Ombudsman’s Office to be “an ally of the victims and of our mission to protect them and to liberate them from the terror regime of crime.”

Marin told Lara that she trusted that “the President and the Government will reflect on the way they communicate operational results, as I requested in my statement.”

De la Espriella’s stroll through the 23 body bags, including those of two minors, was also fiercely criticized in independent and foreign media.
