Kenya’s Konza Technopolis was meant to be Africa’s “Silicon Savannah,” a 2,024-hectare smart city rising from the plains south of Nairobi. Nearly two decades after its 2008 launch, the project has become a case study in how smart cities are financed, and who holds the power.

A flagship project with a US$14.5 billion price tag

Konza Technopolis is a Kenya Vision 2030 flagship, planned as a hub for technology, research and digital government. The estimated total project cost is about US$14.5 billion, a figure that dwarfs Kenya’s annual infrastructure budgets.

Phase 1 horizontal infrastructure began in June 2017 under an Engineering, Procurement, Construction and Financing agreement with Italy’s UniCredit SpA. That contract was valued at roughly KSh 50.4 billion (about US$391 million).

The Italian financing covered the physical groundwork: roads, drainage, water and power corridors. It signalled that European capital still had a role in Africa’s urban future, even as other players moved in.

Chinese credit and the Digital Silk Road

The smart-city core systems tell a different story. The National Cloud Data Centre, smart ICT network, public “safe city” surveillance, smart traffic and government cloud were contracted to Huawei in 2017.

Funding came from a China Eximbank concessional loan of RMB 1.225 billion, signed on 26 April 2019. At the time, that was roughly KSh 17 billion, or about US$172–175 million.

The loan terms are generous but binding: 2% interest, a 19.5-year maturity to 21 September 2038, a 7-year grace period and a 0.5% commitment fee. By 2022, disbursements had exceeded RMB 470 million, with an outstanding balance above RMB 600 million.

China also finances the 400kV Konza substation to guarantee power for the technopolis. This places Konza firmly inside Beijing’s Digital Silk Road, where smart-city systems and surveillance platforms are exported via Huawei and other state-owned enterprises.

The shift to public-private partnerships and local capital

From 2025–26, Kenya’s Treasury began turning to public-private partnerships and domestic capital to ease fiscal pressure. In the 2025–26 financial year, KSh 3.1 billion (about US$24 million) was budgeted for smart cities and the existing data-centre footprint.

In December 2025, the PPP Unit approved a Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer expansion model for the Konza cloud and smart-city facilities. Requests for proposals issued in March–April 2026 explicitly seek local debt and equity, alongside “optional stapled-financing structures.”

Core infrastructure remains in state ownership under the PPP Act 2021 and the Public Finance Management Act 2012. The goal is to blend Chinese concessional credit, Western and multilateral funding, PPPs and local capital markets without surrendering digital sovereignty to any single external power.

Guodong Network and the next phase

In August 2026, Konza signed a framework with China’s Guodong Network. The proposed programme is valued at KSh 38.8 billion, or about US$300 million, covering towers, smart cities, data centres, fibre and cloud.

Kenya has also discussed hosting Guodong’s Africa headquarters. That would deepen the Chinese footprint in Kenya’s digital backbone, even as Nairobi courts European and domestic investors.

The Guodong deal shows how smart-city finance is becoming more layered. A single project now mixes Italian engineering, Chinese concessional loans, PPP structures and potential green bonds.

What smarter finance actually means

For Africa’s smart cities, smarter finance means blending Chinese concessional credit, Western and multilateral funding, PPPs, local capital markets and strong governance. The alternative is fiscal strain and digital dependence on one external power.

Kenya’s experience at Konza is a warning and a template. Low-conditionality Chinese loans and bundled technology give Beijing sway over data, security and standards.

Italy’s UniCredit and the new PPP structures signal European and domestic attempts to rebalance the financial centre of gravity. Whether that rebalancing succeeds will shape not just Konza, but every smart city planned across the continent.

The broader contest for Africa’s digital infrastructure is part of the story covered in Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

The next test is whether the Guodong Network framework translates into signed contracts and disbursed capital. Kenya’s Treasury will also need to show that PPP-driven expansion can attract local debt and equity without stalling.

Investors should watch the China Eximbank repayment schedule, which runs to 21 September 2038. Every disbursement deepens Kenya’s exposure, while every PPP approval tests whether domestic capital can share the load.

The lesson from Konza is already clear: smart cities are not just engineering projects. They are financial and geopolitical bets, and the terms of those bets will determine who controls Africa’s urban data.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Konza Technopolis? Konza Technopolis is a 2,024-hectare smart city in Kenya, launched in 2008 as a Kenya Vision 2030 flagship. It is planned as an “African Silicon Savannah” with an estimated total project cost of about US$14.5 billion. Who is financing Kenya’s Konza smart city? Phase 1 infrastructure was financed by Italy’s UniCredit SpA at roughly KSh 50.4 billion (about US$391 million). Core smart-city systems were built by Huawei under a China Eximbank loan of RMB 1.225 billion (about US$172 million) signed on 26 April 2019. What is Kenya doing to reduce reliance on Chinese loans for Konza? Kenya’s PPP Unit approved a Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer expansion model in December 2025. Requests for proposals issued in March–April 2026 seek local debt and equity, while core infrastructure remains in state ownership.

World.title: Billfish: Another Step Forward in the Eastern Tropical Pacific
World.content:
Some important decisions arrive with headlines, prohibitions, and grand speeches. Others seem much more modest. Last week in Lisbon, we saw one of the latter.

I participated as an observer representing FECOP at the 104th Meeting of the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission (IATTC). Amid discussions about tuna, sharks, bycatch, and other species that cross borders without asking permission, Central America managed to open a specific path forward on something many of us have been saying for years about billfish in the Eastern Tropical Pacific, we need to understand them better. It sounds like a simple conclusion. It is not.

Sailfish, marlins, and swordfish are highly migratory species. In a matter of weeks, they can move through the waters of several countries. They interact with industrial, artisanal, coastal, recreational, and sport fisheries. Some of these species also support an important tourism economy that sustains captains, crews, marinas, hotels, restaurants, transportation services, and coastal communities. Trying to manage them using information from only one country or one fishery is like trying to understand a movie by watching only a few scenes. That has been precisely one of our problems.

Information on billfish in the Eastern Tropical Pacific exists, but much of it remains fragmented. There are still gaps in catch and effort data, biological information, monitoring and data verification, post-release mortality, and our understanding of how different fisheries interact with these species. The proposal presented in Lisbon itself recognized many of these limitations.

For years, pieces that were once scattered have gradually been coming together. At FECOP, working alongside scientific partners and the sportfishing sector itself, we have sought to turn fishing records into useful information to better understand billfish.

Collaborations with researchers from Stanford University, for example, demonstrated the value of recreational fishing records from Costa Rica, Guatemala, and Panama for studying the occurrence of sailfish and blue marlin and their relationship with changing ocean conditions. We have also used historical data generated by sportfishing operations to examine changes in the local abundance of sailfish along Costa Rica’s Pacific coast.

Regional initiatives have added another layer to these efforts. The Pacífico Sostenible project, working with OSPESCA, governments, and private-sector actors, developed a regional pilot focused on recreational fisheries for sailfish and marlin. That process reached a conclusion that is particularly relevant to what later happened in Lisbon, our region needs to strengthen the collection, analysis, and standardization of data generated by recreational fisheries, and we need to do it in a coordinated way across countries and sectors.

An important change has also been taking place within the private sector. Sportfishing organizations in Central America have increasingly understood that asking governments to recognize the economic contribution of our activity is not enough. If we want to participate seriously in conversations about fisherie management, we also have a responsibility to help generate the information needed to make better decisions.

That principle has been part of the work of CASA, the Central America Sportfishing Alliance. Its 2026 agenda placed science and conservation among its strategic priorities and called for progress on regional information about sailfish and the creation of scientific spaces dedicated to billfish. This matters because fisheries discussions have too often fallen into a comfortable trap, each sector arrives at the table with its own numbers, its own experiences and, of course, its own certainties.

Science should help us get out of that trap.

In June 2026, the IATTC Scientific Advisory Committee recommended developing a work plan for billfish data collection and stock assessments, including the costs, staffing needs, and potential sources of external funding required to carry it out. Two months later, Panama, supported by Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua, arrived in Lisbon with a proposal to establish a specialized scientific working group on billfish.

What was ultimately agreed was more gradual, in 2027, a specialized workshop will be held to identify the main information and research gaps, establish priorities, and develop a draft work plan that will later be considered by the IATTC Scientific Advisory Committee. Is that enough? No. Is it important? Absolutely.

For the first time, a clear institutional pathway is opening to turn a concern that different actors have raised for years into scientific questions, research priorities and, eventually, better management decisions. And this is where we also need to accept our share of the responsibility.

Sportfishing holds something extremely valuable for science, thousands of days at sea, encounters with fish, locations, dates, sizes, ocean conditions, fishing effort, and releases. Much of that information is still lost or remains scattered across logbooks, phones, applications, databases, and the memories of captains. Turning that accumulated experience into useful scientific data must be part of the next stage.

But the same must happen with every fishery that interacts with billfish. This is not about proving in advance who is right. It is about building the information that will allow us to find out. That is why I left Lisbon thinking that perhaps the most important progress made at this meeting was the recognition of something quite basic, before we argue over the answers, we first need to agree on the questions.

Sailfish and marlins have been crossing the Pacific for millions of years without recognizing our borders, institutions, or sectoral differences. Perhaps it is time we learned to do the same.



Damián Martínez Fernández

Director de conservación y política pública Federación Costarricense de Pesca FECOP

World.title: Costa Rica Braces for Higher Fuel Prices as Oil Climbs Back Above $100
World.content:
Global oil prices climbed back above $100 a barrel this week, and the increase is on course to reach Costa Rica’s gas stations within weeks. Brent crude, the international benchmark, settled at $101.21 yesterday after a 3.4 percent single-session gain. West Texas Intermediate settled at $96.05.

The trigger was a fresh escalation in the US-Iran conflict, now in its seventh month. US Central Command said American forces destroyed five Iranian crude tankers on Tuesday after attempted attacks on a US warship. A senior Iranian official, speaking to Bloomberg on condition of anonymity, said Tehran was ready for a more intense war rather than back down in the face of the US naval blockade.

The rally is not new territory for this conflict as Brent traded around $72 a barrel on February 27, the day before the war began, and peaked above $126 at the end of April. By early July it had slid back to pre-war levels, and this week’s climb leaves it roughly 40 percent above where it started.

It also runs ahead of official projections. In its outlook released yesterday, the US Energy Information Administration forecast that Brent would average around $90 a barrel in the second half of 2026, already $8 higher than a month earlier. The agency noted that attacks on Saudi shipments through the Bab el-Mandeb strait had cut exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu by about half in August.

Costa Rica imports all of its fuel through the state refiner Recope, leaving it directly exposed. The Regulatory Authority for Public Services (Aresep) sets pump prices monthly from Recope’s actual purchase invoices. International swings therefore reach consumers roughly one to two months later.

That lag explains why the adjustment Aresep approved on Tuesday moved in two directions. Regular gasoline falls ₡51 to ₡707 per liter (about $5.95 a gallon), while super rises ₡22 to ₡726 (about $6.11 a gallon). Diesel jumps ₡82 to ₡688 (about $5.79 a gallon), and the new prices take effect once published in the official gazette La Gaceta.

None of that reflects this week’s spike. Aresep’s monthly review opens on the second Friday of each month, which puts the next one on Friday, September 11, with new prices expected in early October. Based on the timing of previous reviews, it would capture fuel bought as prices rose through August, when Brent averaged $91 according to the EIA.

If crude holds near current levels, the following adjustment, due at the pump in November, would carry a full month of triple-digit oil. That would affect gasoline, diesel and liquefied petroleum gas alike.

The last spike shows how sharp the pass-through can be. The adjustment approved at the end of April, based on shipments from March 13 to April 9, raised diesel from ₡564 to ₡716 per liter and regular gasoline from ₡625 to ₡748. Energy Intendant Mario Mora attributed that increase directly to the Middle East conflict.

A stronger colón offers limited protection this time. The currency has gained about 6 percent against the dollar since early March, a fraction of the rise in crude over the same period. Its larger appreciation since 2022 cushioned gradual fuel increases but cannot absorb a shock of this size.

The stakes extend beyond the pump as the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC) reported year-on-year deflation of 0.17 percent in August, the 16th consecutive negative reading. Consumer prices have now run below the Central Bank’s 2 to 4 percent target range for 40 straight months.

Fuel has been central to that trend since INEC listed gasoline and diesel among the items that pulled prices down most in August. A sustained oil shock would turn fuel from a drag on prices into a source of upward pressure.

Transport costs are already moving in some categories. International airfares were among the things whose prices rose most in August, according to INEC, and airlines typically pass jet fuel costs through to fares. Higher diesel prices also raise costs for freight, public buses and tourism transport.

How long prices stay elevated depends on events in the Middle East. US President Donald Trump said this week the conflict would not end before the November midterm elections and that significant relief at the gas pump was unlikely before then. Goldman Sachs has warned Brent could exceed $120 a barrel if Gulf output stays well below pre-war levels, though that is not its base case. A de-escalation could pull prices down as quickly as they fell after the April peak.

World.title: Costa Rica Immigration Worker Arrested in Residency Scheme
World.content:
An employee of Costa Rica’s immigration agency was arrested this morning on suspicion of manipulating official records to push through a residency card renewal for the partner of an alleged leader of a criminal organization operating in Limón. The Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería said its Policía Profesional de Migración detained the woman, a Costa Rican national surnamed Blandón Reyes, and carried out two simultaneous raids in Limón province. One targeted the agency’s Atlantic regional office, where she worked, and the other her home.

According to the agency, the investigation indicates the employee used the functions assigned to her post to enter documents and false data into the institution’s systems. The purpose, investigators allege, was to complete the renewal of a DIMEX residency card for a Nicaraguan woman surnamed White Rankin, who was entering Costa Rica at the time.

The documents allegedly entered relate to a criminal background record, or hoja de delincuencia, a standard requirement in residency filings. Migración said White Rankin is believed to be in a romantic relationship with a man surnamed Herrera Hernández, whom authorities identify as one of the leaders of “La H,” also known as “Los Hondureños.”

The agency describes it as a transnational criminal organization linked to drug trafficking and a series of homicides in Limón. Following her arrest, Blandón Reyes was transferred to the Ministerio Público at the Second Judicial Circuit in San José, where prosecutors will determine her legal status. No charges had been announced as of Thursday morning, and she has not been convicted of any offense.

The arrest adds to a pattern of alleged misconduct inside the immigration service this year. In July, prosecutors from the anti-corruption unit detained a Migración officer surnamed Barquero at Juan Santamaría International Airport in San Jose on suspicion of simulating the formal entry of a foreign national whom intelligence reports linked to an international terrorist organization. A court later ordered precautionary measures against her, including a 10-month suspension from her post.

Chief Prosecutor Carlo Díaz said this week that the infiltration of drug trafficking networks into public institutions is a documented reality, noting that one of the 23 Costa Ricans detained for extradition in the first phase of a joint effort with U.S. authorities was a former police officer. He announced that the Ministerio Público has prepared procedures for a second phase that could reach officials protected by immunity, though no such request currently exists.

The investigation into La H has intensified in recent months. Prosecutors previously confirmed six raids in Limón as part of the case, amid questions about whether the group had stockpiled assault rifles and whether some of its leaders had already left the country.

The DIMEX is the identity document issued to every foreign resident of Costa Rica, and its renewal depends on the same regional offices and internal systems at the center of Thursday’s investigation. The Ministerio Público has not indicated when it will present its request for precautionary measures.

World.title: Magnitude 5.3 Costa Rica Earthquake Shakes The Southern Pacific Before Dawn
World.content:
A magnitude 5.3 earthquake shook the southern Pacific region of Costa Rica early this morning, surprising residents there and in parts of the Central Valley. The Volcanological and Seismological Observatory of Costa Rica (Ovsicori) at the National University (UNA) recorded the quake at 2:26 a.m. The observatory put the epicenter 53 kilometers (33 miles) southeast of Uvita, Puntarenas, at a depth of 14 kilometers (8.7 miles).

The National Seismological Network (RSN) at the University of Costa Rica reported a magnitude of 5.2 and placed the epicenter 50 kilometers (31 miles) south of Dominical. Both of these numbers are preliminary so differences like these between the two networks are routine. For example, after a quake near Coronado last month, RSN seismologist Lepolt Linkimer explained that each network calculates magnitude from its own set of stations, so readings for the same event can vary slightly without either being wrong.



Residents of Pérez Zeledón, Coronado, San José and Heredia, along with those in the Central Pacific, reported on social media that they felt the shaking. Most described it as light and several people said an earthquake early-warning alert sounded on their phones a few seconds before the movement reached them.

Smaller quakes kept being felt in the same area in the hours that followed and Ovsicori kept the area under close monitoring. At 4:38 a.m., the observatory’s automatic system noted a magnitude 4.5 event about 52 kilometers (32 miles) southeast of Uvita. A separate Ovsicori reading put that event at magnitude 4.2, at a depth of 11.9 kilometers (7.4 miles).

Thankfully, no damage or injuries had been reported as of this writing but the National Emergency Commission (CNE) did report a landslide on a road and minor damage to some structures afterwards. Ovsicori seismologist Marino Protti has previously said that the contact between the plates in this region is relatively weak, and that quakes of this size occur there several times a year.

Anyone who notices new cracks in walls or ceilings, or smells gas, should report it through the 9-1-1 emergency line. Ovsicori also collects public felt reports on its website as these help seismologists map how strongly a quake was experienced.

World.title: Senator Wade defends vote on MCC compact bills
World.content:
Senator Wade defends vote on MCC compact bills

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Senator Louis Wade Jr. has publicly defended his vote in favour of the legislation tied to Belize’s Millennium Challenge Corporation compact.

In a social media post, Wade said the United States is providing US$125 million to Belize in exchange for several legislative commitments.

Those include raising the school leaving age from 14 to 16, introducing national assessment so student performance can be tracked, and restructuring vocational and technical schools to create a standardised qualification for people who study trades.

On the electricity side, Wade said the compact would fund a cable connecting San Pedro, which generates the most expensive electricity in the country, to the cheaper mainland supply.

“In MY OPINION no one needed to pay us to do what is in OUR BEST INTEREST,” he wrote. “So you would really vote against all that?”

Wade said he voted yes alongside all PUP and all UDP senators, while his fellow independent senators chose to abstain.

He added that he and other church leaders negotiated commitments to changes in the Education and TVET bills.

“We love sensational news, without a love for facts,” his post concludes.

World.title: Shyne and 50 Cent bury old feud as rapper turned politician earns public praise
World.content:
Shyne and 50 Cent bury old feud as rapper turned politician earns public praise

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Shyne Barrow’s return to the United States continues to generate attention, this time after a surprise reunion with longtime rival 50 Cent in Miami.

The encounter took place at Serafina, where both men were dining separately before being introduced again.

50 Cent later praised Shyne publicly, saying he was impressed by his growth and referring to him as a “world leader.”

The comments stand in sharp contrast to the pair’s history.

Their feud dates back to the early 2000s, when 50 Cent took aim at Shyne while he was incarcerated. Shyne later responded with the track “For the Record,” and the tension continued for years.

Now, the tone is completely different.

Shyne said he views himself as an elder statesman and believes his role should be about bringing people together rather than carrying old grudges.

He said he has offered olive branches to former rivals and described the reunion with 50 Cent as a sign of maturity and evolution within hip hop.

The meeting also comes as Shyne continues to straddle two worlds, music and politics, with his Belizean leadership role now forming a major part of his international identity.

What was once a feud has now turned into a public show of respect.

World.title: 50 Cent says he wants to visit Belize after making peace with Shyne
World.content:
50 Cent says he wants to visit Belize after making peace with Shyne

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): American rap superstar 50 Cent could be heading to Belize after publicly expressing interest in visiting the country following his reconciliation with former rival Shyne Barrow.

50 Cent made the comment on Instagram while reacting to Shyne discussing their recent reunion and the end of their decades old feud.

The G Unit frontman praised Shyne’s transformation over the years, writing that the Belizean politician had impressed him.

“I’m not gonna front shyne impresses me,” 50 Cent wrote. “world leader, he shown nothing but growth.”

But it was what came next that could generate even more attention in Belize.

“When I get some free time I’ll come to your country,” 50 Cent added.

The comments follow a chance reunion between the two former rivals in Miami, where they reportedly crossed paths while dining at Serafina.

Shyne has since described the encounter as an example of his effort to extend olive branches to people with whom he previously had disagreements.

The relationship between Shyne and 50 Cent was once very different. Their feud stretched back to the early 2000s, when the two exchanged lyrical attacks and public jabs.

More than two decades later, 50 Cent is now publicly praising Shyne and talking about coming to Belize.

No date or formal plans for a Belize visit have been announced, and 50 Cent’s Instagram comment does not confirm that a trip has been scheduled.

Still, the possibility of one of hip hop’s biggest stars visiting Belize following the reconciliation is likely to generate plenty of attention locally.

World.title: Armed robbers hit San Roman Shopping Mall and escape in white SUV
World.content:
Armed robbers hit San Roman Shopping Mall and escape in white SUV

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police are investigating an armed robbery at the San Roman Shopping Mall in the Stann Creek District where two masked men reportedly held up the store owner at gunpoint.

According to police information, officers responded to the business at around 11:35 a.m. on Thursday, September 10, after receiving reports of an armed robbery.

The store owner told police that at approximately 11:15 a.m., two masked men armed with pistol type firearms entered the establishment and held him at gunpoint.

The men then reportedly took an undisclosed amount of cash from the register.

They also stole a black iPhone 16 Pro Max valued at $2,500.

Police say the robbers fled the area in a white Nissan SUV.

No one was injured during the incident.

Investigators visited and processed the scene and reviewed surveillance footage from the area.

Police are continuing their investigation.

World.title: The most consequential election for Belize this year is one no Belizean can vote in
World.content:
The most consequential election for Belize this year is one no Belizean can vote in

By Horace Palacio:

Eight weeks from now, on November 3, an election will be held that will help decide your grocery bill, your light of employment in tourism, and the remittance envelope your family receives from abroad.

You are not invited.

Americans will elect a new Congress that day, every House seat, a third of the Senate, and this newspaper’s news pages have laid out the four channels through which their choice reaches Belizean kitchens, the tourists, the imports, the remittances, the aid. Read that piece for the machinery. This column is here for the meaning, because there is a lesson inside November 3 that stings more than any tariff.

Here it is. Measure how much a foreign election matters to your household, and you have measured, to the decimal point, how sovereign your country actually is.

Call it the exposure index. A fully sovereign nation reads foreign elections the way it reads foreign weather reports, with interest, not anxiety. A dependent nation reads them the way a tenant reads the landlord’s moods. So take Belize’s reading honestly. Seven of every ten visitors who fund our biggest industry carry American passports. More than four of every ten dollars of goods on our shelves arrive from American suppliers. Our families’ lifeline flows from American cities, and our own budget speech already recorded remittances dipping as American migration politics shifted. And beneath it all, our very dollar is the American dollar’s shadow, pegged two to one, importing their inflation without a customs check.

Add it up and face the conclusion like adults. The American voter, a stranger in Ohio who has never heard of Belize and could not place us on a map, sits, functionally, on every Belizean household’s budget committee for the next two years. Unelected by us. Unremovable by us. Deciding, in aggregate, more about the price of our month than most decisions taken in Belmopan.

I wrote a column asking Belizeans to count the kings who actually rule us. Add one more to the census, the American electorate. It reigns over a corner of every Belizean ledger, and on November 3 it holds court.

Now, before anyone reaches for anger, aim it correctly, because there is no villain in Washington here. Americans voting their own interests in their own election owe Belize nothing. That is what elections are for. The wire that runs from their ballot box to your kitchen was not laid by them.

It was laid by us. Wire by wire, decade by decade. Every year we chose imports over production, we laid wire. Every season we marketed to one tourist and ignored the world’s other calendars, we laid wire. Every megawatt we failed to build at home, every export we never shipped, every skill we never trained, wire, wire, wire. Dependence is never an event, my friends. It is an accumulation of small, comfortable choices, and November 3 is simply the day the accumulated wiring hums loud enough to hear.

So what does a serious small nation do with a foreign election it cannot vote in? Three things.

First, watch it like a farmer, not a fan. The farmer does not cheer for rain or curse the drought. He reads the sky and moves early. Whatever November produces, a Congress that squeezes American wallets, a trade fight that lifts prices, an enforcement wave that thins remittances, the Belizean response is the same hedging this column has preached all year. The second tourism market courted now. The export push now. The food grown here now. Every one of those is a levee, and levees are built before the water rises.

Second, run the same audit at home. The household exposed to one employer, one income, one customer, lives at the mercy of moods it cannot vote on, exactly like the nation. The ownership gospel, the skill, the side trade, the titled lot, the shares, is how a family lowers its personal exposure index. Sovereignty, it turns out, is fractal. It is built at the kitchen table with the same materials as at the treasury.

And third, give the country its number. Publish the exposure index alongside the national scorecard this column has demanded, the share of visitors from our top market, the share of imports from our top supplier, the share of household income arriving as remittances. Three numbers, tracked yearly. Not to shame the present, but to steer the decade, because a dependence you measure is a dependence you can shrink, and one you refuse to measure is one you have chosen to keep.

Here, then, is the finish line, and I want every reader to memorize it, because it is the most precise definition of national success this column can offer.

Belize will know it has arrived on the day an American midterm election becomes merely interesting to us instead of consequential. The day we read their results over coffee the way a well-built house hears a storm, aware, unafraid, dry. That day is not granted by anyone. It is constructed, export by export, megawatt by megawatt, market by market, skill by skill.

Americans vote on November 3, once, for their future.

Belize votes every single day, in what it builds or fails to build, for whether their future keeps writing ours.

They will count their ballots in one night.

Ours are counted over a generation. Cast today’s well.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: International News: US Secretary of State ends Latin America tour with push for stronger Regional Security
World.content:
International News: US Secretary of State ends Latin America tour with push for stronger Regional Security

By Zoila Palma: Today, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is wrapping up his South America tour in Peru where he is expected to hold security talks with President Keiko Fujimori as Washington seeks stronger cooperation with conservative governments in the region and intensifies efforts to combat drug trafficking and organized crime.

Rubio arrived in Lima on September 9 following visits to Colombia and Ecuador, where he promoted closer coordination against criminal gangs that the United States has designated or plans to designate as terrorist organizations.

Peru recently joined the “Shield of the Americas,” a US-led coalition promoted by President Donald Trump to combat drug trafficking and organized crime.

Peru, one of the world’s largest cocaine producers, has also experienced a significant deterioration in public security, with homicides rising sharply since 2018, AFP reports.

Peruvian Foreign Minister Carlos Espa said security and preparations for the El Niño weather phenomenon are the country’s two main priorities for Rubio’s visit.

During his stop in Ecuador, Rubio announced that Los Tiguerones, one of the country’s most powerful criminal gangs, would be designated a terrorist organization by Washington. Similar measures have already been taken against other Ecuadorian gangs, Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua and Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel.

Rubio’s regional tour also highlights Washington’s efforts to strengthen its influence in Latin America and counter growing ties between countries in the region and China, Russia and Iran.

World.title: Ministry of Health expands youth outreach on tobacco and alcohol prevention
World.content:
Ministry of Health expands youth outreach on tobacco and alcohol prevention

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Health and Wellness, through the National Drug Abuse Control Council (NDACC), is continuing its nationwide efforts to prevent tobacco and alcohol use among young people and promote healthier communities, in partnership with the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO).

The initiative recently reached the Cayo District, where Youth Forums were held in Belmopan and San Ignacio, along with a Community Sensitization Session.

The engagements provided young people, community members and other stakeholders with information on the risks associated with vaping, tobacco and alcohol use, while creating opportunities to share experiences and discuss practical approaches to strengthening prevention efforts.

The Ministry said the nationwide initiative will continue with upcoming activities in Belize City South Side, Dangriga in the Stann Creek District, and Punta Gorda in the Toledo District.

The sessions form part of ongoing efforts to engage youth, community leaders, educators, parents and other stakeholders in addressing substance use and its impact on communities.

The Ministry said the initiative is focused on empowering young people, strengthening community action and increasing awareness while supporting the development of healthier, tobacco- and alcohol-free environments across Belize.

World.title: Prime Minister wishes Belizeans Happy St. George’s Caye Day!
World.content:
Prime Minister wishes Belizeans Happy St. George’s Caye Day!

By Zoila Palma: Prime Minister of Belize John Briceño has extended St. George’s Caye Day greetings to Belizeans at home and abroad, calling on the nation to reflect on its history and celebrate the identity that has emerged from it.

The Prime Minister encouraged Belizeans to recognize the country’s history in its entirety, including its complexities and the experiences that have shaped the nation over generations.

“As we celebrate St. George’s Caye Day, may we embrace our history in all its complexity and celebrate the Belizean identity forged through it,” Prime Minister Briceño said.

“Happy St. George’s Caye Day, Belize!”

World.title: ‘His heart was broken’
World.content:
File photo Aston Coke, father of 10-year-old Shani Coke, speaking with journalists in Troy, Trelawny. (Photo: Kasey Williams)

TRELAWNY, Jamaica — Aston Coke, the father of slain 10-year-old Shani Coke, died Thursday morning at the Percy Junor Hospital after suffering from a prolonged illness.

It comes just under two weeks after his daughter was laid to rest.

Her partially nude body was found with her throat slashed on July 21. Her murder rocked the usually quiet community of Tyre in Troy, Trelawny.

“He was already gravely ill, and then when his daughter was murdered he took down worse. He was in hospital shortly after the incident and didn’t even get to go to her funeral two weeks ago. His heart was broken,” a family friend told Observer Online.

In a July 22 interview, Aaron Coke said his daughter was well loved and admired by many in her community.

“Her grandmother sent her to the shop, and she did not make it back home. Someone stopped her on the street and disturbed her somehow and slashed her throat… She was loving and caring in the community growing up. Everybody knows her. She knows everyone. She can see you and call you by your full name. She had a sense of humour. She was doing well in school, and she got a lot of academic awards,” said the heartbroken father.

“She decided that she wanted to make something out of herself growing up, because we were driving that into her head, but things just happened overnight,” added Coke, as he alleged that the man believed to have killed his daughter was a habitual offender.

Her alleged killer, Delroy Coke, was mobbed to death while his father was injured during an attack by residents.

World.title: Privy Council introduces free visa process for parties attending London appeals
World.content:
Visa

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Commonwealth citizens travelling to London to attend Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC) proceedings can now access a free, streamlined visa application process.

The initiative, developed by the JCPC in collaboration with the United Kingdom (UK) Home Office and Ministry of Justice, is available to appellants, respondents and members of their legal teams who are attending appeals in person.

The process does not extend to wider family members, the JCPC said in a statement on Thursday.

Once a hearing date has been confirmed, counsel must use the JCPC portal to indicate who will attend the hearing in person and whether they require a visa.

The JCPC will then verify the applicant’s connection to the case before issuing an invitation letter and providing further guidance on the visa application process.

Visa applications will continue to undergo the UK’s usual database checks, and the Home Office may request additional information in some cases, the JCPC said.

JCPC Registrar Laura Angus said the new process reflects the committee’s commitment to open justice, transparency and continuous improvement.

“The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is very pleased to be able to confirm the UK Government’s offer of this service to parties attending appeals in London. We listen to our users’ feedback and this decision underlines the JCPC’s commitment to open justice, transparency and continual improvement. We also routinely offer hybrid hearings for parties who prefer to take part in appeal hearings virtually,” Angus said.

World.title: CASINO CAUTION
World.content:
AS the Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) shores up its anti-money laundering defences ahead of the planned opening of Jamaica’s first casino at Princess Grande Jamaica Resort in Hanover early next year, the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) has issued a warning on key red flags to look out for.

FATF, the global illicit-finance watchdog, published a list of new gaming scams in a report on Wednesday, which it said was based on surveys conducted and included contributions from more than 80 jurisdictions.

The document titled ‘Red Flag Risk Indicators, Risks of Gaming and Gambling’, stated that the industries have changed significantly over recent years and continue to evolve through the expansion of online, cross-border, multi-product, and multi-payment platforms.

FATF said the work offers an updated analysis of money laundering risks posed by the casino sector as well as risks posed by the broader gambling and gaming sectors.

Red flag indicators in customer behaviour at brick-and-mortar casinos included attempts to influence or bribe venue staff to ignore their activities or bypass thorough customer due diligence checks and offering tips and other incentives.

Some casino customers were found to only want to deal with one staff member and avoid other staffers. These schemers use third parties to place cash into redemption terminals and purchase gaming chips, or place bets in an attempt to anonymise gambling.

The report outlined that the schemers also tend to request that winnings be paid in cash up to the threshold amount, but they never return to collect the balance. They also make purchases or attempts to purchase winning claim instruments from another customer and then present it as their own.

The report warned that eyebrows should raise if a player attempts to present a casino value instrument from an unknown source or if they are behaving in an unusual way on premises. It also warned of players acting on behalf of a third party and taking instructions from mobile phones or other customers on the premises.

Other red flags include customers who are reluctant or refuse to provide up-to-date identification documents or inconsistencies in personal information.

The report pointed out that some casino customers also opt to produce documents that are unclear or doctored and prove difficult to authenticate.

Where betting patterns are concerned, some customers were flagged for inconsistent spending that do not match their customer profile, including their known income and background.

In the report, FATF said it examined the scope of the risks associated with brick-and-mortar casinos, sports and novelty betting, other non-casino gambling — including scratch cards, arcades, bingo, lotteries, and slot machines outside of casinos.

“Findings indicate that certain payment methods associated with gaming and gambling activity such as cash, e-wallets, mobile money, and virtual assets are vulnerable to a range of money laundering risks. The variety of payment methods accepted by online gaming and gambling operators increasingly allows rapid, anonymous, cross-border transactions and conversion of value into different forms,” read page two of the 10-page document.

The operators and platforms covered in the report varied in nature and most of the risk indicators provided were related to land-based and online casinos and, to a lesser extent, betting. It was found that land-based operators have similar indicators as do online platforms.

In a statement on Wednesday, Giles Thomas, the president of FATF, said without robust safeguards, these sectors can attract gateways for fraudsters, professional money launderers, and organised criminal networks.

“I urge all governments to take note of the risk factors we have set out today, and put in place appropriate risk-based responses — from strengthening oversight and cracking down on illegal and offshore operators to boosting international co-operation and deepening public-private collaboration,” the FATF president said.

At a recent Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange officials of the CGC declared that they have been engaging in training with the Major Organised Crime and Anti-Corruption Agency (MOCA), the Financial Investigations Division (FID), and the Jamaica Customs Agency in an effort to ensure that strong anti-money laundering guardrails linked to casino gaming are in place when Jamaica gears up to claim its stake in an industry that generated more than US$320 billion worldwide last year.

The partnership with MOCA and FID is one based on capacity-building and information-sharing, support, and investigations.

Damion McKenzie, senior director of enforcement and investigations at the CGC, told Observer editors and reporters the entity recognises that, “Casino gaming is unique here, so some of the typologies and some of the crimes that happen in casinos, they might not be familiar with them. Our initiatives are to ensure that they are aware of those types of instances that can happen in a casino,” said McKenzie as he pointed out that the training of the law enforcement agents included them acquiring an understanding of the workings of slot machines and vulnerabilities.

The commission’s Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen emphasised that the entity is committed to properly regulating the casino gaming industry by ensuring that a multi-pronged approach is taken towards monitoring the sector in order to better protect the financial ecosystem.

“We operate in a space where we don’t have all the resources and all the knowledge, but remember, we operate in a large financial ecosystem. Our approach is focused on keeping us off the blacklist and on the right side of FATF,” Allen said.

He underscored that with Jamaica no longer being on the FATF list of countries that are assessed as having strategic deficiencies in their anti-money laundering/countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) regimes, dubbed a grey list, the CGC is prepared to do all in its powers to help to ensure Jamaica does not find itself back on that list.

In June 2024, then Minister of Finance Dr Nigel Clarke said he was proud to share that FATF, at its plenary in Singapore, welcomed Jamaica’s significant progress in improving its AML/CFT regimes.

As a result, FATF said that Jamaica was no longer subject to an increased monitoring process. With the island acknowledging the importance of remaining off the grey list, the CGC said it plans to ensure there are tight guardrails to protect Jamaica’s good standing with FATF.

Jamaica was placed on the FATF grey list in 2020, which signalled to international financial institutions to take special care when transacting with entities and individuals from the island.

One of the drawbacks of this is that it is more expensive to carry out transactions with countries on the list.

Other red flag indicators to look out for at casinos and other gaming establishments:

*Sudden changes in customer’s betting patterns.

*Co-ordinated or unusual betting activity, including hedged bets, betting on all outcomes and consistent losses to other players in peer-to-peer settings.

*Structuring of deposits into smaller amounts to fall under reporting thresholds.

*Use of short-odds bets and other low-risk mechanisms to justify withdrawals.

*Players making numerous large withdrawals without engaging in significant gambling activity.

*Customers appear to play frequently together, with one always winning and the other always losing.

*Suspected collusion in gambling activities, including gambling on both likely outcomes.

*Customer tries to circumvent note insertion limits by playing multiple machines simultaneously.

*Customer frequently plays games with low returns but with lower risks and a higher chance of winning.

*Customer repeatedly collects winnings just below a customer identification threshold.

*Non-genuine play patterns – wagers are low while large sums are deposited and withdrawn.

World.title: Gov’t looking to add speed to school repairs
World.content:
This file photos shows some of the damage Hurricane Melissa did to Edwin Allen High School last year.

THE Government could look overseas for contractors to speed up the repair and rebuilding of schools devastated by Hurricane Melissa last October.

More than 600 educational institutions sustained damage from the Category 5 storm with 309 severely damaged and ranked priority one for repairs and reconstruction.

At a post-Cabinet media briefing at Jamaica House in St Andrew on Wednesday officials of the Ministry of Education said 57 of those severely damaged institutions were fully repaired when the new school year began on Monday. The ministry said another 95 schools will be fully repaired by the end of September, and another 34 repaired by the end of December.

Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon told the media briefing that school repairs were hampered by a shortage of grade one contractors and the ministry will, among other things, explore hiring external contractors to fill gaps while ramping up efforts to upskill local contractors.

Morris Dixon admitted that the current situation is far from perfect and argued that the need for contractors was even more imperative given the mandate placed on the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA) — the specialised body established to coordinate and accelerate post-disaster rebuilding and long-term infrastructure resilience after Hurricane Melissa.

She pointed out that while the Administration is committed to continue the work to rebuild schools it has been constrained by the number of grade one contractors available in Jamaica.

“When the budget for the project is above a particular amount, you have to use a grade one contractor, and we’re limited with the number of grade one contractors, so that’s a constraint,” Morris Dixon explained.

“We need those contractors for the schools, we need them for the homes, we need them for the businesses, we need them for that beautiful vision that Prime Minister [Dr Andrew Holness] laid out in his budget presentation. And so, one of the things that we are working on, separately, in a different part of the ministry on the skills side, is an initiative between HEART NSTA/Trust and the Development Bank of Jamaica (DBJ)…we have to work to get those who are at grade two up to grade one through financing and otherwise, because that’s a key element of it. And so DBJ is at the table with us, trying to work through that, because our goal is to give the money to the Jamaicans,” Morris Dixon disclosed.

“What we’re looking at is, how we can work with young people who want to be contractors, put them in groupings, provide funding, and provide incubation to them so that we can get more in the pipeline of grade one contractors. Using external sources is something that we’ll have to look at. For example, for the STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) schools, we have done international tenders, and so in some of the big projects, we’ll have to do some international tendering. We’ll see what comes out of that…but right now, our commitment is to our local contractors using them. But of course, they have to show that they can deliver,” Morris Dixon said further.

The education minister, in the meantime, said work was continuing apace to rehabilitate schools listed as priority one which were severely damaged by Melissa with almost continuous afternoon rain in Westmoreland slowing down the process.

“It’s not perfect. Where we are now is not perfect, and we have a lot of people working. We have many contractors. For our very severely damaged schools, which is about 309 schools that were severely damaged… the bills are high. A lot of them are over $100 million, $200 million, $300 million, a billion dollars almost in some instances,” Morris Dixon said.

According to Morris Dixon, the hurricane is being used as an opportunity “to get better school plants, at least in the west”.

Meanwhile, permanent secretary in the Ministry of Education Dr Kasan Troupe said the new school year got off to a fair start on Monday with 92 per cent of schools having all students while two per cent of schools will have to be augmented with temporary learning spaces and utilise some amount of rotation.

“That’s tremendous given what we have been through, and I want to thank all my principals, all my chairmen and board members, and of course, all the teachers,” Troupe said.

She told the media briefing that the ministry has ensured that all schools have been given their operational funds along with furniture and other resources.

“We sent out 30 per cent of the increased grants into our schools in June. The second tranche of that is due in September, the first Friday in September and two weeks ago, we ensured that all the funds were out in all our schools, so we are ahead of time because we understand what it means for our principals to have monies to get the work done. That amounted to $3.05 billion that we have disbursed to our schools, and that will treat with the operations, that will treat with the nutritional support for the learners, and of course, an additional $75 million we sent out to our schools to impact 275 schools to treat with canteen repairs,” Troupe said.

“As it relates to furniture, 41 schools indicated that they need additional support. We are responding to that, but in preparation for this year, we spent $300 million to get furniture out into our schools. So before we started, we distributed over 17,000 pieces, and whilst we were wrapping up on the last weekend, there were 8,000 pieces that we were distributing across our schools,” added Troupe.

According to the permanent secretary, another 20,000 pieces of furniture are being prepared for distribution to the system.

She said the ministry is spending more than $700 million in resourcing high schools with books and more than $300 million in primary schools, making that approximately $1.1 billion of expenditure in providing books for public schools.

World.title: 450 set for Caribbean Music Awards performance
World.content:
450...preparation has been good. We’ve been putting in the work and making sure everything is right.

Dancehall artiste 450 is gearing up to make his debut performance at the highly anticipated Caribbean Music Awards (CMA).

The fourth annual ceremony and showcase will take place on Saturday, September 19 at the National Academy for the Performing Arts (NAPA) in Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago.

For 450, the opportunity to perform on the regional stage represents another significant moment in his career.

“It feels like a big moment for me. The CMA is a major platform for Caribbean music, so it feels like another chapter of the story that my team and I are grateful for,” 450, who is also nominated for Album of the Year, told the Jamaica Observer.

V’ghn, Freetown Collective, Jah Mason, 1T1, and Theomaa are among the artistes slated to perform. The line-up represents a cross section of Caribbean music, spanning soca, reggae, dancehall, bouyon, and contemporary Caribbean sounds.

After three years of staging the awards in New York City, organisers are bringing CMA to the Caribbean for the first time since its inception. The move will also see the celebration expand beyond a single awards night into an immersive weekend of activities.

The weekend is expected to feature networking opportunities, industry discussions, cultural showcases, and opportunities for fans to interact more closely with artistes and other players in the Caribbean music industry.

450 said preparations are well under way for his performance, with his team focused on ensuring his CMA debut makes an impact.

“Preparation has been good. We’ve been putting in the work and making sure everything is right,” he shared.

While not revealing too much about what he has planned, the entertainer promised a high-energy performance featuring some of the songs that have connected with his fan base.

“Energy, good vibes, and some of the songs they know and love. I’m representing Jamaica and dancehall music,” 450 said.

The appearance comes during what the artiste describes as a strong year of career growth, particularly as he continues to introduce his music to audiences outside Jamaica.

“It’s been a really good year. I’ve been able to reach new audiences, perform on bigger international stages, and continue growing the music. There’s still more to accomplish, so mi nah slow down,” he said.

With the final quarter of 2026 under way, 450 has no plans to ease the pace. Beyond his upcoming CMA performance, the dancehall artiste is working on new material and further expanding his international presence.

“I’m working on new music, more visuals, and some exciting international projects. More to come soon,” he added.

World.title: Contractor says all his 7 school jobs almost complete
World.content:
Inside a newly completed grade six classroom with a new roof, ceiling, lighting and ceiling fans at Petersfield Primary School in Westmoreland..

PETERSFIELD, Westmoreland — While several schools in western Jamaica still have a long way to go to repair damage inflicted by last October’s Hurricane Melissa, Petersfield Primary in Westmoreland is now 98 per cent complete. There are only a few doors and windows left to be installed.

The Petersfield project is one of seven being undertaken by Archistruct Limited. Others include William Knibb High in Trelawny and five schools in St Ann. According to owner and managing director of the 14-year-old company Chadwick Lawrence, all the schools are almost 100 per cent repaired.

“The minister [of education] did say she’s holding us accountable, so I take that one seriously. I couldn’t afford to disappoint her,” he told the Jamaica Observer Wednesday.

With a degree in engineering and a master’s in construction project management, Lawrence is supported by a team of qualified construction professionals.

“It is no secret sauce; it’s just a matter of management and execution of tasks based on schedule and procuring materials on time. That is what I do. We use a lot of people from the area, as well as people from different areas, as needed. At Petersfield, we did a lot of night and day work to get it finished,” Lawrence explained when asked the secret to his success in having the schools ready for September.

“It boils down to one expression: Construction is about the joy of creating. It is nice to just see the students inside the classroom; it’s a genuinely nice feeling to see the students in the classroom learning and the teachers teaching in a comfortable space. When you talk with the teachers and the principals and they tell you that they are happy with the product they have received because it’s better than it was before… that really brings the joy of creating,” he said.

The company has been strategic in its approach.

“In terms of the scheduling and procurement of materials, we had ensured that we did that beforehand as we went along. We were doing seven schools, so we were able to buy in bulk and to get everything on spot before we needed it. Now we are at 98 per cent complete and we are happy to say that it is a good September morning. All the kids are out and about, parents and teachers are happy, and we’re just glad to see a satisfied customer,” Lawrence told the Observer.

School board chairman and Custos of Westmoreland Reverend Hartley Perrin, who had initial concerns, is among those pleased with the results at Petersfield Primary.

“I had my doubts. I was very concerned about the progress, or lack thereof… But then, all of a sudden, it started to pick up as if they stepped on the accelerator. They were working longer hours and they seemed to have employed more people. I’m pleased to see the work that has been done and the quality of it. Even the painting is of good standard,” the Custos beamed.

But it has not all been smooth sailing. The type of windows needed for the school projects is not available in Jamaica. The original structures had aluminum window blades.

“We’re doing some… we discussed with the principals and they have agreed to other options for the type of windows,” said Lawrence.

At all seven schools, his team is now adding little touches that make a world of difference.

“We work closely with the principals and teachers. Even now, we are at different locations doing what we call commissioning. There are little things that might be needed — a teacher may need a nail there or a piece of board there for a pin-up board [to place teaching aids] — and we’re there now putting those things in place to make the space as comfortable as possible,” said Lawrence.

At Petersfield, his company has a separate contract to build a new administrative and classroom block. Lawrence confirmed that all materials are on-site and the bending of steel began Wednesday morning.

World.title: THE ULTIMATE TEST
World.content:
World 100m champion Oblique Seville headlines Jamaica’s team for the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest, Hungary. (Photo: AFP)

Technical Leader Maurice Wilson says Jamaica’s athletes will be ready for the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships which starts tomorrow at the National Athletics Center in Budapest, Hungary.

A 32-member team, with 27 athletes set to contest individual events for Jamaica, was named by World Athletics on Monday, based on world rankings for the first of what is set to be an annual end-of-season all-star competition.

Wilson described the event as “a fantastic initiative”, which he said has the potential to take the sport to another level.

“There are changes to the arrangements,” he told the Jamaica Observer, where athletes’ representatives will have “a more hands-on” duty, as national federations such as the Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association (JAAA) will only be responsible for naming relay coaches.

Wilson and Michael Frater have been named by the JAAA to take charge of the mixed 4x100m and 4x400m teams, with the athletes being able to have their personal coaches with them.

“Every major professional sport has annual championships,” Wilson said. “So track and field should not be an exception, and this is something we need.”

Winners of the individual events will receive a bye to the 2027 World Championships as well as US$150,000 (over $23 million) while winning relay teams will share US$80,000 (just over $12 million). Just about every participant will take home a cash prize.

There will also be a US$100,000 ($15.5 million) bonus for breaking a world record, while the champions will get a trophy rather than the traditional gold, silver, and bronze medals.

Newly crowned Diamond League 100m champions Oblique Seville and Tina Clayton have been included in Jamaica’s 32-member team that will compete at the three-day event.

In addition to Seville on the men’s side, Commonwealth Games champions Navasky Anderson, Romaine Beckford, and Demario Prince were also named.

Commonwealth Games champion Sanique Walker and women’s 4x100m relay gold medallists Jodean Williams and Lavanya Williams were also named.

Team Jamaica

Men



Navasky Anderson, Romaine Beckford, Orlando Bennett, Ackeem Blake, Bryan Levell, Tyler Mason, Demario Prince, Oblique Seville, Christopher Taylor

Women

Rushell Clayton, Tina Clayton, Lamara Distin, Brianna Lyston, Ashanti Moore, Ackera Nugent, Nickisha Pryce, Demisha Roswell, Shiann Salmon, Megan Simmonds, Ackelia Smith, Jonielle Smith, Sanique Walker, Danielle Williams, Jodean Williams, Lavanya Williams

Relays

Zandrion Barnes, Kadrion Goldson, Rohan Watson, Assinie Wilson, Shana Kaye Anderson
