World.title: Eight-gold target set as Philippines eyes Asian Games splash
World.content:
EIGHT. Athletes, coaches, and officials during Team Philippines' send-off for the 2026 Asian Games and 2026 Asian Para Games.

Bannered by star athletes Carlos Yulo, Alex Eala, EJ Obiena, and Annie Ramirez, Team Philippines seeks to breach the four-gold mark in an Asian Games edition for the first time since 1962

MANILA, Philippines – Team Philippines has not won more than four gold medals in the Asian Games for over six decades, but the ambitious goal for the upcoming edition in Nagoya, Japan, is to win twice as many.

Philippine Olympic Committee president Abraham “Bambol” Tolentino on Thursday, September 10, said the target for the quadrennial showpiece is at least eight gold medals, believing the 464-strong delegation can surpass the four-gold hauls each in 2018 in Indonesia and in 2023 in China.

“I’m not going to put any pressure on the athletes for this Asian Games. There will be no pressure, but give it everything you’ve got. Give it your absolute best,” said Tolentino in Filipino during the athletes’ send-off at the Rizal Memorial Coliseum.

The Philippines last breached the four-gold mark in the 1962 edition, where it clinched seven gold medals to finish fifth overall.

All but one of the Philippines’ four gold medalists in 2023 are still around, with Gilas Pilipinas, pole vault stalwart EJ Obiena, and jiu-jitsu standout Annie Ramirez aiming to defend their thrones.

Jiu-jitsu veteran Meggie Ochoa, another champion in 2023, has already retired from the national team and transitioned into coaching.

Aside from the three returning titleholders, gold medals are expected from gymnastics ace Carlos Yulo and tennis star Alex Eala.

Yulo, the Philippines’ first and only Olympic double gold medalist, bagged the floor exercise crown in the Asian Artistic Gymnastics Championships in June, while Eala has posted promising results, winning her first-ever WTA Tour title at the Washington Open in August, in between a fourth-round appearance in Wimbledon and a third-round stint in the US Open.

Other gold-medal prospects, according to Tolentino, come from boxing, taekwondo, wushu, mixed martial arts, athletics, esports, and skateboarding.

“There are no replays here. Give it everything you’ve got,” said Tolentino.

In a bid to motivate the delegates, Philippine Sports Commissioner chairman Patrick “Pato” Gregorio announced an additional P6,000 allowance for each participating athlete and coach.

Gregorio also promised bonuses if the country exceeds the four-gold Asian Games tally and 10-gold Asian Para Games yield in 2023.

“Let us achieve more, and when you come back, you will have a very good Christmas, I assure you,” said Gregorio. “Let us make the Filipino nation smile.”

The Asian Games will officially open on September 19 and run until October 4, but the men’s basketball tournament already started, with Gilas Pilipinas kicking off its title defense against Bahrain on Friday, September 11. – Rappler.com

World.title: Get to know the Philippines’ 10 new national artists
World.content:
Among the newly named national artists are four luminaries who are being conferred with the honor posthumously

MANILA, Philippines – Every three years, a new set of Filipino individuals receive the country’s highest honors for their contributions to Philippine arts and all its forms. These pioneers are chosen and vetted by the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) and the Cultural Center of the Philippines (CCP), and later conferred by the president of the Philippines.

The last set of national artists were named in 2022 and included screenwriter and novelist Ricky Lee, dancer Agnes Locsin, stage director and theater actor Antonio “Tony” Mabesa, cartoonist Lauro “Larry” Alcala, poet Gemino Abad, fashion designer Salvacion Lim-Higgins, soprano Fides Cuyugan-Asensio, actress Nora Aunor, and director Marilou Diaz-Abaya.

This time, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. named 10 new national artists under Proclamation No. 1414 across the fields of literature, film and broadcast arts, visual arts, architecture, music, fashion design, and dance.

Get to know them and their legacies here.

Gregorio Brillantes (Literature, posthumous)

Born and raised in Camiling, Tarlac, Gregorio Brillantes was a decorated author who was dubbed the “master of the Filipino short story” and “the godfather of Philippine speculative fiction.”

Brillantes stood as one of the most defining voices in Philippine fiction in English as we know it today. He published a vast array of influential works that cut across generations, such as The Distance to Andromeda and Other Stories; Faith, Love, Time, and Dr. Lazaro; and The Apollo Centennial.

He also wrote and edited for the publications Sunburst, The Manila Review, Focus, Asia-Philippines Leader, and the Philippines Free Press.

Brillantes received his BLitt degree, major in journalism, from Ateneo de Manila University in 1952. He racked up several accolades throughout his decades-long career, including being inducted into the Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards for Literature Hall of Fame and receiving the Gawad CCP para sa Sining, among many other awards.

He died on September 26, 2025, at 92 years old.

Armando “Bing” Lao (Film and Broadcast Arts, posthumous)

Armando “Bing” Lao was a filmmaker, director, editor, and screenwriter regarded as a pillar in Philippine cinema.

He was the man behind the screenplays of the iconic films Takaw Tusko (1986), Itanong Mo sa Buwan (1988), Hati Tayo Sa Magdamag (1989), Fetch a Pail of Water (1999), La Vida Rosa (2001), and Biyaheng Lupa (2009), to name a few.

Lao was named New Wave Best Director and took home the title of New Wave Best Feature Film at the 2013 Manila Film Festival for his film, Dukit. He was also the recipient of one FAMAS award for Hati Tayo Sa Magdamag and five Gawad Urian awards for Takaw Tukso, Itanong Mo sa Buwan, Fetch a Pail of Water, Larger than Life, and La Vida Rosa, among other awards.

In 2024, he received the lifetime achievement award from the Film Development Council of the Philippines during its annual Parangal ng Sining, which recognizes luminaries in local cinema.

He passed away on June 18, 2024, at 75.

Gabriel Formoso (Architecture, posthumous)

Born on April 9, 1915, in Manila, University of Santo Tomas alumnus Gabriel “Gabby” Formoso was a soft-spoken master builder who was regarded as the “Architect of a Modernizing Philippines.”

He was one of the first 100 architects of the Philippines. He was nominated for the National Artist honors as early as 2003.

Over 80 landmark buildings and 159 private homes bear his handprint, including the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Complex, the wood-accented Asian Institute of Management, The Manila Peninsula, and the historic Club Filipino clubhouse.

He graduated with an architecture degree from UST in 1937. Admired by the United Architects of the Philippines, he received the UAP Likha Award and Gold Medal.

He died at the age of 81 on December 22, 1996.

Teodoro Hilado (Theater, posthumous)

Born on May 15, 1938, in Silay City, Negros Occidental, Teodoro “Teddy” Hilado was a theater administrator who was dubbed the “Father of Lightning Design in Philippine Theater.”

Hilado served as the resident technical director for the CCP from 1969 to 1973, and a theater director of the Folks Arts Theater from 1973 to 1986.

He brought back to life hundreds of iconic dance, drama, and opera productions for organizations like Ballet Philippines and the Bayanihan Philippine National Folk Dance Company — where he met the love of his life, Rosky Balahadia. Their heartwarming, real-life romance at the CCP later became the soul behind the award-winning music video for the Itchyworms’ “Di Na Muli,” where Rosky returned to the CCP stage after over 20 years to dance once more under the spotlights designed in Teddy’s honor by his former protege, Shakira Villa-Symes.

Play Video

Beyond traditional theater, he also designed ecosystem installations, including the Dr. Jose P. Rizal Light and Sound Presentation located at Rizal Park. He racked up several awards throughout his career, including being the first recipient of the Gawad CCP for Excellence in Lightning Design and Technical Theater in 1997, receiving the CCP Centennial Honors for the Arts in 1998.

Hilado died at the age of 77 on December 23, 2015.

Imelda Cajipe-Endaya (Visual Arts)

Imelda Cajipe-Endaya is a Manila-based painter and printmaker known for her mixed media depictions of children, the environment, gender, empowerment, and Filipino identity, among many other disciplines. The 76-year-old is the first woman to be named national artist in the visual arts category.

She earned her bachelor’s degree in fine arts from University of the Philippines (UP) in 1970 and later completed her graduate studies in art history and criticism in 1975 and 1976, respectively.

In a video feature by Silverlens Galleries in 2025, Endaya confessed that she had long been labeled by writers as a feminist before she even knew what that concept was.

“I was simply painting about my own experience as a woman through the years,” she said.

To date, Endaya has received countless major awards for her work, such as the CCP’s Thirteen Artist Awards in 1990, the Araw ng Maynila Award in 1998, the CCP Centennial Honors for the Arts in 1999, and the NCCA’s Ani ng Dangal in 2009, to name a few.

Nunelucio Alvarado (Visual Arts)

Hailing from Sagay, Negros Occidental, Nunelucio “Nune” Alvarado is a 76-year-old painter whose works explore social realism. He paints through his battle with dementia through portraits of farm workers and vivid portrayals of community, political injustice, and struggle.

He is a progressive figure in the local art scene and the pride and joy of Negros Island, channeling his activism into spotlighting the marginalized sectors in his community through his paintings.

Alvarado was a recipient of the CCP’s Thirteen Artists Awards in 1992, and in 2004 received the Patnubay ng Sining at Kalinangan sa Larangan ng Pintura, a lifetime achievement award given by the same government agency.

In May, Alvarado’s hometown Sagay put up a 30-meter-tall mural to honor his legacy as a living art pillar and continue to inspire the youth.

Alfredo Buenaventura (Music)

Born in 1928, Alfredo Buenaventura is a composer and conductor hailing from Santa Maria, Bulacan. He has composed over 1,000 works throughout his career, spanning operas, chamber music, symphonic poems, ballets, and many more. He has also composed numerous religious songs.

He was also an organist at the Manila Cathedral.

Some of his well-known masterpieces include “Lakambini,” “Mabuhay March,” “Bayan Kong Mahal,” “Dulambuhay,” and “Planting Rice.”

Buenaventura took up music at UST, the Centro Escolar University, and the Gregorian Institute. He served as the dean of CEU’s Conservatory of Music for 30 years.

Buenaventura received the Republican Cultural Heritage awards in 1964 for his composition of “Maria Makiling,” and in 1972 for his “Kayumanggi Symphony,” according to a Daily Tribune report.

Nicanor Tiongson (Literature)

Born in 1946 in Malolos, Bulacan, Nicanor Tiongson is a playwright, cultural scholar, and critic in the disciplines of history, literature, film, theater, popular culture, and art. He is professor emeritus at UP Film Institute and also served as dean of UP’s College of Mass Communication. As a cultural scholar, he was also the artistic director and vice president of the CCP.

In 1976, he co-founded the Manunuri ng Pelikulang Pilipino alongside Behn Cervantes, Nestor Torre, Petronilo Daroy, Pio de Castro III, Clodualdo del Mundo Jr., Justino Dormiendo, Mario Hernando, Bienvenido Lumbera, and Manny Pichel. This film circle is the award-giving body behind the Gawad Urian, which honors Filipino films and the people behind them.

Among his works, he wrote an impactful trilogy of essays on Philippine theater, which, as a whole, explores different art forms in theater, the evolution of local theater, and theater groups in the Philippines from the 1970s to the 1980s and the productions they mounted.

He wrote the historical book The Women of Malolos and Komedya sa Parañaque: Kasaysayan at Estetika, which tracks the growth of the comedy genre in San Dionisio and Don Galo in the city. The Ateneo de Manila University Press also published a compilation of Tiongson’s plays and musicals: Revitalizing Tradition and Resurrecting History.

In 2015, he won the Grand Goodman Prize for his “substantial contributions to Philippine historical studies.”

Maria Beatriz ‘Patis’ Tesoro (Fashion Design)

Born in Iloilo in 1950, Patis Tesoro initially dreamed of becoming a painter but would later be dubbed the “Grand Dame of Philippine Fashion” for her decades-long work reviving and reinventing Filipiniana.

Tesoro built her name by transforming indigenous Filipino textiles into barongs, kimono jackets, Maria Clara gowns, ternos, caftans, and richly embroidered tops, working piña, jusi, abaca, and cotton into pieces heavy with hand embroidery and indigenous patterns.

Her work has been staged in exhibitions and shows both locally and abroad, including “Piña: From Fabric to Couture” at the Hotel InterContinental Madrid in 2013, and “Kasuotang Filipino: Mga Likha ni Patis Tesoro” at the Museo ng Makati in 2023.

Tesoro pursued her education at Marygrove College in Detroit, Michigan, training to become an art educator before turning to fashion as a livelihood. Her revival of Filipiniana deepened through her collaboration with cultural advocate Ado Escudero on Katutubong Filipino, a project aimed at reviving the country’s dying traditional textiles.

Rafael ‘Nonoy’ Froilan (Dance)

Born on October 24, 1950, in Calbiga, Samar, Rafael “Nonoy” Froilan is one of the Philippines’ most celebrated male ballet dancers and has come to be known as the country’s premier danseur.

Froilan trained with the University of the East Dance Troupe before joining the CCP Dance School in 1972 and Ballet Philippines the following year.

For more than two decades, he served as principal dancer of Ballet Philippines, originating roles created specifically for him, including Norman Walker’s Songs of a Wayfarer and National Artist Alice Reyes’ Rama Hari and Carmina Burana. He also famously danced opposite Dame Margot Fonteyn and Yoko Morishita.

He has spent decades teaching at the Philippine High School for the Arts.

In 2020, he received the Gawad CCP Para sa Sining for Dance. – with reports from Arabella Grace Sta Ana and Jade Tan/Rappler.com

Arabella Grace Sta Ana is a Rappler intern studying BA Philosophy at UP Los Baños.

Jade Tan is a Rappler intern studying AB Journalism at UST Manila.

World.title: EXPLAINER: Why senators don’t need Senate clearance for personal trips
World.content:
IN SESSION. Senate President Win Gatchalian opens the second regular session of the 20th congress on July 27, 2026.

Two more senators have left the country amid the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte and Senate deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027.

On Thursday, September 10, the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed that Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano and Senator Pia Cayetano had flown abroad, amid social media posts showing the senator-siblings allegedly arriving in Singapore on Wednesday evening, September 9.

A separate social media post also alleged that Taguig Mayor Lani Cayetano, Alan’s wife, flew to Singapore early Thursday.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said he had yet to receive formal information about the Cayetano siblings’ departure but clarified that senators leaving the country for personal trips do not need to obtain travel clearance from the Senate.

Play Video

“I have yet to receive formal information if they left or not. The photos we are seeing on social media may be old pictures. However, senators leaving for abroad for personal reasons may do so without seeking clearance or notifying the Senate leadership,” Gatchalian said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Senator Loren Legarda, who remains on extended medical leave, also flew out of the country in August without seeking travel clearance.

Travel authority

Unlike official foreign trips, personal trips by senators do not require prior approval from the Senate president under current Senate rules.

Senate Policy Order No. 2016-003, approved by then-Senate president Franklin Drilon in July 2016, amended the Senate rules on official local and foreign travel.

The policy order struck out the provision stating that “all personal travels abroad of officials and personnel of the Senate shall be subject also to the approval of the Senate President.”

The amended provision instead states that official foreign travel by Senate members, officials and employees covered by the policy shall be subject to the prior approval of the Senate president.

“It was a personal trip and we don’t know the reason for it. We have no policy they need to seek permission for personal trips,” Gatchalian said.

“They need travel clearance for official trips, especially if the Senate needs to cover some of their expenses such as hotels, tickets, and staff allowance. Senators and employees need travel clearance when traveling on official notice,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Albay declares state of calamity over dengue outbreak
World.content:
CROWDED HOSPITALS. Albay Governor Noel Rosal visits the Josefina Belmonte Duran Albay Provincial Hospital in Ligao City on September 9, 2026, where at least 100 dengue patients are currently confined.

Facing 14 fatalities and more than 1,700 active dengue cases, Albay has mobilized its quick response fund to secure additional emergency medical kits and contain the outbreak

ALBAY, Philippines – The Provincial Government of Albay declared a state of calamity after recording 1,785 dengue cases and 14 fatalities as of Thursday, September 10.

According to data from the Albay Provincial Health Office (PHO), Legazpi City logged the highest number of active cases at 378, with five fatalities, followed by Bacacay town with 254 active cases, and Daraga with 188 active cases and two fatalities. Active cases are currently being monitored across 15 other municipalities.

The declaration allows the provincial government to mobilize emergency response efforts, implement immediate containment measures, and access quick response funds to procure critical medical supplies and testing kits.

Albay Governor Noel Rosal said the declaration was deemed necessary as dengue cases continued to surge. He issued the declaration recommendation a day earlier, Wednesday, September 9.

“We are already beyond the epidemic level compared to the last three years, according to the Department of Health Region V,” Rosal said. “Let us continue the barangay brigades and clean our respective areas.”

Rosal had earlier issued Executive Order No. 51 on September 2, mandating sustained and community-based dengue prevention and control measures.

“The province shall strengthen the Albay Aksyon Barangay Kontra Dengue as a mechanism for mobilization, source reduction, health education, early identification of public health concerns, reporting, referral, and coordination with appropriate health authorities,” the order stated.

The Albay PHO urged residents to actively participate in community sanitation to halt transmission.

“The continuous increase in cases is a clear call for more intensified, sustained, and collective action to prevent further illness and loss of life,” the PHO stated. “Let us not wait for another case to emerge or another life to be lost before taking action. Every area we clean and every mosquito breeding site we eliminate is a step toward stopping dengue and saving lives.”

This marks the province’s first dengue-related state of calamity since 2019, when a similar declaration was issued alongside a national epidemic alert. – Rappler.com

World.title: Aira Villegas, Albert Ian delos Santos PH flag bearers in Asian Games
World.content:
DELIVER. Boxer Aira Villegas and weightlifter Albert Ian delos Santos in action for the Philippines.

The flag-bearing duties for the Asian Games opening ceremony fall on Olympic boxing medalist Aira Villegas and weightlifting junior world record holder Albert Ian delos Santos

MANILA, Philippines – Two of the Philippines’ top medal prospects in the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, will serve as flag bearers as boxer Aira Villegas and weightlifter Albert Ian delos Santos are tasked to lead the delegation in the opening ceremony.

Philippine Olympic Committee president Abraham “Bambol” Tolentino made the announcement on Thursday, September 10, during the send-off event for athletes competing in the Asian Games and Asian Para Games.

Villegas, 31, is best known for winning a bronze medal in the 2024 Paris Olympics, contributing to the Philippines’ finest Summer Games campaign led by gymnastics double gold medalist Carlos Yulo.

The pride of Tacloban, Leyte, has also won silver and bronze medals in the Southeast Asian Games.

“It is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to be given this honor, to be a flag bearer for Team Philippines in a competition of this magnitude,” said Association of Boxing Alliances in the Philippines president Marcus Jarwin Manalo. “I think Aira will be a good ambassador of the Philippines at the Asian Games.”

“I think she is really deserving of this great honor.”

Meanwhile, 20-year-old Delos Santos is fresh from a dominant campaign in the Asian Youth and Junior Weightlifting Championships in August in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, where he set multiple continental and world records.

Delos Santos completed a three-gold sweep in the junior men’s 70kg division and established new Asian and world records in clean and jerk with 180kg and total lift with 321kg.

Hailing from Zamboanga City like Olympic weightlifting champion Hidilyn Diaz, Delos Santos also captured a silver medal in the 2025 Southeast Asian Games in Thailand, where he finished behind home bet and reigning world champion Weeraphon Wichuma.

Tolentino said tennis star Alex Eala was considered for flag-bearing duties, but plans did not push through as she is set to compete in the Singapore Open, which begins on September 21, two days after the Asian Games opening ceremony on September 19 at the Paloma Mizuho Stadium.

While the quadrennial showpiece has yet to official open, the men’s basketball tournament already tipped off, with Gilas Pilipinas opening its title defense against Bahrain on Friday, September 11. – Rappler.com

World.title: Apart from timing, what else is ‘unusual’ about Romualdez’s hospital confinement?
World.content:
EX-HOUSE LEADER. Speaker Martin Romualdez graces the first meeting of the Visayas Caucus of the 20th Congress in the House of Representatives on August 7, 2025.

Romualdez’s admitting physician reveals that he did not see nor examine the former House speaker when he was confined on September 7 because the attending physicians barred him from entering the room

Apparently, the condition of former House speaker Martin Romualdez was not an emergency case when he rushed himself to the hospital on September 7, the day Sandiganbayan 3rd Division issued an arrest warrant against him for plunder.

Dr. Kurt Allen Sibayan, Romualdez’s admitting physician, said this in court on Thursday, September 10, during the hearing on the former speaker’s motion for hospital confinement.

Rappler saw a copy of Romualdez’s medical certificate, which did not indicate the number of days the former speaker needed for recuperation. On the floor, Office of the Ombudsman Deputy Special Prosecutor Omar Sagadal reiterated this point twice: Romualdez doesn’t need confinement.

“There’s nothing here that says the patient requires confinement,” said Sagadal.

Romualdez is currently confined at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City after admitting himself at around 4 pm on Monday. He gave a list of diseases, including hypertension and heart problems.

He was served the arrest warrant by the Philippine National Police on Monday, but he has yet to be transferred to a jail facility because of his condition.

During the hearing, Sibayan also revealed that he prepared the abstract, but did not see nor examine Romualdez. The physician said he was told that resident doctors were not allowed to go inside the room.

It was attending physician Dr. Rosalio Torres (hematologist), Romualdez’s hospital “team manager,” who told Sibayan this.

“Residents are not allowed inside the room,” said Sibayan.

Asked whether it was unusual for a resident doctor to be barred from a room, Sibayan answered in the affirmative.

According to Sibayan, apart from Torres, two other physicians made separate diagnoses of Romualdez — cardiologist Rody Sy and neurologist Rogelio Libarres. He said he was only tasked with adding the diagnoses to the medical abstract.

On Thursday, the 3rd Division transferred Romualdez’s custody from the Philippine National Police-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) to the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology. After the resolution on his request for hospital confinement, the former speaker will be detained at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas.

The court also scheduled Romualdez’s arraignment on September 7, the phase where he will be read his case and asked to enter either a guilty or not-guilty plea.

A clearer timeline

Echoing what Interior Secretary Juanito Victor “Jonvic” Remulla had said, the doctors confirmed that Romualdez checked in at around 4 pm.

CIDG Metro Manila chief Police Colonel John Guiagui said the former speaker has moved to another hospital room, which is being guarded by law enforcers.

Torres said on Thursday that months ago, staff of Romualdez asked him if he would be willing to manage the former speaker’s hospital care. He accepted, so he formed a team of specialists to take care of Romualdez.

On September 7, the doctor said he received a call from Romualdez’s staff between 9 am and 10 am because the congressman complained of chest pains. Due to the former speaker’s history of heart problems, Torres immediately suggested confinement for Romualdez so he could be examined.

But why was Romualdez confined immediately, bypassing the emergency room? Torres explained that, in consultation with Sy, they advised the former speaker to be admitted for confinement and evaluation.

And if Romualdez had already complained of chest pains that morning, why did they wait until 4 pm to admit him?

“[Maybe] he wanted my advice,” said Torres.

Play Video

Romualdez is in a private room and not under intensive care. Torres said his patient needed “active monitoring.”

“It can be an impending heart attack, unstable angina,” said the physician.

Further, Torres said it was “high risk” to transport Romualdez because of the possibility of a heart attack. This was raised repeatedly because Remulla had earlier said the former speaker should be transferred to the PNP General Hospital in Camp Crame — and, of course, given the court’s commitment order for Romualdez, to Payatas.

The 3rd Division will continue the hearing on Friday, September 11, when more of Romualdez’s doctors are expected to take the witness stand. – Rappler.com

World.title: Orange heavy rainfall warning up in Bataan, Zambales on Sept. 11 morning
World.content:
Several areas in Bataan and Zambales are placed under the orange heavy rainfall warning on Friday morning, September 11, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration says. Image from Pagasa/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Several areas in Bataan and Zambales were placed under the orange heavy rainfall warning on Friday morning, September 11, according to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa).

The orange warning means that affected areas will experience rainfall between 15 millimeters (mm) and 30 mm within an hour, and this will continue in the next two hours.

In its heavy rainfall warning advisory at 5 a.m., the state weather bureau said the orange warning applied to Morong, Hermosa, Dinalupihan, Samal, Orani, Bagac and Abucay in Bataan; and Castillejos, San Antonio, Subic and Olongapo in Zambales.

Article continues after this

World.title: Habagat rains to weaken on Friday – Pagasa
World.content:
Satellite image from Pagasa

MANILA, Philippines — The southwest monsoon, or habagat, may bring lighter rains in some areas across the country as it weakens on Friday, Sept. 11, the state weather bureau said.

Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) weather specialist Leanne Loreto said in its 5 a.m. weather advisory that the effects of the southwest monsoon may weaken starting Friday.

READ: WALANG PASOK: Class suspensions on Friday, Sept. 11 amid habagat rains

Article continues after this 

“Good news for our fellow citizens here in Luzon, as the southwest monsoon weakens and will continue to weaken over the weekend,” she said.

The southwest monsoon may bring between 50 and 100 millimeters of rain over Pangasinan, La Union, Benguet, Zambales, and Bataan, according to Pagasa.

Gloomy skies with scattered rains may prevail over Metro Manila, the rest of Luzon, Western Visayas, and Northern Samar due to the habagat.

“In other parts of Luzon, we will still experience cloudy weather, but there will be longer periods where the sun will shine through,” she reported.

Meanwhile, a low-pressure area (LPA) is being monitored 900 kilometers (km) west of Southwestern Luzon.

Article continues after this 

It has a medium chance of developing into a tropical depression within the next 24 hours, according to Pagasa.

“We expect this LPA to move away from the country, pulling the southwest monsoon along with it. It is moving in a west-northwestward direction, and we anticipate it will head toward northern Vietnam,” Loreto said.

Article continues after this 

A second LPA was estimated 2, 145 km east of Eastern Visayas and has a low chance to develop into a tropical cyclone within the next 24 hours.

“However, we expect it to continue moving west-northwestward over the weekend and potentially enter the area of responsibility,” she added. /das

World.title: Survey shows more Filipinos see better year ahead
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — Overall personal optimism among Filipinos improved in June, with 48 percent (“optimists”) expecting their quality of life to improve in the next 12 months.

According to the Social Weather Stations (SWS) survey conducted from June 20 to June 29, eight percent saw it worsening (“pessimists”) while 31 percent said it will stay the same (“no change”).

This resulted in a net personal optimism (percentage of “optimists” minus percentage of “pessimists”) of +40, which is classified by the SWS as “excellent.” This was also 17 points up from the “high” +23 in March and slightly above the 2025 average “very high” score of +39.

Article continues after this 

The June score was the highest since the “excellent” +41 recorded in June 2025.

READ: SWS: 33% of Filipinos say quality of life improved

Excellent

Among regions, net personal optimism was highest in Luzon outside Metro Manila at an “excellent” +49, up 27 points from the “high” +22 in March. It was followed by Metro Manila at a “very high” +36 (up 8 points from a “high” +28), the Visayas at a “very high” +33 (up 6 points from a “high” +27), and Mindanao at a “very high” +31 (up 11 points from a “high” +20).

The June survey also found that 33 percent of adult Filipinos said their quality of life improved compared to 12 months ago (“gainers”), while 33 percent said it worsened (“losers”). On the other hand, 34 percent said it stayed the same (“unchanged”).

Among these groups, net personal optimism was higher among the “gainers” at an “excellent” +60, followed by “unchanged” at an “excellent” +40 compared to “losers” at a “fair” +12.

Article continues after this 

The SWS classifies net personal optimism scores of +40 or more as “excellent,” +30 to +39 as “very high,” +20 to +29 as “high,” +10 to +19 as “fair,” +1 to +9 as “mediocre,” -9 to 0 as “low” and -10 and below as “very low.”

The survey used face-to-face interviews with 1,200 adults nationwide with sampling error margins of plus-or-minus 3 percent for national percentages and plus-or-minus 6 percent each for Metro Manila, Luzon outside Metro Manila, the Visayas and Mindanao. /das

World.title: BI: No reason to stop Cayetanos from leaving
World.content:
Bureau of Immigration building. — File photo by Niño Jesus Orbeta/INQUIRER

MANILA, Philippines — Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano and his sister, Sen. Pia Cayetano, boarded a flight to Singapore on Wednesday, arriving at Changi Airport hours later, according to the Bureau of Immigration (BI).

“The Bureau of Immigration confirms that Senators Alan Peter Cayetano and Pia Cayetano are currently out of the country,” it said in a statement on Thursday.

“Based on BI records, there were no hold departure orders or derogatory records against the two senators, as of departure date, that would legally prevent them from leaving the country,” it added.

Article continues after this 

READ: BI confirms Cayetano siblings traveled out of the country

The BI did not say that Cayetano’s wife, Taguig City Mayor Lani Cayetano, also left the country on Wednesday night, as confirmed by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian the next day.

According to Gatchalian, while he does not know the reason for the departure of the Cayetanos, he sees nothing wrong with it as senators do not need to seek permission from the chamber to travel for personal reasons.

He said only senators traveling on official business need permission from the Senate. “For example, if the Senate is paying for hotels, tickets and staff expenses, there must be an official notice filed with the Senate,” Gatchalian told reporters.

Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente Sotto III said the same thing. In a separate message, he explained that “senators are not compelled to ask permission to leave the country.”

Article continues after this 

In contrast, government employees must apply for a travel authority from their office whenever they leave the country, even for personal trips. They are required to present the document to immigration agents at the airport before departure.

Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri also said it was okay for the Cayetanos to go on a personal trip, particularly for “health reasons.”

Article continues after this 

“I think it’s a personal trip. I think it’s for health reasons. I wish them well. That’s okay, there’s no problem with that,” he said.

Not an issue

In a social media post, Sen. Panfilo Lacson, who has been engaged in a word war with Alan Peter Cayetano over alleged irregularities in flood control and reclamation projects in Taguig City, called his departure a nonissue.

“This is not an issue as of the moment. Let’s make him take a break from the stress caused by issues that he himself created,” Lacson said.

READ: Cayetano to Lacson: Stop the theatrics, let evidence speak

He added that he wished his colleague well, despite their differences. “[I]f it is simply health-related, I sincerely wish him well despite our animosities.”

Alan Peter Cayetano is currently being investigated by the National Bureau of Investigation as well as the Office of the Ombudsman in connection with alleged irregularities in the country’s hosting of the 2019 Southeast Asian Games, where he served as chair of the Philippine Southeast Asian Games Organizing Committee.

Lacson and his office have also formally submitted to the Ombudsman at least 45 case studies backed by official documents detailing “systemic anomalies” in flood control infrastructure projects in Taguig City, the political bailiwick of the Cayetanos.

The Ombudsman has since launched a fact-finding investigation into the reported irregularities.

World.title: Get to know the next 10 national artists
World.content:
The National Artist medallion — Photo from the National Commission for Culture and the Arts via Philippine News Agency

MANILA, Philippines — Ten Filipino cultural luminaries are entering the esteemed circle of national artists, making up the largest single batch of awardees since the honors were established in 1972.

Through Proclamation No. 1414, series of 2026, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has conferred the Order of national artists on the following:

• Nicanor Tiongson (for Literature)

Article continues after this 

• Gregorio Brillantes (Literature)

• Imelda Cajipe-Endaya (Visual Arts)

• Nunelucio Alvarado (Visual Arts)

• Gabriel “Gabby” Formoso (Architecture)

• Rafael “Nonoy” Froilan (Dance)

Article continues after this 

• Maria Beatriz “Patis” Tesoro (Design)

• Armando “Bing” Lao (Film and Broadcast Arts)

Article continues after this 

• Teodoro Hilado (Theater)

• Alfredo Buenaventura (Music)

Formoso, Lao, Brillantes, and Hilado received the recognition posthumously, while Cajipe-Endaya became the first female national artist for visual arts.

READ: Palace names National Artists for 2025, 1st woman in visual arts

The proclamation was signed by Marcos on Sept. 1, according to the chief of the Presidential Communications Office, Secretary Dave Gomez. The date of the conferment ceremony is yet to be announced.

The new batch raises the number of total awardees to 91 since the recognition started during the first Marcos administration. The award is the highest national recognition given to Filipinos who have made significant contributions to the development of Philippine arts and letters.

The selection is based on the recommendations of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts and the Cultural Center of the Philippines (CCP). Aside from a gold-plated medallion minted by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, the honorees will receive a cash award, a lifetime monthly stipend, life insurance, state funeral benefits, and a place of honor in state functions and cultural presentations.

The following notes offer a glimpse of the latest awardees’ work and legacy:

Gabriel Formoso

Formoso was born in Manila on April 9, 1915. He finished high school at Ateneo de Manila in 1933, then enrolled at the University of Santo Tomas School of Architecture where he graduated in 1937. He would go on to start his practice in architecture two years later in 1939, becoming one of the first 100 licensed architects in the Philippines. Formoso’s technical mastery was seen in his over 200 works, composed of residential, industrial, and commercial edifices.

Among his most renowned designs are the Asian Institute of Management Building, Doña Narcisa Building, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Complex, Philippine National Bank Financial Center, Bank of America-Lepanto Building, United Coconut Planters Bank, Dusit Thani (then Hotel Nikko/Manila Garden Hotel), Pacific Star Building, Peninsula Manila, Heritage Hotel, and PLDT Sampaloc complex.

His awards include the Likha Award from the United Architects of the Philippines in 1990; the 1979 Outstanding Architect of the Year Award from the Professional Regulation Commission; and the 1977 Patnubay ng Kalinangan Award from the Commission on Arts and Culture.

Formoso passed away on Dec. 23, 1996.

Rafael ‘Nonoy’ Froilan

Froilan was born on Oct. 24, 1950 in Calbiga, Samar. He received his degree in Business Administration from the University of the East (UE), Manila, in 1971, and a degree in Education at the University of the Philippines Diliman in 1977. Having begun his career as a folk dancer in UE Dance Troupe in 1968, he later joined the CCP Dance School in 1972.

From 1973, he was a principal dancer in Ballet Philippines, and acted as a teacher for modern dance from 1975 to 1980. He later received the cultural award in dance from the Metro Manila Commission on Culture in 1981. That same year, he became an instructor of jazz at Shoe Mart Dance Arts in Quezon City.

Froilan is known for his roles in landmark productions, including “Songs of a Wayfarer,” “Song of Adarna,” “Roi David,” and productions of “A Midsummer Night’s Dream,” “Romeo and Juliet,” “Amada,” “Itim Asu,” and Misang Pilipino, among many others. As a choreographer, he also contributed to Filipino dance through original works, such as “Danzas” (1986), “One Afternoon” (1987), “Iba’t Ibang Salita” (1988), and “Amparo (1990).”

Patis Tesoro

Known as the “grand dame of Philippine fashion,” Maria Beatriz “Patis” Tesoro got her start in fashion learning from her dressmaker mother while growing up in Iloilo. Born on Dec. 29, 1950, she learned how to embroider in high school, and later learned the business of making sustainable indigenous and traditional art from her mother-in-law. After attending Maryknoll (now Miriam College) from 1959 to 1968, she began studying art education at Marygrove College in Detroit, Michigan. She also began designing ready-to-wear clothing in the early 1970s. By 1982, she launched her own label, “Patis,” followed by her first fashion show in 1984.

READ: Patis Tesoro preserves Filipino couture with every stitch

In 1992, Tesoro became the organizer of the Katutubong Filipino Foundation, an organization devoted to providing tribal and rural-based Filipinos with livelihood opportunities while preserving their traditional arts and crafts.

Having devoted over 30 years of her life to preserving the use of traditional Filipino fabrics, Tesoro has also helped revive the piña fabric industry to ensure its longevity, bringing it to the world stage. She has also sought to modernize and revive other traditional Filipino fabrics, such as abaca, jusi, and silk. She received the Gawad Tanglaw ng Lahi Award from Ateneo de Manila University in 2016 for her commitment to the revival of Philippine traditional textiles.

Armando ‘Bing’ Lao

Armando “Bing” Lao was born in Davao City on Sept. 6, 1948. He began his career in film in the 1980s. Respected for his “substantial body of work in Philippine cinema,” Lao was the recipient of several Gawad Urian awards, including the best screenplay honors for “Takaw-Tukso” in 1987, “Itanong Mo sa Buwan” in 1989, “Oras-Oras, Araw-Araw” in 1990 and “Tuhog” and “La Vida Rosa” in 2001. In April 2024, he was among the “Parangal ng Sining” awardees of the Film Development Council of the Philppines (FDCP), a recognition given to exemplary Filipino artists or organizations who had significant impact to the Philippine cinema.

He was also the screenwriter behind the films “Serbis” (2008) and “Kinatay” (2009) which competed at the prestigious Cannes Film Festival. Aside from his work as a screenwriter, Lao also directed “Biyaheng Lupa” (2009), “Ad Ignorantiam” (2012) and “Dukit,” and served as the creative consultant of numerous films.

He also established the “Found Story” School of Filmmaking where he conducted workshops that “[guided] aspiring and professional storytellers in creating films that resonate deeply with audiences.”

Lao passed away in June 2024 at the age of 75.

Gregorio Brillantes

Gregorio Brillantes was born on Dec. 18, 1932, in Camiling, Tarlac, which also served as the setting for a number of his stories. He attended the Ateneo de Manila University from 1948 to 1952, where he completed a bachelor of letters degree, major in journalism. He would later go on to teach English at Ateneo High School as well as literature and creative writing at the Far Eastern University, all while contributing short stories to national magazines.

READ: Gregorio C. Brillantes, 92: Master of the ‘fine story’

He won the Philippines Free Press’ annual short story contest several times, receiving the top prize in 1953 (for “The Living and the Dead”), 1954 (for “A Wind over the Earth”), and 1956 (for “The Distance to Andromeda”). “Faith, Love, Time, and Dr Lazaro” received the second prize at both the Free Press contest and the Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards in 1960.

Brillantes received the Catholic Mass Media Award of Merit for Best Book for “The Apollo Centennial” in 1981; the South East Asian Writers or SEA Write Award in 1982; and the Patnubay ng Sining at Kalinangan award from the city government of Manila in 1983.

He died in September 2025.

Nicanor Tiongson

Nicanor Tiongson was born in Malolos, Bulacan, on Jan. 10, 1946. He is an essayist, playwright, and cultural administrator. He authored “The Cinema of Manuel Conde,” “The Urian Anthology,” and “The Women of Malolos,” and edited the 10-volume “CCP Encyclopedia of Philippine Art.” His plays include “Pilipinas Circa 1907,” “Basilia ng Malolos,” “Noli at Fili Dekada 2000,” and “Mabining Mandirigma.”

Tiongson received several awards over the years for his significant works. One of his recent awards include the Lifetime Achievement Award in 2024, given to him by the FDCP through its Parangal ng Sining.

Alfredo Buenaventura

Alfredo Santos Buenaventura was born in Santa Maria, Bulacan, on Oct. 14, 1929. He is a composer, conductor, and teacher. He composed a number of operas, symphonic poems, vocal works and chamber music.

Among his notable pieces are “Bayan Kong Mahal,” and “Mabuhay March,” as well as the 1961 musical composition and orchestra “Maria Makiling” which earned him the Republic Cultural Heritage Award in 1964. The artist received the same award in 1972 for his “Kayumanggi Symphony.”

Teodoro Hilado

Teodoro “Teddy” Hilado was born in Silay City, Negros Occidental, on May 15, 1938. He was a lighting designer and technical director. He was recognized by many as the father of lighting design in Philippine theater.

Hilado was the technical director of the CCP from 1969 to 1973 and designed most of its important theatrical events. He was also a theater director of the Folk Arts Theater from 1973 to 1986. He was bestowed the Gawad CCP Para sa Sining in 1997.

Hilado died of brain cancer at the age of 77 on Dec. 23, 2015.

Imelda Cajipe-Endaya

Imelda Cajipe-Endaya, 76, was born in Manila on Sept. 16, 1949. One of the pioneers of feminist art in the Philippines, she is a printmaker and a painter, consistently exploring the themes of national identity and people empowerment, gender, race, migration, displacement and globalization in her artworks.

READ: Imelda Cajipe-Endaya: Woman and artist for all seasons

Some of her major works are in the following collections: “Bintana ni Momoy” (Momoy’s Window), 1983, Ateneo University Art Gallery; “Pasyong Bayan” (A Nation’s Passion), 1983, Metropolitan Museum of Manila; “Sa Lupang Golgota,” 1984, Fukuoka Asian Art Museum, Fukuoka, Japan; “Mansanas sa Almusal” (Apple for Breakfast), 1988, CCP; and “Solidarity Sisters,” 1999, Central Bank of the Philippines.

She also earned local and international recognition, such as the gold medal in printmaking from the Art Association of the Philippines in 1979, Mayi Critics’ Choice in 1980, CCP Thirteen Artists Award in 1990, Cheju Pre-Biennale Special Award in 1995, Patnubay ng Sining at Kalinangan Award from the City of Manila in 1998, RP Centennial Honors for the Arts in 1999, artist in residency at Ecole Cantonale d’Art du Valais, Switzerland, in 1999 and awards from the American Society of Contemporary Artists in 2009.

Nunelucio Alvarado

Nunelucio “Nune” Alvarado was born in Fabrika, Sagay City, Negros Occidental, on May 5, 1950. He is celebrated for his progressive artworks depicting the plight and struggles of the Negros-based “sakada” (seasonal cane workers), or laborers hired from outside the region. He developed a distinctive style marked marked by bold colors, emotion, and strength.

He has had many solo exhibitions of works of strong social impact, including his first show “Hampang-Hampang Lang ’Ni Pero Tuod Tuod” (Playful But True), 1979, Sining Kamalig, Manila. He has also taken part in major group exhibitions in the country, such as “Piglas: Art at the Crossroads” (To Be Free: Art at the Crossroads), 1986, and “Terra non Terra” (Earth Ground), 1992, both at CCP.

Alvarado was among the Thirteen Artists awardees of the CCP in 1992. He also received the Grand Prize in the Philip Morris Philippine Art Awards in 1997 and 1999. INQ /das

World.title: Ahead of arraignment, Sara suffers setback in another case
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte. — File photo by Grig C. Montegrande/INQUIRER

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte suffered a legal setback after the Taguig City Prosecutor’s Office dismissed her perjury complaint against her alleged former aide Ramil Madriaga for “insufficiency of evidence.”

The dismissal came a day after Quezon City prosecutors threw out a complaint filed by Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, accusing several lawmakers and Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) officials of illegally disclosing bank transactions involving him and Duterte during a congressional hearing. Prosecutors said they had no jurisdiction because the respondents were public officials with Salary Grade 28 or higher and acted in their official capacities.

In a 19-page decision, Taguig prosecutors said the evidence failed to show that Madriaga knowingly and willfully made materially false statements under oath, as required under Article 183 of the Revised Penal Code.

Article continues after this 

“Accordingly, the complaint must be dismissed for insufficiency of evidence,” they said.

READ: QC prosecutors junk VP husband’s complaint over release of bank records

Duterte filed the complaint after Madriaga submitted an affidavit to the Office of the Ombudsman in March alleging that he had delivered large sums of money to various people on her instructions. He claimed to have served as her “bagman” or courier for diverted confidential funds.

Duterte denied knowing Madriaga or having personal or professional dealings with him. She filed another perjury complaint in August, submitting about 1,000 pages of documents that she said “thoroughly exposes Madriaga’s malicious and deliberate falsehoods.”

The prosecutors, however, found the evidence insufficient to support a criminal charge.

Article continues after this 

They noted, however, that the ruling does not resolve whether Madriaga’s affidavits hold evidentiary value and whether he is credible as a witness in other judicial proceedings.

Another courtroom battle

The back-to-back setbacks came as Duterte was set to face another legal battle.

Article continues after this 

She is due to be arraigned at 8:30 a.m. on Friday before Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98 on three counts of grave threats over her Nov. 23, 2024, remarks about having President Marcos, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and then Speaker Martin Romualdez killed if she were killed.

READ: Spox: Sara Duterte to attend Friday arraignment for grave threats case

Duterte has denied the charges and posted P360,000 bail last Saturday.

On Thursday, Duterte urged the Supreme Court to immediately resolve her Sept. 7 petition for a temporary restraining order and/or writ of preliminary injunction as she asserted that she has immunity from suit as a sitting impeachable official.

Her spokesperson, lawyer Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr., confirmed with the Inquirer that Duterte will attend her arraignment.

National Capital Region Police Office officer in charge Brig. Gen. Christopher Abrahano assured that they will provide necessary security measures for the Vice President.

Meanwhile, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said Duterte had yet to seek the withdrawal of her more than 300 security escorts despite saying last Saturday that she no longer trusted the police, the court or even her security team.

World.title: 4 retired SC justices giving views on ‘2/3’ conviction vote
World.content:
On its 23rd day of proceedings at the Senate in Pasay City on Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, the impeachment court continues its evaluation of Article I, which focuses on allegations surrounding Vice President Sara Duterte’s misuse of confidential funds. Prosecution and defense panels presented arguments as the court scrutinized evidence and witness testimonies related to the alleged irregular liquidation of government funds. — Photo by Niño Jesus Orbeta/INQUIRER

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court is turning to four retired Supreme Court justices to settle a question that could decide Vice President Sara Duterte’s fate: Does it still take 16 votes to convict when four senator-judges are not taking part in the trial?

The impeachment court on Thursday named retired Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban, Reynato Puno and Hilario Davide Jr., and retired Associate Justice Adolfo Azcuna as amici curiae, or legal advisers to the court, on the potentially decisive voting issue.

Panganiban (who writes a column, “With Due Respect,” in the Inquirer), Puno and Azcuna will appear before the impeachment court on Sept. 16. Davide will submit a legal memorandum that will become part of the record, according to impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol.

Article continues after this 

READ: Barbers: Expert views on VP Duterte voting needed before taking issue to SC

“The impeachment court is not leaving constitutional math to guesswork or chance,” Tongol said, adding that the four legal luminaries were tapped to provide guidance on the contentious issue.

Their intervention came after Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo on Tuesday asked presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero to revisit his July 6 ruling that 16 votes would be needed to convict an impeachable official.

“When we refer to all members, who exactly are we counting?” Tulfo had asked.

Article XI, Section 3(6) of the 1987 Constitution provides that an impeached official cannot be convicted “without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate.”

Article continues after this 

The dispute centers on whether “all members” should mean all 24 senators regardless of their ability to participate, or only those legally able to take part in the impeachment proceedings and final vote.

Four senators are currently unable to attend the trial: Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, who is in hiding amid an International Criminal Court arrest warrant; Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, who are facing nonbailable plunder charges before the Sandiganbayan; and Loren Legarda, who is reportedly in France on an extended medical leave since Aug. 3.

Article continues after this 

Estrada, Marcoleta and Dela Rosa have not attended a single impeachment trial. Their absence prompts the question of whether the 16-vote requirement should remain despite the reduced number of participating senator-judges.

What conviction means

If Duterte is convicted by the Senate acting as an impeachment court, she will immediately lose her position as Vice President. The impeachment court may impose an additional penalty of perpetual disqualification from holding any public office, permanently barring her from running for government positions or public service in the future.

A conviction does not preclude separate criminal or civil proceedings, meaning she can still face trial in regular courts for civil and criminal liabilities.

The three retired justices who will appear on Sept. 16 are expected to present their legal views and answer questions from the senator-judges.

The prosecution and defense panels will present their own oral arguments on Sept. 23, with each side given 15 minutes.

The senator-judges are then expected to vote on whether to overturn Escudero’s ruling on the threshold.

Tongol said the amici curiae would not be cross-examined because they would provide legal doctrine, not factual evidence. The prosecution and defense panels would only listen to their presentations.

“Since an amicus curiae provides legal doctrine, not factual evidence and the constitutional right to cross-examine applies only to fact witnesses, not scholars advising the bench, the legal panels will just sit and listen during the whole presentation,” Tongol said.

READ: Senate impeachment court revisiting ‘2/3’ conviction rule

Heavyweights

The four advisers bring extensive constitutional and judicial experience to an issue that could affect the outcome of the impeachment trial.

Panganiban and Puno both served as chief justice of the Supreme Court. Puno was later appointed chair of the Consultative Committee that reviewed the 1987 Constitution under President Rodrigo Duterte.

Davide was among the 50 members of the 1986 Constitutional Commission that drafted the 1987 Constitution. He later chaired the Commission on Elections and joined the Supreme Court in 1991.

Then President Joseph Estrada appointed Davide chief justice in 1998, making him the presiding officer of Estrada’s impeachment trial.

Azcuna was also a member of the Constitutional Commission. He later served as presidential legal counsel and spokesperson to then President Corazon Aquino before being appointed to the Supreme Court as an associate justice by President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo in 2002.

While the impeachment court tackles the voting issue, the prosecution is preparing to open Article 2, which accuses Duterte of having unexplained wealth.

Bicol Saro Rep. Terry Ridon said on Thursday that the prosecution had asked the court to subpoena three witnesses: retired Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang, Karen Batu, officer in charge of the Office of the Ombudsman Records Division, and Gerardo del Rosario, director of the Securities and Exchange Commission’s (SEC) Company Registration and Monitoring Department.

Cabotaje-Tang is expected to testify on public accountability and integrity in public office, including mechanisms for addressing undisclosed or unexplained wealth and prohibited business interests.

Batu will testify on Duterte’s statements of assets, liabilities and net worth, or SALNs, particularly those she submitted to the Ombudsman.

Del Rosario will authenticate and identify SEC records involving companies registered in Duterte’s name.

Target timeline

The three witnesses are expected to lay the legal and documentary groundwork for the prosecution’s case involving Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth and business interests.

Ridon said the prosecution hoped to open and finish Article 2 within two to three weeks, depending on the length of the hearings.

Batu and the SEC officials earlier testified before the House justice committee when it heard the impeachment complaints against Duterte.

Cabotaje-Tang retired from the Sandiganbayan in November 2024 upon turning 70. President Benigno Aquino III appointed her presiding justice in October 2013.

Before joining the anti-graft court, she served at the Office of the Solicitor General, eventually becoming assistant solicitor general. She represented the government before the Sandiganbayan, including in efforts to block a plea-bargaining agreement with former military comptroller Carlos Garcia. /das

World.title: AFD 2026 Delivers New Agreements, Market Instruments for Regional Growth
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026: Delivering Impact. Capital in Action concluded with a series of agreements and new financial instruments to strengthen regional financial cooperation, sustainable finance, digital assets, aviation finance and access to capital.

Held on Sept. 9-10, the forum brought together 8,000 participants from 90 countries, including representatives of major global financial institutions and asset managers collectively managing more than $26 trillion. The forum also featured renowned Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen.

Expanding regional financial cooperation

Several agreements signed during the forum focused on regulatory cooperation and improving cross-border access to financial markets.

The Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA) signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the National Bank of Georgia on mutual access and recognition in financial services. The agreement establishes a framework for closer regulatory cooperation between the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) and Georgian financial markets in selected areas.

AFSA also signed an MoU with the Croatian Financial Services Supervisory Agency (HANFA) to strengthen regulatory cooperation and further develop cooperation between the two authorities.

The agreements complement discussions held during the forum on reducing fragmentation between regional financial markets and facilitating cross-border capital flows.

The Astana International Exchange (AIX) and the Kyrgyz Stock Exchange (KSE) also agreed to strengthen cooperation and engagement between Kazakhstan’s and the Kyrgyz Republic’s capital markets.

New instruments for sustainable finance

A major development on the second day was AIX’s launch of trading in voluntary carbon credits verified under the international Verified Carbon Standard (VCS).

AIX became the first exchange in Central Asia to provide its own infrastructure for trading voluntary carbon credits. London-based Valor Carbon became the first supplier, with Standard International Market, an AIX broker and Trading Member, facilitating transactions.

The new exchange-based model is designed to provide transparent trading rules and market-based price discovery for carbon credits, creating an additional mechanism for climate projects in the region to access financing.

The initiative builds on the AIFC Carbon Platform and expands AIX’s environmental products, following the earlier introduction of I-REC renewable energy certificates.

The forum also advanced cooperation in sustainable finance through agreements involving the AIFC Green Finance Center, First Carbon Group, Green Investment Group and HYT-CAPITAL. The agreements aim to support sustainable projects, develop financial instruments and attract investment through capital markets in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.

Aviation and digital assets

Aviation finance was another area where discussions moved toward practical cooperation. The AIFC and Development Bank of Kazakhstan agreed to cooperate on projects related to sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

The forum also highlighted the development of Kazakhstan’s aviation finance ecosystem. Jupiter Jet completed its first aircraft leasing transaction with an American lessor with support from the AIFC Aviation Finance Hub.

Digital finance and tokenization featured prominently throughout AFD 2026. Tech Hub Ltd. and ōzen signed a framework cooperation agreement to develop a music royalty tokenization platform in Kazakhstan and Central Asia.

Other agreements involving CodeCoin Tech Ltd., Delta DA Ltd. and Altyn Bank focused on cross-border financial services, fintech, asset management, trade finance and payment infrastructure.

From discussion to implementation

The agreements signed at AFD 2026 reflect the forum’s broader focus on turning investment opportunities into practical projects and market infrastructure.

The first day centered on sovereign and institutional capital, financial infrastructure, tokenization and the transformation of global finance. The program also included the launch of the AIFC Junior Mining Platform’s investor activities, with 23 early-stage mining projects presented to potential investors.

On the second day, the focus shifted further toward implementation – from carbon-credit trading and aviation finance to regional regulatory cooperation and new digital instruments.

As AIFC Governor Renat Bekturov said at the opening of the forum, competition for capital increasingly depends on the ability to transform opportunities into real projects and investments.

Against this backdrop, the agreements and market initiatives announced during AFD 2026 demonstrate the AIFC’s efforts to position Astana as a platform connecting international capital with investment opportunities in Kazakhstan and across Central Asia.

World.title: Dimash Calls for Investment, Infrastructure to Unlock Kazakhstan’s Creative Potential
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh singer, composer and producer Dimash Qudaibergen called for greater investment, infrastructure and legal support for Kazakhstan’s creative industries during the opening ceremony of Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026 on Sept. 9.

AFD 2026 is a two-day event bringing together more than 5,500 participants from over 80 countries to discuss capital markets, investment, artificial intelligence, innovation, real-economy financing and cross-border capital.

While on stage, Qudaibergen performed “Aqerke,” “Stranger” and “Weekend,” as well as the traditional Kazakh kui “Adai” on dombra.

Following the performance, Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) Governor Renat Bekturov spoke with Qudaibergen about the potential of Kazakhstan’s creative economy, attracting investment to the sector, intellectual property protection and the challenges artists face when entering international markets.

Qudaibergen said the development of the creative industry requires not only investment, but also stronger legal protection for artists and mechanisms to connect creators with investors.

“Artists need legal protection and support from creative industry development funds. These funds can become a bridge between investors and new creative projects,” Qudaibergen said.

Bekturov noted that Kazakhstan’s creative sector brings together thousands of companies and more than 140,000 people, while its contribution to the economy remains relatively small, highlighting the need to develop the sector as a source of future growth.

When asked why investors should consider creative industries, Qudaibergen pointed to Kazakhstan’s culture, history and music as assets with strong international appeal.

“Our culture, our history and the music are truly unique, and that makes them interesting to an international audience,” he said, drawing on his experience of performing around the world.

Protecting creative independence

For Qudaibergen, attracting investment should not come at the expense of an artist’s independence or ownership of intellectual property.

He said the decision to share rights with investors or business partners is ultimately personal, but artists should understand the financial and contractual side of their profession before making such decisions.

“I choose the second option, because for me it is essential to keep both creative independence and ownership of my intellectual property,” he said.

Qudaibergen stressed that financial literacy is part of an artist’s professional responsibility, allowing creators to better understand contracts, finances and the business side of the industry.

“Education everywhere is very important,” he said, adding that understanding contracts, finances and the business side of the industry allows artists to make informed decisions and retain control over their work.

He also cited his own career as an example of how an artist can gradually move from performer to producer and entrepreneur.

Qudaibergen said he now works directly with business partners and operates his own label, established by his father, which promotes not only his work but also young artists.

His transition into production included an international vocal project on China’s Hunan TV, where he first gained international recognition through “I’m a Singer” show. Returning to the network as a producer, he said, gave him an opportunity to introduce other Kazakh talents to a global audience.

From Kazakh roots to global audiences

Qudaibergen said Kazakhstan’s cultural identity can become a competitive advantage internationally when traditional heritage is combined with contemporary approaches.

“Our uniqueness comes from combining respect for our roots with a desire to innovate,” he said. “We can make traditional things feel fresh and turn something authentic into a modern trend.”

During his tours, Qudaibergen has introduced audiences to musicians from his team and traditional Kazakh instruments, including dombra and kobyz. He said some international fans also became interested in Kazakhstan’s history, language and traditional music.

He also encouraged young Kazakh artists to remain connected to their identity while pursuing international careers.

“To become an international artist, you have to follow your own path, first of all. And then you need to believe in yourself,” he said.

He warned young artists against changing direction simply because of short-term financial opportunities.

“Professional career management means thinking long term,” he said. “You shouldn’t accept every offer just because it looks profitable today. You always have to remember the goal you are moving towards.”

Building a system for young talent

Qudaibergen said Kazakhstan’s creative sector needs a more systematic approach to developing talent, particularly in management, professional training, broadcasting and distribution.

He identified a shortage of qualified professionals as one of the industry’s key challenges, arguing that talented artists need more than opportunities to perform.

“We have not yet become a full-fledged industry with a clear system. So, we need to do our best to train professionals,” he said.

He also pointed to the limited presence of creative projects across television, radio and large-scale distribution platforms.

“The main task is to build professional infrastructure and create a clear, systematic path to international markets,” Qudaibergen said.

Qudaibergen said this was particularly important because young artists should not have to rely on chance encounters or simply hope that someone will discover them.

“This is exactly what I was missing when I started,” he said, recalling his own experience as a young artist from Aktobe who had little understanding of how to build an international career.

“Right now, it has become one more mission,” he said. “Young talents should grow inside a real creative development system, instead of simply hoping that one day they will get lucky and someone will invite them somewhere.”

Qudaibergen’s own career, from a young performer in Aktobe to an internationally recognized artist and producer, illustrates the potential of such opportunities. Reflecting on his journey, he emphasized that talent alone is not enough to build a lasting career.

“Hard work is also very important. It’s the most important thing,” he said. “When the universe turns to your side, you need to be ready.”

Qudaibergen is now preparing his new Dimensions world tour, continuing his international career while expanding his work as a producer and supporting young Kazakh artists.

World.title: AFD 2026: Creative Industry Pushes Investors to Rethink What Counts as Financial Asset
World.content:
ASTANA – What if a song, a game, a digital creator or a piece of intellectual property could be treated not only as a cultural product, but as an investable asset? For Kazakhstan’s emerging creative economy, that shift in thinking could be as important as the creative output itself.

The question was at the center of discussions on the second day of Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026, held on Sept. 10 and dedicated to creative industries as an asset class, moderated by David Tuganov, president of the Creative Industries Alliance of Qazaqstan (CIAQ), the panel brought together Aizatulla Hussein, founder of Õzen; Olzhas Akparov, CBDO of Cyber Temple; Julia Kushnir, head of business development for Eastern Europe and Central Asia at TikTok; and Askar Bilisbekov, CEO of Alem Capital Management Limited.

Tokenization of the song?

One of the clearest examples of that shift came from the music industry, where Õzen is working on what Hussein described as a new way to turn music intellectual property into a financial asset through blockchain-based tokenization.

“For the last seven years that we have been working in the music industry, our core business has been the distribution of music content in the digital space. But music is not simply entertainment. It is a full-fledged financial asset that can generate income over many years, and that income continues to grow,” Hussein said.

The concept is to tokenize music rights through smart contracts and allow investors to acquire a fractional economic interest in a song, with returns linked to the income generated by the underlying music.

“What we are doing now is tokenizing the music asset, the music intellectual property, through smart contracts. Now we give anyone the opportunity to come and buy a piece of this song, and when the income comes to the artist, proportionally to how many tokens they have acquired, they will receive those payments,” Hussein said.

The model, he said, could effectively create an internal marketplace for music, where investors can assess the performance and potential of individual compositions using data generated across digital platforms. Õzen’s model is still building the necessary legal and regulatory framework, with Hussein identifying jurisdiction as the key challenge rather than the technology itself.

“In principle, the technology is not a problem at all. These technologies have already been developed. The only serious thing that we need to implement correctly is the jurisdiction, how we can turn a contract into tokens,” he said, noting that the company hopes to launch pilot projects by the end of the year.

The move is significant because it changes the conversation around creative industries from one centered primarily on grants, promotion and audience growth to one centered on ownership, cash flows and investment returns.

Shift in investors’ mindset

Bilisbekov also emphasized this shift in investor thinking, noting that the main obstacle facing creative entrepreneurs in Kazakhstan is often not a lack of talent, but an insufficient understanding of how to present that talent as a business proposition.

Drawing a comparison with Hollywood’s film industry, he said investors have long understood that creative investments can be approached through venture capital strategies, where a number of projects are financed with the understanding that some will fail while a smaller number generate significant returns.

“In Hollywood, the principle was quite simple: invest in a large number of films, knowing and understanding that most of the films will fail,” Bilisbekov said.

He said similar venture-style approaches already finance creative projects globally, while Kazakhstan’s creative sector remains constrained by a fragmented market and a limited understanding of the investor relationship.

“In the creative industry in Kazakhstan and in our region, the attitude toward investors is always somewhat residual. Why? Because there is no understanding that an investor is, first of all, your partner,” he said.

For Bilisbekov, that means creative entrepreneurs also need to change how they themselves approach investment.

“We need to change our mindset,” he said, highlighting that creative founders must be able to understand the financial side of their businesses, communicate their models clearly and demonstrate that they can operate beyond the strength of an idea alone.

“One investor has never bought into a company simply because you are talented, simply because you have an idea,” he said.

From creativity to business value

The point is particularly relevant as the creative economy increasingly intersects with technology. TikTok, for example, is no longer simply a platform for entertainment, according to Kushnir, but part of Kazakhstan’s broader digital creative economy, giving creators, entrepreneurs and businesses direct access to audiences.

“The platform is part of Kazakhstan’s digital creative economy,” Kushnir said, emphasizing what she described as the democratization of creativity.

“Absolutely any person has all the tools and all the opportunities to interact with an audience,” she said, noting that creators do not necessarily need millions of followers or an established public profile to find an audience.

For businesses, that audience can translate into commercial value, with TikTok’s research with the Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs showing that 80% of surveyed small and medium-sized businesses said the platform helps them attract new customers, 79% said it helps them retain customers, and around 70% said it helps them differentiate themselves from competitors. The next step, however, is converting reach and creativity into durable businesses and investable assets. That is where the convergence of creativity, technology and capital becomes particularly important.

Where AI meets creativity

Akparov described how artificial intelligence is already changing parts of game development, including early-stage concept work and the creation of visual references, while Bilisbekov said that Kazakhstan’s strongest competitive advantage may ultimately lie in its human capital.

“Our brains are absolutely competitive. There are simply a little bit more efforts needed in this direction. There will be more of these startups,” Bilisbekov said.

Hussein likewise pointed to a growing convergence between Kazakhstan’s technology and creative communities, arguing that the two sectors need to become less separate.

“IT people should come to creatives, and creatives should come to IT,” he said, describing them as two communities that have traditionally developed in parallel rather than together.

That convergence could become increasingly important as AI lowers some of the technical barriers to building digital products and puts greater value on ideas, storytelling, design and other forms of creative input.

For Kazakhstan, however, panelists suggested that the missing piece is still capital. Hussein noted that the country needs to create conditions for creative talent to develop into sustainable businesses, while Bilisbekov pointed to two priorities: dedicated programs for the creative industries and a deeper capital market.

“We don’t have, as far as I know, even a single acceleration program that has been launched for the creative industry. That is something that needs to be launched,” Bilisbekov said.

He also stressed the importance of developing Kazakhstan’s capital market more broadly, saying creative businesses need financing mechanisms that go beyond traditional business models.

“It is very important to develop the capital market. What we unfortunately lack today is exactly that,” he said.

That is perhaps the broader investment question emerging from Kazakhstan’s creative economy: not whether the country has talent, but whether it can build the financial, technological and regulatory infrastructure needed to turn that talent into assets that can be valued, financed and scaled.

The tokenization initiative being developed by Õzen offers one early example of what that could look like, moving music from a product consumed by an audience toward an asset in which an investor could potentially hold an economic interest.

For a country seeking to deepen its capital markets while developing a new generation of creative businesses, the shift may ultimately require both sides of the equation to rethink their roles: creatives need to become more financially literate, and investors need to become more comfortable assessing assets whose value may be built around intellectual property, audience, technology and cultural relevance rather than factories, equipment or conventional balance sheets.

World.title: ADCB Kazakhstan Plans to Triple Project Financing in Kazakhstan
World.content:
