World.title: Azerbaijan expands investments in its economy for 8M2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 11. Investments in the Azerbaijani economy grew from January through August 2026.

Trend's calculations based on the State Statistics Committee's data show that over 12.6 billion manat ($7.4 billion) was invested in the country's fixed capital during the reporting period. The figure rose by 10% year-on-year.

During the period, 8.4 billion manat ($4.9 billion) was invested in Azerbaijan's non-oil and gas sector, up 1.4% from the same period last year.

The Chairman of the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA), Taleh Kazimov, said at a July 31 press conference on the parameters of the interest rate corridor that the CBA had revised its economic growth forecasts amid an increase in lending activity.

"We forecast economic growth of 0.5% in 2026, while GDP growth in the non-oil and gas sector is expected to reach 2.4%. In 2027, we expect economic growth of 2.6%, while growth in the non-oil and gas sector is projected at 3.9%," the chairman said.

Kazimov noted that the central bank had revised its economic growth expectations compared with its previous forecasts. The previous forecast had projected GDP growth of 1.1% in 2026 and 3.2% growth in the non-oil and gas sector. For 2027, the corresponding forecasts had been 3.2% and 4.7%.

The CBA chief stressed that despite global economic developments, there was no need for the central bank to change its current monetary policy course.

"The Central Bank has action plans for various scenarios within its monetary policy framework and is able to respond promptly to changing economic conditions. There is currently no basis for switching to a ‘Plan B,’ and therefore such a scenario is not being discussed," he noted.

According to him, current macroeconomic indicators provide sufficient grounds for continuing the existing policy.

"The macroeconomic environment and current regulatory indicators provide grounds for continuing the current policy course. Therefore, we are continuing to implement the strategy we have chosen," he said.

The official added that all central banks prepare alternative action plans to address potential risks.

"One of the key conditions for successful monetary policy is making the right decision in a timely manner in response to changing circumstances. We believe that the monetary policy we are currently implementing will adequately address potential challenges the economy may face in the medium and long term," he emphasized.

World.title: Live: Rams and 49ers arrive at MCG ahead of historic Australian NFL match
World.content:
(Getty Images)

Here's a pub quiz stat for you: the MCG will become the fifth stadium to host an NFL game and the opening/closing ceremony of an Olympic Games.

The Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum (1932, 1984), Berlin's Olympiastadion (1936), London's Wembley (1940) and the Estádio do Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro (2016) have all hosted an Olympic Games opening ceremony, as did the MCG in 1956.

The Stade de France (closing ceremony at Paris 2024) will join that list when it hosts its first game later in the season.

Given the Rams are the home team, they will now have hosted matches at two different Olympic stadiums, having played at the Coliseum between 1946 and 1979 and 2016 and 2019.

(Getty Images)

Perhaps less surprisingly, the MCG is the first stadium to have hosted a Cricket World Cup final and an NFL regular-season game, so there is that.

At 100,022, the stadium has the largest capacity of any that the league will use this season.

World.title: Bigger and hungrier: What we know about 25 proposed new data centres
World.content:
Dozens of approved but yet-to-be-built AI data centre projects will escape the federal government's proposed restrictions around energy and water use because the new rules are not expected to be retrospective.

ABC analysis of planning records and company documents has revealed this new generation of data centres will be significantly bigger and power hungrier than existing ones.

Earlier this year, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the federal government would create Australian standards to quell community concerns about the environment, while attracting the investment of major tech companies.

With the government aiming to pass a law to establish these rules by early 2027, the uncertainty has not slowed the breakneck speed of development.

Business has welcomed the tens of billions of dollars being invested in building the physical infrastructure powering the generative AI boom, although not all of the approved data centres will likely be built.

Know more about this story? Email Cam Wilson on wilson.cameron@abc.net.au or his secure email cmwlsn@protonmail.com

Bigger, hungrier

ABC analysis of upcoming projects includes developments from Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, AirTrunk, CDC and NEXTDC, as well as property groups Goodman and Stockland, each of which was contacted for confirmation.

The list has been verified by analysts from commercial renewable energy project mapper RenewMap and real estate construction analytics firm CBRE.

Advocacy group Data Centre Australia published a report saying Australia had 162 data centres with a combined IT capacity of 1.5 gigawatts as of March of this year.

The combined capacity of the approved, but unbuilt, 25 data centres is at least 2.9 gigawatts, based on each company's statements of computing power and the state planning-approved energy capacity.

One project approved last week is property developer Goodman's five-storey data centre Project Apollo in Sydney's north.

It will take two years to build and be one of Australia's biggest data centres by computing capacity if it existed today, according to the facility's proposal.

While not subject to the federal government's rules, its approval came with conditions from the NSW government relating to water and energy use.

Australia has more than 160 existing data centres and dozens more in development. (ABC News)

RenewMap co-founder and director Alex Thompson said the development pipeline had accelerated in recent months, with proposed centres generally much larger than those already operating.

He said NSW and Victoria were the main growth areas, particularly western Sydney and Melbourne's outskirts, while developers were also pursuing regional locations alongside wind, solar and battery projects.

Mr Thompson said even though they have been approved, "not all of these data centres will get built".

Environmental concerns

For software engineer and western Sydney resident Jack Tollefsen, the expansion is happening close to home.

He lives in Horsley Park and works down the road from NEXTDC's S4 development, which is under construction and expected to provide 365MW of capacity.

Jack Tollefsen takes pride in his community garden on Sydney's western fringe and is worried about a massive data centre being built in the area. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Mr Tollefsen has started a petition opposing the data centre and others being built in suburban areas.

An environmentalist who opposes AI, Mr Tollefsen said he had raised his concerns with local and state representatives.

"My main concerns with this are largely the environmental impact, the impact it has on the ecosystem, the native wildlife in the area," he said.

Mr Tollefsen said he was disappointed the federal government had not already introduced minimum standards for data centres.

He said he hoped NEXTDC would at least reduce its water usage by designing it with a closed-loop system, a more water-efficient approach that requires more energy.

NEXTDC's data centre, being built on Sydney's western fringe, is expected to be bigger than existing projects. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

The proposed national standards are intended to address energy, water and land-use impacts of large data centres, but state and territory governments will retain their planning responsibilities.

The exact details of the proposed legislated standards have not yet been released.

So far, the federal government has said it will require data centres to underwrite new renewable energy to cover their consumption, cover the connection costs, be as water-efficient as possible, and be built in appropriate locations.

Some of the approved data centres may meet these standards, even if they are not legally required to comply.

Australia wants investment on our 'terms'

In July, Mr Albanese delivered a landmark speech detailing how Australia would respond to the opportunity and challenges presented by AI.

The prime minister said Australia had both the desire and capacity to attract investment from major AI companies, including data centres, as long as they met certain requirements.

Anthony Albanese attended national cabinet last month, discussing rules for AI data centres. (ABC News)

He said the government would pass a law in early 2027 setting rules to force data centres to minimise water use and maximise energy efficiency.

"We can set the terms, we can determine AI's social licence," he said, claiming the standards would create certainty for investors, too.

But the prime minister later told ABC Radio Sydney the rules would not apply to projects already approved or under construction.

"You can't retrofit. But as well, many of the centres which are under construction tend to be smaller ones," he said.

A Department of Industry, Science and Resources spokesperson said Australia had far fewer large data centres built and in construction than the United States, citing research from S&P Global Ratings.

"Current investment trends suggest the number of large data centres will increase. The Australian government wants this investment to be sustainable and aligned with our national interests," they said.

Call to stop building until rules in place

Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young has been leading calls for a ban on data centre construction until the government establishes minimum standards.

She said communities were already facing pressure from developments being proposed and built, and argued standards introduced after projects were approved would not provide the protections the government was promising.

"In the absence of a moratorium on building and approving new data centres, then these rules must be retrospective because otherwise they're worthless," she said.

Senator Hanson-Young said the government risked losing community support for AI if it did not take concerns about energy, water and local benefits seriously.

Is Australia prepared for the data centre boom? As data centres rapidly come online to meet demand, governments are urged to ensure development does not outpace adequate planning.

Data Centres Australia chief Belinda Dennett said her industry was already taking steps to meet the government's expectations around power and water use.

"Members will continue to meet those requirements until the new rules are in force — but they cannot comply with something that isn't yet established or even articulated."

Investment continues

Kate Muller, a partner in Ashurst Perkins Coie's projects and energy transition practice, said the delay and uncertainty around national standards was not dampening investor interest.

Ms Muller said Australia was attractive to major technology companies because of its security, and a government and policy environment similar to US-headquartered businesses.

She said developers were used to dealing with some regulatory uncertainty.

Kate Muller's work includes advising on data centre projects. (ABC News: Nickoles Coleman)

"The degree of debate, guideline and regulation is unlikely to deter that investment and we certainly haven't seen that in our practice and with the people that we're speaking to around industry," she said.

Ms Muller said clear expectations could help ensure projects delivered benefits for Australians, while public debate could help address their potential detrimental effects.

"Indeed, we expect to see a genuine drive toward more data centre development in Australia," she said.

Two federal parliamentary inquiries are examining data centres and AI respectively, and will report back later this year.

World.title: 'Art is central to our political power': 50 years of land rights celebrated in art award
World.content:
When Elizabeth Ngwarraye Bonney received the prestigious 2026 Vincent Lingiari Art Award, she was not there to accept it.

She was sitting under the stars on her country a few hundred kilometres north-east of Alice Springs.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains images of people who have died, used with permission.

"The land holds stories, and when we are there, we feel them," she said in a statement read on her behalf.

Elizabeth Ngwarraye Bonney says her mother has been fighting for their country for 40 years. (Supplied: Central Land Council/Artists of Ampilatwatja)

Her winning painting, titled My Grandmother's Country, is layered and deep, featuring river systems, desert wildflowers, hills and valleys and gums — almost alive and moving.

Ms Bonney, of Artists of Ampilatwatja, is a traditional healer and painter.

Her mother, Eileen Bonney, fought for her country as part of the Wakaya-Alyawarre land claim for 40 years.

Elizabeth Ngwarraye Bonney's painting, My Grandmother's Country. (ABC News: William Green)

"[It was] one of the longest-standing land claims in the Northern Territory, and now she is passing it over, so we can pass it over to our children," Ms Bonney said.

" My mother had to fight because this was her mother's country. "

Intersection of art and land rights

The theme of this year's Vincent Lingiari Art Award (VLAA), presented by the Central Land Council (CLC) and the peak for central Australian Aboriginal art centres, Desart, on Thursday night, is Our country, our culture: 50 years of land rights.

The famous image of Gough Whitlam and Vincent Lingiari. (AGNSW: Mervyn Bishop)

In the room of finalists, the artworks are as diverse as the nine CLC regions they hail from, all across the central Australian desert.

The exhibition features ceramics, soft sculpture, traditional topographical paintings of land, painted fuel caps and even a Kaytetye Ned Kelly who wears bright pink pants.

Dr Josie Douglas says the power of Aboriginal art has always been central to First Nations political power. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

CLC general manager Dr Josie Douglas said Aboriginal art remained integral to fighting for country and land rights.

"The power of our art has always been central to our political power," Dr Douglas said.

"You can see that in the 1988 Barunga Statement and the artwork from that statement, which was danced up and presented to prime minister Bob Hawke.

"You can also see it in 1993, ahead of the Mabo decision, when the former chairman of the CLC, Wenten Rubuntja presented prime minister Paul Keating with a painting titled Yeperenye Dreaming."

Josie Douglas says Aboriginal art is frequently used to substantiate land claims. (Supplied: Central Land Council)

Dr Douglas said her favourite painting in the collection was the Kaytetye Ned Kelly.

It's a self-portrait by Ned Kelly, who continued to fight to keep his country safe, culminating in a High Court ruling last month to set aside the NT's largest groundwater extraction licence at Singleton Station.

The artworks in the VLAAs are as diverse as the regions they hail from. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Warumungu and Luritja curator of the VLAA, Kelli Cole, said it was important to celebrate all Mr Lingiari had achieved.

She said marking the 50th anniversary of the Aboriginal Land Rights Act, through the exhibition, felt vital.

Warumunga and Luritja curator of the VLAA Kelli Cole says celebrating Vincent Lingiari's legacy is vital. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

"Vincent Lingiari, a Gurindji man, led the Wave Hill Walk-Off in 1966; he and many others, and he had the struggle … he pursued equal rights and payment for working on country," Ms Cole said.

"For me, it's so important to honour his legacy."

The diverse range of works linked to the award theme, 50 years of land rights. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Land council award

Last month, more than 1000 people gathered in Kalkaringi for the Freedom Day Festival to mark the 60th anniversary of the Wave Hill Walk Off, led by Vincent Lingiari in 1966.

Photographs of the VLAA finalists were taped to the side of council four-wheel-drives in a travelling bush exhibition so that CLC representatives at the celebrations could crown the winner of the CLC Delegates Choice Award.

They chose Warumungu leader and translator Joseph Williams Jungarrayi's arresting piece 'Three Brothers'.

Mr Williams said his piece, depicting three faces against an old mining map of the Tennant Creek area, was about reclamation.

Joseph Williams Jungarrayi says his painting is about reclamation. (Supplied: Central Land Council/Anna Miers)

"Transforming a document that once marked extraction and disruption into one that carries culture, story and identity," he said.

"Fifty years on from land rights, this work speaks to reclamation — of land, of narrative and of identity.

" It honours the enduring presence of ancestors and recognises that our stories are still embedded in country, no matter how it has been mapped, divided or used. "

Desert Mob, now in its 35th year, continues across the weekend in Alice Springs with artist talks today, a marketplace and workshops on Saturday and satellite events at various art centres on Sunday.

World.title: Country council says four-day week has been a game-changer
World.content:
A small country shire in southern Western Australia says its decision to adopt a four-day work week has almost solved the challenge it faces in attracting and keeping key workers.

The Shire of Boyup Brook is six months into a trial of a four-day week for all full-time office workers, with plans to roll out the measure to outside crew next year.

The local government, 260km south of Perth, is among the sector's earliest adopters of the four-day work week, alongside the New South Wales shire of Murrumbidgee, set to start a trial next year.

Council staff compress the hours of a normal five-day week into four, working 9.5 hours each day, with no change to opening hours or service delivery for locals.

The shire of Boyup Brook has a population of about 1,700 people. (ABC News: Jacquie Lynch)

Bid to attract workers

Boyup Brook chief executive Leonard Long said the shire needed to find ways to attract workers to the small town.

With a population of just 1,700, the shire's limited rates base also means it is not able to pay as much as larger local governments.

"Being in a regional area, it's difficult to attract staff in the first instance," he said.

Leonard Long says a compressed work week helped the shire attract staff. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Mr Long said the trial had already proved successful, with the shire able to recruit for a senior position it had been unable to fill before the trial.

"He took it because of the four-day week," Mr Long said.

" He did have other options to go to, which would have been closer to home and paying more. "

The shire has more than a dozen office staff, split into two teams, with each team taking either Monday or Friday off, allowing no disruption to services.

Boyup Brook says its four-day work week model is working well. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Administrative officer Jimina Shaw-Sloan said working four longer days afforded uninterrupted time to work and meet outside usual opening hours.

"I find it really good, just mainly for having some really solid blocks of time that you're not forward-facing to clients," she said.

Jimina Shaw-Sloan says a compressed work week has many benefits. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Four-day week just one way to attract staff

WA Local Government Association president Mark Irwin said remote councils were trying different ways to attract staff, with nine-day fortnights also common.

Mark Irwin says there is a skills shortage across local governments. (ABC News: Jacqueline Lynch)

"Ninety per cent of local government reported a skill shortage in recent surveys we did," he said.

" We see a lot of people who are effectively working remotely; I was talking to one shire where many of their staff were not only interstate, but even overseas. "

Workplace and organisational behaviour expert Libby Sander said research into four-day work weeks internationally had shown positive results, including increased productivity.

While a compressed five-day week had benefits, Dr Sander said it would likely not be as beneficial to staff as an overall reduction in hours each week.

Libby Sander studies organisational behaviour at Bond University. (Supplied: Dr Libby Sander)

But she said the Shire of Boyup Brook's decision to introduce a standard four-day week across all its administrative staff, rather than ad-hoc rostered days off, was significant.

"It reduces that psychological pressure to keep working [on a day off], which we know Australians feel quite keenly," Dr Sander said.

" That 'I feel like I'm slacking and there might be something my team is dealing with, that I need to deal with'. "

Australian Services Union WA secretary Wayne Wood also noted that the Boyup Brook model was different from a "genuine" four-day work week, where employees work fewer hours with no loss of pay.

But he welcomed the new approach.

"We have long advocated for these types of flexible arrangements," he said.

"Particularly for WA local governments facing challenges attracting and retaining skilled staff, especially in regional areas."

World.title: MATES charity aims to prevent suicide in heavy industries
World.content:
Warning: This article contains discussions of suicide.

Sydney mother Maggie Pearce says her son Ben was loud, had a lot of friends and was dedicated to his job as a shopfitter.

"He was just a beautiful soul," Ms Pearce said.

She says her 21-year-old son, who took his own life in 2018, had struggled with drinking.

Maggie wanted to turn that grief into fuel for change and started facilitating conversations about mental health in her transport workplace where she looks after a depot of staff.

She now volunteers as a connector with MATES, which specialises in heavy industries including construction, mining, energy and manufacturing.

Ms Pearce says she has had hundreds of important conversations with her workmates since, including when someone has had a bad day or when a major event is affecting staff broadly.

"I don't want to see another mother in the same position that I am," she said.

"I think the only way that we can do this is to increase awareness for people to say that it's OK to reach out for help.

" We spend so much time at work that you might pick up on signs in people that they're not OK that they may hide from their family. "

Maggie Pearce (left) volunteers as a connector with MATES at her workplace. (Supplied: MATES)

Trades are the most common occupation among male suicides

Deaths by suicide among men are highly represented in heavy industry.

In 2023 and 2024, 1,383 men died by suicide who worked as technicians or in trades, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

This figure represented the most common occupation among suicides, making up 27.6 per cent of suicides in males.

Ms Pearce says the long hours and living away from loved ones may be leading to some mental stresses to those in this line of work.

She also says some occupations like mining and construction on big sites are reasonably well paid, which is sometimes fed into gambling.

"They're working long hours, so then their, I would call it 'playtime', is probably not the best things," Ms Pearce said.

Brad Parker says it is important to have people available for important conversations at worksites. (Supplied: MATES)

MATES in Construction NSW CEO Brad Parker says there's many other factors too, including the long working hours and culture of heavy alcohol use and occasionally bullying.

"One of the big things is job insecurity in our industry," Mr Parker said.

" The life of the project is as good as the life of the job. "

"It is the only industry that I know of in the world where we work so hard to work ourselves out of a job."

Network of carers looking out for workmates

The charity was initially set up in 2007 in Queensland as Men Actively Talking to Each other on Sites (MATES) in response to research showing higher rates of suicide among construction workers compared to other professions.

Mr Parker says MATES has since grown to around 37,000 volunteers nationally reaching around 330,000 colleagues to have potentially life-saving conversations.

In 2021 the World Health Organization recognised their work as an example in their implementation guide for suicide prevention in other countries.

Mr Parker said the key is having a network of people on the ground at workplaces where they are accessible for the important conversations.

"[Workers] spend more time at work with their workmates than they probably do with their loved ones, family or friends," Mr Parker said.

"We need our people on the ground."

The NSW organisation is mostly funded by government, while its national arm received around 43 per cent of its funding from government sources.

Ms Pearce says while attitudes towards mental health have become more open in the last decade, there's still work to be done to make it more accessible.

Ms Pearce hopes governments can help fund programs to set up similar support networks in small businesses, like where her son Ben worked, which was too small to have the kind of support networks that larger sites have.

"I don't believe they have the resources or funding within the smaller companies," Ms Pearce said.

"That will help break down some stigma around mental health."

MATES 24/7 Helpline: 1300 642 111

World.title: Live: ASX set to fall as oil passes $US109 and bond yields surge
World.content:
Capital Economics senior markets economist James Reilly gives eight reasons why he thinks the S & P 500 looks like it's in a "late-stage bubble" that will inflate a bit further this year before popping next year.

The first is valuation.

"Shiller's cyclically adjusted PE [price-to-earnings ratio] (CAPE) has risen close to its dotcom peak," he writes. "And the S & P 500's valuation compared to that of US Treasuries (i.e., the equity risk premium), is around its most stretched since the dotcom bubble."

The second is unprecedented earnings expectations around artificial intelligence-related firms.

Long-term earnings growth forecasts for S&P 500 companies (Capital Economics)

"We think AI will indeed boost productivity and support stronger earnings. But not to the extent priced," Reilly argues. "Any signs of earnings disappointing expectations at these firms would take a heavy toll on the S & P 500 index."

Renegade Australian economist Steve Keen put out a very interesting YouTube video on this theme earlier this week.

The third is the rapidly shrinking free cash flow and surging debt of the AI hyperscalers.

"The combined free cash flow for the hyperscalers at the heart of the AI boom is expected to turn negative in 2027 amid huge CapEx [capital expenditure] plans," Reilly writes. "The pace of corporate debt issuance has increased to record highs and hyperscalers' issuance has now more than doubled since last year."

Reilly argues a significant rise in market volatility is also a warning sign, pointing to the massive gyrations in South Korea's KOSPI driven by AI-related stocks.

The extreme market concentration in what is known as the "Magnificent Seven" has been worrying many analysts for some time.

Market concentration is at record highs (Capital Economics)

"Index concentration is alarming," Reilly warns. "Narrow leadership raises idiosyncratic risk and is often associated with unsustainable rallies. "Measures such as the 10 largest firms' weight in the S & P 500, or that of the 400 smallest firms, are at extreme levels."

Share sales are also approaching previous bubble peaks. Unsurprisingly, corporate insiders tend to raise more funds by selling shares in their companies when they think valuations are near their peaks.

US equity raising is approaching previous bubble peaks (Capital Economics)

"With more blockbuster IPOs [initial public offerings] and share sales by AI hyperscalers looking likely, a further wave of equity supply looks set to be unleashed," writes Reilly. "On past form, this suggests that the end of the bubble is just months away, rather than years."

He also cites a record-high share of foreign ownership in US stocks and a steady increase in leverage (debt-funded share purchases) as the final factors that make him think there is a stock bubble and that it's nearing its peak.

World.title: Opals knocked out of World Cup as luckless captain's torn ACL confirmed
World.content:
The Opals have been knocked out in the quarterfinals of the Women's Basketball World Cup in a 23-point loss to Spain just hours after receiving more devastating injury news about captain Ezi Magbegor.

Half an hour before the tip-off in what turned out to be a comprehensive 89-66 loss to Spain, Magbegor's WNBA team, the Seattle Storm, revealed the star forward had torn her ACL.

Magbegor, who only returned to the court in early July after partially tearing her Achilles in March, went down early after taking a knock to her right knee in Australia's qualification final win over Italy.

"It makes me emotional when I see anyone go down," Opals coach Sandy Brondello said after the loss to Spain.

"But Ezi's come back from an injury and it's just another injury. [It's] just really unfortunate. She's a key part of what we want to do. It sucks, but that's sport isn't it?

"She's got to have a great recovery and she'll get back, I don't have a doubt about that. Just disappointed for Ezi that she's going through another rehabilitation."

The inexperienced Opals struggled without some of their biggest stars. (Supplied: FIBA)

Magbegor joined fellow stars Alanna Smith (leg injury) and Jade Melbourne (illness) on the sidelines, while veteran Sami Whitcomb was ruled out before the tournament with injury and Cayla George did not play due to pregnancy.

Smith suffered a lower-leg injury in the opening game of the tournament, while Melbourne played only three minutes against Italy and could not take the floor in the quarterfinal.

The Opals made a great escape after surrendering a 20-point three-quarter-time lead against the Azzurre thanks largely to a 30-point explosion by 21-year-old Izzy Borlase, but the missing players were too much to overcome in the final-eight showdown.

Ally Wilson was Australia's top scorer with 13 points as the team shot just 40 per cent from the field and had 23 turnovers.

Veteran Steph Talbot said she her young team's lack of big-tournament experience was evident in the game, and said it was a strange experience hitting the court with only eight teammates.

"It's very weird. It was very quiet, very unusual. We were all looking around like, 'Is this it?'" she said.

"But a job's a job and we fought hard to the end. I'm really proud of the effort they put in. It's definitely a different experience."

Brondello said the difficult World Cup would be valuable experience for the team, which boasted seven players in their first major international tournament, with the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics looming large on the horizon.

World.title: How this Perth man keeps Dockers fans pumped up from the top
World.content:
"Get a haircut and get a real job" is a popular saying, but it was his luscious locks that helped Troy Nababan land a plum job.

He's the Fremantle Dockers guitarist, rocking Queen and AC/DC covers from the top of the 60,000-seat Perth Stadium.

The 38-year-old Morley father is one of a handful of people who can boast that they have played to a sold-out crowd at the stadium, among the likes of Ed Sheeran and Coldplay's Chris Martin.

Troy Nababan is one of a few musicians who can say they've played to a sold-out Perth Stadium, strapped in a harness, right on top. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

"I dreamed I would [play stadiums] when I was very young, but I thought that opportunity had maybe disappeared as I got a little older," he said.

" It's not the sort of gig you get to have every day … during the game the sound of the crowd is immense. "

A long way to the top

The gig is not for the faint-hearted.

The platform at Perth Stadium where Nababan stands is 42 metres high, or a 12-storey drop to the grass below. There are no handrails and worst of all, the metal grate is see-through.

It's a long way to the top - the platform at Perth Stadium where Nababan stands is 42 metres high. (ABC News: Nicolas Martyr)

Even after hundreds of games, Nababan — who is anchored to the platform by a harness — says he still does not look down.

"It does get slippery if it rains. I had a little trip maybe two or three weeks ago, went a little bit too hard and my sneaker got caught," he said.

But even that does not seem to faze Nababan. He says his biggest risk is rocking too hard and giving himself a wedgie.

Nababan says he doesn't look down when he's rocking the crowds. (Supplied: Instagram)

"This is not the sort of gig you can do passively. They [the crowd] pump me up, I try and pump them up. I try and run around as much as possible," he said.

" The way the harness grabs is like a seatbelt. If I jump up a little too much, it sort of grabs, and I am wedgied. "

'A bit of a strange gig'

It all started with a "random phone call" in 2019.

Nababan said his booking agent was looking for a long-haired guitar player for what they called "a bit of a strange gig".

His luscious locks got him the gig as the Fremantle Dockers' guitarist. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

"They said 'we want you to play on top of Perth Stadium', and I'm like 'alright' but I was thinking 'is that safe'?" he said.

"My philosophy from when I was much younger was always say yes. If there's an opportunity, just go for it."

For years, footy held little appeal for music-obsessed dad from Morley. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Playing AC/DC covers was a natural transition. The guitarist is inspired by 80's hair metal like Mötley Crüe and Whitesnake.

In the purple haze of his recording studio, 30 guitars hang on the walls, most of them electric and more than one covered in rhinestones.

Nababan keeps more than two dozen guitars in his studio. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

When he is not rocking the stadium, the father of two is a recording engineer who also teaches students at TAFE.

Rocking the bandwagon

Nababan goes to the park every weekend with his son to kick the footy but admits his love of the sport is relatively new.

Like many musicians, he dreamed of playing stadiums when he was very young. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

"It was a slow transition, I'd watch the first quarter and head home, then it was watching the first half … and now unfortunately it's a big obsession of mine," he said.

"Every day it's what footy media is on YouTube, what podcast can I listen to … I just can't seem to get enough of it at the moment.

" The energy of this stadium this whole season has been really, really powerful. There's so much positivity, it's electric. "

The musician is now firmly on the roller-coaster of being a Fremantle fan. He is still recovering from last week's upset defeat the minor premiers suffered against Hawthorn.

Dockers wilt against masterful Hawthorn So good for so long this year, Fremantle chose an inopportune time to put in — by some distance — their worst shift of the season, going down by 32 points to a brilliant Hawthorn.

"It wasn't the best feeling, but I am choosing to be positive about it. I think the supporters are very firmly behind the club," he said.

Before tonight's elimination and his last gig of the year, the man behind the leather jacket and long hair said he would consume a lot of coffee, a lot of sugar and do his damnedest to create an electric atmosphere.

As for his hair care, a generous dollop of coconut oil stops it from drying out in the wind.

World.title: Survey reveals how many young motorists take risks on road – and number is rising
World.content:
NationalQueenslandRoad safety Survey reveals how many young motorists take risks on road – and number is rising Dominique Tassell September 11, 2026 — 9:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than a quarter of Queensland’s younger motorists admit they get behind the wheel without wearing a seatbelt and almost as many say they have driven while on drugs. The number of young Queenslanders who admit to driving without a seatbelt has risen. The figures in RACQ’s 2026 Annual Road Safety Survey indicate a deeply concerning trend, says Josh Cooney, the motoring club’s executive manager of road safety. According to the survey, 28 per cent of Queenslanders aged 18 to 24 admitted to driving without a seatbelt, an increase of 9 per cent from the previous year’s figure. Just over 22 per cent of those polled admitted to driving under the influence of drugs, up from 15.9 per cent of drivers in that age bracket.



And while the number of young drivers who admit to speeding had fallen, it remained high at three in five drivers, or 63.2 per cent. Related Article Sponsored

IAG Australia How smart car technology could prevent one in five road casualties “Young drivers continue to be overrepresented in serious and fatal crashes on our roads, and

these latest results are worrying,” Cooney said. “In 2025, P-plate drivers and riders were involved in 10 per cent of deaths on Queensland roads – a

tragic reminder that inexperience, risk-taking and poor decisions behind the wheel can have

devastating consequences. “Every time someone drives without a seatbelt, speeds or gets behind the wheel intoxicated, they

are putting their life and the lives of others at risk.”



Cooney called for more random breath tests, more roadside drug tests and mandatory drug

testing for every crash police attended to increase the chances dangerous drivers were caught

before they caused serious harm. Related Article Exclusive

Traffic Driving past this huge Brisbane school? Here’s how fast traffic moves at drop-off time “The more visible police are on our roads to deter and detect dangerous behaviours, the better

our chances of curbing this road safety crisis that’s tragically killing far too many Queenslanders,” he said. Queensland has recorded 185 road deaths so far this year. Last month, the RACQ raised concerns about the road toll surpassing last year’s. More than 300 people lost their lives on Queensland roads in 2025, marking the highest road toll in 16 years.



Road deaths in 2026 are on track to be even higher. To raise awareness of the expected toll, 107 life-sized silhouettes were installed in King George Square. RACQ said the message behind the campaign was simple: the number of people represented by the silhouettes had not yet been lost. World.title: NFL Melbourne LIVE: NFL stars dress to impress as crowds, celebs flock to the MCG for historic Rams-49ers clash
World.content:
Freezing cold or burning hot weather, a cold beer, food out of your truck, and the company of your new and old friends. Tailgating is one of American Football’s greatest traditions.

At your average American tailgate, you will see everyone decked out head to toe in the merch of whichever team they support. In some cases, people will get a blow-up costume of their team’s mascot. Don “Bearman” Wachter is an example of someone who goes all out for his team, the Chicago Bears. Wachter dresses in a taxidermy bear head with the rest of his clothes having fur sewn onto them, making the “Bearman”.

Tyrone Harris and Rampage pose for a photo at the Rams Tailgate Experience. Zoey Duchene

In the US, where most stadiums are surrounded by giant, open car parks, the true tailgating experience lies in grilling out of the back of a truck. It is reminiscent of family, with crowds growing from a few close friends to strangers who happen to be “friends of friends”.

Australians might not call it tailgating but they do get together in carparks before big games. President of the Croydon Rangers, which is one of the teams a part of the Gridiron Victoria American football club, Brock Lynch and his family have already had their own experience with it. Back in 2008, they hosted their own tailgate outside of the MCG before the Hawthorn-Geelong grand final.

World.content:
Iranian strikes damaged multiple American military aircraft this week on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, a US official told Reuters.

A US official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said Iran’s attack hit one A-10 Thunderbolt II, known as the Warthog, leaving it with a missing wing, while about eight F-15s sustained light damage and were returned to service.

Iran’s strike on the US base in Jordan came after US forces said they destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers. The US said its strikes were in response to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeting a US Navy warship with ballistic ​missiles twice over the previous two days.

The Iranian attack required US forces to fire roughly 30 Patriot interceptors to counter the missiles, the US official said, amid increasing concern about the inventory of American air defence interceptors and other missiles.

While specific inventory numbers are classified, the Centre for Strategic ​and International Studies has estimated that about 65 per cent of US Patriot interceptors were expended between February and July, with fewer than 850 left on hand, down from 2330 before the Iran war began.

World.title: ‘Chilling’: AI giant Anthropic says it blocked possible efforts to build biological weapons
World.content:
TechnologyAI ‘Chilling’: AI giant Anthropic says it blocked possible efforts to build biological weapons Dustin Volz September 11, 2026 — 6:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anthropic said it had disrupted several potential plots this year by scientists who used its leading artificial intelligence models to conduct research that could have helped develop biological weapons. In a report describing misuses of its AI models, Anthropic said it could not determine whether the research served a legitimate or nefarious purpose because valid biological inquiry — the kind that can lead to breakthroughs like vaccines — can also help engineer dangerous pathogens. In the face of that uncertainty, Anthropic said it erred on the side of caution because the consequences of missing malicious activity could be severe. The potential for cutting-edge AI models to facilitate the development of known or entirely new biological pathogens is among the gravest concerns experts have about a technology that is developing so rapidly that even its leading architects doubt whether humans will be able to fully control it. AP “You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, ‘Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,’” Jacob Klein, the head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, said in an interview. “It’s an incredibly nuanced situation.” The potential for cutting-edge AI models to facilitate the development of known or entirely new biological pathogens is among the gravest concerns experts have about a technology that is developing so rapidly that even its leading architects doubt whether humans will be able to fully control it.



Compared with the threat of catastrophic cyberattacks or AI agents that fail to align with human intentions, biological misuse has gained less attention as an existential risk of AI, in part because past examples have generally been shown only in research settings rather than in the real world. Andrew Weber, a senior fellow on the Council on Strategic Risks who reviewed Anthropic’s report before its release, said the findings were “chilling examples of state-sponsored biological weapons developers tapping into the rapidly advancing capabilities” of leading AI models. Related Article AI ‘Could kill us all’: Anthropic insiders say AI has more than 10% chance of ending humanity – soon The lengthy report Anthropic published on Thursday catalogued a litany of misuses of its AI models, including the chatbot Claude, over the past eight months. Some examples were similar to past disclosures from Anthropic and other AI labs, including suspected Chinese and Iranian government-linked actors targeting dissident and diaspora communities for surveillance. The report also highlighted cases of Russian state media using Claude to generate online propaganda masquerading as independent reporting, including fabricated claims about an election in Moldova.



Anthropic documented another genre of abuse it said was new: attempts to use Claude to develop software for conventional weapons design and development, including firearms, missiles, armed drones and bombs. It detailed three cases in China, two in Russia and one in Yemen. The report does not identify by name which parties were involved in the Yemeni case, but the context makes clear that it is referring to the Iran-backed Houthi militia. AI use by terrorist networks is a growing concern among US security officials. But among all the categories of threats shared in the report, none may be as worrisome as the biological research cases. Anthropic did not disclose the names of researchers or institutions that it blocked, their countries of affiliation or the specific biological agents at issue, in part because of its uncertainty about their aims. The lengthy report Anthropic published on Thursday catalogued a litany of misuses of its AI models, including the chatbot Claude, over the past eight months. AP Photo/Patrick Sison Still, Anthropic said the scientists circumvented its controls intended to prevent users from blocked regions from gaining access to its AI models and worked to “obfuscate the purpose of their research to evade our safeguards.” The company banned accounts associated with the research.



In one example from May, a scientist sought Claude’s help with writing a grant application for funding to conduct research intended to experiment on the chikungunya virus, a mosquito-borne malady that can lead to months of severe pain and other symptoms. Such research, known as gain of function, can be legitimate and lead to vaccine development, but it can also create superbug versions of viruses. In this instance, the scientist wanted to engineer mutations to the virus that would make it more harmful as it repeatedly infected live animals. Anthropic said it believed the particular research was worrisome in part because it could discern that the work was intended to be performed at a military research institute. The findings are ‘chilling examples of state-sponsored biological weapons developers tapping into the rapidly advancing capabilities.’ Andrew Weber, a senior fellow on the Council on Strategic Risks “What we don’t know is if the research was meant to be weaponised,” Klein said. “But a military institution doing gain-of-function research is concerning.” Anthropic said evaluations from last year of its older models demonstrated that they were not yet able to meaningfully assist in conducting dangerous biological research. Its current models are more able to complete complex scientific research, the company said, which spurred tighter safeguards intended to restrict access to a wide range of dual-use biological research queries.



Susan Monarez, a microbiologist and public health expert who oversaw a review of national biosecurity preparedness in the Obama administration, also reviewed the Anthropic report before its publication. She said the findings provided real-world evidence to support concerns that bad actors were trying to covertly use advanced AI “to improve their chances of building biological pathogens that could cause significant harm.” Related Article Analysis

AI ‘We must be stopped’: Why Australia needs to listen to the experts on AI Monarez, who briefly served as the director of the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention last year, said AI held enormous promise to usher in an era of medical breakthroughs that save and extend lives. But the same abilities that make that possible, she added, could also “let bad actors hide in plain sight, using seemingly legitimate research to create pathogens we may not see coming and may not be able to stop once released.” Weber of the Council on Strategic Risks, who also served as the assistant secretary of defence for nuclear, chemical and biological defence programs during the Obama administration, called for limiting access to AI tools capable of this level of biological research to trusted researchers only. “The fact that Russia, China and North Korea continue to develop prohibited biological weapons makes it imperative that we deny their researchers access to these extraordinarily capable models,” he said.



This article originally appeared in The New York Times. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: ASX set to slump, Wall Street falls as oil climbs to its highest mark since May
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slump, Wall Street falls as oil climbs to its highest mark since May Stan Choe Updated September 11, 2026 — 6:27am ,first published 5:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil prices keep climbing as the war with Iran keeps clogging the global flow of crude, and they leaped Thursday to their highest levels since before the summer. That worsened worries about inflation and cranked up pressure within the bond market, helping to send stocks lower again on Wall Street. The S&P 500 fell 0.6 per cent for a fourth straight loss, its longest such streak since June, though it’s not far from its all-time high set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 316 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.7 per cent. Oil climbed to its highest mark since March. AP The Australian sharemarket is set for another day of heavy losses, with futures at 6.13am AEST pointing to a loss of 81 points or 0.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX shed 1 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was lower at US71.56¢. US stocks sank under the weight of rising oil prices. Brent crude, the international standard, climbed another 6.3 per cent and briefly topped $US108 per barrel for the first time since May before settling at $US107.63.



Related Article Energy Australia softens local gas supply rules, easing fears in Asia It’s jumped from less than $US72 in early July as hopes fade that the war with Iran will allow oil to flow freely again from the Middle East anytime soon. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that oil prices likely won’t come down until after the US midterm elections in November. The jump has vaulted the price for a gallon of regular gasoline to an average of nearly $US4.28 across the United States, according to AAA. That’s up nearly 34 per cent from a year earlier and is not only costing people more at the pump but also through higher prices for all kinds of products that move by truck to store shelves. A report on Thursday said inflation at the US wholesale level accelerated to 5.4 per cent last month from 4.8 per cent in July, and retailers could eventually pass such increases in prices onto shoppers. A report is coming on Friday that will show how much inflation US consumers are feeling. The typical move to rein in high inflation is for the Federal Reserve to raise its main interest rate, the federal funds rate. Such a move then filters out through the rest of the bond market, makes it more expensive for US households and businesses to borrow money, slows the overall economy and undercuts prices for investments. That hopefully would remove some of inflation’s fuel.



A report on Thursday suggested the US job market may remain solid, with fewer workers applying for unemployment benefits last week. That could give the Fed more confidence that the economy could withstand higher interest rates. Following Thursday’s reports, traders see a roughly 73 per cent chance the Fed will raise the federal funds rate at its meeting next week. That’s up from the 61 per cent probability seen the day before, according to data from CME Group. That’s also despite Trump’s consistent lobbying for interest rates to go lower rather than higher. The Fed’s counterpart in Europe, the European Central Bank, raised its own interest rates on Thursday in hopes of getting inflation in check. It cited “the conflict in the Middle East” and how it “continues to generate inflation pressures.” It all pushed the yield on the 10-year Treasury up to 4.95 per cent from 4.83 per cent late Wednesday, which is a significant move for the bond market. It’s up from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran began and is back to where it was in the autumn of 2023. That was after the Fed cranked the federal funds rate higher to get super-high inflation coming out of the COVID pandemic under better control.



Higher yields mean investors can make more money putting their money into bonds, which can in turn make investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other investments that are riskier than bonds. Some investors see a 5 per cent yield on the 10-year Treasury as the next potential flashpoint. But strategists at Bank of America’s Research Investment Committee suggest 7 per cent may be the more important threshold, pointing to peaks for expensive stocks around that point in the past. Related Article Opinion

Bonds Trump’s ‘top bond salesman’ is getting a reality check Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In the meantime, the rising 10-year Treasury yield is making mortgages more expensive and hurting the housing industry. One report on Thursday said the average long-term US mortgage rate hit its highest level in over 14 months, while a second one said sales of previously occupied US homes fell in August to their slowest pace in more than a year. That helped sent stocks of homebuilders lower, including drops of 3.5 per cent for Lennar and 2.4 per cent for D.R. Horton.



Elsewhere on Wall Street, Macy’s fell 4.7 per cent even though the retailer reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. While raising its forecast for earnings this fiscal year, it warned that “there are macroeconomic and geopolitical factors that could influence” how much its customers feel comfortable spending. Macy’s said it received $US116 million ($162 million) in tariff refunds from the government — $US98 million during the quarter and another $US18 million after the quarter ended. Macy’s CEO Tony Spring told The Associated Press Thursday that it’s using some of the proceeds to lower prices on certain items like furniture and other big-ticket purchases. All told, the S&P 500 fell 44.66 points to 7,591.70. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 316.56 to 52,064.10, and the Nasdaq composite sank 171.62 to 26,081.72. In stock markets abroad, indexes slipped across much of Europe and Asia. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 1.3 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves. World.title: This rising indie rock star has done his 10,000 hours, and it shows
World.content:
CultureMusicReview This rising indie rock star has done his 10,000 hours, and it shows Annie Toller and and John Shand September 11, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nate Amos’ earworms are always catchy but rarely too sweet. This Is Lorelei, The Singer in My Band ★★★★ By the time his first official, label-anointed album came out in 2024, Nate Amos had done his 10,000 hours. Over the years he’d uploaded scores of releases to Bandcamp under the name This Is Lorelei – work that, until recently, was just a side project to his long-running art-pop outfit Water From Your Eyes. Now, it’s coming into its own. The years of compulsive attention to craft have paid dividends: his latest album, The Singer in My Band, is a tight, affecting collection of songs, flitting deftly between power-pop, alt-country and pop-punk.



There are goofy moments – like single Billy Came Back, a zippy jangle-pop tale of a local karaoke legend blowing back into town – but gut punches too, especially in the resonant, open-stringed numbers that fill the album’s second half. The arrangements are always catchy but rarely too sweet: even the earworm hook and cascading harmonies of highlight Oh No Now My are paired with a taut, digitally tortured guitar solo. This Is Lorelei’s Nate Amos has taken his one-time side project to centre stage. Eve Alpert Though billed as a road album, written and recorded amid a relentless touring schedule, The Singer in My Band was finished at Amos’ family home with cameos from his father and sister, both professional bluegrass musicians. It feels like a grounding moment in his trajectory – a return to centre as a solo artist, led by songwriting-first principles. Annie Toller



A sophisticated sense of mischief fuels the jazz group’s new album. Zela Margossian Quintet, Remedy ★★★★ You know that feeling when you revisit a home from your past, to find the furniture changed and walls repainted, so any familiarity or nostalgia are jumbled with an unsettling newness? This third Zela Margossian Quintet album is like that.



The familiarity of the snaking melodies of Margossian’s Armenian roots, and of her rigorous classical training being entwined with jazz’s open-endedness, are still there, but her compositions are even more sophisticated and varied, with a delightful sense of mischief sometimes creeping in. The band, meanwhile, is joined by guest artists on four pieces, swelling the already expansive palette of colours generated by Margossian’s piano, Stuart Vandegraff’s saxophones, Jacques Emery’s bass, Alexander Inman-Hislop’s drums and Adem Yilmaz’s array of percussion. Phil Slater’s trumpet cries gently over a lament called Indifferent World – a reality with which we’re all familiar. The stateliness of Jenny Eriksson’s viola da gamba features on What If, the title possibly asking what would happen were that instrument added to this already exotic band. The answer? A dreamy timelessness. Virna Sanzone applies her plush voice to the Armenian lyrics of How I Wish, and flamenco guitarist Damian Wright makes Kintsugi glisten like sunlight on water. World.title: Sex, drugs and a legend redefined: it’s time to meet the real Marianne Faithfull
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Marianne Faithfull died last year, directors Iain Forsyth and Jane Pollard had been working on a film about her for four years. Watching Broken English, named for the hit album she made in 1979, you can see what a compelling subject she was. A ’60s survivor, still probably best known to an older generation as Mick Jagger’s ex-girlfriend and the subject of scandal, she emerges as a formidable woman who was also a singer, writer and actor, the kind of liminal artist who popped up in collaborations with professional fans from Metallica to Nick Cave. In her ’70s, she is in a wheelchair, hooked up to an oxygen tank: the result of long COVID. Whatever, she still commands the room. Broken English isn’t so much an account of her life as a response to it, pitched somewhere between documentary, essay and fiction. Archive footage is sprinkled between interviews with Faithfull herself. These are set within an imaginary “Ministry of Not Forgetting”, the questions asked by “an archivist” played by 1917 star George MacKay. Derek Jacobi narrates the film and Tilda Swinton plays the head of the ministry, who at one point lists Faithfull’s many achievements before concluding: “And yet, to the world at large, she’s still just Mick Jagger’s girlfriend. Well, f--- that.” Tilda Swinton stars in the unconventional documentary. In his role as archivist, MacKay wears an earpiece to hear the directors urging him to push a point or drop it, depending on Faithfull’s answers. Clearly, they never aimed to cover Faithfull’s entire life. The juiciest scandal from her Stones era is left out. Her youthful heroin addiction is in there, but the gruesome details of her life on the street that she described in her autobiography aren’t. And while her first husband, John Dunbar, appears with her, Jagger does not. “I didn’t know how to make him a part of it,” Pollard says with a short laugh. “I really enjoyed reframing it, looking at that period of her life from the perspective of her childhood, growing up in a commune.”



With the Stones, she says, “they all felt they were all working towards something that felt really important”. But, as Faithfull reflects herself, that wasn’t how she was seen. She was cast as a rock’n’roll casualty. She was the woman arrested in a drug raid wearing only a fur coat. For the tabloids, she was a terrific story. The filmmakers set out to tell a different story. Their approach to the years Faithfull spent with Jagger, for example, was to shift their gaze away from the usual catalogue of disasters. We learn how Faithfull took Jagger to see the Royal Ballet with Rudolf Nureyev, knowing he would love it; we see that she joined in a poetry event with the Beat poets and became a lifelong friend of Allen Ginsberg. Marianne Faithfull with George MacKay in Broken English. Madman Films “All these cultural things that she was absorbed in and that she was sharing with Mick, things that felt a lot more relevant and interesting than just who at the end of the day she was going to bed with,” Forsyth says. “I hope that as much as the film is a story about a life, it’s just as much a film about how we choose to tell that story.” Forsyth and Pollard are best known to Australian audiences for their inventive 2014 film about Nick Cave, 20,000 Days On Earth. They first became interested in Faithfull because Cave and his musical partner Warren Ellis knew her well; Ellis worked with her as a producer and toured with her, playing in her band. “In the year before the lockdown, we would chat to Warren a lot,” says Pollard. “He was working on the poetry album She Walks in Beauty with her when she got COVID and went into a coma. He was just heartbroken, in the studio working on the poems, not knowing if she would ever hear them. I think at that point, our hearts found her in a different way. We began to care about her a lot, just vicariously, through him.” Marianne Faithfull with her friend and collaborator Warren Ellis. Rosie Matheson



The interviews with MacKay at the Ministry of Not Forgetting were among the first things they did, afraid that Faithfull’s precarious health would collapse again. After that, they worked on the film’s mosaic structure of memories and other interviews, showing her assembled segments as they went along. From the start, they expected that by the time they finished the work, she would no longer be with them, but they never intended it as an obituary. “The film needed, in some way, to acknowledge her passing, but not to change,” says Forsyth. “We were so determined it wasn’t going to be like a standard text with dates. That felt so at odds with it; it’s so alive with her humour and artistry and brilliance – with her defiance, actually.” George MacKay is 34. He had worked several times with Pollard and Forsyth on art projects, but he knew almost nothing about Marianne Faithfull. “I knew one or two of her songs without knowing they were hers,” he says. He threw himself into research. When he saw how she was pilloried and derided in the press during her Stones period, he was aghast. “It was awful, just on a human level, what was said about her,” he says. “The misogyny she came up against was so intense.” Although he worked from a script, he says the interviews felt like improvisations. “Because Marianne had never seen those scripts – and you have to follow wherever the interview goes.” The Ministry of Not Forgetting sounds as if it could have come from a Harry Potter novel, but it is a key idea for the filmmakers. “Not forgetting was a deliberate act, to make remembering active,” says Forsyth.



“If you choose not to forget, you make the effort. Whereas remembering something is an accident. Do I remember where I left my car keys?” Pollard chips in. “It’s also about learning lessons. The act of remembering seems loaded with a kind of sentimentality; it feels wistful in a way, whereas not forgetting is a recalibration. It has an urgency.” Broken English was billed at last year’s film festivals in Sundance and Venice as a documentary, but Forsyth isn’t sure that holds. “For us, the idea of going into a project saying ‘we are going to make a documentary’ just seems so alien, so limited from the start,” he says. “I think we were going into it thinking, ‘We are going to make a film that tells a story, and we want to make the best film and tell the best story we can.’ For me, ‘non-fiction’ works as well as anything because the story we’re telling is not fiction, although we might be using some of the devices of fictional storytelling. I think the story we’re telling is full of emotional truth. Which is not the same as journalistic truth.” Related Article Cinema Crash to classic: How Practical Magic’s box-office hex marked the spot for Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock For Pollard, the real discoveries in the film are the expressions that flicker across Faithfull’s face as she looks at the old footage of her younger self, beautiful and damaged but still holding up her end of things. “There’s a piece from Weekend World in 1974 or ’75, an interview she probably should have said ‘no’ to, when she had just come out of rehab,” she says. Watching it, Faithfull initially looks dismissive of that young idiot, opining on life. “Then she starts to align with her. And I’m looking from face to face, and I’m seeing the same eyes, I’m seeing the same smile, and I’m seeing the same willingness to be open. We all can all read a face – and cinema is the best way for us to do that. That’s when the film is revelatory.” Broken English opens nationally on September 17.

World.title: Survey reveals how many young motorists take risks on road – and number is rising
World.content:
NationalQueenslandRoad safety Survey reveals how many young motorists take risks on road – and number is rising Dominique Tassell September 11, 2026 — 9:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than a quarter of Queensland’s younger motorists admit they get behind the wheel without wearing a seatbelt and almost as many say they have driven while on drugs. The number of young Queenslanders who admit to driving without a seatbelt has risen. The figures in RACQ’s 2026 Annual Road Safety Survey indicate a deeply concerning trend, says Josh Cooney, the motoring club’s executive manager of road safety. According to the survey, 28 per cent of Queenslanders aged 18 to 24 admitted to driving without a seatbelt, an increase of 9 per cent from the previous year’s figure. Just over 22 per cent of those polled admitted to driving under the influence of drugs, up from 15.9 per cent of drivers in that age bracket.



And while the number of young drivers who admit to speeding had fallen, it remained high at three in five drivers, or 63.2 per cent. Related Article Sponsored

IAG Australia How smart car technology could prevent one in five road casualties “Young drivers continue to be overrepresented in serious and fatal crashes on our roads, and

these latest results are worrying,” Cooney said. “In 2025, P-plate drivers and riders were involved in 10 per cent of deaths on Queensland roads – a

tragic reminder that inexperience, risk-taking and poor decisions behind the wheel can have

devastating consequences. “Every time someone drives without a seatbelt, speeds or gets behind the wheel intoxicated, they

are putting their life and the lives of others at risk.”



Cooney called for more random breath tests, more roadside drug tests and mandatory drug

testing for every crash police attended to increase the chances dangerous drivers were caught

before they caused serious harm. Related Article Exclusive

Traffic Driving past this huge Brisbane school? Here’s how fast traffic moves at drop-off time “The more visible police are on our roads to deter and detect dangerous behaviours, the better

our chances of curbing this road safety crisis that’s tragically killing far too many Queenslanders,” he said. Queensland has recorded 185 road deaths so far this year. Last month, the RACQ raised concerns about the road toll surpassing last year’s. More than 300 people lost their lives on Queensland roads in 2025, marking the highest road toll in 16 years.



Road deaths in 2026 are on track to be even higher. To raise awareness of the expected toll, 107 life-sized silhouettes were installed in King George Square. RACQ said the message behind the campaign was simple: the number of people represented by the silhouettes had not yet been lost. World.title: NFL Melbourne LIVE: NFL stars dress to impress as crowds, celebs flock to the MCG for historic Rams-49ers clash
World.content:
Freezing cold or burning hot weather, a cold beer, food out of your truck, and the company of your new and old friends. Tailgating is one of American Football’s greatest traditions.

At your average American tailgate, you will see everyone decked out head to toe in the merch of whichever team they support. In some cases, people will get a blow-up costume of their team’s mascot. Don “Bearman” Wachter is an example of someone who goes all out for his team, the Chicago Bears. Wachter dresses in a taxidermy bear head with the rest of his clothes having fur sewn onto them, making the “Bearman”.

Tyrone Harris and Rampage pose for a photo at the Rams Tailgate Experience. Zoey Duchene

In the US, where most stadiums are surrounded by giant, open car parks, the true tailgating experience lies in grilling out of the back of a truck. It is reminiscent of family, with crowds growing from a few close friends to strangers who happen to be “friends of friends”.

Australians might not call it tailgating but they do get together in carparks before big games. President of the Croydon Rangers, which is one of the teams a part of the Gridiron Victoria American football club, Brock Lynch and his family have already had their own experience with it. Back in 2008, they hosted their own tailgate outside of the MCG before the Hawthorn-Geelong grand final.

Iranian strikes damaged multiple American military aircraft this week on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, a US official told Reuters.

A US official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said Iran’s attack hit one A-10 Thunderbolt II, known as the Warthog, leaving it with a missing wing, while about eight F-15s sustained light damage and were returned to service.

Iran’s strike on the US base in Jordan came after US forces said they destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers. The US said its strikes were in response to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeting a US Navy warship with ballistic ​missiles twice over the previous two days.

The Iranian attack required US forces to fire roughly 30 Patriot interceptors to counter the missiles, the US official said, amid increasing concern about the inventory of American air defence interceptors and other missiles.

While specific inventory numbers are classified, the Centre for Strategic ​and International Studies has estimated that about 65 per cent of US Patriot interceptors were expended between February and July, with fewer than 850 left on hand, down from 2330 before the Iran war began.

World.title: ‘Chilling’: AI giant Anthropic says it blocked possible efforts to build biological weapons
World.content:
TechnologyAI ‘Chilling’: AI giant Anthropic says it blocked possible efforts to build biological weapons Dustin Volz September 11, 2026 — 6:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anthropic said it had disrupted several potential plots this year by scientists who used its leading artificial intelligence models to conduct research that could have helped develop biological weapons. In a report describing misuses of its AI models, Anthropic said it could not determine whether the research served a legitimate or nefarious purpose because valid biological inquiry — the kind that can lead to breakthroughs like vaccines — can also help engineer dangerous pathogens. In the face of that uncertainty, Anthropic said it erred on the side of caution because the consequences of missing malicious activity could be severe. The potential for cutting-edge AI models to facilitate the development of known or entirely new biological pathogens is among the gravest concerns experts have about a technology that is developing so rapidly that even its leading architects doubt whether humans will be able to fully control it. AP “You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, ‘Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,’” Jacob Klein, the head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, said in an interview. “It’s an incredibly nuanced situation.” The potential for cutting-edge AI models to facilitate the development of known or entirely new biological pathogens is among the gravest concerns experts have about a technology that is developing so rapidly that even its leading architects doubt whether humans will be able to fully control it.



Compared with the threat of catastrophic cyberattacks or AI agents that fail to align with human intentions, biological misuse has gained less attention as an existential risk of AI, in part because past examples have generally been shown only in research settings rather than in the real world. Andrew Weber, a senior fellow on the Council on Strategic Risks who reviewed Anthropic’s report before its release, said the findings were “chilling examples of state-sponsored biological weapons developers tapping into the rapidly advancing capabilities” of leading AI models. Related Article AI ‘Could kill us all’: Anthropic insiders say AI has more than 10% chance of ending humanity – soon The lengthy report Anthropic published on Thursday catalogued a litany of misuses of its AI models, including the chatbot Claude, over the past eight months. Some examples were similar to past disclosures from Anthropic and other AI labs, including suspected Chinese and Iranian government-linked actors targeting dissident and diaspora communities for surveillance. The report also highlighted cases of Russian state media using Claude to generate online propaganda masquerading as independent reporting, including fabricated claims about an election in Moldova.



Anthropic documented another genre of abuse it said was new: attempts to use Claude to develop software for conventional weapons design and development, including firearms, missiles, armed drones and bombs. It detailed three cases in China, two in Russia and one in Yemen. The report does not identify by name which parties were involved in the Yemeni case, but the context makes clear that it is referring to the Iran-backed Houthi militia. AI use by terrorist networks is a growing concern among US security officials. But among all the categories of threats shared in the report, none may be as worrisome as the biological research cases. Anthropic did not disclose the names of researchers or institutions that it blocked, their countries of affiliation or the specific biological agents at issue, in part because of its uncertainty about their aims. The lengthy report Anthropic published on Thursday catalogued a litany of misuses of its AI models, including the chatbot Claude, over the past eight months. AP Photo/Patrick Sison Still, Anthropic said the scientists circumvented its controls intended to prevent users from blocked regions from gaining access to its AI models and worked to “obfuscate the purpose of their research to evade our safeguards.” The company banned accounts associated with the research.



In one example from May, a scientist sought Claude’s help with writing a grant application for funding to conduct research intended to experiment on the chikungunya virus, a mosquito-borne malady that can lead to months of severe pain and other symptoms. Such research, known as gain of function, can be legitimate and lead to vaccine development, but it can also create superbug versions of viruses. In this instance, the scientist wanted to engineer mutations to the virus that would make it more harmful as it repeatedly infected live animals. Anthropic said it believed the particular research was worrisome in part because it could discern that the work was intended to be performed at a military research institute. The findings are ‘chilling examples of state-sponsored biological weapons developers tapping into the rapidly advancing capabilities.’ Andrew Weber, a senior fellow on the Council on Strategic Risks “What we don’t know is if the research was meant to be weaponised,” Klein said. “But a military institution doing gain-of-function research is concerning.” Anthropic said evaluations from last year of its older models demonstrated that they were not yet able to meaningfully assist in conducting dangerous biological research. Its current models are more able to complete complex scientific research, the company said, which spurred tighter safeguards intended to restrict access to a wide range of dual-use biological research queries.



Susan Monarez, a microbiologist and public health expert who oversaw a review of national biosecurity preparedness in the Obama administration, also reviewed the Anthropic report before its publication. She said the findings provided real-world evidence to support concerns that bad actors were trying to covertly use advanced AI “to improve their chances of building biological pathogens that could cause significant harm.” Related Article Analysis

AI ‘We must be stopped’: Why Australia needs to listen to the experts on AI Monarez, who briefly served as the director of the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention last year, said AI held enormous promise to usher in an era of medical breakthroughs that save and extend lives. But the same abilities that make that possible, she added, could also “let bad actors hide in plain sight, using seemingly legitimate research to create pathogens we may not see coming and may not be able to stop once released.” Weber of the Council on Strategic Risks, who also served as the assistant secretary of defence for nuclear, chemical and biological defence programs during the Obama administration, called for limiting access to AI tools capable of this level of biological research to trusted researchers only. “The fact that Russia, China and North Korea continue to develop prohibited biological weapons makes it imperative that we deny their researchers access to these extraordinarily capable models,” he said.
