World.title: ASX set to slump, Wall Street falls as oil climbs to its highest mark since May
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slump, Wall Street falls as oil climbs to its highest mark since May Stan Choe Updated September 11, 2026 — 6:27am ,first published 5:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil prices keep climbing as the war with Iran keeps clogging the global flow of crude, and they leaped Thursday to their highest levels since before the summer. That worsened worries about inflation and cranked up pressure within the bond market, helping to send stocks lower again on Wall Street. The S&P 500 fell 0.6 per cent for a fourth straight loss, its longest such streak since June, though it’s not far from its all-time high set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 316 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.7 per cent. Oil climbed to its highest mark since March. AP The Australian sharemarket is set for another day of heavy losses, with futures at 6.13am AEST pointing to a loss of 81 points or 0.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX shed 1 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was lower at US71.56¢. US stocks sank under the weight of rising oil prices. Brent crude, the international standard, climbed another 6.3 per cent and briefly topped $US108 per barrel for the first time since May before settling at $US107.63.



Related Article Energy Australia softens local gas supply rules, easing fears in Asia It’s jumped from less than $US72 in early July as hopes fade that the war with Iran will allow oil to flow freely again from the Middle East anytime soon. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that oil prices likely won’t come down until after the US midterm elections in November. The jump has vaulted the price for a gallon of regular gasoline to an average of nearly $US4.28 across the United States, according to AAA. That’s up nearly 34 per cent from a year earlier and is not only costing people more at the pump but also through higher prices for all kinds of products that move by truck to store shelves. A report on Thursday said inflation at the US wholesale level accelerated to 5.4 per cent last month from 4.8 per cent in July, and retailers could eventually pass such increases in prices onto shoppers. A report is coming on Friday that will show how much inflation US consumers are feeling. The typical move to rein in high inflation is for the Federal Reserve to raise its main interest rate, the federal funds rate. Such a move then filters out through the rest of the bond market, makes it more expensive for US households and businesses to borrow money, slows the overall economy and undercuts prices for investments. That hopefully would remove some of inflation’s fuel.



A report on Thursday suggested the US job market may remain solid, with fewer workers applying for unemployment benefits last week. That could give the Fed more confidence that the economy could withstand higher interest rates. Following Thursday’s reports, traders see a roughly 73 per cent chance the Fed will raise the federal funds rate at its meeting next week. That’s up from the 61 per cent probability seen the day before, according to data from CME Group. That’s also despite Trump’s consistent lobbying for interest rates to go lower rather than higher. The Fed’s counterpart in Europe, the European Central Bank, raised its own interest rates on Thursday in hopes of getting inflation in check. It cited “the conflict in the Middle East” and how it “continues to generate inflation pressures.” It all pushed the yield on the 10-year Treasury up to 4.95 per cent from 4.83 per cent late Wednesday, which is a significant move for the bond market. It’s up from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran began and is back to where it was in the autumn of 2023. That was after the Fed cranked the federal funds rate higher to get super-high inflation coming out of the COVID pandemic under better control.



Higher yields mean investors can make more money putting their money into bonds, which can in turn make investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other investments that are riskier than bonds. Some investors see a 5 per cent yield on the 10-year Treasury as the next potential flashpoint. But strategists at Bank of America’s Research Investment Committee suggest 7 per cent may be the more important threshold, pointing to peaks for expensive stocks around that point in the past. Related Article Opinion

Bonds Trump’s ‘top bond salesman’ is getting a reality check Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In the meantime, the rising 10-year Treasury yield is making mortgages more expensive and hurting the housing industry. One report on Thursday said the average long-term US mortgage rate hit its highest level in over 14 months, while a second one said sales of previously occupied US homes fell in August to their slowest pace in more than a year. That helped sent stocks of homebuilders lower, including drops of 3.5 per cent for Lennar and 2.4 per cent for D.R. Horton.



Elsewhere on Wall Street, Macy’s fell 4.7 per cent even though the retailer reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. While raising its forecast for earnings this fiscal year, it warned that “there are macroeconomic and geopolitical factors that could influence” how much its customers feel comfortable spending. Macy’s said it received $US116 million ($162 million) in tariff refunds from the government — $US98 million during the quarter and another $US18 million after the quarter ended. Macy’s CEO Tony Spring told The Associated Press Thursday that it’s using some of the proceeds to lower prices on certain items like furniture and other big-ticket purchases. All told, the S&P 500 fell 44.66 points to 7,591.70. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 316.56 to 52,064.10, and the Nasdaq composite sank 171.62 to 26,081.72. In stock markets abroad, indexes slipped across much of Europe and Asia. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 1.3 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves. World.title: This rising indie rock star has done his 10,000 hours, and it shows
World.content:
CultureMusicReview This rising indie rock star has done his 10,000 hours, and it shows Annie Toller and and John Shand September 11, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nate Amos’ earworms are always catchy but rarely too sweet. This Is Lorelei, The Singer in My Band ★★★★ By the time his first official, label-anointed album came out in 2024, Nate Amos had done his 10,000 hours. Over the years he’d uploaded scores of releases to Bandcamp under the name This Is Lorelei – work that, until recently, was just a side project to his long-running art-pop outfit Water From Your Eyes. Now, it’s coming into its own. The years of compulsive attention to craft have paid dividends: his latest album, The Singer in My Band, is a tight, affecting collection of songs, flitting deftly between power-pop, alt-country and pop-punk.



There are goofy moments – like single Billy Came Back, a zippy jangle-pop tale of a local karaoke legend blowing back into town – but gut punches too, especially in the resonant, open-stringed numbers that fill the album’s second half. The arrangements are always catchy but rarely too sweet: even the earworm hook and cascading harmonies of highlight Oh No Now My are paired with a taut, digitally tortured guitar solo. This Is Lorelei’s Nate Amos has taken his one-time side project to centre stage. Eve Alpert Though billed as a road album, written and recorded amid a relentless touring schedule, The Singer in My Band was finished at Amos’ family home with cameos from his father and sister, both professional bluegrass musicians. It feels like a grounding moment in his trajectory – a return to centre as a solo artist, led by songwriting-first principles. Annie Toller

World.title: Sex, drugs and a legend redefined: it’s time to meet the real Marianne Faithfull
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Marianne Faithfull died last year, directors Iain Forsyth and Jane Pollard had been working on a film about her for four years. Watching Broken English, named for the hit album she made in 1979, you can see what a compelling subject she was. A ’60s survivor, still probably best known to an older generation as Mick Jagger’s ex-girlfriend and the subject of scandal, she emerges as a formidable woman who was also a singer, writer and actor, the kind of liminal artist who popped up in collaborations with professional fans from Metallica to Nick Cave. In her ’70s, she is in a wheelchair, hooked up to an oxygen tank: the result of long COVID. Whatever, she still commands the room. Broken English isn’t so much an account of her life as a response to it, pitched somewhere between documentary, essay and fiction. Archive footage is sprinkled between interviews with Faithfull herself. These are set within an imaginary “Ministry of Not Forgetting”, the questions asked by “an archivist” played by 1917 star George MacKay. Derek Jacobi narrates the film and Tilda Swinton plays the head of the ministry, who at one point lists Faithfull’s many achievements before concluding: “And yet, to the world at large, she’s still just Mick Jagger’s girlfriend. Well, f--- that.” Tilda Swinton stars in the unconventional documentary. In his role as archivist, MacKay wears an earpiece to hear the directors urging him to push a point or drop it, depending on Faithfull’s answers. Clearly, they never aimed to cover Faithfull’s entire life. The juiciest scandal from her Stones era is left out. Her youthful heroin addiction is in there, but the gruesome details of her life on the street that she described in her autobiography aren’t. And while her first husband, John Dunbar, appears with her, Jagger does not. “I didn’t know how to make him a part of it,” Pollard says with a short laugh. “I really enjoyed reframing it, looking at that period of her life from the perspective of her childhood, growing up in a commune.”



With the Stones, she says, “they all felt they were all working towards something that felt really important”. But, as Faithfull reflects herself, that wasn’t how she was seen. She was cast as a rock’n’roll casualty. She was the woman arrested in a drug raid wearing only a fur coat. For the tabloids, she was a terrific story. The filmmakers set out to tell a different story. Their approach to the years Faithfull spent with Jagger, for example, was to shift their gaze away from the usual catalogue of disasters. We learn how Faithfull took Jagger to see the Royal Ballet with Rudolf Nureyev, knowing he would love it; we see that she joined in a poetry event with the Beat poets and became a lifelong friend of Allen Ginsberg. Marianne Faithfull with George MacKay in Broken English. Madman Films “All these cultural things that she was absorbed in and that she was sharing with Mick, things that felt a lot more relevant and interesting than just who at the end of the day she was going to bed with,” Forsyth says. “I hope that as much as the film is a story about a life, it’s just as much a film about how we choose to tell that story.” Forsyth and Pollard are best known to Australian audiences for their inventive 2014 film about Nick Cave, 20,000 Days On Earth. They first became interested in Faithfull because Cave and his musical partner Warren Ellis knew her well; Ellis worked with her as a producer and toured with her, playing in her band. “In the year before the lockdown, we would chat to Warren a lot,” says Pollard. “He was working on the poetry album She Walks in Beauty with her when she got COVID and went into a coma. He was just heartbroken, in the studio working on the poems, not knowing if she would ever hear them. I think at that point, our hearts found her in a different way. We began to care about her a lot, just vicariously, through him.” Marianne Faithfull with her friend and collaborator Warren Ellis. Rosie Matheson



The interviews with MacKay at the Ministry of Not Forgetting were among the first things they did, afraid that Faithfull’s precarious health would collapse again. After that, they worked on the film’s mosaic structure of memories and other interviews, showing her assembled segments as they went along. From the start, they expected that by the time they finished the work, she would no longer be with them, but they never intended it as an obituary. “The film needed, in some way, to acknowledge her passing, but not to change,” says Forsyth. “We were so determined it wasn’t going to be like a standard text with dates. That felt so at odds with it; it’s so alive with her humour and artistry and brilliance – with her defiance, actually.” George MacKay is 34. He had worked several times with Pollard and Forsyth on art projects, but he knew almost nothing about Marianne Faithfull. “I knew one or two of her songs without knowing they were hers,” he says. He threw himself into research. When he saw how she was pilloried and derided in the press during her Stones period, he was aghast. “It was awful, just on a human level, what was said about her,” he says. “The misogyny she came up against was so intense.” Although he worked from a script, he says the interviews felt like improvisations. “Because Marianne had never seen those scripts – and you have to follow wherever the interview goes.” The Ministry of Not Forgetting sounds as if it could have come from a Harry Potter novel, but it is a key idea for the filmmakers. “Not forgetting was a deliberate act, to make remembering active,” says Forsyth.



“If you choose not to forget, you make the effort. Whereas remembering something is an accident. Do I remember where I left my car keys?” Pollard chips in. “It’s also about learning lessons. The act of remembering seems loaded with a kind of sentimentality; it feels wistful in a way, whereas not forgetting is a recalibration. It has an urgency.” Broken English was billed at last year’s film festivals in Sundance and Venice as a documentary, but Forsyth isn’t sure that holds. “For us, the idea of going into a project saying ‘we are going to make a documentary’ just seems so alien, so limited from the start,” he says. “I think we were going into it thinking, ‘We are going to make a film that tells a story, and we want to make the best film and tell the best story we can.’ For me, ‘non-fiction’ works as well as anything because the story we’re telling is not fiction, although we might be using some of the devices of fictional storytelling. I think the story we’re telling is full of emotional truth. Which is not the same as journalistic truth.” Related Article Cinema Crash to classic: How Practical Magic’s box-office hex marked the spot for Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock For Pollard, the real discoveries in the film are the expressions that flicker across Faithfull’s face as she looks at the old footage of her younger self, beautiful and damaged but still holding up her end of things. “There’s a piece from Weekend World in 1974 or ’75, an interview she probably should have said ‘no’ to, when she had just come out of rehab,” she says. Watching it, Faithfull initially looks dismissive of that young idiot, opining on life. “Then she starts to align with her. And I’m looking from face to face, and I’m seeing the same eyes, I’m seeing the same smile, and I’m seeing the same willingness to be open. We all can all read a face – and cinema is the best way for us to do that. That’s when the film is revelatory.” Broken English opens nationally on September 17.

World.title: Political aftershock of 9/11 still being felt 25 years later - Helen Clark
World.content:
Twenty-five years later, former NZ Prime Minister Helen Clark is lamenting the unlearnt lessons from political mistakes make in the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks on New York's World Trade Center.

Clark was at the helm of the nation and en route to Europe, when terrorists flew planes into the 'Twin Towers', triggering a US response that reverberated around the world and forced other countries to choose sides in the Middle East.

"What I remember is being in the lounge at Hong Kong Airport and seeing these images coming through on the TV screen, no sound, of what appeared to be smoke coming out of skyscrapers," she told John Campbell on RNZ Morning Report.

"We had no idea what was going on - where was this, what was happening - and got on the next flight.

Helen Clark discusses being PM during 9/11 attacks Morning Report Download MP3 8m

"Jim Anderton was deputy prime minister and had taken command of issuing statements for the government.

"I landed in Rome and quickly made the decision that I would have to go back, because - for those who weren't around at the time or don't have a clear recollection of it - it was just such an incredibly dramatic and tragic event.

"No-one quite knew if this was the start of a series of more attacks or what we were heading into. There was considerable confusion at home and abroad about what was happening."

Clark's passage home ran into further obstacles, when she encountered an Ansett airline strike in Melbourne, which saw her complete the journey on an NZ Air Force Lockheed P3 Orion.

El Quaeda operative flew planes into New York's World Trade Center. AFP/SETH MCALLISTER

Over the months that followed, New Zealand had to decide what part to play in the American quest for revenge against El Quaeda, who were hiding in the White Mountains of Afghanistan.

When the ruling Taliban refused to co-operate with the US, it also became a target.

"In late 2001, when this shocking attack happened, the world was with the US," Clark recalled. "Whatever people around the world may have thought of the US, they were deeply shocked to see, in the American heartland, there were innocent people being killed from terrorist bombs.

"Here we start to unpick what went wrong.

"Firstly, I think the Taliban were so isolated, they didn't see the seriousness of the American resolve to go after the El Qaeda headquarters, so when they didn't co-operate, the US went after them.

"That was always an issue in terms of international legality, because there were those that argued the Taliban gave El Qaeda sanctuary, so they had a responsibility, and there were others that said this is El Qaeda operating out of caves, what could the Taliban have done about that anyway.

"There was that kind of debate going on."

Under Clark, New Zealand opted to support the Afghanistan invasion, but not the subsequent extension of that campaign into Iraq, which was accused of building 'weapons of mass destruction'.

"In the end, there was quite a large international response in Afghanistan, which led to quite a long presence or us and for others," she said. "Where things spun out was the US, having taken out the Taliban at the end of 2001, then thought why not move onto Iraq, and that was where they went many steps too far and that became a terrible tragedy for Iraq.

Saddam Hussein's downfall left a power vacuum in Iraq. AFP / FILE

"No-one particularly mourned the going of Saddam Hussein, but that war was said to have killed, in rough figures, from 500,000-700,000 people, and who knows how many died because of the poverty, marginalisation and hunger that came from that."

Clark saw alarming similarities between the Iraq war and the action against neighbouring Iran in recent months.

"A lot has happened in the last 25 year and, with the benefit of hindsight, we an see the points at which things went badly wrong.

"I think more the similarity is the spurious reasons for going to war. There was never any evidence of weapons of mass destruction.

"I myself went to see the United Nations inspector in charge off getting rid of the Iraqi nuclear weapons towards the end of 2002 in New York and he assured me they could find absolutely nothing.

"Fast forward to February this year and the attacks on Iran on the basis they were on the imminent point of developing a nuclear weapon. This was never true and it takes me back to the allegations of the Vietnamese using 'Yellow Rain' or whatever - that was never true either.

"Before countries go to war, citizens should be demanding what is this proof. I think we had our eyes open in 2003 and knew there was no proof.

World.title: Auckland CBD business owner eager for CRL opening after years of disruption
World.content:
Businesses gear up for opening of City Rail Link Morning Report Download MP3 4m

The City Rail Link has held its official opening in Auckland, with a bar owner saying he's looking forward to reaping the rewards of staying afloat during its construction.

A symbolic ribbon was cut on Friday morning at the vast Te Waihorotiu Station, which runs between Victoria Street West and Wellesly St. It's expected to become New Zealand's busiest train station.

The ceremony was attended by a large contingent of officials and politicians, including Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown and representatives from Ngati Whatua Orakei.

Minister for Rail Winston Peters spoke at the opening too - and even showed off his singing skills with his best Johnny Cash impression.

The City Rail Link took ten years to complete and cost $5.5 billion dollars.

It has also caused significant disruption for businesses along the route.

Craig Wright told Morning Report it's been a long slog to keep Northern Line Bar and Social open near Karanga-a-Hape Station, and he's hoping for consistency and continuity once the new rail loop is running.

"When you're faced with three metre hoardings, literally, you know, a metre and a half from your doorway, the view isn't great for the customers to sit and look at.

"Neither is the noise or the smell or the dust."

Auckland City rail link construction on Karanga-a-Hape road in 2019. RNZ / Kymberlee Fernandes

He said the business made it through those years with "good luck and duct tape".

"I think it's probably a testament to the staff that I have have been consistent over the few years that we just stuck in there, we could see, pardon the pun, light at the end of the tunnel."

He said the support of the local Karanga-a-Hape road community went a long way and everyone had pitched in to help eachother.

As construction hoardings came down and first look events took place, there have been some better days but Wright said he was now hoping for more consistency.

"We need people to be coming into the city to work and to enjoy activities in the city, but also that they can leave from our stations to go on to other events."

He said as exciting as the opening was he was hoping the stations and rail link would be maintained well over a long period of time.

"Without sounding pessimistic, the day we see rail replacement buses, our hearts are going to drop.

"So hopefully the maintenance and the future proofing is going to be the proof in the pudding."

World.title: Watchdog clears Police Commissioner Richard Chambers of any wrongdoing
World.content:
The police watchdog has cleared Police Commissioner Richard Chambers of any wrongdoing.

RNZ revealed in June that an investigation was underway in relation to complaints about Chambers. It is understood the complaints related to alleged conduct towards women.

RNZ understands that one of the complainants was believed to be a former police staffer. It is understood the other complaint was from a woman Chambers dated more than two decades ago.

As part of the investigation, RNZ understands staff from the National Integrity Unit visited the complainant in Australia. It is understood her allegations are historical.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

In a statement, Chambers said he welcomes the outcome of the investigation.

"While I have always strongly rejected the allegations made, it is important such allegations are investigated thoroughly and with due process. That has now been done.

"I am getting on with my job, supporting the frontline to keep our communities safe. Due to the significant privacy issues involved, I won't be making any further comments on this matter."

On Friday, the IPCA released a summary report, saying in December they received a complaint from a former partner of Chambers.

Richard Chambers. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"The complainant and he had been in a long-term romantic relationship in the 1990s.

"The complaint related primarily to allegations of stalking and digital surveillance. It also included an allegation of sexual assault dating back to 1999."

The IPCA said the police investigation was assigned to "highly experienced detectives" from the Police National Integrity Unit (NIU).

"Our investigation into the alleged recent conduct included making several enquiries and reviewing records and other evidence gathered by the NIU on our behalf.

"This included examination of exhibits which the complainant believed provided evidence substantiating her concerns."

The IPCA found no evidence to support any of her concerns about stalking and digital surveillance and "found evidence that contradicted many of her claims".

"Whilst we accept that she genuinely believed what she told us, we conclude that there was no evidential foundation for any of these allegations."

The IPCA advised her of the outcome in July.

The investigation of the complainant's allegation of historic sexual assault was led by the NIU with active oversight by the authority.

"From the outset, the welfare of the complainant was a critical consideration for the authority and police.

"As far as was possible, the investigation followed standard Adult Sexual Assault investigation protocols."

The IPCA said when the complainant agreed to be interviewed by police, she formalised a criminal complaint.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"After the first police interview, the complainant made further allegations of historic sexual assaults and she was re-interviewed."

The IPCA monitored police's interview of the commissioner and independently interviewed him without police present.

"The commissioner co-operated fully throughout."

The IPCA said police had completed a "thorough and robust investigation and that all reasonable lines of enquiry have been followed up".

The IPCA agreed with the conclusion reached in the report that the evidential test for prosecution is not met.

"Whilst the authority considers that the police investigation impartially investigated the historic sexual offences, the outcome of the investigation into the allegations of stalking and digital surveillance raised unavoidable reliability issues that Police had to consider as part of their assessment.

"It is the authority's view that, when all the evidence is considered in totality, police reached the only outcome reasonably available."

Following the IPCA's review, police sent their investigation report and documents from the police file to a Crown Solicitor for a further independent review.

The Crown Solicitor agreed with the conclusion that the evidential test for prosecution was not met, the IPCA said.

"We commend the professionalism of the police officers involved in this investigation and the steps taken to ensure its confidentiality and integrity.

"The authority will not be commenting further on the nature of the allegations or the reasons for its findings. We appreciate there is a strong public interest in reporting publicly on this investigation.

"However, we must balance the public interest in this investigation with the needs of all affected parties, especially those of the complainant."

The IPCA said they had also provided a confidential report to the Public Service Commission.

Deputy Commissioner Mike Pannett. RNZ / Louis Dunham

Last week, Deputy Commissioner Mike Pannett said in a statement to RNZ that NZ Police had completed its criminal investigation.

"The IPCA will publicly release its findings in due course. As the matter remains before the IPCA, police has no further comment at this time."

In an earlier statement to RNZ, Chambers said he had been advised that the IPCA and police were investigating complaints against him.

"I strongly reject the claims that have been made."

He said he would co-operate fully with the investigation and looked forward to having the matter dealt with.

"I acknowledge the public interest in this, but it is important the investigation takes its course. I cannot make further comment at this point."

In response to earlier questions from RNZ, an IPCA spokesperson confirmed that the IPCA received an anonymous letter raising concerns about Chambers in November last year.

"We received a complaint concerning the commissioner on 1 December 2025.

"We decided we would independently investigate both matters on 3 December 2025. Our investigation began shortly after this. The complainant was interviewed by police on 4 June 2026."

Police Minister Mark Mitchell. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

In an earlier statement to RNZ, Police Minister Mark Mitchell said he was "aware that complaints have been received about the Police Commissioner."

"They are now being investigated by police and the IPCA. I have no further comment at this time."

In an OIA received by RNZ, Mitchell said he had received two complaints related to Chambers.

World.title: Tech outage in central NZ fixed after hours offline, Health NZ says
World.content:
Access to radiology images and patient administration systems in Health NZ's central region has been restored after several hours offline overnight on Wednesday.

The region covers Whanganui, Hawke's Bay, MidCentral, Wairarapa, Hutt Valley, Wellington, and Kāpiti.

Health NZ's Gary Baird, national director of digital services and technology, said in a statement the issue was resolved on Thursday morning.

But, it had caused intermittent delays accessing radiology images during the night and in the early morning.

"Staff managed the issues using established contingency processes and maintained acute radiology services. No acute or planned cases were deferred and no data was lost because of the issue," he said.

Health NZ did not say what had caused the issue.

It's the latest in a number of outages across Health NZ's systems nationwide, most recently, in Waikato.

World.title: Greyhound foster mum urges others to take in ex-racing dogs waiting for 'forever families'
World.content:
Greyhound adoptions surge after racing ban Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Families across New Zealand are eager to adopt greyhounds after racing was made illegal last month.

Agencies say the demand for adoptions is overwhelming, but they're desperate for foster homes to get the dogs used to life as a pet.

Janelle Broadhurst has been fostering greyhounds since 2017. She says it's the dogs' quirky attitudes that have kept her going for almost 10 years.

"You always meet new personalities, you look at them and they're obviously gorgeous and elegant, but they've also got these goofy, fun, cheeky personalities," she said.

"You really want to help them transition from the kennels, and fosters can do that."

She wasn't alone in loving greyhounds. Lisa Philp, the manager of Greyhounds as Pets, said she had received hundreds of applications for adoptions in the past month.

"The demand has been enormous, we saw a huge upsurge in applications so we have several hundreds now to process, and we're very excited about that.

"We redeployed a couple of staff and have taken on a couple more staff to help with the applicant load."

But she said the rehoming process had been bottlenecked by a shortage of foster homes. The kennels were full, and many of the dogs needed to be trained before they could be adopted permanently.

"What we're also working on doing at the moment, and one of our new staff is working on this, is building up our foster network throughout the whole country but especially in the North Island because we're a wee bit behind there," she said.

"Because if we have dogs able to go into foster homes it just gives us a lot more capacity."

Tyson, the greyhound Broadhurst had been fostering, was nine years old and had gum disease. He moved into her care when his previous family could no longer afford to pay his vet bills.

"A change of circumstances, y'know, with the financial climate and everything. They went down to one income so they were unable to care for him any longer, so that's how Tyson came into my hands," she said.

"So he's been here waiting for his forever home."

Broadhurst said she had fostered about 15 dogs over the years, most for a few weeks to a few months. But she'd had Tyson since January.

"Everyone absolutely loves him when we go and do pats and chats at Petstock or Animates every Saturday morning, they absolutely love him," she said.

"Then we say his age and that he's got gum disease and people are like, 'Oh, I'm sorry, I'm not in that position.'"

By providing a foster home, she said Tyson could afford to wait until his forever family arrived.

"It's that vital transition that they need between kennel and the new home," she said.

"Because the matching has to be damn perfect so the dog stays in their forever home forever, that family might not be there right then, so it's really important to have fosters."

Janelle Broadhurst (R) and Tyson. RNZ / Felix Walton

She said the ex-racing dogs were easy to take care of as many had already been trained.

"They're already house trained, it's a big bonus compared to getting a puppy from the pound. Greyhounds have been handled, trained, walked on lead, so they come with all the most amazing essentials already."

But she said it wasn't always easy to say goodbye when the time came.

"The first couple were really hard, but the beauty of it is you get to stay in touch and you get to visit them, or they visit you, or you catch up at the greyhound walks that are held weekly and monthly," she said, "and you know they've been matched with the right family."

World.title: Wellington City Council not seeking refund for flawed report
World.content:
Wellington City Council won't be asking for a refund for a $435,000 report which officials have said contains flaws, and which the mayor has described as largely written by AI.

Andrew Little said he stood by his view of the report - and he's still concerned by it after errors were discovered in August.

The Deloitte Future Fit Pōneke report, commissioned by council chief executive Matt Prosser and released in 2025, claimed the council had 330 more staff than it should based on the number of full-time employees per 1000 households.

Recently, council staff pointed to errors in the report, including the use of more than three-year-old data on full-time employees from the Taxpayers' Union, and that duplicate roles were calculated by considering roles with the word 'project' in the title were the same.

Council officials also said Deloitte had counted all employees as full-time in its calculation of total people costs. They said there was a $21.5 million difference in the council's figures for total people costs and Deloitte's.

Officers said the incorrect data meant the assumptions used to come up with the 330 excess staff figure were "inherently flawed" - and a more accurate number was an excess of 284 full-time staff.

This week, a Wellington City Council spokesperson said executives were not seeking a refund for the report.

The report had included a disclaimer that its estimates were indicative and needed further testing before being relied on, the spokesperson said.

"Some aspects of the staffing analysis were identified as requiring further validation, consistent with the report's disclaimer that additional verification and financial modelling would be needed before relying on the findings."

Wellington City Council confirmed its decision to cut 47 roles this week, in a drive to save over $4 million - including from the Creative Capital, Economic and Engagement, Planning and Environment and Property and Capital Projects team.

The council spokesperson said job cuts weren't made solely as a result of the Deloitte report.

The report included recommendations that were being worked on already, including to improve contract management, workforce planning, organisational design and cost efficiency.

The Guardian has reported Deloitte provided a partial refund to the Australian government when errors were found in another report it did, partly written AI.

Little said while it is the council officials' decision whether or not to seek a refund, he stood by his assessment of the report as containing "large parts drafted by AI".

"That's probably a standard these days. What I was concerned about is that too much of the report wasn't properly tailored to the needs of Wellington City Council.

"It was effectively off-the-shelf, generic drafting - that continues to concern me."

Little said he was unsure whether Deloitte's AI agent referred to out-of-date data, rather than the recent data the council had provided.

"That is a matter that is yet to be resolved in my view."

Deloitte did not answer questions about how the errors came about.

However in a statement, a spokesperson said the company stood by its report and recommendations - and was confident it had been useful.

"In respect of AI, Deloitte uses a range of tools and technologies across its work, including AI-enabled tools where appropriate.

"These tools, where applied, were used to support and speed up aspects of the work process, rather than replace human analysis, judgement, or review."

World.title: All Blacks make changes for final Springboks Test
World.content:
All Blacks coach Dave Rennie has named Richie Mo'unga in his side to play the Springboks in the fourth Test in Baltimore on Sunday (NZT), the No.10 being one of five players to make their first starts in the series.

The Springboks lead the series 2-1 and while they have only made two changes to their starting 15 from the third Test, Rennie has made a number, calling in prop Fletcher Newell, lock Patrick Tuipulotu, flanker Ethan Blackadder and centre Anton Lienert-Brown to also make their first starts for the series.

In all, there are eight changes from the starting side that lost to the Springboks 29-24 in Soweto last weekend, as the All Blacks attempt to draw the series. One of them also involves a position swap, with Tupou Vaa'i shifting from lock to the side of the scrum.

Codie Taylor will captain the side after being dropped for the third Test, while prop Ethan de Groot and lock Josh Lord return to the 23 after missing the second and third Tests because of concussion. De Groot will start the match while Lord is on the bench with Sam Darry and Patrick Tuipulotu forming the second row.

Codie Taylor has been named All Blacks captain for fourth Test against Springboks. © Photosport Ltd 2026 www.photosport.nz

Josh Moorby comes in on the left wing, replacing Leroy Carter, who missed a few crucial tackles in the third Test in Soweto last weekend and drops out of the 23.

Injuries have forced Rennie's hand, with skipper Ardie Savea, Luke Jacobson and Quinn Tupaea ruled out while lock Fabian Holland is also unavailable because of illness.

But he has made other changes as well, with Mo'unga replacing Ruben Love at first five being a strong talking point.

Rieko Ioane and Beauden Barrett are named on the bench as back cover, as Lienert-Brown takes Tupaea's place in the run-on side.

Peter Lakai will play at No.8, joining Blackadder and Vaa'i as the new loose forward combination, while the front row is different too, with Taylor and De Groot returning and Tyrel Lomax dropping to the reserves with Newell preferred as a starter.

Rennie said the selection group had always planned for a number of changes for this match.

"Every player here has worked incredibly hard over the last seven weeks to prepare the team for the seven games we've played so far, and all those selected for this Test fully deserve it," Rennie said.

Coach Dave Rennie. Chris Symes / www.photosport.nz

"We have everything to play for on Saturday. It is our chance to draw the series and end the tour with a performance to be proud of.

"We have had incredible support travelling with us throughout the tour and amazing support back at home. We want to put in a performance that shows how much we appreciate that. We also want to honour the players and management who have returned home early but contributed so much."

If reserve halfback Kyle Preston takes the field, he will be the only player to have taken part in all eight games on the All Blacks tour.

All Blacks v Springboks, 4th test at Baltimore

1. Ethan de Groot, 2. Codie Taylor (captain), 3. Fletcher Newell, 4. Patrick Tuipulotu, 5. Sam Darry, 6. Tupou Vaa'i, 7. Ethan Blackadder, 8. Peter Lakai, 9. Cam Roigard, 10. Richie Mo'unga, 11. Josh Moorby, 12. Jordie Barrett, 13. Anton Lienert-Brown, 14. Will Jordan, 15. Damian McKenzie.

Reserves: 16. Asafo Aumua, 17. Xavier Numia, 18. Tyrel Lomax, 19. Josh Lord, 20. Wallace Sititi, 21. Kyle Preston, 22. Rieko Ioane, 23. Beauden Barrett.

World.title: Meteorologist, parrot trainer, former All Black captain and a DJ want your vote in Tukituki
World.content:
What does a meteorologist, a parrot trainer, a former All Black captain and a DJ have in common?

They're all vying to be the next MP for Tukituki in Hawke's Bay. The bellwether seat is currently held by National MP Catherine Wedd, who is up against five newcomers.

Over their morning coffee in Havelock North, some locals in the Tukituki electorate have their minds made up already.

"I'm very comfortable with who the candidates are and yes, I know who I'll be voting for - the people who focus on the economy," said one man.

"To be honest I'm going to go with ACT or TOP. I'm not supporting the current prime minister and I've always been a right-wing voter all my life," said another.

One woman told RNZ she'd usually give both votes to Labour, but that's unlikely this time around.

"The Labour person, whoever it is, for around here isn't very visible so I'm a bit disappointed in that. Not too sure who I'll give my vote to in the electorate, but the party vote will probably go to Labour."

Others are feeling rather unsure.

"There's a lot of uncertainty. I don't like either of the two main parties so where are we going to go?" said a local pensioner. "And certain candidates I'm not fond of. I don't know... it could be very interesting seeing what happens."

"I'm concerned," said another voter. "Concerned because the polls and what they're showing. Not sure I believe the polls, but it creates that degree of uncertainty,."

Taine Randell. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Six very different candidates are vying for the job in a historically blue electorate that flipped to red in 2020 when Labour's Anna Lorck won the seat.

Former All Black captain Taine Randell, who was a student at Lindisfarne, has stepped into the political contest for New Zealand First.

"We've got a few issues in New Zealand and I don't have a great deal of confidence in the people that we've got there that they are going to solve those issues, so with my experience I'm going to throw my hat in the ring and see if I can do better."

His key priority is economic growth.

"There's no progress without growth. Through my experience in small and medium businesses, from zero employees up to 120, that's where the potential is for growth in New Zealand. We've just got to make sure they stop getting punished by banks, energy companies and out-of-control Government regulation."

Something people might not know about Randell, who played 52 tests for New Zealand, is that in 2008 he was working as an oil broker in London right before the global financial crisis happened.

"My wife and I decided we were coming back to New Zealand, so I made sure I'd been paid and then handed in my resignation. It turned out to be the same day that Lehman's bank went bust. The biggest insolvency in the history of mankind - talk about good timing," he laughed.

Rachel Ward. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Putting up giant billboards of her face on fences is all rather new to Opportunity candidate Rachel Ward.

"I'm not sure you ever get used to that," Ward said.

The mother of two has resigned from her conservation job managing Cape Sanctuary to dip her toes into politics because she's frustrated about the "conservation bureaucracy and environmental short-sightedness of the current coalition government".

"It's just too important and I have a really strong gut feeling that this is what I should be doing, if I can make things better for our environment and for my kids in the future."

As well as being able to do back flips on the trampoline, she's also New Zealand's only certified parrot trainer.

"I do have a business in Australia that is a parrot behaviour and training business - it seems wacky and out there, but in Australia one in three people have a pet parrot - and they're all pretty naughty and bite and do all sorts of things."

Ward wants to focus not only on protecting the environment, but also on unifying New Zealanders.

"There are policies and bills going to Parliament that are dividing our country... it really upsets me, and we can do so much more together when we celebrate our differences and culture.

"Watching politics around the world and the division... we don't need to be like that and we don't need to follow that trajectory."

Dan Scott. Supplied

Labour's candidate for Tukituki is 22-year-old meteorologist Dan Scott.

"I grew up in Hawke's Bay and I've been watching, especially since the cyclone hit, and I've been really concerned that there's not been the investment or the thought put into what the people of Hawke's Bay really need and deserve," he said.

His campaign is focused around healthcare, the cost of living, climate change adaptation and jobs. The closure of the McCain factory in Hastings really struck a nerve with him.

"I'm really worried there is no planning from Government in terms of how to follow that up. It's crucial we have food processing continue in Hawke's Bay so we can still have food from New Zealand growers and not rely on imported items."

Asked what's something people don't know about him, his response is unexpected.

"I have always had a fear of public speaking growing up... the fact I've managed to turn that around and run for Parliament might give people a bit of a surprise."

If successful, Scott plans to split his time between Hawke's Bay and Wellington, where he works as a meteorologist and forecaster.

Mark Longworth. Supplied

The fourth political newcomer for Tukituki is Green Party candidate Mark Longworth. The natural medicine grower lives in Central Hawke's Bay and is a former DJ.

Longworth said he decided to stand for Parliament after feeling uninspired by the options at last year's local elections.

"If I couldn't cast a vote for my values from what was on offer, I felt it was important for those votes to go somewhere... to be counted and do more good.

"No option wasn't good enough for me so I felt the need to put my hand up for the general election."

He has three priorities.

"Grow the Green Party vote, get more people enrolled to vote, especially our rangatahi, and make this coalition a one-term government."

Rob Douglas. Supplied

ACT's Rob Douglas is standing again for Tukituki, after having a run at the job in 2023.

He's a property valuer in Hawke's Bay, and told RNZ he is not aiming for the electorate vote.

"I'm not asking people in this election to actually vote for me personally, I'm asking the voters of New Zealand to give their party vote to ACT.

"We've got two really clear objectives - we're trying to lock Labour out and unlock NZ's potential."

A little-known fact about Douglas is that he struggled at school.

"Against all my objections at school I was given a lot of remedial reading... it's made a real difference in my life.

"I now write valuation reports for a living, something I couldn't have done without that base knowledge I picked up then. I feel it's so important for Kiwis to get the opportunity to get that core knowledge."

A billboard for Catherine Wedd. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Incumbent National MP Catherine Wedd is hoping she'll keep the job come 7 November.

"It's been an absolute privilege to represent Hawke's Bay Tukituki for the last three years and I feel we have a lot more to do," she said.

Her main priority for the region is the economy, as she wants to see more growth in the farming and horticulture sectors.

"That's why I've been a really staunch advocate for water security. We're one of the only regions in the country without large-scale water storage. If we can get that in Hawke's Bay it will unleash so much potential for the district and the region."

Something people might not know about the MP is that she used to work as a journalist for 1 News and the BBC.

World.title: Crows' quest for premiership glory just beginning as they prepare to take on Lions
World.content:
A week is a long time in footy, but an hour can feel like a lifetime.

In the space of 30 minutes last Saturday, Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks jumped from zero to hero, whilst hours earlier at the SCG the Lions went from premiership favourites to staring down a straight sets exit.

When the Bulldogs piled on three rapid fire goals to erode the Crows' 20-point lead, the tension at Adelaide Oval was palpable; but after Izak Rankine snapped a magical goal to seal Adelaide's first finals victory in nine years, everything changed.

The home crowd rose as one to give their embattled senior coach a standing ovation; drawing a smile from the man whose future was publicly in the spotlight and uniting a football club that has been fractured since its 2017 grand final collapse.

Izak Rankine sealed Adelaide’s first finals victory in nine years with a spectacular goal from a ridiculous angle. (AAP: Matt Turner)

Adelaide premiership player and former board member Rod Jameson couldn't hold back his emotions post-game on ABC Sport.

"'Get stuffed' is probably what you want to say," he said.

"It's been against the odds.

"I feel really happy for Matthew Nicks that he's actually got one … so what's the narrative now next week?"

That's the big question in a relentless news cycle. Despite the pressure valve being released, Adelaide's quest for glory is just beginning with an upcoming semi-final at the Gabba to face a Lions side who handed them their biggest loss of the season back in round 7.

But the heat has certainly shifted to the qualifying final losers Fremantle and Brisbane, with both teams facing the daunting possibility of becoming the 13th side in 13 years to be eliminated in straight sets.

Matthew Nicks claimed his first AFL finals win since he began coaching the Crows. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Reigning premiers Brisbane were stunningly blown away by an undermanned Swans. Sydney's passion was unrelenting; winning the tackle count by 15, contested possessions by 19 and beating the Lions at their game with a whopping six goals to one from centre bounce.

"They were desperate from the start, and all you want as a fan is the effort … that was perfect finals footy," dual premiership winning Swan Ryan O'Keefe said on ABC Sport.

"When was the last time 36 scoring shots were kicked against an opposition in a final? That's unbelievable."

It’s a blueprint that will build belief for the Crows ahead of Saturday’s semi and could dictate the result. Adelaide is one of the best pressure sides in the competition. The six times they have lost pressure differential this season they’ve been defeated, whilst the Lions are 13-0 when winning it.



Adelaide’s other advantage is their forward firepower, with the team averaging 109 points per game in their last five matches. The Lions conceded 14 goals to key forwards last week, have leaked 100 points eight times this season and are sitting 13th for points against per game.



"The defence is the difference this year," premiership Magpie Luke Ball said after the Lions loss at the SCG.

"It looked too easy to score against them. They're going to have to defy history."

Lachie Neale starred for the Brisbane Lions with 42 disposals. (AAP: James Ross)

The final and most pivotal factor is likely to be the midfield. The Lions kicked five goals to none from centre bounce back in their round 7 mauling on top of 27 extra points from stoppage. Lachie Neale starred with 42 disposals and Will Ashcroft had 36 touches and a goal.



It's a concern for the Crows who conceded three unanswered goals from the middle against the Bulldogs on Saturday night. They made up for it in their defence with Josh Worrell nabbing a career high 34 disposals and a massive 19 intercepts. Adelaide kept the Bulldogs to a 14 per cent inside 50 to goal efficiency.



Brisbane are no strangers to doing it the hard way. This is the eighth consecutive year they’ve made it to a preliminary final or semi-final with a record of 3-2 in the latter.

The Crows, meanwhile, have got the monkey off their back, snapping their September shackles and now can take a swing at the reigning premiers at a venue they haven't won at since 2018.

"I don't think it can be understated how much pressure was on this side coming into this contest," All-Australian midfielder Josh Francou said after the elimination final.

"They were challenged and in the end they got the job done and in the end they go to up to Brisbane with a free hit."

You can hear ABC Sport call the semi-final between Adelaide and the Brisbane Lions from 5:30pm CST on 891 ABC Adelaide and on ABC Listen.

World.title: Recent finals history is against Freo, but these numbers could save them
World.content:
Keeping hold of form and momentum on the footy field is often like trying to catch lightning in a bottle. Just ask Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir.

Few, if any, would question that Fremantle has been the best and most complete football team across the 2026 AFL season.

The shortest player in the AFL has become a big part of the Fremantle Dockers Plucked from state footy three years after being passed over by all 18 AFL clubs at the national draft, Isaiah Dudley reflects on his improbable rise as the Dockers look to bounce back in the finals.

The Dockers' excellence has spanned weeks, months, time zones and weather seasons.

In the middle of the year, the question was more of when they were going to lose rather than if anyone would challenge them for the minor premiership.

But just as winter turns to spring the fortunes of all football teams change.

Now instead of wondering about the pack chasing them, the Dockers are now frantically searching for how they can regain that torrid early season form.

The development of how we play football in Australia — in all codes — often means that the best team of the year doesn't win the title.

Instead, it is often taken out by the team in the best form or with the best fitness when the finals comes around.

Once upon a time, it was almost a foregone conclusion that a side in Fremantle's current position would rally to redemption in week two of the finals.

In the first decade of this century, more qualifying final losers went on to win a premiership than to suffer the indignity of a straight-sets exit.

But as the Dockers would remember better than many sides, things have changed since then.

Fremantle, along with Geelong, broke new ground in 2014 when both experienced back-to-back finals losses.

With rising performance standards and more equalisation measures in the league, footy is more competitive than ever, and straight-sets exits have been the single most common fate for top-four losers since those breakthrough losses.

Half of the two dozen semifinals since 2014 have been won by the nominal underdog.

With time rapidly running out on season 2026, Fremantle is looking for that ephemeral sense of what kept them ahead of the pack before their season is over.

Standing in Freo's way this week is the side with the current longest winning streak — and a side who knows how to measure efforts for September — Geelong.

Winning the whole thing

Fremantle's loss to Hawthorn last week was its first home defeat in 13 games at Perth Stadium this season. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

Usually when a team starts to dip there is a reason. It is very rare for the rest of the league to raise their level to that of the competition heavyweights.

The league leaders are always the most studied, and the most scrutinised.

Over the course of the season threads are pulled at potential weaknesses until they are unravelled by the best of the rest.

When looking Fremantle's dip the biggest story is what is happening at the contest — or more importantly what isn't happening.

Fremantle's midfield and front half group is blessed with attacking talent, able to turn a half-chance into a broken line or shot at goal.

They are sometimes less able to control the ball when it hits the deck, especially when there are even numbers at the contest.

Against disciplined midfields, the Dockers have struggled to find the supply they need to churn the scoreboard over.

While they are still outsourcing teams at stoppage, the Dockers are beginning to be outscored when the ball hits the deck in general play.

Opposition sides have become increasingly accustomed to not overcommitting to competing in the air to counter the Dockers plethora of tall contested marking options, and instead focusing the ball on the inevitable battle when it hits the deck.

When GWS downed Fremantle in round 17, the Giants were able to win the post-clearance ground ball battle 65 to 49.

Despite losing ground in the air, the Giants were more than able to make it up on the ground.

It is a template other sides have been able to follow, cruelling the ability for the Dockers to score from broken play.

Last week, Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell was very clear on their focus around keeping extra numbers at the contest.

Hawthorn's smalls such as Nick Watson (right) dominated groundballs all night in the qualifying final. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

"Our forwards' work rate was a real highlight. We didn't always use the ball at our best, but the way they created outnumber after outnumber was huge," Mitchell said after the win over Fremantle.

While the Dockers broke even at post clearance contests in the game, the Hawks scored an extra 27 points from intercepts.

This was the big difference in the contest, and the key reason that the Dockers are playing again this week.

"I just thought [the] contest was pretty even, but I thought their contest method was a lot better than ours. I thought they were probably a little bit more decisive to get it to the outside [and] buffer pressure," Longmuir said after the match.

Part of the deal that Mitchell made with the outnumber was to leave their defence more isolated against the dominant Dockers key forward set up.

But that was a calculated gamble due to the match-ups that presented themselves.

Hawthorn captain James Sicily (right) was excellent in defence and nullified Fremantle's tall forwards time and time again. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

"I think having a bit of extra time to watch them. Credit to Kade Simpson, the backline coach, he did a great job preparing the boys. Whether it was, you know, Barrass, Battle, Sicily, Weddle, we sort of had good match-ups [on Fremantle's forwards]," Mitchell said.

The Dockers were only able to get two goals from their tall forward triumvirate of Josh Treacy, Patrick Voss and Jye Amiss — the first time since round 6 that they were kept to less than three as a group.

Although the Dockers managed nine marks inside 50, the set shots they managed were from unfavourable situations and none are renowned sharpshooters from those positions.

But despite the downward turn in form, there is definitely still a clear path to the club's maiden AFL premiership cup.

The path back

Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir has put up a defiant front in the lead-up to the semifinal against Geelong. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

The silver lining for Fremantle is last week's loss wasn't a season-ender.

Instead, Longmuir has a fair amount of hope for their chances to come.

"There's still a path there. So everything we've been working on across the course of the year, we've got to lean into that now," Longmuir surmised in the wake of the loss to Hawthorn.

"[I] understand that the outside noise might turn a little bit from positivity to negativity. I understand that aspect of it, but as a group, we've got to lean into each other and try [to] find our best footy before next week," he said.

" We're not dead and buried. "

But the road to glory has become significantly harder than it looked a week ago.

Instead of a week off to recoup before a home preliminary final, the Dockers instead face one of the most feared sights in footy; Geelong when it matters most.

After floating through the season in fits and spurts, Geelong found its feet as September drew closer.

Geelong rode a six-match winning streak coming into the finals, albeit against some softer opposition.

Last week's win over Carlton was dominant but still left the indication that there is room to grow.

The Cats are also one of the few sides who know what it is like to beat the Dockers this year, splitting their two home and away clashes with the minor premiers.

In both games, control over the ball was perhaps the most critical element.

In round 1 the Cats claimed 50 more marks than the Dockers on their way to a 10-point win, while in round 15, the Dockers gained a 22-mark edge over the Cats in their nine-point win.

Limiting the Dockers ability to control the ball via the kick-mark game — and instead forcing the ball to deck — is one of the ways that teams can blunt their attacking influence.

Notably, Fremantle has suffered three losses in four of its matches where it has registered its lowest marking totals of the season.

The messier the game is, the harder it often is for the Dockers to dominate.

However, the Cats present a vastly easier challenge to the Dockers inside defensive 50 than Hawthorn did last week.

Geelong's defence has not been as strong as it has been in previous years and most key defensive indicators have deteriorated in the last part of the year.

Geelong has conceded marks and shots inside 50 at a bottom-four rate in the last ten matches, and during that time, the Dockers probably should have beaten them by more in their return match.

There's a quiet — if not cautious — confidence that the Dockers will be able to break the trend of straight sets exits if they can get the game back on their terms.

"I think you [have] to lean into physicality from the start. Contest is really key and then [we need to] try and lock it in our front half," Fremantle co-captain Andy Brayshaw told the media during the week.

If the Dockers can return to their brand of football, their hopes of their maiden premiership may still be alive in 2026.

World.title: The FIFO Rams may have lost the battle for hearts and minds
World.content:
The NFL has long been a pioneer in blending the barrier between entertainment and legitimate sporting competition.

Today's clash at the MCG between the San Francisco 49ers and the LA Rams is a historic moment for the league — after all, playing a regular-season game on the other side of the world is pretty outlandish.

But as close to 100,000 people cram into the Melbourne Cricket Club's hallowed halls and stare into the far distance at the gridiron imprinted upon its hallowed turf, the question has to be raised as to why it's happening, who is benefiting most, and why the two teams are taking such wildly contrasting approaches to the contest ahead of a busy season.

First things first. Why is this happening?

Modern Australian sports fans are far too educated to be left staring in wonder at the strange code of football being played in front of them when they turn up.

Most, if not all, of the people in the stands later today will not only know the rules, but have their favourite players and likely even have a team they can claim to support year in, year out.

This Australian San Francisco 49ers fan has been a fan long before there was ever a suggestion of a game being played on these shores. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Josh Chadwick)

More than a handful of Australia-based supporters would likely confess to spending Monday mornings with one eye on a pop-out window on their computer screen — or at their phone — to keep up with Sunday Night Football as it plays out Stateside.

In short, people already have their favourites.

Anecdotally, when attending previous international matches as a supporter in London over the years, you are far more likely to see fans wearing unrelated jerseys to those teams actually playing — especially in the nascent years of the NFL's English experiment.

So those people heading to the MCG today will, by the law of averages, be watching two teams they don't support.

This should clearly be a detrimental situation to the nominal home team, the Los Angeles Rams.

However, the Rams' pitiful backing from locals at SoFi Stadium, which results in more away-team invasions than anywhere else in the NFL, especially against San Francisco, suggests that playing in front of a hostile crowd at home probably isn't anything they're not used to.

"It's cool for us always to have an advantage of having, what I see, as one home game a year in LA," coach Kyle Shanahan told reporters earlier this week.

"Just the way our fans take over that stadium … [but] I have a feeling they won't be much different here. I expect to have a good showing."

The San Francisco 49ers have been training at AAMI Park this week. (AP Photo: Asanka Brendon Ratnayake)

Shanahan made those comments in Melbourne on Monday.

The Rams didn't even arrive until Thursday morning, about 24 hours before kick-off, in a bold fly-in fly-out plan to avoid the jet lag that comes from a 12,748-kilometre, 16-hour trans-Pacific flight.

Melbourne's NFL game is a battle of opposing jet lag strategies The San Francisco 49ers arrived a week in advance of their Melbourne NFL game, while the Rams will arrive the day before. A sleep expert says both strategies have merit, but one may have a slight edge.

How effective this plan will be on the field will come in time — not just after the MCG contest, but in the next couple of games and throughout the year.

But off the field, it's hard not to think that the Rams have fumbled the ball in their own end zone and given a free pass to San Francisco to take over the running of the narrative, which gets us onto the question of who is benefiting.

According to an investigation by The Athletic, the 49ers are the most popular team in Australia.

NFL games were first being shown on Australian TV during the 1980s, first by Channel Nine, Channel 10 and then the ABC, with effervescent host Don Lane bringing a new audience to professional American Football.

Joe Montana led the 49ers during their greatest era. (Getty Images)

Given that the 1980s were the 49ers' greatest era, with the side winning four of their five Super Bowls that decade thanks to Bill Walsh's famed West Coast Offence and the talents of quarterback Joe Montana, the Niners' enduring appeal makes sense.

Australians love a winner.

So having the 49ers play the first game on Australian soil makes perfect sense.

But there is a complication.

Starting in January 2022, the NFL launched its Global Markets Program, a formalised approach that gives NFL clubs access to international territories for marketing and fan engagement.

The (Inter)National Football League The NFL will open its 2026 season with a match in Melbourne, Australia, this week, one of a record nine matches to take place overseas this season. And it shows no signs of slowing down yet.

All 32 teams now have an overseas presence via this program, with 22 different countries targeted, including Australia.

These markets are not exclusive. Germany is the most popular market, with 11 NFL teams snapping up their options there, while some areas, including Colombia, Japan, Greece, Ghana and Nigeria, have been taken by just one team each.

But Australia is proving to be of interest too, with four teams nominating this great southern land as their territory to harvest in the NFL's own brand of sporting and commercial imperialism.

Those four teams that picked Australia are the Las Vegas Raiders, Philadelphia Eagles, Seattle Seahawks and the Los Angeles Rams.

So, if the Rams have commercial rights in Australia, why did they fly in the day before the game and not spend time winning over hearts and minds among supporters in the build-up?

Loading Instagram content

Have they missed a trick by failing to turn up to their own party?

It's almost as if the Rams are turning up to their holiday home, only to find that the 49ers have already unpacked the suitcase in the master bedroom and are sitting on the couch with their feet on the coffee table.

For a start, Australia is not the Rams' only overseas operation; they also have the rights in China, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, New Zealand and the United Arab Emirates, with Japan, South Korea and China exclusively theirs.

It would be wrong to say the Rams organisation has done nothing in Melbourne.

The cheerleaders have been out and about all week, and the team has collaborated with Melbourne fashion label-turned-homeless charity HoMie and various events at "Rams House" on the Crown Riverwalk.

But San Francisco has done all that too, and then some.

Melbourne Victory players Louis D'Arrigo and Philipp Ziereis exchanged jerseys with San Francisco 49ers star Fred Warner at AAMI Park. (Supplied: Melbourne Victory)

The 49ers' stated aim is to paint Melbourne red, and it seems, externally at least, to be doing a great job: hosting open training sessions in front of 2,000 local children at AAMI Park, watching the Geelong-Carlton game at the MCG on Friday night, a training run with Special Olympics athletes, setting a cheerleading record at Federation Square, visiting the local children's hospital, partaking in a Bunnings sausage sizzle. This is hearts and minds 101 from the 49ers team.

Shanahan and the 49ers' decision to give the players a week to adjust to the time zone and the rigours of international travel seems to make sense to anyone who has travelled across the world and then had to work.

"It took a couple of days to adjust," he said on Monday.

"But [I'm] feeling real good today."

The biggest interest for sports science types will be how two sets of experts came to such wildly different conclusions about how to approach the longest road trip in NFL history.

The San Francisco 49ers Gold Rush cheerleaders led 1,424 people in a record-breaking cheer dance event. (Getty Images: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Ye Myo Khant)

The Rams felt that the team would be far better served doing all their prep at home and keeping the players' body clocks on US Pacific Coast time.

They did something similar last year when playing the Jaguars in London, a 10-and-a-half-hour, 8,780km journey from LA, a game they won comprehensively.

The 49ers have decided that getting into the Melbourne time zone would serve them best, training in the late morning to adapt to the earlier-than-usual kick-off time.

Which perhaps leads to the crux of the issue: the purpose of these international games.

Are they meant to spread the gospel of the NFL into new markets, or are they primarily about building commercial relationships?

"For us, this is a year-round effort," Kevin Demoff, president of the Rams, told CNB.

"I would much rather win the game and grow the market the other 51 weeks a year than focus on having our players here for that week."

That said, questions about the approach have clearly struck a nerve, as Demoff responded to San Francisco Standard reporter David Lombardi's tweet criticising the strategy.

Lombardi wrote on X: "An actual 'business trip' would involve the Rams taking the time actually to grow their brand. There's a reason the Rams don't even own LA. It's related to their current mentality. Moving to Anaheim and then St. Louis severely hurt the cultivation of a fan base. 49ers benefit."

Demoff accused the writer of being "obsessed with the Rams brand" in a startlingly thin-skinned response.

As much razzmatazz as the NFL collects around itself, this is also a serious sports league where, with just 17 regular-season games to establish your case for sporting immortality, teams simply cannot afford to throw away a single chance for a win.

The conflict between the front-of-house commercial imperatives and the back-end business of winning football games is being thrown into stark relief this week.

The Los Angeles Rams are coming to Australia for one thing only, to win. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/Greg Fiore)

The 49ers have embraced Australia, and Australia has embraced them in turn.

The Rams, as a sporting operation, are treating this like a business trip, focused on getting a W to start their season, commercial considerations be damned.

And who knows, should the Rams' smash-and-grab approach work out, and they claim the victory, that puts them on the path to Super Bowl LXI — which is taking place at their actual home, SoFi Stadium, next February — then it might not matter how many proverbial babies they kissed or hands they shook.

That would give the Rams the unique status of being able to say they won a Super Bowl on home turf, after starting the season by laying down roots at a distant home away from home.

Such a victory would forever tie Australia to a team of winners.

And Australian sports fans do love a winner.

World.title: Joyce vague on details, Albanese wins tennis match amid golf grant saga
World.content:
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

Barnaby Joyce has always been a disruptor; it’s one of the reasons Pauline Hanson wanted to woo him to One Nation.

Few have had a career quite like Joyce, who was once described by Tony Abbott as Australia’s best retail politician. The man who had two turns as Nationals leader could connect with voters. He was loved and despised (in some seats) in equal measure.

His defection to One Nation was designed to bolster the party’s legitimacy. His performance as its Treasury spokesperson this week did anything but.

Joyce struggled as he was sent out to sell the party’s superannuation policy. Under the plan, renters and mortgage borrowers would be able to divert a quarter of their super contributions to their income for up to three years.

Across a series of interviews (including one he conducted from the Qantas Chairman’s Lounge) he was asked about the proposal’s inflationary impact and what this would mean for a person's foregone retirement savings.

“Interest rates keep rising,” Hanson had said as she announced the policy at a rare press conference in Parliament House. Economists told the ABC the policy, if ever adopted, would only tempt the Reserve Bank to push them higher.

Loading...

Joyce claimed the extra cash wouldn't drive up inflation because the money already sits in superannuation funds, so it's already in the economy. Economists don't share that view, with history suggesting people would most likely spend and not invest any extra money.

Joyce snapped at the ABC's Sarah Ferguson on 7.30 on Monday night for not providing questions on retirement savings losses ahead of time. He declared he was not Jesus Christ, as if that was ever in question.

He is, though, an accountant by trade (a fact he pointed out) and someone who has been on the policy sell many a time. It became clear One Nation never modelled the proposal. Joyce later claimed they didn't have the staff to do so — an argument that fails to acknowledge One Nation could've asked the Parliamentary Budget Office to help as other parties do.

Whether the policy has merit is one thing. But inflation is already running hot. Having some idea of the inflationary impact before releasing should be the bare minimum for a Treasury spokesperson.

A subplot to this is it's the second time in as many months the Coalition was reportedly gazumped by One Nation on policy (first being the tobacco excise). A similar proposal was said to have been drafted under Sussan Ley. The opposition downplayed the question of a leaker within their ranks, but it again begs the question of discipline.

The similarity between offerings from the Coalition and One Nation is something the government continues to leap on. It plays into the argument the government thinks it can win and is probably why a noticeable chunk of Labor's questions to itself in QT were about super.

Hastie v Hanson

A fight between Hanson and Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie has been brewing for a while.

The spat came to a head this week over a One Nation cartoon that called the former SAS captain a "traitor" eight times across nine minutes for testifying in Ben Roberts-Smith's failed defamation case. He was subpoenaed to do so.

"It's a slur on me. It's a slur on other veterans who have given under oath evidence to the federal court," Hastie said.

Several Liberals also condemned the cartoon. As did fellow veteran Jacqui Lambie, who echoed Hastie in calling the One Nation leader a "bloody coward".

Hastie served in Afghanistan. He's drawn the ire of One Nation and backer Gina Rinehart for giving evidence against the Victorian Cross recipient. Hanson and Rinehart say Roberts-Smith has been unfairly targeted over war crime allegations.

Andrew Hastie is taking issue with a cartoon published on Pauline Hanson's X account. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Roberts-Smith was this year charged with five counts of the war crime of murder over the alleged killings of five Afghan men between 2009 and 2012. He has not yet entered a plea but has denied the allegations.

Hastie's seat of Canning covers a large part of the state electorate of Secret Harbour, which One Nation won in a by-election last month. It's put a target on the seat as one the party thinks it can win at the next federal election.

Hastie's ruled out legal action over the video. It would be too costly of an exercise, he says, thanks to Rinehart's backing. Instead, he wants to "impose costs politically".

Hanson, and Joyce, have insisted she hasn't personally called Hastie a traitor despite the video. Earlier this week though, she did say she'd call him a "wanker".

Coalition deals it itself out

While he wouldn't agree with Hastie's description of Hanson having a "glass jaw," Opposition Leader Angus Taylor did back the call for the video to be pulled down.

It's an ironic point for him to make at the press conference where he was rallying against the government's Digital Duty of Care legislation – a bill he declared amounted to political censorship.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

The government released draft legislation earlier this week. It's designed to force social media companies to identify and mitigate harm on their platforms. It would also force platforms to provide users with choice between an algorithmic feed and a feed simply made up of people you actually follow.
