Tech.title: August 2026 Was the Hottest Month Ever Recorded: Copernicus Data
Tech.content:
August was the planet’s hottest month ever recorded, capping a remarkably grim summer of heat records. With El Niño strengthening—and climate change continuing to heat things up—more records are likely in store well into next year.

Data from Copernicus, the European Union’s climate agency, shows that last month tied with July 2023 for Earth’s hottest month. (July is also usually the hottest month of the year.) This July also tied with July 2024 for the second-hottest July on record, while June 2026 was the second-hottest June ever recorded. The news comes on the heels of a separate announcement on Wednesday from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which declared this was the hottest summer for the US, beating a previous record set during the Dust Bowl.

The sweltering summer is a grim sign of how burning fossil fuels is pushing temperatures up around the globe while unleashing more intense and longer heat waves.

“August 2026 was a remarkable month in the global climate record,” Samantha Burgess, the strategic lead for climate at the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, said in a statement. “Combined with record global sea surface temperatures and the warmest summer on record for Western Europe, these observations show how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans. The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies, and ecosystems across the world.”

The global average temperature for August was 1.65 degrees Celsius (3 degrees Fahrenheit) above the preindustrial average, according to Copernicus. While it was hot globally this summer, the impacts played out with dangerous and sometimes deadly results locally.

Tech.title: Which iPhone 18 Model Should You Buy?
Tech.content:
With a fresh folding form factor, the new iPhone Duo is Apple’s most radical redesign in years. It lands alongside the more familiar-looking iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. There’s no regular iPhone 18, or at least, not yet. Rumors suggest we may see a more affordable base model, perhaps flanked by an iPhone 18e and a second-generation iPhone Air, in spring 2027.

The two new Pro iPhones are available to preorder on September 12 and ship on September 18. You can preorder the iPhone Duo from October 16, ahead of a full release on October 23. But which iPhone 18 model is right for you? I’ll break down the differences and what these phones have in common, so you can choose with confidence. For options beyond the iPhone 18 lineup, read our Best iPhones guide.

Why You Might Not Need to Upgrade

Before you drop all those hard-earned dollars, remember that you probably don’t need the latest iPhone. If you have an older iPhone, Apple does a good job of updating the software (the iPhone 11 Pro is still supported), and for hardware issues, your iPhone might be repairable; maybe it needs a battery replacement or these troubleshooting tips. Don’t feel like you have to spring for Apple’s shiny new thing.

Sadly, Apple raised iPhone Pro prices this year, so both models are $100 more expensive than the iPhone 17 Pro series.

If you’re set on upgrading, consider raising funds by selling your old iPhone. Just be sure to back up your iPhone, and factory reset it before you sell or give it away. Once the new device arrives, we have tips on how to set up your new iPhone and what settings to change to get the most out of it.

Which iPhone 18 Is Right for You?

The Similarities

We’ll start by looking at what’s the same across the iPhone 18 models this year.

The Processor

All three new iPhones have Apple’s A20 Pro chip inside, and, you guessed it, this is Apple’s most powerful chip ever. Now, iPhones are already the most capable phones for raw compute power, but the A20 Pro promises a significant jump in performance (around 20 percent faster and 30 percent more efficient than the last generation). It also packs a new neural engine to power on-device AI and a new thermal design with a larger vapor chamber to keep things cool. For the iPhone Duo, the A20 Pro has a display engine to ensure smooth transitions between two screens. While Apple doesn’t list the RAM, every model is rumored to have 12 GB.

The Display

While they come in different sizes and the Duo has two, every iPhone features an OLED screen that Apple calls a Super Retina XDR display. They also have ProMotion technology, otherwise known as a 120-Hz refresh rate. These adaptive refresh rates can drop as low as 1 Hz when there's little activity on the screen, enabling features like the always-on display without draining the battery too much.

The displays are protected by the scratch-resistant and antireflective Ceramic Shield 2, the same as last year’s iPhone 17 range. And they can go from 1 nit up to 3,000 nits of brightness. Only the iPhone Duo has a custom nano-texture finish on the interior screen, giving it a matte look that’s designed to reduce glare and crease visibility.

The Usual Specs

All the phones have an IP68 rating for water and dust resistance, meaning they can survive a short dunk in fresh water. They all come in four storage options (256 GB, 512 GB, 1 TB, or 2 TB), support Qi2 magnetic wireless charging (MagSafe), USB-C 3.2, Dual SIM, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, and Ultra-Wideband (UWB). It also has Siri AI, Apple Intelligence, Emergency SOS via Satellite, and Crash Detection.

The Differences

Tech.title: Best Robot Lawn Mowers (2026): 12+ Models Tested Over 3 Years
Tech.content:
Other Robot Mowers I Tested and Liked

Photograph: Simon Hill

Photograph: Simon Hill

Video: Simon Hill Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Roborock Rockmow Z120 Lidar Shop Now

Roborock Rockmow X120H Lidar for $3,200: Better known for its robot vacuums, Roborock also makes robot mowers, and the X120H Lidar is its flagship model (discounted to a far more reasonable $2,000 at the time of writing). I actually tested the UK model, the identical Z120 Lidar (£2,299). This mower employs Lidar and AI vision, so it can cut without satellite connections, with no RTK antenna required. It also supports 4G and comes with a 3-year data plan. It is Four Wheel Drive (4WD) and has ingenious front wheels that pivot and turn independently to navigate tight areas smoothly, with minimal churning of your lawn. There’s a single disc underneath with six cutting blades and a reasonably wide, 9.5-inch (24 cm) cutting width. It supports a 0.8 to 2.7-inch (20 to 70 mm) cutting height, can cover up to around 21,500 square feet, and, most impressively, can handle an 80 percent (up to 39-degree) slope. A full charge gives you 110 minutes of mowing time, and it takes around 50 minutes to charge.

After some minor setup hassles (battery error), the Rockmow Z120 has impressed me. It looks to be the most capable mower I have tested yet for navigating uneven terrain. Apparently, it can automatically create maps, but it defaulted to the manual mode for me, prompting me to remote control it around the borders of my lawn. Edge mowing is the big disappointment, with the mower regularly leaving a strip on one edge of my lawn. I’m not keen on the optional PreciEdge Module (£150) that promises to reduce edges to 3 cm. I haven’t tested it, but feel it should be included in a mower this expensive. Why is it optional? Who doesn’t want their edges properly cut? It avoided most obstacles just fine, but was occasionally oversensitive, avoiding plants swaying over the border edge. The Rain Protection mode is a little too sensitive, preventing the mower from starting several hours after rain, so I had to override it. It also lacks a Spot Mode, though it is so heavy I would not want to carry it between lawn areas. I think this design, with the rotating wheels, has real potential if Roborock can improve the AI/software. Unfortunately, it's not currently available in the US right now, but hopefully be back in stock soon since it was released just this past summer.

Eufy Robot Lawn Mower E15 for $1,300: This is another wire-free mower that uses a camera system to automatically map lawns and avoid obstacles. It’s very similar to my top pick and also has a super handy Spot Mode that lets you drop and mow on unmapped areas. But even after a big price drop from its original RRP, it’s still more expensive than the TerraMow, and it’s not as good at cutting edges. It can cover up to 0.2 acres (8,700 square feet), cut from 1 to 3 inches, and handle up to 18-degree slopes. It is also fairly quiet and has GPS tracking, but you must have Wi-Fi coverage in your backyard, or you'll need a 4G data subscription. I found the setup lengthy due to a firmware download, but the mapping and the first cut were decent. Object avoidance is very good. The E15 can only run during the day and doesn't cope very well with inclines. I also found it frequently failed to cut the edges of the lawn and doesn't perform well if the grass is damp. The more affordable Eufy C15 (£999) is very similar, but designed for smaller lawns (up to 5,300 square feet) and only available in the UK and Europe right now.

It kept my back lawn neat without issues, but my front lawn has a dip and ill-defined border that it struggled with. That said, every time it looked as though it might get stuck, it managed to maneuver out of trouble. There’s a dial to adjust mowing height for the C15, whereas you can do it in the app with the E15. Both come with a covered charging base, which often costs extra with rivals. If you’re interested, watch out for a sale event (I’ve seen the E15 drop below $1,000, which makes it far more tempting).

Segway Navimow X430 for $2,249: My backyard is both a Wi-Fi and 5G dead zone. Before manually mowing the yard I save all my podcasts and music to offline mode, and I let my fiancee know she’ll need to deploy a carrier pigeon if she needs to get my attention. So, it was a relief to see just how quickly the navigation system of the Navimow X430 recognized the unit across the treacherous triple lot that surrounds my house. It connected within seconds of beginning the initial setup and 20 minutes later, the robot mower was on its way using the handy auto-mapping function. As it turns out, I didn't need the three beers I'd brought with me when I embarked upon this process, assuming it would be on par with the weeks-long headache it took to get the Mammotion Luba 2 connected and operational last summer.

It did an above-average job on its first pass despite the endless flurry of compost piles, stray bushes, fencing and detritus from half-finished gardening projects that litter my half-acre lawn, though I opted for manual mapping to take advantage of its aptitude at hugging the wobbly brick borders of some raised beds with relative ease. The sites claims that it can handle “tall, thick and dense grass," which I had the perfect scenario to test. After a two weeks of dealing with an endless cycle of torrential downpours and blistering heat, I was left with few open windows for a good mow before my patchy, crabby grass got too unwieldy for the Navimow’s 4-inch height maximum. I watched with disappointment as it casually drove over some stray blades that went to seed without making any impact whatsoever. Despite that, the Navimow X430 has impressed me with its ease-of-use. We'll update our impressions here with additional testing, but so far so good.—Pete Cottell

Photograph: Simon Hill

Sunseeker X7 Gen 2 Wireless Robot Lawn Mower for $2,700: If you have a large, challenging lawn, this could be a mower worth considering. It combines built-in NET-RTK, GPS, and AI vision, has floating dual disc blades for uneven terrain, and can work at night thanks to an Indirect Time of Flight camera. It is also all-wheel drive (AWD) and can handle 70 percent slopes up to 35 degrees. It can cover more than 32,000 square feet. I love the wide 14-inch cutting width, the relatively quiet operation (it never went over 60 decibels but was usually even quieter), even though I’d advise against mowing at night because of the risk to wildlife. Sadly, the automatic mapping was mediocre, and there’s no Spot Mode for a drop-and-mow. This Gen 2 mower brings a raft of improvements over the original, including night vision, faster processing, enhanced durability and traction, a built-in screen, and onboard RTK without a separate antenna. But only the original Sunseeker X7 ($2,700) is available to buy on Amazon. You currently have to go through a dealer to get the Gen 2.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Husqvarna Aspire R6V for £999: While the reliable Husqvarna 410XE Nera was my top pick for a long time, you can get more affordable mowers now, without the hassle of RTK antennas. The Husqvarna Aspire R6V is just such a mower. It uses a combination of GPS and AI vision with a camera on the front. It was easy to set up and map the lawn in the app, but you will need a good Wi-Fi signal across your yard for it to work effectively. I was a little disappointed in the sensitive obstacle avoidance, as it left large uncut strips around the edges of my lawn. I was able to reduce the verge a little with some tinkering, but it was still larger than the recommendations above. Note: This model is currently not available in the US.

Anthbot Genie 3000 for $900: This often-discounted mower was my budget pick for a while, but mowers have moved on, so you can get better performance without the satellite antenna now. It offers auto-mapping, but the remote-control option works better. The mower cut my lawn effectively, but even after repeated map updates, it left an uncut verge. The obstacle avoidance works well, and it cuts in neat lines. It had no issues returning to charge or following a schedule. The voice that says it has connected or started mowing began to annoy me, but thankfully, it can be turned off. There were some glitches with rain alerts that prevented it from mowing, even long after the rain had stopped. I also experienced some flaky connection issues with the GPS, and it occasionally got stuck. While there is support for multiple areas, the mower often struggled picking up a signal in my front yard. Ultimately, this is still a decent mower when discounted, provided you have a modest-sized, straightforward lawn.

Mova Lidax 2000 for $1,199: With a sleek design and a mixture of 360-degree lidar for 3D mapping and a camera with AI vision, this mower proved very effective. Setup was straightforward, and there’s no need for wires or an antenna, though I did have to adjust the map manually. You can set multiple areas, and its navigation is generally very good. It mowed in neat lines, successfully avoided thin posts for the badminton net and other obstacles, and completed an excellent edge pass at the end. With some of the closest edge mowing I’ve seen, I was all set to recommend this mower, but then it got stuck. A couple of times, it seemed to be stuck, then managed to free itself, but an uneven problem spot proved to be its nemesis, and it chewed up a patch of grass trying to get free. Eventually, I had to make that spot a no-go zone. This mower is still worth considering, particularly if you see it on sale; just be prepared to tweak the map. The 2000 covers up to half an acre. If you have a quarter of an acre or less, the Mova Lidax 1000 ($1,299) is much cheaper but has the same features.

Avoid These Mowers

Stiga A6V Photograph: Simon Hill

Stiga A6V: I like that this mower only needs the charging station and has no need for an antenna. The buggy setup was my first red flag, as a firmware update failed and had to be repeated. Once up and running, I found the mower always left a big verge, even after adjustment. The AI vision camera is very slow to react to obstacles and not very good at navigating around them. It hit the ball several times in my test, and I had to hit the stop button as it got too close to my cat. It lacks useful features like automapping and spot-mow, and there are better options for the money above. The yellow finish is a bit garish for my tastes too.

EcoFlow Blade Photograph: Simon Hill

EcoFlow Blade: While it was easy to set up and cut my lawn nicely without the need for any boundary wire, the EcoFlow Blade sometimes struggled with GPS navigation and ended up stuck in a flower bed. It also left an untouched strip around the edge of my lawn. The object avoidance was solid, and it can be automated in the app, though it occasionally failed to start a scheduled cut for me. EcoFlow seems to have discontinued this model, though it is still on sale in Europe. Probably best to avoid.

Yardcare E400 Photograph: Simon Hill

Yardcare E400: Curious about the budget end of the robot mower market, I agreed to try the Yardcare E400, but this mower was an unmitigated disaster from start to finish. It’s a boundary wire model, so you must run wire around the area you want mowed. Yardcare suggests it can cover up to 4,300 square feet and cut grass between 0.8 and 2.4 inches. The problem is that it gets stuck frequently and struggles to even get on and off its charging station reliably. After trying multiple fixes to no avail and going through customer support, I had to conclude that this model has a serious design flaw.

How Do Robot Lawn Mowers Work? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Perhaps counterintuitively, the setup instructions for your robot lawn mower will likely tell you to start by cutting the grass. Robot mowers mostly can’t deal with long grass. Unlike traditional mowers, these robots don’t collect grass cuttings; they mulch instead, and they are designed to cut frequently, keeping your lawn short and simply leaving the cuttings on the ground, which can also improve lawn health. Most robot mowers are designed to run two or three times a week during the growing season (from late spring to early fall). They have rechargeable batteries onboard and can last from half an hour to several hours on a full charge. They return to the charging base and recharge automatically when their power runs low. Most mowers have simple controls, a small display, and an emergency stop button. You can generally start and stop mowing, set schedules, and create or edit mapped areas using the onboard controls or the companion mobile app, very much like a robot vacuum. What Features Should I Look For in a Robot Mower? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron There are many factors to consider in choosing a robot mower, and the best choice for you often depends on your yard. Lawn Size and Shape Robot lawn mowers are generally rated to cover a specific square footage, with wider coverage requiring models with larger batteries. Alongside yard size, you should consider the shape and topography of your lawn, as most robot mowers will struggle with steep inclines. While you can often map out separate areas so your robot mower can mow front and back lawns, for example, it will generally need you to lift and carry it between those areas. If you have an uneven garden or steep slopes, look for a four-wheel-drive (4WD) or all-wheel-drive (AWD) mower and check the manufacturer's rating for inclines. Navigation Type There are a few types of navigation that robot mowers employ. We’ve tested five different approaches, though some mowers combine multiple technologies for better performance. Satellite : Often employing something called Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) Global Positioning System (GPS), these mowers need a satellite signal to navigate and will have a receiver that must be placed in the open with a clear line of sight to the sky. Satellite navigation mowers are not suitable for areas with tall trees or buildings.

Satellite navigation mowers are not suitable for areas with tall trees or buildings. Light Detection and Ranging (lidar) : This technology sends out rapid laser pulses to 3D map the terrain (it is also used by self-driving cars). It enables mowers to cut grass under thick tree canopies or near tall buildings where GPS signals usually fail.

It enables mowers to cut grass under thick tree canopies or near tall buildings where GPS signals usually fail. Cameras : Cameras and onboard AI are used for obstacle detection and avoidance. AI vision can automatically map areas and cut the grass while avoiding obstacles it encounters, much like how most robot vacuums navigate a home to clean the floors.

Wire boundary : These mowers require you to install a perimeter wire as a boundary around your lawn that marks out the border the mower should not cross. It's a messy job that can be tricky.

: These mowers require you to install a perimeter wire as a boundary around your lawn that marks out the border the mower should not cross. It's a messy job that can be tricky. Remote control: You mow your lawn from the comfort of your home using a remote controller or an app on your phone. Some only work via remote control, while others can also cut automatically. Power and Charging Robot mowers generally come with large charging docks, and you’ll need to earmark a suitable spot for yours. They usually have extensive weatherproof cabling, but you will have to find a route to an outdoor socket. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth To connect to your mower and schedule a mow, update the firmware, or remote control it where supported, you need a decent Wi-Fi signal or a Bluetooth connection. It’s best to set up your mower’s charging station within range of your Wi-Fi network. Some mowers also need a strong Wi-Fi signal to operate effectively, so you might consider adding an outdoor mesh router. If you want to connect your phone via Bluetooth, you will have to get quite close. How Noisy Are Robot Mowers? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Most robot mowers are far quieter than their traditional counterparts. You can expect them to operate at around 55 decibels, though they may go as high as 75 decibels. We only tested battery-powered mowers, but expect gas mowers to be louder. While the operation is often quiet, I did find that several mowers made annoying beeping sounds when backing up or had a loud recorded voice during setup or upon receiving a command. Do Robot Mowers Work in Any Weather? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Robot mowers and their charging stations usually have IP ratings and can cope with rain, but you should pack up and bring your mower indoors during the winter months. Many robot mowers have some kind of rain sensor and will pause mowing when it gets too wet. Some mowers may need to be paused manually. The wheels can churn up your lawn and get caked in mud if mowers continue to labor in the rain, especially with larger and heavier models. How Well Do Robot Mowers Cut? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Mowers of different sizes will have varying cutting widths, denoting the width of the strip they can cut on each pass. Most also have floating cutting decks that enable you to choose the length of grass you want (typically 1 to 3 inches). Many robot mowers seem to struggle with cutting around the edges of a lawn, especially if there’s a wall or fence that prevents them from getting close enough. It’s common to find an uncut verge around the edge of your lawn, so you might need to occasionally get the string trimmer out. Every robot mower I’ve tested has also struggled to cut the area around the charging station, so I recommend placing the unit on a deck or pavement if possible. Can I Install a Robot Mower Myself? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron ​Yes, most robot mowers can be installed by anyone, but you might want to set aside an afternoon to work out any snags. Finding the best spot for the receiver for a satellite mower can be tricky. The mapping process can also take a while; usually, the mower will prompt you to remote-control it around the border you want to set. After the first mow, you should review its performance and make tweaks to ensure it’s covering the entire area you want to cut. Can Robot Mowers Mow at Night? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Some models are capable of mowing at night in the dark using headlights, Lidar, and Time of Flight sensors, alongside their usual navigation capabilities. This can be convenient and also removes the risk for pets or children playing on the lawn during the day. However, there is a risk of injuring nocturnal wildlife, like hedgehogs in the UK and Europe. Mowers are also more likely to make mistakes and get stuck in the dark. It may be better to schedule mowing for dawn or dusk. How I Test Robot Lawn Mowers AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron I test each robot lawn mower for at least a month, on at least two different lawn areas, assessing the ease of setup, the mapping process, automatic scheduling (where available), navigation, obstacle avoidance, and the quality of the final cut, looking for length, uniformity, and any missed patches. Where applicable, I try extra features, tweak settings in the app, and check how the mower handles different weather conditions. I also keep an eye on battery performance and charging time to ensure it aligns with the manufacturer's claims.

Tech.title: Charlie Kirk Was Shot a Year Ago. The Conspiracy Theories Are More Rampant Than Ever
Tech.content:
In the days after the assassination of conservative activist and Turning Point cofounder Charlie Kirk, the online reaction was a mess. Graphic videos of the shooting were everywhere within minutes of his death, far-right figures called for violence and vengeance, and right-wing lawmakers and influencers called for the cancellation—and worse—of anyone celebrating. Then, the conspiracy theories began.

It’s been one year since Kirk’s death, and conspiracy theories about the shooting have persisted, supercharged by social media algorithms and right-wing influencers like Candace Owens, who has used her huge following to push baseless allegations about the incident.

Experts believe these conspiracy theories will continue for a long time to come. “There’s no reason to believe conspiracy theories about Kirk’s murder will lose steam anytime soon,” Jared Holt, senior researcher at Open Measures, tells WIRED. “If anything, I expect them to escalate further as the criminal trial against Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing Kirk, plays out over the next year or so. The trial is bound to draw major media attention and offer conspiracy theorists a source of new material to work from.”

In the immediate aftermath of Kirk’s death, some conspiracy theorists claimed the assassination was a false flag operation designed to deflect attention away from President Donald Trump’s connections to Jeffrey Epstein. Others claimed the entire thing was staged. There was the AI-powered gun theory, the claim that the shooter was a Kirk supporter, and even claims that Kirk was still alive.

But ultimately, the baseless claim that persisted is that someone close to Kirk, or operating on behalf of Israel, was responsible for his death, that Robinson was simply a patsy, and what really killed Kirk was an exploding microphone. This is the narrative that has been central to Owens’ monthslong conspiracy theory campaign. Her Kirk content has racked up hundreds of millions of views.

Owens’ success is fueled in large part by the way that social media platforms today encourage their users to post content. “X and YouTube are rife with speculation about Kirk’s death, where it is both still possible to recruit new audiences and monetize them,” Joan Donovan, assistant professor of journalism and emerging media studies at Boston University, tells WIRED.

Tech.title: Best Bluetooth Speaker (2026): JBL, Sonos, Marshall, and More
Tech.content:
Part of LG’s xboom collaboration with producer, Black Eyed Peas star, and tech obsessive will.i.am, the Stage 501 is a mighty 25.8-pound party starter. Its 2.2-channel setup combines twin 5.25-inch woofers with two 2.5-inch full-range drivers. Together they’re capable of 160 watts on battery or 220 watts plugged in. In simpler terms: It easily filled a huge workshop space with rave-ready bass, and enough volume for a proper party.

What surprised me more than the party capabilities was that it also sounds acceptable at low volume in my office. I was expecting a pint-sized PA system, but dialled back to casual listening volume and it remained composed. Often, speakers designed for loud really struggle with quiet, and just sound muddy, but that wasn’t the case here. Yes, it prefers it when people are dancing, but it manages well when you’re chilling out too.

The xboom app is excellent, with EQ, AI Karaoke, synchronized lighting, and some cheesy but irresistible DJ punch buttons. LG has also included two very sensible smartphone/tablet stands that position your device at the perfect angle for karaoke nights. It comes with two mic inputs, but you will need to buy microphones separately.

Battery life is “up to” 25 hours, and the battery itself is replaceable. It’s big, and not as grown-up sounding as the Soundbox Mix, but it is cheaper and has a surprisingly good LED light show feature that I expected to hate, but didn’t. Party on dudes.

Honorable Mentions

Bang & Olufsen Beosound A1 (Gen 3) for $399: Gorgeously designed, flawlessly finished, and one of the most covetable Bluetooth speakers around. The brushed aluminum puck has barely changed since 2016, which says plenty about the strength of Cecilie Manz’s original design. The latest version adds a richer, more powerful 360-degree sound from its 3.25-inch woofer, 0.6-inch tweeter, and 60 watts of amplification. It is IP67 rated, lasts up to 24 hours, and is appreciably more repairable and upgradable. I love it, but it’s just a little too expensive when the KEF Muo exists and sounds as good as it does.

Soundboks Mix for $799: The 21.4-pound Soundboks Mix is tremendously loud, with a 10-inch woofer, 1.2-inch tweeter, and 40-hour replaceable battery. WIRED writer Parker Hall measured 111 decibels from a meter away, and was surprised at how musical it remained rather than just battering you with volume. IP65 protection, sturdy handles, and rubberized tennis-ball style corners make it particularly well suited to outdoor parties. It’s expensive and heavy compared to the new breed of party speakers from brands like LG and Sony, but it is superb at what it does.

Tech.title: ‘Killmonger Locs’ Are Everywhere in Video Games. This Artist Is Sick of It
Tech.content:
When the life-simulation game Paralives was released in early access, Danielle Udogaranya’s hand ached at the thought of making new Black hairstyles for it.

It wasn't because she didn't want to create for the game. Udogaranya, better known as Ebonix, has spent over a decade creating custom content for life-simming games with the goal of helping people see themselves on digital screens. Her hesitation stemmed from the physical toll it takes to craft the perfect digital coil, braid, and kink—painstakingly long hours and tedious precision.

“I thought to myself, why am I still having to do this?” Udogaranya, a technical artist who has a degree in psychology, tells WIRED.

Fans of games like The Sims spend time flipping through her sites, downloading custom hair packs inspired by real-life styles not otherwise available in-game. As of now, the Ebonix Patreon has over 115,000 members, and hundreds of both free and paid content items.

The reason behind the demand for custom content in life-simming games is both simple and disappointing: Natural Black hairstyles have been historically underrepresented, and the technology used to make them has been slow to improve.

“With new games coming out now, I'm still seeing the issues, and I'm still seeing the ‘Killmonger locs.’ God forbid we get more than three options,” Udogaranya says, in reference to the stiff, short-dreaded style featured by Michael B. Jordan’s character in Black Panther that became a go-to for many games as well as some other films. Similar examples can be seen in old and new franchises alike, including Tekken 8, Spider-Man 2, Apex Legends, Horizon Zero Dawn, and more. The reason for this Black hair default? Textured hairstyles in games have been reliant on code that was not made for them.

Tech.title: Everything New You Can Do With Siri AI
Tech.content:
Siri made its debut on the iPhone in 2011, five years ahead of Google Assistant and 11 years before ChatGPT would open up to the public. Despite the head start, Apple's voice AI has been comprehensively overtaken in recent years, and made to look rather primitive compared to the many generative AI rivals it’s now up against.

With the launch of iOS 27, Apple and Siri are fighting back. There's a new name—Siri AI—and a host of new capabilities that are coming to your iPhone.

These are the new features that you'll be able to make use of once iOS 27 appears on your handset, if you're running the iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 15 Pro Max or later (including, of course, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo). Only these latest phones have the necessary on-board silicon to meet the higher AI processing demands.

Get More Personal Context

You'll notice when Siri AI arrives that it spends some time indexing everything on your iPhone. That's so it can dig deep into your texts, emails, calendars, and whatever else you have stored on your phone (everything is kept on-device though—nothing gets sent back to Apple).

It means you can ask natural questions about text conversations, email interactions, and appointments—"What day is my work appraisal happening?" for example, or "Where did I say I'd meet Mom?"—and get informed, personalized answers back, based on what's already stored in your apps.

This works for photos and videos as well. Open up the Photos app and you're able to ask Siri AI to show you all the pictures of your pet, or the images you took on your last vacation, or all the photos of trees you've collected, via simple, conversational prompts.

Ask About Anything on the Screen

Siri AI knows what you're looking at while you're using your iPhone—perhaps even better than you do. Whereas before you would've had to take a screenshot and give it to Siri to look at, now you can just ask.

So if you're on the web in Safari, you can say "Hey Siri" and then get it to summarize the text onscreen or identify a landmark in an image in an online article. You can ask what certain options mean in Settings, or look up more details about a game you're thinking about downloading from the App Store.

The same sort of visual processing is available through the iOS Camera app too: Just switch to Siri mode using the selector by the shutter button, and ask Siri AI about anything that's in view (nutritional information about an item on a menu, for instance).

Tech.title: Jell-O and Beer May Hold the Keys to Brewing Houses on Mars
Tech.content:
Establishing life on another planet is a multifaceted process with many problems. Housing is one major challenge, but a new study suggests researchers have found a way to build living quarters on Mars using materials already present on the planet, along with a couple of other clever ingredients.

The study, published on Sept. 10 in the journal Chem Circularity, reports that researchers found a way to turn the sand on Mars into what is functionally low-grade concrete using little more than gelatin, yeast, and the natural Martian environment. Combine the three ingredients, and the dry, cold, low-pressure environment of Mars freeze-dries the mixture, turning it into a porous, foam-like material strong enough to build houses on the red planet.

“My inspiration came from freeze-dried fruits that become harder,” senior author Jishen Qiu of The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology said in a statement. “So, I asked myself if we can take advantage of that and make some materials.”

According to Qiu, the concrete produced by this method measures 10 to 12 megapascals (a metric unit of pressure), putting it on par with low-grade concrete here on Earth. This concrete is strong enough to build a one- or two-story house on Earth, and since Earth has three times the gravity of Mars, it’s more than strong enough to build structures on Mars too.

The gelatin is run-of-the-mill porcine gelatin, which means it’s made from pigs, and it’s quite literally the same stuff that Jell-O uses to make its jiggly dessert. For the yeast, Qiu created a specially engineered version covered in the same proteins mussels use to attach themselves to rocks. These two ingredients, along with pounded-up Martian rocks and water, create the material.

Mars’ frigid cold, low-pressure environment effectively freeze-dries the material, causing water to sublimate, which means it turns directly from a solid to a vapor, leaving the Martian concrete behind. Because this process is so fast, items must be 3D-printed in real time to work properly.

The team tested it by 3D printing two small beehive-shaped structures about the size of a wine cork in a simulated Martian environment, but the team believes the process can scale up. Once the structures have reached the end of their usefulness, people on Mars can break them down, mix them in a bioreactor, and brew a new building with the same materials, as long as there’s still yeast alive to reproduce.

An elegant solution to a long-standing problem

Houses on Mars made with this method would resemble beehives, but be made of what is essentially concrete. Nin Liu

Delivering humans to Mars is already a tall order. Elon Musk tried to get it done by 2025 and missed the mark by at least a decade. However, getting people there is only half the battle. Once there, they need a place to live that can withstand the Martian environment, which includes temperature swings of nearly 100 degrees Celsius and virtually no radiation protection from the sun due to the thin Mars atmosphere.

There are many ideas about the subject, ranging from inflatable domiciles to the idea of letting self-propagating fungi grow whole buildings. Some enterprising scientists from the Indian Space Research Organisation even made space bricks from Martian soil, guar gum, urea, nickel chloride and a bacterium called Sporosarcina pasteurii, which converts urea and calcium into calcite. This lets the soil harden into something resembling concrete.

NASA held a habitat challenge from 2015 to 2019 that tasked companies and researchers to 3D-print homes using unique methods and materials. The winners took home over $2 million in prizes. In short, no stone has been left unturned, and people are using all sorts of exotic materials to try to find the best solution for habitats on Mars, including Qiu.

“I always ask myself: Is there any physical law or fundamental mechanism that prevents us from doing this?” Qiu said. “I can’t see any at this point in time. We are confident in scaling it up. It would surprise me if materials for future Martian engineering will not be as diverse as those used in Earth engineering, and biology will certainly contribute.”

Tech.title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: The Highest-End Phones Compared
Tech.content:
Apple’s $1,299 iPhone 18 Pro Max now stands tall as the company’s newest nonfolding high-end flagship phone. Announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday, it packs big camera and battery upgrades. But with a starting price that’s $100 higher than the iPhone 17 Pro Max, the phone’s 256GB model is now priced closely to Samsung’s $1,300 Galaxy S26 Ultra.

While every iPhone received a $100 price increase that’s likely influenced by the ongoing RAM shortage, Apple’s topline iPhone appears to be a close rival to the S26 Ultra in several key areas, especially when it comes to battery life and cameras.

The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra design and display

While Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro Max and Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra are big phones, their design aesthetics are quite different. The 18 Pro Max sports a similar aluminum unibody design to the one that debuted on last year’s 17 Pro Max. It comes in burgundy red, glacier blue, silver and black colors. Its shape gives it a hefty appearance, but one that fits in well when the phone is being used as a professional camera for events like Apple TV’s Major League Baseball broadcasts. And at 249 grams (8.8 ounces), the 18 Pro Max isn’t lightweight by any stretch. The phone has a 6.8-inch OLED display that should be quite expansive for videos, websites and games.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra has a slightly bigger 6.9-inch AMOLED display, but at 214 grams, it’s notably lighter than the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It also comes in six colors: pink gold, silver shadow, cobalt violet, sky blue, white and black. The S26 Ultra is also the thinnest in its line, but its Privacy Display is its most unique feature. The S26 Ultra’s display can make specific apps or notifications difficult to see from off-angle viewing, making it easier to hide content from prying eyes without needing to apply a privacy screen protector. No other company has replicated Samsung’s Privacy Display, which does make the phone stand out.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max in glacier blue. Apple/CNET

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra battery capacity

Both phones have big batteries. While Apple doesn’t disclose its battery specs in the US — instead citing that it can play 45 hours of video — its Ireland website claims the physical SIM edition will have a 5,391-mAh capacity. That’s slightly higher than the 5,000-mAh capacity on the S26 Ultra and might be even higher on the eSIM model that will be sold in the US.

Apple hasn’t yet disclosed the charging speed for the iPhone 18 Pro Max, but this is an area where Samsung already excels — the S26 Ultra has 60-watt wired charging and won our CNET Lab Test award for fastest wired charging phone by recharging from 0% to 76% in 30 minutes. That said, last year’s iPhone 17 Pro Max had a 40-watt charging speed that was one of our top performers, recharging 0% to 69% in the same 30-minute test. We look forward to testing out the 18 Pro Max to see how it fares.

You can turn on Privacy Display in Quick Settings to prevent others from seeing what’s on your screen. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra cameras

Both phones also have their respective companies’ highest-end cameras, with Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro Max now featuring a variable-aperture camera that can physically open or close to take better photos in darker or lighter environments. This feature comes with the Pro Max’s three-camera setup that includes a 49-megapixel wide camera, a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera and a 48-megapixel telephoto camera with a 4x optical zoom. While the S26 Ultra doesn’t include a variable aperture, it has four cameras on the back that include a 200-megapixel main camera, a 50-megapixel ultrawide, a 50-megapixel telephoto with a 5x optical zoom and a 10-megapixel telephoto with a 3x optical zoom.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra processor, features

Apple’s A20 Pro processor powers the company’s latest AI features, headlined by the new Siri AI assistant that is built with Apple’s collaboration with Google’s Gemini. It can help you look up specific information buried in your emails and texts and turn them into actionable items like new reminders or calendar events. Apple also made a point of showing off the A20 Pro’s gaming abilities and how the phone’s vapor chamber helps keep it running cool while pushing intensive graphics.

But Samsung’s phone includes Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 for Galaxy processor, powering its own slate of Galaxy AI features focused on proactive suggestions, along with photo editing. It’s also quite capable of high-end gaming.

Check out the specs below to compare both phones further.

Tech.title: Apple Hikes iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max Prices by $100
Tech.content:
Planning to scoop up a new iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone 18 Pro Max after watching the Apple event this week? Hope you have an extra $100 in your pocket. Apple confirmed at Wednesday’s live Surprise and Shine event that the two phones will cost $100 more than the previous versions. The iPhone 18 Pro will start at $1,199 and the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max will begin at $1,299. Both of those prices include 256GB of storage.

Both phones will be available for preorder this Saturday, Sept. 12, and will launch on Sept. 18.

The price increase was expected, and was actually lower than some observers predicted. The $100 price hike matches Samsung’s cost hikes for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Flip 8, and Google’s hikes with the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro.

Andrew Lanxon, CNET editor-at-large, notes that the new phones are packed with Apple’s latest tech, including upgraded cameras, new A20 Bionic processors, and fresh colors, including a much-buzzed-about dark cherry, labeled burgundy.

Tech.title: Over 153 Million Driver’s Licenses Were Stolen by Hackers. Here’s What to Know
Tech.content:
If you’ve used your driver’s license to verify your information either in the real world or online, there’s a chance that some of your driver’s license information was stolen by hackers in a security breach against the ID verification giant IDScan that was reportedly active for a year.

“On or around Sept. 1, 2026, IDScan.net received information indicating that certain data may have been accessed without authorization,” IDScan said in a statement on Sept. 4. “Upon this discovery, we took immediate steps to secure our systems and engaged a team of third-party specialists to help determine the full nature and scope of the incident.”

The hack is discussed in more detail by Brian Krebs, a security researcher who runs the website Krebs on Security. He says he was first made aware of the breach after a source alerted him to a post on a Russian cybercrime forum from a hacker offering digital scans of identity documents for more than 170 million people from a service called Nexus.

Krebs was able to access Nexus and verify that it did indeed have the documents it said it had, including a scan of his own driver’s license.

The data includes 153 million driver’s licenses, 10 million ID cards, 3 million travel documents like passports and, according to Krebs, “at least 579,000” medical cards. Most of these records are for US residents, but about 1.1 million Canadian driver’s licenses were also found.

Per IDScan, hackers weren’t able to get every piece of information from those documents, but most likely obtained full names, driver’s license numbers and government-issued ID numbers.

The hackers who ran Nexus boasted that they had obtained the information by “continuously exfiltrating new data for over a year” into a private database from “a major identity verification company.”

The data collected likely came from a range of sources. Krebs says the leak of his information could have resulted from renting a car from Hertz, which uses IDScan to verify driver’s licenses. Other companies that use IDScan include FedEx, Target, GameStop and over 1,000 cannabis dispensaries, car rental agencies and gun shops across 19 states. IDScan reported that it scanned 150 million IDs in 2024 alone.

The New Orleans field office of the FBI is investigating the matter. The FBI has not responded to a request for comment.

Here’s what you can do

IDScan says it will notify everyone who was affected by the breach and “provide access to free credit monitoring and identity protection services” for those people. If you end up being one of them, IDScan says to contact it at 1-833-516-2980 (Monday-Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. ET) to enroll in those services.

Those concerned they may have been affected have a few options. The easiest and quickest is a credit freeze, which makes it much more difficult for cybercriminals to open new accounts in your name. CNET has a guide for that if you need help. Freezing your credit is free, but it requires you to set up individual accounts with the three major credit bureaus.

Since cybercrime can strike anywhere and at any time, it’s also good to follow some tips to keep yourself safe, including using strong passwords, familiarizing yourself with the latest AI-powered phishing scams and considering using a VPN to help obfuscate your online presence so you can’t be tracked.

The unfortunate reality is that cybersecurity breaches are getting bigger, and companies are telling consumers less about what’s happening, so it’s worth staying vigilant, even if your driver’s license wasn’t stolen.

Tech.title: Ninja Takes on Caraway With Cheaper, ‘More Durable’ Ceramic Cookware
Tech.content:
One thing about Ninja, the company is going to keep its customer base happy with new release after new release. On the heels of launching its first water filter, the HydraSense, Ninja’s first-ever ceramic-coated cookware is now available, too.

The cookware is dishwasher-safe and oven-safe up to 550 degrees Fahrenheit. The pieces are stackable for easy storage, and the handles on the lids can be pushed down to save even more space. Ninja says the ceramic cookware is twice as durable as competitor Caraway, but the company didn’t share what type of testing, if any, was conducted to support that claim. We also haven’t gotten our hands on the Ninja NeverQuit lineup yet to independently test its durability or do a side-by-side comparison with Caraway or other ceramic cookware.

However, Ninja’s new cookware is more affordable than Caraway. The NeverQuit three-piece frying pan set is $250 while Caraway’s three frying pans with lids set is currently available for $395.

Ceramic-coated cookware is often favored because it’s nonstick, easy to clean and can be made without chemicals typically used in non-stick cookware, such as PTFE (Teflon). Ninja says the NeverQuit coating is “designed without lead, cadmium, PFAS, PFOA, PTFE or hard anodization.”

It is available in a three-, six- or 12-piece set. The 12-piece set includes 8-inch and 10.25-inch frying pans, a 4-quart pan with lid, a steamer basket, a spatula, a pasta ladle, a 6-quart stock pot with lid, a 6-quart metal strainer basket and a spoon rest.

Ninja also teased an upcoming stainless-steel cookware line named “Ninja Eversear,” but hasn’t announced a launch date just yet.

Tech.title: Don’t Sleep on Apple’s Audio Intelligence. It Reveals a Lot About Where We’re Headed
Tech.content:
The first five minutes of John Ternus’ first keynote as Apple CEO weren’t a product unveiling or a recap of Apple’s history. Instead, they were a redefinition of the iPhone as an “intelligent personal hub.”

Of all the devices Apple makes, the iPhone doesn’t need to be described or explained to anyone. But this new framing of it as a hub not only set up the debut of the foldable, category-straddling iPhone Duo, an iPhone/iPad hybrid of sorts — it also suggested an AI-infused wearable device future that Apple’s already dipping its toes into.

Of all the things Apple announced during its “Surprise and shine” event this week, the one that hit hardest for me wasn’t the Duo. It was the reveal of Audio Intelligence, a new AI-powered assistive toolset that will live on the latest Apple Watches and even a range of recent iPhone models.

Siri will store Recaps of conversations had previously, provided the always-listening feature is turned on. Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Audio Intelligence: A memory-keeping tool, or a listening device?

Audio Intelligence listens. And in listening, it can make memories. Or recall things. Or, in a sense, act like the sort of AI-enabled wearables I’ve been trying in various forms over the last few years. Live Rewind can check back on things said up to 15 seconds ago, while Siri Recap ambiently summarizes and transcribes conversations when it’s turned on.

Apple promises that Audio Intelligence is encrypted and that no actual audio recordings are saved. But what it does reminds me of Plaud’s AI wearables, or features like the “Conversate” transcription function on the Even Realities G2 smart glasses. Or Looki’s AI conversation summaries.

It’s designed, it seems, to run in the background and record conversations as you’re having them — transcribing them and summarizing them so you can read the text transcriptions later, or on the fly, and available in Siri to search as needed. And if you happen to miss what someone’s saying in a chat, there’s “Live Rewind” that replays the last 15 seconds of a real-life chat, like some real-life version of asking your Apple TV what someone just said on that Netflix show.

Seen here: Meta’s Ray-Bans. Apple’s expected to have its own smart glasses next year. Scott Stein/CNET

A stepping stone for visual intelligence wearables next year

Audio Intelligence also recognizes real-life sounds like sirens or doorbells, something that was already part of Apple’s assistive suite of Apple Watch and AirPod features.

What will it feel like to use Audio Intelligence on an Apple Watch? I don’t know. Maybe like wearing an AI pendant on my wrist. But also, I wonder what Apple is preparing us for next.

Recaps and summaries equal memories. Audio is easier to record than photos and video. But Visual Intelligence, a camera-based way to use Siri to analyze, translate or remember things that you see, already exists on iPhones, iPads and the Vision Pro, and Apple’s eventual next-gen AirPods are expected to have cameras in them to use Visual Intelligence in the real world — maybe in a very similar way to how Audio Intelligence seems to work on the Apple Watch.

And then there are smart glasses. Apple’s expected to have glasses next year, and the smart glasses already out there lean heavily on AI… and are starting to be feared as privacy-invading gadgets. Meta’s bearing the brunt of that anti-smart-glasses anger now, but will Apple find a way to ease people into feeling like assistive, continuously aware (and perhaps recording) AI devices are helpful, or comfortable, or acceptable? Audio Intelligence feels like one delicate foot into a zone that’s getting more intimate and strange every year.

Apple’s making big privacy claims, but will it help? Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Can Apple convince us it’s safe?

Apple needs to advance its AI to find true assistive uses on glasses, but it also needs to nail down privacy concerns for always-recording wearables. I said this back in June when the debut of the new Siri clearly pointed to a framework for AI wearables and smart glasses to come.

Apple has to start somewhere. And that somewhere looks like Audio Intelligence on the new Apple Watches. And if it works in a way that feels useful and not creepy, then maybe it’s the first part of the next phase of the “intelligent hub” that Ternus’ iPhone ecosystem is heading towards in 2027 and beyond.

Tech.title: What an Ex-Anthropic Researcher’s Warning About Human Extinction Really Means
Tech.content:
A string of posts on X from an AI researcher who says he quit a job at Anthropic over ethical concerns has gone viral, prompting thousands of responses and reigniting debate over the potential future dangers of artificial intelligence.

Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who also worked at OpenAI on pretraining AI models, resigned from Anthropic over concerns that AI development could lead to human extinction. “Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote. “They are racing to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Superintelligence refers to a hypothetical scenario in which AI’s “cognitive” abilities vastly exceed those of humans across every domain — science, math, strategy, creativity and problem-solving.

The threaded post on X from Coxon has more than 156 million views as of this writing and has been liked more than 752,000 times.

I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives. More thoughts below. — Jacob Coxon (@hilbertspaess) September 9, 2026

The statement quickly spread on social media and was featured on major news sites. It even drew a comment from Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who responded on X, “It’s becoming more clear the threat AI poses to humanity, so I’m calling for immediate action from the industry and Washington.”

In less than 24 hours, the statement also drew responses from others at Anthropic who, rather than debating with Coxon, confirmed that the threat that AI will overtake and potentially eliminate humans is not a wild fantasy but a reality for AI researchers.

“Jacob [Coxon] is correct here,” wrote Evan Hubinger, a team leader at Anthropic in AI alignment stress testing, on X. Hubinger wrote in his response, “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”

Hubinger said, “I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”

Representatives for Anthropic and OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Resignations that act as warning signs

It’s difficult to dismiss Coxon’s concerns for one big reason: He’s not the first researcher at a major AI company to leave for these reasons. In February, a safety lead at Anthropic, Mrinank Sharma, resigned from the company, telling followers on X, “The world is in peril … We appear to be approaching a threshold where our wisdom must grow in equal measure to our capacity to affect the world, lest we face the consequences.”

In the same month, OpenAI researcher Zoë Hitzig wrote in a New York Times column that she quit the company in part because it was following Meta’s path of putting profits ahead of ethics. Days later, she reposted a poem she’d written on X, titled “How We Programmed the Apocalypse.”

Thinking about this old poem of mine this week – pic.twitter.com/RITOGz3mTp — Zoë Hitzig (@zhitzig) February 17, 2026

Since then, AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have walked back some of their previous comments about AI’s potential for harm or whether it will create mass unemployment. Anthropic publicly acknowledged earlier this year that it has loosened some of its safety standards to keep up with competitors, including OpenAI and a swath of Chinese companies that have been releasing cheaper, high-performing AI models.

That competition, with both OpenAI and Anthropic hurtling toward initial public offerings, has raised concerns that, instead of moving cautiously in deploying AI models, industry leaders are rushing into the unknown and releasing models that could pose present and future dangers. This was the case when Anthropic released advanced AI models, which ended up being pulled or temporarily restricted due to major cybersecurity risks.

In the case of Coxon, whose resignation has caused the largest stir yet among those who’ve left AI companies, the dangers of contributing to the technology’s accelerating pace outweighed any financial gains. “I left before any of my equity vested,” he told the news site Axios.

Ironically, both OpenAI and Anthropic have taken the stance that if they slow down, someone less concerned with safety will drive AI’s future.

“Coxon is right that competition is driving the speed,” said Shama Hyder, a professor of AI at Link School of Business. “Every one of these companies believes slowing down hands the lead to someone less careful, so even the people who understand the risk have a reason to accelerate. “

AGI and superhuman AI

How quickly AI poses an imminent threat to humanity may depend on when the technology reaches two purported benchmarks that have become increasingly blurred: superhuman AI (also known as artificial superintelligence or ASI), which Coxon mentioned in his viral post, and AGI, or artificial general intelligence.

AGI would mark the hypothetical point at which AI meets (or exceeds) the capabilities of a human mind. Some predict that AI will achieve that benchmark in just a few years, or at least sometime before the end of the 21st century. That timeline has also been thrown into doubt by some AI leaders, such as Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who downplayed the importance of such markers on a recent earnings call where he said, “For many tasks, we could say that we have already achieved AGI.” The milestones, he said, “are kind of senseless at this point.”

The goalposts are also varied. Some may choose to measure AGI using specific tests, while others would consider AGI achieved only if AI could act autonomously in ways that surpass human capabilities.

ASI would be further down the road, after AGI, and would theoretically mark the point at which AI could outperform all humans across all tasks, particularly in deep thinking and cognitive understanding. The timeline for that is much fuzzier, but the speed at which AI is advancing has researchers such as Coxon suggesting it’s sooner than many people think.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (left) and US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick (right) on stage at the G20 forum this month. Altman has acknowledged the risks of AI while trying to sway the public on the technology’s benefits. Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

A recent event that may have some adjusting their timeframes is the incident exposed in July in which OpenAI agents went rogue, plotted together and hacked Hugging Face, an AI community that was acquired by Nvidia. The speed at which the Hugging Face incident played out and the likelihood that it could happen again — this time without warning — have fueled warnings about the dangers of autonomous AI systems.

Doomers vs. boosters

The debate over whether or not AI will kill all humans by 2030 mirrors the broader discussion over AI doomers versus boosters, and the lack of nuance in the middle. While AI boosters typically hype AI by emphasizing its extraordinary potential, such as huge productivity gains, AI doomers hype it in the opposite direction, emphasizing job loss and human extinction.

As Emily Bender and Alex Hanna argue in their book The AI Con, both AI boosters and doomers rely on science-fiction tropes to frame superintelligence as either a utopian savior or an apocalyptic threat, despite a lack of evidence that such technology is near. Many AI critics argue that either narrative functions as corporate marketing, with the same underlying premise, falsely presenting an all-powerful AI future as an absolute inevitability.

The speed at which Coxon’s post went viral and the response it’s drawing may be an indication that the AI industry has another PR crisis on its hands in a year when AI data centers are under fire and trying to change their image, and social media companies, including Meta, are reeling from multibillion-dollar judgments over issues like tech addiction.

One approach that AI leaders like Altman have taken is to focus the public’s attention on what AI brings to the table and what it could offer beyond job losses and mass death — in other words, swapping doomer rhetoric for booster rhetoric.

“Abundance” has been a buzzword that’s been thrown around of late, promising a world in which AI’s advances and benefits will eliminate scarcity and improve life for everybody by lowering barriers to creating new goods and services and providing them more cheaply, and not just for those who can afford the costs of advanced AI technology.

Hyder said that what was missing from Coxon’s post was guidance on what people outside the AI industry can do. “The extinction debate belongs to a few hundred people who control training runs and the regulators who can inspect them,” she said.

The question ultimately boils down to what humans want to do with the technology. “If AI is powerful enough to do the dramatic things people fear, it’s powerful enough to do the dramatic things we’ve been hoping for in medicine and science,” Hyder said.

So far, the hyped-up abundance argument has been met with skepticism, especially when it keeps public attention and fascination focused on AI. Boosterism benefits the companies that are guzzling investment dollars and promoting the billions (or trillions) their companies’ IPOs may represent.

Who cares about abundance, you could argue, if there are no humans left in the world to enjoy it?
